descriptions.fe021c51-e3fb-407d-9f6c-b770ba056f15: Human remains dating to 41,000 BC place this cave at the frontier of Homo sapiens settlement in Europe. Modern humans and Neanderthals overlapped here in a four-storey labyrinth of galleries.
descriptions.dd0f3348-710e-4e66-b50e-45bd71b61e12: A single rampart and ditch crown this 90-metre hill above the Vale of White Horse — proposed as the 5th-century Battle of Mons Badonicus site, now wooded and known as Badbury Clump.
descriptions.fd8def6a-360b-43ea-be95-f451dca3b19d: Three concentric earthwork rings — each higher than the last — define this Durotriges hillfort above east Dorset. A Roman-era town known as Vindocladia stood just to the south-west.
descriptions.ab4f6f19-ab67-4c4b-9ed9-16a0c0e4ab96: A 2nd-century BC Roman town whose economy ran on garum — fermented fish sauce. The factory vats are still visible, and the smell reportedly lingered for centuries.
descriptions.5b0b6371-1e89-434a-b125-fcc7349de5db: Commanding a ridge above the Voghji River, this fortress served as the last capital of the Syunik kingdom before Seljuk forces ended it. Its walls span from the 4th to the 12th century AD.
descriptions.3db7a812-6b3a-4574-b804-840a2390cdad: A Roman resort town from the 1st century BC where emperors and senators vacationed. Half the town has since sunk beneath the sea due to volcanic ground subsidence.
descriptions.b2b1beee-00c6-4dfa-a616-89f7be1b86b7: A 300–600 AD stucco frieze depicts earth monsters, jaguars, and kings emerging from the underworld across a single facade. The site covers 25 hectares around this one monumental core.
descriptions.2fb4a171-fe52-40c9-8bcb-195cd068b55d: A 60-tonne boulder balanced on five smaller stones. Whether glaciers placed it or humans did around 8000 BC has been debated for over two centuries.
descriptions.da2f5fea-80b2-4c88-a5d1-738c054512b5: A jawbone unearthed here — BH-1 — is between 397,000 and 525,000 years old, making it the easternmost Middle Pleistocene human fossil in Europe. Neanderthal teeth also found in 2022.
descriptions.1a9242d4-250f-4ffb-8dad-dae849c10798: A Maya cave near Chichén Itzá sealed for centuries with offerings to the rain god Tlaloc still arranged around a massive stalagmite. The ritual assemblage was found untouched.
descriptions.c4d2251b-b64a-4615-a6f9-5a71ff6f3955: A 400-1200 AD village of around 90 circular stone foundations spread across a hillside. Circular architecture is distinctive — most Mesoamerican buildings used rectangular plans.
descriptions.7260c83f-718a-4d70-9126-516ecd7db7a7: A 1st-century AD Roman gateway in ancient Camulodunum (Colchester), the first capital of Roman Britain. It is the largest surviving Roman gateway in the country.
descriptions.83711b0a-71a6-4022-88f9-060aada84ea6: A Neolithic court tomb also called the "Giant's Grave." Court tombs get their name from the open-air courtyard where mourners gathered before entering the burial chambers.
descriptions.55da0a74-b7fc-4b66-a104-e6b32df0e8e3: Neolithic cup-and-ring rock carvings from the 4th-2nd millennium BC. These spiral motifs appear across Atlantic Europe, but no one has decoded what they mean.
descriptions.d2db72cb-3a9d-429f-98ad-e56925fcdc43: A Neolithic chambered tomb from 3300 BC with an unusual multi-chambered design. The cairn contains both cist burials and entrance graves in one structure.
descriptions.0dfe2efe-0699-4300-8f2e-04852c23ab55: Aboriginal rock art from 3770 BC to the 19th century, carved into sandstone. The engravings include fish and marine animals — recording thousands of years of coastal life.
descriptions.e1b8b97e-0344-4248-8a0f-86d3b956c759: A 1700 BC wedge-shaped gallery grave. Wedge tombs are the most common megalithic tomb type on the island — over 500 have been recorded.
descriptions.62406daa-7d26-4ffa-a9d9-54a8be76456e: A 4.45-hectare prehistoric landscape with multiple monument types spanning millennia. Tombs, standing stones, and field boundaries all share the same patch of ground.
descriptions.f4e3fdef-07f1-4327-b0db-c01c671bfafc: A Neolithic tripod portal tomb balanced on three upright stones. The capstone looks precarious but has survived in this position for over 5,000 years.
descriptions.3dd0bac8-4618-4f61-a2b2-4dd229a76e45: Four uprights bear a tilting capstone at the north-west tip of Islandmagee — known locally as the Druid's Altar, dating to around 2000 BC or the stripped remains of an earlier passage grave.
descriptions.f6b6e039-36f1-4107-b730-dc2aa34b7a92: A Neolithic cairn also known as Dooey's Cairn, with a U-shaped forecourt leading to gallery chambers. Excavation revealed cremated bone, pottery, and flint tools.
descriptions.ed559418-30ca-4d1b-b0d0-9e13982d5949: A Neolithic portal tomb from 4000-2500 BC. Its massive capstone, supported by three uprights, creates a chamber just large enough for crouched burials.
descriptions.35d7d24f-f520-472b-9799-3897b9833255: A 3rd-millennium BC ritual landscape with standing stones, a henge, and cairns clustered in one glen. The concentration of monuments here rivals Stonehenge in density.
descriptions.ac2c74ff-d861-4609-8589-67a8c3eceb3c: A Neolithic stone circle 35 metres wide with over 50 upright stones. A mound inside the ring held cremated remains, hinting at rituals spanning millennia.
descriptions.26b6f958-d33e-4d59-843e-f233ba117170: A group of Bronze Age cairns from 2000 BC with passages aligned to the midwinter sunset. Only about 50 cairns of this type exist, all clustered in one region.
descriptions.37bdb6b2-e689-46c4-8c55-a0576e39d407: A port city with origins in the Scytho-Parthian era, later taken by Arab conquerors in the 8th century. Three distinct layers of fortification walls map each era of rule.
descriptions.b300f71d-88f7-4a2a-bdf0-b9bb33a53c73: Single-bank fort enclosing 1.2 hectares near Okeford Fitzpaine; the rampart reaches 15 metres wide where best preserved, though ploughing has flattened much of the site.
descriptions.72f50344-3b9f-4390-929c-78d72d7a6e01: A Neolithic hilltop enclosure with two non-concentric earthworks spotted only from aerial photography in 1990. Surveys reveal three distinct periods of activity.
descriptions.ccb3de8b-5c50-4204-ae6f-46cdda2e081d: A settlement with 4,000 years of continuous use, famous for its vivid red-painted pottery. Bronze tools found here rewrote the timeline of Southeast Asian metallurgy.
descriptions.c0d65355-96d2-407f-bda3-b4e63897266d: Settled by 4000 BC on a coastal river plain, Bandurria combined a fishing economy with monumental stone terraces — the first ceremonial architecture yet found in the Americas.
descriptions.ad2b103b-1296-40b2-895d-98f7dc8558be: Over 300 petroglyphs carved onto cliff faces from 7000 BC onward depict whales, tigers, and hunting scenes. They are the earliest evidence of whaling in human history.
descriptions.ae2ca7b1-89da-46cb-8924-f9d04dd5da2e: A city sacred to the Greek god Pan, inhabited for 2,000 years until 1967. A shrine to Pan was carved directly into the rock beside one of the Jordan River's main sources.
descriptions.2048dfe4-9b29-494f-8807-881c71023f22: Named Banna -- Celtic for "horn" -- this fort occupies a triangular spur above the River Irthing. The western wall abuts the longest surviving stretch of Hadrian Wall still standing.
descriptions.339e7c39-0bd9-49c4-8e91-5dfe48c8e140: Fortified staging post on Watling Street -- today the A5 road -- where travellers paused between larger Roman towns. The town straddles the boundaries of Norton and Whilton in Northamptonshire.
descriptions.77aa7ece-0acc-4765-b8ae-be5e0763d9ef: A village site with 11 prehistoric phases spanning Neolithic to Iron Age, including 640 burials. The graves reveal one of Southeast Asia's earliest bronze-working cultures.
descriptions.820ff35d-d611-4865-b4e3-27e09843aa9a: A Roman legionary fort and town whose name derives from the Celtic Banostra. The 12th-century monastery founded here by ban Belos gave the village its modern name.
descriptions.1724deb2-8bac-4a38-971b-4d1542745e0b: Eight-metre-diameter Bronze Age entrance grave on the Isles of Scilly, set on a low platform 12 metres across. Directly below lie the remains of the Iron Age village of Halangy Down.
descriptions.8b8c6154-987e-4d54-b9ca-fac19630061b: Ramparts rise 4 metres high in places around this North Somerset fort, with artefacts spanning the Stone Age and Bronze Age. A local folktale links a nearby carved cross to a miraculous origin.
descriptions.13c39c81-106b-4f1d-9975-b729226ab99d: An ancient settlement with a Roman temple dedicated to Zeus Bomos, a local name for the god Baal. Two early Christian churches were later built among the ruins.
descriptions.3cf8d34b-fa9a-421f-8e8a-f21d910affe2: The largest Roman bath complex north of the Alps, built in 2nd-century Trier. At 172 metres long, it dwarfed the city's earlier forum baths.
descriptions.4d28794b-71ae-4418-b2b5-47972a341a6b: Three temples built to honour Enki, the Sumerian god of wisdom and fresh water. A natural spring inside the temple held deep spiritual significance for Dilmun worshippers.
descriptions.8dd50bbd-b629-4c5f-8214-647324df6fce: 16 overshot waterwheels in a 2nd-century Roman mill complex near Arles -- the greatest concentration of mechanical power assembled before the Industrial Revolution. Output fed roughly 12,000 people.
descriptions.437d6dda-8c48-4142-91fe-575c140b961a: A stone circle on Ramsley Moor with one tall standing stone and 11 smaller ones, ringed by a rubble bank. It sits in a broader cairn field dotted with burial monuments.
descriptions.230e6523-3000-4234-a12e-1336ed82b012: Twin deep ditches and ramparts crown this Wiltshire hilltop on the ancient Ridgeway. In 556 AD Saxons fought a decisive battle here that helped forge the future kingdom of Wessex.
descriptions.ff76a431-09d7-40b4-8dc5-b80211b2e246: Founded by Romans as Barcino in the 1st century BC, the colony was tiny -- just 10 hectares. A Temple of Augustus still stands embedded in the medieval Gothic Quarter.
descriptions.643b79ca-d609-475e-839e-28c9858fa00a: A Neolithic passage grave with decorated stones bearing spiral and zigzag carvings. Identical motifs appear across the Irish Sea, tracing ancient cultural connections.
descriptions.70c09eab-cdac-4a95-ad5b-160bba0aace7: Petroglyphs spanning from 4000 BC to the Iron Age carved on the same rock face. Newer figures were carved directly on top of older ones across thousands of years.
descriptions.39dd0b66-f565-4698-934f-37da9ff624dd: An inscription at the city gate records its construction in 371/372 AD. Bargala was a city in the Roman province of Macedonia Salutaris and a major religious centre of the Bregalnica region.
descriptions.1c486e79-c7b2-4466-934f-1dd448d32974: An ancient citadel captured by Alexander the Great, with layers going back to 1700 BC. Continuous occupation from the Chalcolithic through the Kushan period.
descriptions.348770cd-a3a2-4b6e-83f7-bd5f5d699022: Dating to 4800 BC, this Breton cairn is 72 metres long with 11 burial chambers and megalithic art. Its construction predates the pyramids of Giza by more than 2,000 years.
descriptions.eae0879c-2e4a-422d-8626-2fbf21adb227: A 5,000-year-old chambered cairn 22 metres across, with a roof of two massive stone slabs. Despite partial collapse, visitors can still enter one of its burial chambers.
descriptions.2817ce5e-3b43-445e-9a10-d4115a7036bb: A Bronze and Iron Age site with continuous occupation, featuring rectangular stone houses from the First Iron Age. Imported Phoenician trade goods show Mediterranean contacts.
descriptions.3f888db6-1b30-44c7-b2f6-3effec34f650: A 1.4-million-year-old site that yielded a child's milk tooth -- the earliest anatomical evidence of humans in Western Europe at the time of its dating.
descriptions.97eeca75-a0d6-4365-a610-c3b5044a3043: About twenty menhirs and monoliths on a wooded hilltop, the tallest standing 4 metres high. Whether this is a dolmen or a cromlech remains an open question.
descriptions.bf730d05-edd1-42cf-8746-a081c4ac78a6: At 1,200 metres above sea level, Barriles yielded stone sculptures of warriors standing atop captives — signs of ranked society and conquest culture by 300 AD.
descriptions.23ee2849-5bee-4742-91b1-29a35361fcf7: A 5,300-year-old bowl barrow 30 metres across that kept being reused for burial. Anglo-Saxon warriors were later interred in the same mound, 4,000 years after its builders.
descriptions.1b82a32d-cf01-4735-94c2-7df578796ce5: A Khitan city from the 4th century AD with a ruined octagonal brick pagoda near its walls. Mud walls 4 metres thick and 2 metres high still trace the 1.6 x 1.8 km footprint.
descriptions.300c7075-942d-447e-a3eb-cce1fcd5d3a0: An Iron Age enclosure surrounded by archaeological remains including settlements, field systems, and cairns. The circular earthwork shares the landscape with Carn Euny.
descriptions.94f496b6-5e15-4a5a-9bd2-0cb1885864bf: A Roman tumuli cemetery with the tallest Roman barrow north of the Alps, standing 15 metres high. Seven grand burial mounds suggest an elite family of extraordinary wealth.
descriptions.7e45502b-80d5-404a-9b46-cfd630d2be3a: A Maya cave where pottery and human remains were placed on ledges deep inside. The Maya treated caves as entrances to Xibalba, the underworld of the dead.
descriptions.4e240612-152f-48a1-aee8-59dd9027a990: To the southwest lies Sharpenhoe Clappers, a hilltop stronghold over 2,000 years old. Barton-le-Clay appears in the 1066 Domesday Book, though the fort predates that record by a millennium.
descriptions.a57d3d87-6660-4136-a523-434165373169: A Gaulish oppidum built by the Rauraci tribe after their defeat at Bibracte in 58 BC. It was abandoned within decades as Roman conquest reshaped the region.
descriptions.bfcc8547-38c2-4af1-bb54-79a47c79daea: A Roman palace basilica containing the largest surviving hall from antiquity -- 67 metres long, 33 metres high. The floor was once black-and-white marble with heated walls.
descriptions.3dfa5ceb-3772-4f22-9817-1b56cb246c57: Built as Roman public baths in the 4th century AD, this Metz building was converted to a Benedictine chapel in the 7th century -- among the oldest standing churches in Europe.
descriptions.f4f9740d-f83e-4252-a014-f34c09583cf7: Remote 5th-century BC Temple of Apollo Epicurius combining Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian columns in a single structure -- the earliest confirmed use of the Corinthian order anywhere in antiquity.
descriptions.17c73394-bfd9-4c62-99d4-4b062994f8bb: The second-largest town in Roman Syrmia, after Sirmium, connected by a road to Singidunum. Only a small fraction of the ancient city has been preserved above ground.
descriptions.05ca5b20-5645-4bc5-b922-6e0605c918e4: A Sican complex with 50 identified pyramids built between the 8th and 12th centuries AD. The site sits inside a protected forest sanctuary that still covers the ruins.
descriptions.85664eb7-5761-407b-854b-aec846d137e6: A Roman road whose medieval name means "road to the bath town" -- it led to the spa at Buxton. Sections of the original route are now protected monuments.
descriptions.02941d88-16e9-42c6-8abf-e7d5b5b38821: Mesolithic flint scatters mark the earliest human use of this limestone plateau; later came Bathampton Camp, a hilltop fort or stock enclosure. Human activity here spans at least 10,000 years.
descriptions.8d0fb4aa-7eda-4d61-a313-5f270a2f5b8c: A sunken Lycian city visible beneath clear Mediterranean waters, with submerged harbour, bathhouse, and fish sauce workshops. Earthquake and sea-level rise drowned it.
descriptions.7703241e-28d5-4d8e-a75d-241ed0477a26: Eight silver-plated coins spanning 102 BC to 350 AD were found here by schoolboys in 1983. Two stone ramparts and two ditches ring this 213-metre hilltop above Dunster in Somerset.
descriptions.aed60d2e-9dec-442b-a7bf-86647aca27b9: In 2008, detectorists uncovered a 3rd-century battlefield where Roman forces clashed far beyond imperial reach. Coins suggest a date during Severus Alexander or Maximinus Thrax.
descriptions.da9a2764-3ac6-4e5a-9e4c-9d15b3b7aef8: Bivallate fort near Warminster with triple ditches on its most exposed sides; the ramparts follow the natural hill contour, making the western and northeastern faces nearly impregnable.
descriptions.b3f7a897-e4b1-4c2f-b7fd-c91efd9523ae: A show cave occupied by humans since the Stone Age and open to tourists since 1649. Devonian limestone formations inside have been growing for hundreds of millions of years.
descriptions.51dd742c-bf32-46f2-a76f-3452c860b101: Rock-cut caves from the 2nd-3rd century AD containing artworks of both Buddhism and Jainism side by side. The dual iconography is rare for caves of this period.
descriptions.2fb9ef2d-55be-497a-9759-735df4f80db8: A mysterious 150-metre stone wall and five-sided building of unknown origin. Theories range from a sheep pen to a military fortification -- no one has proven either.
descriptions.1b68e8c4-22fd-4e5a-8708-92fb516034f0: High ground above this Shropshire village preserves both an ancient hilltop fort and a Roman settlement. The Domesday Book records the area, but occupation began over 2,000 years earlier.
descriptions.9dcc1c87-49c7-44f9-9d09-13b9b2b6671f: At 261 metres, this Hampshire hill carries an 80-hectare fort visible from the nearby A34 road. The hill derived its name from its historic role as one of many signal beacons across the country.
descriptions.57ced914-514c-4de1-97d9-63e5c23e3bc3: A Bronze Age hillfort site on a peak 248 metres high, making it the second-highest point in its county. The fort's defensive purpose exploited the natural vantage point.
descriptions.b7cc5073-ffca-4cd3-a168-3062908d4959: A hilltop enclosure from the Late Bronze Age whose defences were renewed in the Late Iron Age. The single rampart and ditch protected a settlement for centuries.
descriptions.782afd80-c3e6-4678-99b0-adc7c3074b7f: Seven stone circles, stone rows, and cairns hidden under peat until the 20th century. The name means "big place of birch trees" -- Neolithic farmers cleared the woodland.
descriptions.ee3d64b9-9207-4bff-8b91-3007ee811ecb: A 1-km Roman canal built for salt extraction, with pottery sherds and saltern sites nearby. The waterway remained in use for centuries, its line still traceable today.
descriptions.ad61addd-d62b-4c88-972c-18ebf465a900: Pre-Classic Maya city founded by 550 BC with a surrounding ditch and earthwork ramparts. Temple structures in the distinctive Rio Bec architectural style rise across the site.
descriptions.89be3bc4-f58c-4641-b56d-fb76041392f8: A Roman coastal hamlet where milefortlets guarded the shore beyond Hadrian's Wall. These small fortlets extended the Wall's defensive system along the Cumbrian coast.
descriptions.fa2037ed-54b7-425a-9650-27f0e25ac274: A Neolithic stone avenue curving southwest from Avebury, now vanished except for a single stone called Adam. Excavations revealed parallel rows of buried stone sockets.
descriptions.5801a79b-8780-405a-9e1b-6a6016c5438b: A Neolithic henge with 13 small standing stones forming an oval horseshoe that echoes the earliest form of Stonehenge. Its name translates as "Arthur's Grave."
descriptions.6cb3213a-bb68-4b7b-b45f-fab324033b3c: Round Bronze Age cairn in Ceredigion, about 2 metres long, with its capstone fallen and side slabs still in position. The grave bears no proven connection to the 6th-century poet Taliesin.
descriptions.baece784-4e12-4344-b9e4-bb4ed232ac3e: The name translates as "Giant Tomb." Set on a natural inland promontory at Cefnmeiriadog in Denbighshire, this fort commands views over the River Elwy valley from 800 BC onward.
descriptions.ffa6977e-a160-4bd9-a5ba-f529ab34bba8: A group of Buddhist rock-cut caves carved in the 1st century BC on an ancient trade route. Monks chose the route between coast and plateau to intercept passing merchants.
descriptions.8e131607-f575-485f-8115-275c68dda764: A massive Iron Age ditch 30 metres wide and 10 metres deep running for nearly a mile. It may have served as a tribal boundary rather than a military fortification.
descriptions.0de3da9b-5aeb-45a2-8f72-31ac1ad74a13: A prehistoric moorland landscape dense with cairns, burial mounds, and guidestones. The gritstone upland preserves monuments spanning the entire Bronze Age.
descriptions.dfc58d6f-44da-4159-b6e0-5fee86690841: A 2,000-year-old underground quarry that supplied stone for cathedrals across the region. The soft limestone was prized for its carvability in door and window surrounds.
descriptions.b68028d2-2617-41e8-9346-7c2a0404fc4e: A Thracian rock sanctuary reused for over a thousand years, featuring a 150-tonne rock balanced on the ground. A stone sun-clock and labyrinth mark the ritual landscape.
descriptions.2094fe27-b71c-4059-82d0-3891880600a5: A multilingual inscription carved 100 metres up a cliff face by Darius the Great around 520 BC. Like the Rosetta Stone, it unlocked the decipherment of cuneiform script.
descriptions.3c612fb4-3639-4124-8e26-58457c82376a: The largest prehistoric settlement ever found on this island, with over 1,600 burial sites across 10,000 square metres. The earliest remains date to the 4th millennium BC.
descriptions.8e70d0a6-40bb-46df-85ca-77997735c625: A rock-cut temple built by Ramesses II and dedicated to four deities. Relocated in the 1960s to save it from rising Nile waters behind the Aswan Dam.
descriptions.5ea4b4c5-9a5d-492d-aa71-5458b78d07a0: The ruins of Maresha, a major town during the First Temple period, sit alongside Roman-era Eleutheropolis. Underground burial caves and mosaics riddle the hillside.
descriptions.b2db3feb-e9a8-490b-a0ec-f0549f17d389: A small Maya city from the 4th century AD, subservient to the larger El Zotz. It lies within a protected biotope in the dense jungle.
descriptions.5b27b64f-8c83-4685-8644-8a2076d83322: Originally a Dacian settlement known as Aiadava, later Romanized as Remesiana. The town's name, Bela Palanka, means "white town" -- a name carried through the centuries.
descriptions.85ee60a8-9452-4359-89a6-3a937c5523d8: A Roman-era villa rustica where excavations uncovered gold and silver jewelry and 322 coins. The high-quality finds suggest an unusually wealthy rural estate.
descriptions.f0365431-b2a9-42a7-9cff-877433b51551: False entrance at the north end deceives tomb robbers; the actual burial chambers are hidden in the sides of this 3000 BC Cotswold mound. Four chambers contain the remains of at least 38 individuals.
descriptions.42ddb06e-547a-4f8e-b093-a6efcf2a8e2c: More a fortified estate house than a castle, this Armenian-built structure has a single rectangular keep. A single ground-level entrance was its only way in.
descriptions.c2bbac8e-a9d7-44be-a639-1920ef0dc640: A Hellenistic mausoleum built from an estimated 2,500 cubic metres of marble quarried locally near Ephesus. The sheer volume of stone rivals some of the grandest ancient tombs.
descriptions.033b359c-dc2e-4fea-a61e-cd2ad0ca9bbe: A fortress at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers, fought over by 115 armies across two millennia. Celts, Romans, Byzantines, and Ottomans all held it.
descriptions.7efae859-7199-4dd9-bde0-fcee0163a19e: Thracian cult plateau in the Rhodopes carved with round holes, stepped trails, and niches. Evidence points to a sanctuary of the Bessi tribe dedicated to the god Sabazios.
descriptions.00d711e5-2c6b-40c5-9c5c-a0f673cac312: An oval hillfort of 2.4 hectares that once sat on an island of firm soil surrounded by fens. Its moat was natural -- waterlogged marshland on every side.
descriptions.da99f5e5-6c0b-4700-a1d1-5f452f06538f: 64 stones -- some reaching 2 metres -- form this Donegal circle dated circa 2100-700 BC. The monument aligns with the sunrise on the Celtic festival of Beltane, which gave the site its name.
descriptions.81ac6019-eba7-4117-846e-e10dadb4dfe5: An elevated stone platform used as an orator's podium in ancient Athens. From this bema, speakers addressed the assembly on matters of war, law, and democracy.
descriptions.2715f436-40ec-4225-b5b6-8cc9523b2048: A pyramid that changes angle partway up -- 54 degrees at the base, 43 at the top. Engineers likely shifted the angle mid-build to prevent collapse, creating its bent shape.
descriptions.7e88e3ce-568c-4cea-aa71-79713b290df1: Saka kurgans from the 5th-3rd century BC that contained golden jewelry and horses buried beside their owners. Permafrost preserved organic materials in extraordinary detail.
descriptions.4054acf6-3542-4023-846b-bc13d419d79b: Mid-7th-century BC settlement at the Dnieper-Bug Estuary mouth, among the first permanent outposts in the northern Black Sea. By the 5th century BC it was largely abandoned as Olbia grew dominant.
descriptions.84f1b5af-954a-4b0a-aa4f-7911bb2adc74: Clifftop fort at 140 metres on the Devon coast, part of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site. Coastal erosion steadily consumes the ramparts -- the sea is slowly reclaiming the site.
descriptions.4c6645cc-de9a-4a21-b932-809f7600337c: An Iron Age headland fort with two ramparts up to 5.2 metres high. Its cliff-edge position gave defenders a natural wall on one side.
descriptions.5b413fb7-8c04-4923-8b60-cdc126069114: 1st-or-2nd-century BC fort in Worcestershire. The name "Berry" derives from burgh — a defensive position; local tradition also calls it "Danes Bury" after a Norse raiding legend.
descriptions.923f9b29-d79d-41a2-b815-c1a433d37679: A univallate hillfort following the ground's natural contours to enclose about 3 hectares. Its oval shape and single defensive ring are typical of early Iron Age design.
descriptions.8de5905a-6fa0-4b74-a68e-2e9c5da8c212: A sacred mountain rising 382 metres above the Caspian shore, known for mythical stories across the Caucasus. Pilgrims still visit this five-fingered rock formation.
descriptions.d26b2b27-e58b-438d-bdb1-8203b0c73549: Royal burial complex of the Semirechye-Saka tribe in the Altyn-Emel National Park, covering 2 square kilometres. The name "Besshatyr" means "Five Tents" in the local Turkic language.
descriptions.06f66762-c2a9-465c-bc9e-a31052ec7ce6: A Roman gate into the Acropolis built almost entirely from recycled stones of a demolished 4th-century BC monument. The original dedicatory inscription is still visible.
descriptions.3c771af0-6d1d-4a43-94ec-89ad5b476255: A Roman outpost fort north of Hadrian's Wall named Fanum Cocidi -- "Shrine of Cocidius," a war god worshipped in northern Britain. It served as an intelligence post.
descriptions.11d5d105-4613-4bd5-9e52-b17ce6a5c87d: Twenty-two Buddhist rock-cut caves on an ancient trade route between the Arabian Sea and the Deccan Plateau. Stupas carved inside the caves mark early monastic life.
descriptions.465c2630-67b7-42fe-95ac-e2a66a733531: A ruined Buddhist stupa with a cruciform plan, home to a 1,700-year-old statue of the Buddha attaining enlightenment. It is the oldest such statue in the world.
descriptions.6005666e-206a-4e73-b72a-72fbe8ffc6cf: Oldest layer of ancient Taxila, with grooved Red Burnished Ware pottery dated to around 800 BC. Together with nearby excavations, it forms the Ruins of Taxila -- a World Heritage Site since 1980.
descriptions.3c56c4c5-f5a8-48bb-8b93-9e3a92feac09: The capital of the Aedui tribe and one of Gaul's most powerful hillforts. Julius Caesar defeated the Helvetii nearby in 58 BC, and Vercingetorix was proclaimed leader here.
descriptions.c8d3dff0-b501-4ffa-8ef7-4f0605d8d091: Sole confirmed Iron Age hillfort in east Kent, occupied from about 350 BC. Sling bullets found on site are consistent with a violent assault by Julius Caesar's legions around 54 BC.
descriptions.a4057ca6-8123-45d9-b213-91e18a1b9193: A large Roman courtyard villa with some of the most complete mosaic floors in the country. Intricate geometric and mythological designs cover the heated rooms.
descriptions.113ce1a7-3e6a-49cb-9120-e6e230191646: A Mesoamerican centre of the Cotzumalhuapa culture from 600-800 AD. Its stone monuments depict human sacrifice, ballgame scenes, and cacao-themed rituals.
descriptions.23576019-c749-4ee9-95b1-cdae21f5ff06: Birthplace of the poet Martial around 40 AD, this Roman city features frescoes from its baths and townhouses. Recent excavations are revealing its full scale.
descriptions.b60c114a-7ee2-4f67-b3ff-a3d3d3e55d15: A Roman house in Londinium with well-preserved underfloor heating intact beneath the streets. The east wing had hypocausts, and the building sat at the Roman waterfront.
descriptions.89823dee-539f-45c3-aebf-e6a84cd0151f: Five stupas from the 1st century BC near Jalalabad, famous for the Bimaran Casket -- a gold reliquary bearing a very early depiction of the Buddha in human form.
descriptions.48130c20-c762-482d-bf8f-1474186dda0f: Triangular promontory in Wiltshire with steep natural defences on all sides except the south. Pottery found here is Roman or later -- the supposed Iron Age origin remains archaeologically unconfirmed.
descriptions.eb347510-7433-420e-aee8-adb0cdec43aa: An Iron Age earthwork enclosing coastal hillside along the Jurassic Coast. Its main rampart and ditch run over 2 km parallel to the shoreline.
descriptions.13bdea38-cb6c-4c6b-85cb-402a31427819: Two Chalcolithic funerary hypogea -- the oldest evidence of human presence on Menorca. Megalithic stone facades front burial chambers cut into the living rock.
descriptions.b9fdfd6f-b222-4c64-9953-b04fef1f55aa: Celtic name Banna -- "horn" -- describes the triangular spur above the River Irthing, bounded by cliffs south and east. Among the best-preserved of the 16 forts along Hadrian Wall.
descriptions.b1135e25-0b17-4daf-ab6f-57b3cfb9a1fa: Petroglyphs spanning 6,000 years at an ancient Palaeolithic and Neolithic site. The rock carvings are inscribed into sandstone formations across a vast desert landscape.
descriptions.8424266d-c9ed-42b0-b04c-004e21cd06de: Roman ala fort near Weissenburg on the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes, now a World Heritage component. Partly subterranean ruins and a reconstructed bathhouse complex survive at the site.
descriptions.ab0a09e4-2350-42b5-b864-6a9330e4670f: A double-ringed Bronze Age stone circle from 1700-1400 BC. The outer ring has 15 stones, the inner has 10 -- none taller than 60 centimetres.
descriptions.a1441245-1be1-457c-8de6-ae331f12007e: Sasanid city from the 3rd century AD built on a rigid perpendicular street grid — the first such urban layout in the ancient Near East. It uniquely fused Zoroastrian and Roman artistic traditions.
descriptions.5fb67acb-15e7-4e73-ab27-3d729a0b74b9: One of the eastern gates of Roman London's defensive wall, marking the start of Ermine Street to York. It was rebuilt twice before final demolition in 1760.
descriptions.3867504c-c199-4a59-9609-9b2340905467: An 8th-century BC fortified settlement with over 100 houses arranged in neat rows inside timber-and-earth walls. It sat on a marshy peninsula for natural defence.
descriptions.f3c2a268-f63e-41be-b587-1885a7e1cfae: Island in Lake Malaren housing Birka, a Viking-age trading town active 750-975 AD declared a World Heritage Site in 1993. The oldest relic on the island predates the Viking settlement.
descriptions.9f611d23-894b-45e0-ad29-a692e6d46241: Rampart 3 metres high with a 2-metre ditch rings this Somerset summit. Stone tower foundations were visible at the start of the 20th century but have since disappeared entirely.
descriptions.2b8e45c1-ca98-4c5f-8790-1b64f32e965f: Hilltop fort on a Devon ridgeline above valleys formed by Coly River tributaries. The terrain provided natural defence on three sides, concentrating fortification on the exposed eastern approach.
descriptions.b7696395-7934-4067-b84a-34d7834e5610: Earthwork fort at 185 metres above the River Avon in Devon, its outline still readable in the hilltop landscape. Little survives beyond the ditch-and-bank silhouette.
descriptions.7fe4bb17-d008-4886-a097-c03c66b43f76: A Neolithic stalled cairn from 3000 BC with compartmented burial chambers. Its oblong form measures 22.5 metres, typical of the Orkney-Cromarty tradition.
descriptions.91e451d3-977c-45fd-824b-b3ab93908ed9: Two parallel ramparts -- the taller reaching 5.2 metres -- defended this Cornish headland above St Austell Bay. A ditch 2.1 metres deep lies beyond the outer rampart.
descriptions.5e7bedef-ef5e-44b4-b479-ec462b3ba954: An ancient Hohokam fortification atop a lava-capped mesa rising 305 metres above its base. Stone walls, petroglyphs, and pottery sherds mark the summit.
descriptions.8a93ea1c-7dc4-4b11-b68e-39524fa0b8bc: Black limestone obelisk from 825 BC with bas-relief carvings of King Shalmaneser III's conquests. Only two complete Assyrian obelisks survive -- this is the more historically significant.
descriptions.775b2ff8-3307-475c-a3d8-c0d8e7aecea0: A fortress complex near a town where settlements existed from prehistoric through Roman times. Fortifications crown each of the summit's highest points.
descriptions.d0dab028-351d-48e1-b749-821e89458654: A group of standing stones near the Hole of Horcum on the North York Moors. The tallest stone stands 1.9 metres but is much weathered and leaning.
descriptions.81112e4f-9b95-4dcf-be7b-0c62b9580c19: Small Roman fort positioned on an old military road between Old Carlisle and Papcastle in Cumbria. Beyond its function as a 2nd-century waypoint, little historical record of the garrison survives.
descriptions.cf261948-6565-4fab-962f-c57620305e53: Chalk hill with a single-rampart fort active from the 4th or 5th century BC. A stockade-enclosed settlement preceded it, built in the 5th or 6th century BC -- making this a two-phase site.
descriptions.39896f94-30a7-4b94-8974-b880b83bdca4: The ancient Ridgeway passes just south of the parish, and Blewburton Hill -- half inside the village boundary -- is topped by a prehistoric fort. Bronze Age sites cluster across the chalk downland.
descriptions.6ff3e4f1-8f21-410a-9c93-d4468c91a762: A Mesolithic spring site near Stonehenge with 4,000 years of continuous habitation. Over 35,000 worked flints and 2,400 animal bones have been excavated from the spring.
descriptions.614fd061-151e-45e3-8806-f5ec033241a0: Dacian fortress built under King Burebista in the 1st century BC to resist Roman expansion. Part of a defensive network of hilltop strongholds across the Orastie Mountains.
descriptions.763e4a8b-eed2-495d-81db-35f83a3d5d82: A perforated sarsen stone that produces a booming sound when blown through its natural holes. Legend says King Alfred used it to summon troops against the Danes.
descriptions.dc7674a8-0723-455e-ab0b-9378c4491da9: A chalk hill containing the Medway Megaliths, including Kit's Coty House. These Neolithic tombs are among the oldest known monuments in southeast Britain.
descriptions.3951e459-d0f1-4580-bda1-8e6163ddbd13: A standing stone 2 metres tall on a moorland route, standing since pre-Roman times. Traces of blue paint and a carved date of 1841 mark its later reuse as a boundary stone.
descriptions.25cf40c9-4d5a-4818-9d6a-254bc7e097a7: Henge 1.6 km from Stonehenge, once holding bluestones now removed -- only the ditch and empty stone sockets survive. It linked Stonehenge to the River Avon in a ceremonial Neolithic landscape.
descriptions.1b69bb27-aebb-4675-8ee0-e9d6007a4cee: Giant figures etched into the desert floor near the Colorado River, the largest 52 metres long. Best seen from the air, their purpose remains unknown.
descriptions.037e3715-f5f7-4345-8216-8aa26f404009: An island with ancient carved stone figures -- Janus-faced anthropomorphic sculptures unique in style. One figure has two faces looking in opposite directions.
descriptions.69fb9773-3709-4e8e-8682-96c75f57dfc6: Around 10,000 rock engravings cover 6 square kilometres in Nuevo Leon. Charcoal from ancient ovens dates occupation back to 6960 BC; images range from astronomical symbols to fertility scenes.
descriptions.884eefd5-fec7-49da-972f-dfd3a8c099ab: A stone circle of 16 standing stones around a central slab, with an associated stone row of five stones. An ogham stone was found nearby but has been moved.
descriptions.190fd91a-8c04-4665-9121-b89eff26130f: A Neolithic dolmen with three uprights supporting a robust wedge-shaped capstone. A large flat stone nearby may be the collapsed remains of the original structure.
descriptions.df056ae9-c7c1-4a2d-93f9-76e9d6bd0f93: Greco-Roman theatre seating 13,000 at ancient Halicarnassus -- city of the Mausoleum, a Wonder of the Ancient World. The theatre dates to the 4th century BC.
descriptions.8afd1020-1c36-499b-ae38-8aaa9f9d4170: A treasury dedicated in the Archaic period at the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi. Pausanias never mentioned it -- by his time, the building may already have been destroyed.
descriptions.7d711cde-9765-499f-a664-0409651a90e8: A Buddhist rock-cut hillock covered with monolithic stupas surrounding a great central platform. The dome of the main stupa was built of brick atop the carved stone.
descriptions.15264f9b-f57b-4562-b577-fbfdec72227f: A 5.7-km linear earthwork that may date to the Bronze Age and was reactivated in the 4th century AD. A Roman road was cut through it, then the dyke was rebuilt across it.
descriptions.08088896-dddb-43de-a2d3-188c2cf4f61a: A petroglyph of a reindeer so finely carved it has been called the finest rock carving in its country. Newer figures from later millennia were added to the same rock face.
descriptions.55231dfd-fc7a-4bdf-a490-7ee5de43e975: An Iron Age underground passage, or fogou, unusual for having more than one entrance. Its original purpose -- storage, refuge, or ritual space -- is still debated.
descriptions.d48e9c91-2bb0-4960-be2b-a80eeb957d62: The first aqueduct in Naples, built by Greeks around 400 BC. It tapped an aquifer fed by Mount Vesuvius's eruptions and ran 10 km to reach the city gates.
descriptions.3a1d65e1-389c-4ceb-9eb1-50af9efeec1e: Headland fort at 60 metres above Hope Cove in Devon, defended inland by a single linear earthwork. Little physical evidence of the structure remains above ground today.
descriptions.08508ff0-053d-4b8e-b2a3-6382818c6735: A small Maya settlement famous for the finest known Maya murals, depicting battle scenes and court life in vivid colour. The paintings survived because the city was abandoned.
descriptions.045e2515-7952-4245-9cc3-e335f0341484: A late Neolithic barrow cemetery on the heath, with the largest barrow reconstructed from its original excavation. Six closely packed burial mounds survive.
descriptions.7d93ed41-cb1c-4f2c-a935-d81b4fa7d87c: A Megalithic temple from 2500 BC paired with a Bronze Age fortified village -- the earliest known fortification on the island. Cart ruts and silos surround the complex.
descriptions.3bfe34ae-3a60-48fe-9773-8cd0ec838b46: A major Neolithic temple sharing design features with the famous Ggantija and Hagar Qim temples. Nearby cart ruts and a dolmen add to the ritual landscape.
descriptions.b4d3bc67-e38d-4d6e-9b03-0ca72a0d4398: An Iron Age and Roman earthwork on a hilltop in woodland. The site has been closed to visitors since 2016 due to erosion from foot traffic.
descriptions.52c6e083-90a9-44d1-83f8-d3c2cbd0e9e3: A passage grave built with heavy boulders and capstones, assigned to the Funnelbeaker culture. The cemetery also contains unchambered long barrows and other tumuli.
descriptions.ccf25f6a-36aa-458a-9d43-5b33ef8c119c: A hill with Bronze Age barrows, two Iron Age hillforts -- one the fourth largest in all of Britain -- and a Roman villa. Four thousand years of occupation on one summit.
descriptions.bebeb092-4bf8-41da-accd-cf2a8b640343: A Roman villa built inside the ramparts of a larger Iron Age fortress. A bath suite with mosaic floors was among the rooms uncovered during 19th-century excavations.
descriptions.5281654c-51d5-443c-9a00-9824f323f61b: A raised bog where three bog bodies from the Late Bronze Age were found preserved in peat. A nearby fortified settlement from the 4th century BC was one of northern Europe's largest.
descriptions.66b6fcb0-605a-4988-9c26-50d92bdb45dd: 19 upright stones set in an ellipse 24.9 by 21.9 metres, with a leaning central stone just south of centre. A west-facing gap in the ring may mark a deliberate entrance to this Cornwall circle.
descriptions.e99aac35-d2da-448f-8cd2-d07c02ae007c: A Neolithic entrance grave considered one of the smallest and best-preserved burial monuments in all of Britain. The unique Scillonian type is found only in two areas.
descriptions.c22fa6c5-6691-4f76-a6fe-83ee0b7e0dbf: A stone circle traditionally called the Nine Maidens, though the original number of stones was likely greater. Some stand barely 60 centimetres above the moorland.
descriptions.cb2f9081-0b6b-469c-ba0d-16d21149fa3a: Standing stone 2.4 metres high with a rectangular cross-section; the back face has two carved steps -- unusual detail absent from most Penwith menhirs. Located 3 km northeast of St Just in Cornwall.
descriptions.9085faef-619a-4d87-bd91-1f33780fe58f: A hamlet with a standing stone whose description is thin, but the surrounding Shropshire moors contain guidestones and cairns spanning thousands of years of use.
descriptions.a9a32ee2-bd62-4fe4-8515-0ccdda65a7ee: A submerged Mesolithic settlement in 11 metres of water, discovered when a lobster was seen tossing worked flint tools from its burrow. Dates to around 6000 BC.
descriptions.792dd8d0-be86-45d9-9cfd-bfc7da7c0082: Fifteen pairs of parallel stone monoliths forming alley menhirs oriented east to west. The paired rows may represent a solar cult from the 4th millennium BC.
descriptions.7748176f-48aa-4377-8b17-f9f64dc5c525: A ridge with cross dykes, tumuli, and long barrows spanning the Neolithic to Iron Age. The concentration of burial monuments shows millennia of reverence for this hilltop.
descriptions.db3840fb-0dfd-444c-be07-ed15ee4874cc: A Roman courtyard villa on the Isle of Wight with fine mosaics, built after the 2nd Augusta Legion conquered the island in 44 AD. A fire damaged the villa but mosaics survive.
descriptions.ed7d0f05-9dd1-4452-915c-11be01ecd9cc: Excavations in the 1960s at this Norfolk village revealed a Roman bath house alongside nearly 140 pottery kilns -- a density pointing to industrial-scale ceramics production for the wider region.
descriptions.6d28ceb7-10be-442f-be2e-cab319d32763: A Neolithic entrance grave considered one of the smallest and best-preserved in Britain. The circular mound is built of rubble and soil, typical of the Scillonian entrance type.
descriptions.a1efde92-3c4f-47dd-b101-fd4951c4cfa1: A Roman fort whose Celtic name may mean "fort of the raven," built in the 230s to guard the Wash. It became part of the Saxon Shore defence system against raiders.
descriptions.b719c2bb-3424-4eab-8648-9e72bf83bdac: Two circuits of ditch and bank enclosing 9.3 hectares on Bratton Down. Rampart slopes rise 5-6 metres above the ditch bases along the Salisbury Plain escarpment.
descriptions.ced822e8-13cd-49db-9011-808dc23aac45: An ancient city with a sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia, protector of women in childbirth. Young girls performed a bear-dance ritual here before they could marry.
descriptions.44354857-115b-44d3-b155-cae373565602: The Acropolis sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia, of unusual trapezoidal shape. It had no formal temple -- just an open precinct with a stoa to display offerings.
descriptions.611a3218-4df9-4018-8d46-c1e731f04b2a: A limestone promontory extending 2.5 km into the Bristol Channel with human activity spanning from the Bronze Age through Roman times. A 4th-century AD temple was found here.
descriptions.6724235d-289c-411b-9b85-ac18229a0212: A Victorian-era naval fort built in the 1860s to defend the Bristol Channel. Though modern, it sits atop a headland with a much longer history of human occupation.
descriptions.2cd65076-e10c-401f-a997-296f99badf9c: The summit of this hill bears the remains of Kemerton Camp, an Iron Age hillfort. A mutilation burial of 50 men found near the entrance suggests a violent end.
descriptions.4154478d-f0ff-4f48-b577-48a8f647595c: Steep-sided hill at 367 metres near Welshpool with a hilltop fort and roundhouse foundations inside. Archaeological evidence ties it to the Cornovii tribe and their resistance to Roman conquest.
descriptions.a0dd99a4-37b3-4b2d-bf8b-0bbaf3c2f53a: Roman fort at Rochester far north of Hadrian Wall along Dere Street, garrisoned into the 270s AD -- longer than most frontier outposts in hostile northern territory.
descriptions.5d5f1cc8-18af-42b2-860a-65862b328498: Timber fort built at Ribchester around 72 AD by Petillius Cerialis, guarding a River Ribble crossing. Rebuilt in stone in the 2nd century and garrisoned for over 300 years by cavalry units.
descriptions.8b1abd85-fc57-40d7-a4c6-c987d4d0bc29: Woodland promontory enclosure at 175 metres above the River Bray near South Molton in Devon. The earthwork occupies a natural spur, with the river providing defence to the west.
descriptions.51ab44fd-823d-4c9c-aed4-b4e188a22408: Hilltop fort at 311 metres near South Brent in Devon, its summit position providing the primary defensive advantage across the surrounding landscape.
descriptions.dba6e82d-3388-4b6c-beba-63f8f440ba0b: 137-metre hill dominating the flat Somerset Levels, visible for miles. The fort covers 1.6 hectares; the hill has been occupied since at least the Bronze Age around 2000 BC.
descriptions.5b9668cf-d08f-4877-ab48-c4f3b47f5117: The Roman town of Varvaria stood here, later becoming a medieval stronghold of the powerful Subic family. The hilltop location controlled the surrounding agricultural region.
descriptions.21ac323f-7214-4891-9499-74e55c3d7d56: A 2nd-century Roman hypocaust survives in the cellar of a medieval building with Chester Rows. Roman underfloor heating, 1,800 years old, sits beneath a working shop.
descriptions.3696838c-9f7e-4e20-aaf8-841af9e7690d: A village where Romans built a villa to take advantage of clean spring water. The site dates from the earliest period of Roman occupation.
descriptions.262b6a28-de86-4e63-bdba-398a67236618: 24 broad upright stones form a 24-metre oval on Dartmoor -- roughly half the original number. Located 300 metres from Ringmoor Stone Row and Cairn Circle in the Upper Plym Valley.
descriptions.6645e3f5-bc18-46f5-854c-5b89dd96650e: A large boulder cairn surrounded by a stone ring and a human effigy figure, dating to about 1400 AD. The effigy is one of few such figures found on the northern plains.
descriptions.c7d33a59-e6ed-46e1-ad3f-5598b699727b: Herefordshire Beacon's shape is entirely determined by the terraced Iron Age earthworks, compared to a giant wedding cake. A Norman castle was added later atop this 2nd-century BC fortification.
descriptions.8d4f7a98-2c79-4a0e-ae9b-c8f4a665902f: A Roman ruin site that was repeatedly uncovered by storms in 1520, 1552, and 1562, then entirely eroded away by the sea. Nothing of the original fortress remains today.
descriptions.186eeb54-e6a0-4370-87c6-fbcaae023a33: A Neolithic burial chamber within a hedge bank, with a megalithic chamber and single entrance passage. Part of the original cairn still survives around the tomb.
descriptions.36bcb120-d684-4d2b-82d2-e41311e02bb4: Roman fort at Brougham near Penrith, with early occupation linked to the revolt of Venutius around 70 AD. Artefacts from the excavated cemetery span the 2nd and 3rd centuries.
descriptions.2e2617fe-2aa6-48ba-b8f1-4b3725e25e8d: Cliff-top broch on Mainland Orkney, 20 metres above sea. External diameter 17 metres; walls 3.5 to 5 metres thick -- the double-skin dry-stone construction typical of the form.
descriptions.1d873464-bd56-415a-984e-67026294d00c: Headland broch on North Ronaldsay separated from the mainland by defensive earthworks. The entrance passage has a guard cell and bar-holes for securing the door against intruders.
descriptions.ce979635-b9c3-4645-838d-a7a30da06854: An unexcavated coastal broch with views to Foula, Vaila, and Fair Isle. A massive triangular lintel stone still sits over the entrance despite centuries of collapse.
descriptions.17191c2e-9ebc-41e5-865f-1bb6be790eb5: Central tower once reaching about 10 metres, surrounded by stone buildings housing a substantial community from around 500-200 BC. Two drystone skins make up the tower walls.
descriptions.918025af-8cfa-47db-a273-b4b715590e0c: Tallest surviving broch in existence, built around 300 BC on Mousa in Shetland. Among the best-preserved Prehistoric structures in Europe, it still stands to its full original height.
descriptions.90bd1f84-149e-4ee7-98c4-9c14b56298f1: A broch on a rocky islet accessible only at very low tide, once connected by a causeway now lost. The entrance is blocked with rubble but the lintel still holds.
descriptions.aa4988d2-aa09-48db-a515-71e38576824b: The southern gate of Diocletian's Palace, originally a sea gate where the emperor entered by boat. Today it is the main entry from the waterfront promenade.
descriptions.b99fab00-abbf-4c9d-b03b-42b66bb04814: Village on the A66 trans-Pennine road, built over the Roman fort Verterae that guarded the Stainmore pass. The modern road follows the route the Romans established nearly 2,000 years ago.
descriptions.577f59ce-ea47-4d39-a1f0-c5a0fd6e84d1: The highest hill in its county at 540 metres, with several Iron Age hillforts. Quarrying destroyed two of the three forts, leaving only Nordy Bank intact.
descriptions.6ffc6cd5-4065-430e-881f-32d6cb2e3445: Burial mound near Marple in Greater Manchester. Excavation in 1809 yielded cremated bones, burnt stones, and a preserved acorn; a nearby barrow held a funerary urn.
descriptions.970e9f98-8206-46d0-a591-b20b2df667ba: A portal tomb with a capstone weighing an estimated 150 tonnes -- the heaviest in Europe. How Neolithic builders raised this colossal stone remains a mystery.
descriptions.353f7688-f230-41ef-a181-8bd9341448cf: Bronze Age cairns sit atop the highest point of Bodmin Moor at 420 metres. The hill shifts from a conical peak to a multi-peaked crest depending on the vantage point.
descriptions.9d58f665-8cc3-4438-9dc5-99885deb90d0: Ring structures made of broken stalagmites found 336 metres deep in this cave date to 176,000 years ago. They are the oldest known constructions by Neanderthals.
descriptions.9afe9a14-d2a8-495a-b0d3-ddb86a761a31: A Bronze Age cairn with 18 thin jagged stone pillars jutting from a low mound like a crown. Originally 30 pillars stood here before 19th-century treasure hunters disturbed it.
descriptions.bca65486-49fb-4c72-acff-8df9d0d7f0b3: A Neolithic passage tomb that began as a henge and was later transformed into a burial mound. A carved pillar inside the chamber and a mysterious "Pattern Stone" remain.
descriptions.770a7347-7227-408d-97e0-cf0c02b57157: An Iron Age farmstead with three excavated roundhouses, two of which have been reconstructed at a national museum. The buildings were rebuilt mainly by volunteers.
descriptions.26de5254-9e5e-4611-9439-35f3086d9ab5: The tallest standing stones on the island, nearly 4 metres high. An 18th-century account described them as part of a ruinous circle of eight stones.
descriptions.d2968d12-d344-43d1-b192-ad3436cd38c1: Summit enclosure at 300 metres on Mynydd-y-Gaer, defined by a single circular bank and ditch enclosing 1.1 hectares. A Bronze Age burial mound survives inside the walls.
descriptions.0ed9dd74-23c1-45e4-9d4e-8b80dfe46b0c: Lymington fort with timber-revetted ramparts of wall-and-fill construction. Excavation in 1935 found upright beams and walls built from cut and laid turves preserved beneath the earthwork.
descriptions.41ff8c60-d10d-44cf-905c-e2d1a39e5d3f: Most thoroughly investigated Roman villa complex on the Isle of Purbeck, with occupation from the 1st through 6th centuries AD. Mosaic and hypocaust evidence survives from multiple phases.
descriptions.b1e4d609-9b3a-4b93-8ad0-e890a880a5dc: A Roman villa with an aisled hall and bath house, rebuilt multiple times over four centuries. A new bath complex was added in the 2nd-3rd century as the villa expanded.
descriptions.3e27c892-40de-4be9-a3fd-396e17d3c86d: Buddhist caves carved during Emperor Ashoka's reign in the 3rd century BC. They are the earliest monastic settlement in the area, hewn directly from rock.
descriptions.916b8b05-0c42-4af3-b05e-9be842a23c5b: A valley of Buddhist rock carvings in the Swat region, once a sacred landscape of monasteries. Sculptures and inscriptions welcomed pilgrims as they entered the valley.
descriptions.d41a3ab6-2d5d-4fd4-bdb5-e581f27b9bdb: A small Megalithic temple from the Tarxien phase, partly built over by a modern hotel. The coralline limestone facade and trilithon entrance are still partially visible.
descriptions.ceff34a3-d6a5-4d8c-8c58-4a8cc27460a5: A Minoan palace fresco showing a figure vaulting over a charging bull. The artist had to simultaneously mold and paint wet stucco at height -- an extraordinary feat.
descriptions.563693f3-5fa9-485d-940f-66f26210a9f4: A bronze bull dedicated at Delphi to commemorate an exceptional tuna fish catch. The citizens of Corfu considered the haul so miraculous it warranted a monument to Apollo.
descriptions.9724373d-f4f0-4a4b-b460-d01dd5b4b2ee: Plateau fort concealed in heavy Hampshire woodland, defended by three concentric bank-and-ditch rings at 65 metres altitude. The earthworks are eroded but still visible on close inspection.
descriptions.0529af31-7573-467e-88ff-12dbca48f94d: Four granite bull sculptures associated with the Celtic Vettones people. Hundreds of similar "verracos" exist, but these are among the most famous examples.
descriptions.8c624c02-31b5-4058-8551-f7cec08e6359: A settlement with ceramics resembling Dalma-type pottery from northwestern Iran. The painted wares link this site to a broad cultural network spanning the 5th millennium BC.
descriptions.8b9f8fb9-7f39-455b-bf0e-bec8e76fb45d: Multivallate fort measuring 579 by 187 metres near Old Radnor in Powys. Offa's Dyke -- the great 8th-century earthwork demarcating the border -- passes near the base of Burfa Bank.
descriptions.8729144c-61a4-49e3-9883-c04538725739: One of nine Roman Saxon Shore forts built to defend against Saxon raiders. Its walls still stand, measuring roughly 205 by 100 metres and up to 4.5 metres thick.
descriptions.eb56629d-c8e4-4f74-bebf-85b06ee5ba20: A unique underground structure: stone steps descend to a spring-fed chamber with a carved frieze and sunken basin. Whether it served ritual or practical purposes is unknown.
descriptions.3b512b0e-f4d7-4d81-8467-87796cdf405a: Trans-regional hilltop settlement in southern Styria, active 800-600 BC. The surrounding necropolis originally held at least 2,000 burial mounds -- the densest Iron Age cemetery in central Europe.
descriptions.3c1e886f-d77b-4d46-899b-2aaf26861a4d: A burial ground of the Chernyakhov culture with 315 burials — 253 cremations and 62 inhumations. It is the most studied Chernyakhov site in Right-bank territory, excavated from 1973 to 2000.
descriptions.e473f682-8b9c-4d5c-b2cc-0ca24fcc06bc: Single-rampart fort on the southern edge of Bishop Sutton in Somerset, investigated in 1955, 1959, and 1966. Excavations revealed postholes, ditches, and pits inside the enclosure.
descriptions.050ff0e8-d181-4b9a-8c1b-9a5f1a5d48bb: Hilltop fort at 220 metres above the River Lew near Lydford in Devon. A Norman motte-and-bailey castle was added below it to the northeast -- two fortifications from different eras on one hill.
descriptions.6f2ea7d4-4858-46e6-a24f-0c9d49109741: An ancient woodland with a Bronze Age earthwork enclosure hidden among beech trees several hundred years old. The deadwood ecosystem makes it a nationally important habitat.
descriptions.118c6bd0-cfa1-4376-8f42-34e75bec43d3: Five stone circles about 4,000 years old clustered on a hillside. The largest, Brat's Hill, has 42 stones forming an irregular ring 30 metres in diameter.
descriptions.00daa905-2060-4b9c-8369-eb5e6878f6a6: Low-lying fenland between Cambridgeshire and Suffolk yielding a hoard of Bronze Age artefacts -- among the largest found in western Europe. Mesolithic finds show activity spanning millennia.
descriptions.21c68897-6da3-4cbc-abda-41e45a0c0f3c: A Bronze Age burnt mound -- an oval heap of fire-cracked stones 14 metres across -- hidden in a park with no marker. Its purpose, whether cooking or bathing, is debated.
descriptions.bd536ec2-bdb9-4da0-8489-e6c58fec5921: A Roman legionary camp and town where several legions were stationed in succession. Remains include an amphitheatre and aqueduct along the Adriatic coast.
descriptions.0fa0df95-200a-40bf-805d-51a1f530f973: Shetland broch with outer walls around 4.5 metres thick -- unusually massive even for the form. Walls on the seaward east side still stand over 4 metres high.
descriptions.c8d56e70-25e4-4814-b5c5-13cd14e68808: Hilltop fort at 150 metres above the Yeo and Bradiford rivers near Barnstaple in Devon. Only the outline of the earthwork defences survives above the surface today.
descriptions.99685d28-2f4f-409e-9f18-04a1215a04d1: Oval univallate fort above Burrington Combe in the Mendip Hills. The combe below has produced cemetery finds of long human occupation, including at Aveline's Hole nearby.
descriptions.3d8cb484-8b57-41fa-ab0d-203449c1c821: Carboniferous limestone gorge with cave entrances occupied for over 10,000 years. A hillfort was built beside the combe in the Iron Age, and human bones dated 10,400-10,200 BC were found inside.
descriptions.1be281ba-d8dd-4260-85c9-39aa02b15567: Univallate promontory fort at 210 metres in Leicestershire, with Mesolithic artefacts showing this was among the first settled hilltops in the area. The fort itself dates to the early Iron Age.
descriptions.1949a2b8-9e93-4091-b404-915fb9bd8f52: Well-preserved broch at Shapinsay with drystone walls up to 4 metres thick. A complete chamber survives off the entrance passage, and stone fittings remain visible inside.
descriptions.c0aefb21-c09e-4b5d-a149-031232e56632: A tidal island with a rampart enclosure and an Iron Age presence linked to the Celtic saint Cenydd. Hermit traditions and archaeological remains overlap here.
descriptions.d047cd4f-0416-4547-9bcc-20034e2c8819: Two ramparts enclose 2.2 hectares atop a Staffordshire hill, following the natural contours. The fort is traditionally associated with Wulfhere, 7th-century King of Mercia.
descriptions.4c5cee5c-42d5-443a-871a-730a8e584e89: A multivallate hillfort on a triangular promontory, enclosed by a ditch 4 metres wide. Two spurs of a river valley provided natural defences on most sides.
descriptions.1b8b5fd4-d6b2-4ae0-9783-6e4e39a1314f: Spur fort in Somerset with steep drops on the north, east, and south. The bank reaches 1.6 metres high; the ditch drops 2 metres below -- small in area but well-chosen for its natural advantages.
descriptions.96cc1d5e-207e-4b43-b14e-a0854e10e7c2: Elliptical Shropshire hillfort with up to four concentric ditches and two well-preserved entrances ringing the summit of Sunnyhill. The neat oval shape earns it a reputation as a spectacular example.
descriptions.a90e4406-25e6-4646-ae73-0730696a22d4: Two-phase fort enclosing 8.9 hectares near Andover: an earlier single rampart, then a stronger double rampart overlaid to the south and east. Both phases remain visible in the earthwork profile.
descriptions.fc553d2e-73db-4bfb-b3a7-ba8f95597304: Sandstone ridge promontory at 160 metres near Weston-under-Redcastle, enclosing about 8 hectares. Steep slopes protect all sides but the north, which received the heaviest fortification.
descriptions.18c1589b-3ebd-4267-8567-effd7e549792: A Bronze Age barrow near Stonehenge that produced some of Britain's most spectacular grave goods, including worked gold objects. It marks a burial of the Wessex elite culture.
descriptions.021e7e01-8d62-4480-ae4a-454bc7d78b7f: Roman lakeside settlement on the Obersee shore, positioned at the junction of roads to Zurich, Winterthur, and Chur. A 1st-century waystation on the Alpine road network.
descriptions.2df3baac-05ae-4af8-9e6e-d6b709fa78f3: A bivallate hillfort with double bank and ditch on two sides and a single bank on the others. It encloses 4.4 hectares within a private wooded estate.
descriptions.f80f56c0-949f-4009-8658-f47cc3ca13fa: Buddhist stupa near Mingora enlarged five times, each phase encapsulating the previous structure. Dating to the 2nd century BC, built during the Mauryan period in the Swat Valley.
descriptions.17c94d52-2df2-44ba-83f1-41c26ee6eea3: A Greek, Roman, and early Christian city that was abandoned after a major earthquake flooded it. A UNESCO site, it spans from Chaonian tribal settlement to Roman colonia.
descriptions.f1349cdf-a245-414f-a199-fa6c5e7e7cd7: The remains of a 3rd-century BC Greek theatre with well-preserved lower cavea and orchestra. Almost nothing of the original Greek stage survives the Roman renovation.
descriptions.74af1ed2-4221-4e13-8a96-e63631d01cc7: The ruins of a Roman bathhouse in the ancient port city of Phaselis. The city thrived as a trade hub on the Lycian coast between East and West.
descriptions.9b3bade9-0410-4e3d-8c00-89cdc1b776ed: Non-concentric layout: a 1.2-hectare inner enclosure inside a larger 4-hectare outer ring on Keynston Down. The offset arrangement reflects two distinct phases of construction.
descriptions.c08d8ce8-6103-4f32-bb80-9e59c0a97a17: Paleolithic cave at 1,640 metres altitude near the Zuvandchay River. Stone tools and animal bones dated to 30,000 BC place it among the highest-altitude ancient habitation sites in the Caucasus.
descriptions.b347415b-f65c-4377-bbf2-3c4f553f8804: Flat-topped limestone hill on Anglesey at 164 metres, its name meaning "Arthur Table." The natural topography required minimal additional fortification to secure the perimeter.
descriptions.8944e529-490d-499c-94d2-9c81cace802b: Paeonian city from the 6th century BC near Knezhje. In 2008 the main gate was found intact -- confirming this as a major early urban centre and reshaping understanding of Paeonian civilization.
descriptions.3fb0fb63-6af0-4da6-9b5a-132ee05dd28f: An ancient Illyrian city with massive walls built before the end of the 4th century BC. It later acquired Greek-style public buildings, including a theatre and stoa.
descriptions.98299c91-a01b-4dfc-bc31-f8f8ce1b84a5: A well-preserved Roman temple dedicated to Azizos, later converted into a church. Two phases of Christianization altered the ancient structure.
descriptions.b7ce5331-6c35-46bb-ac93-fdccf2b208e0: A ceremonial mound complex spanning 2,000 years of coastal occupation. The Huaca de los Reyes features dramatic adobe reliefs of fanged jaguar faces.
descriptions.8b190e2c-f9ea-4d46-803a-11750b5119ba: Third-millennium BC copper smelting community in Huelva, achieving furnace temperatures of 1,200 degrees Celsius. It provides very early evidence of copper metallurgy in Atlantic Europe.
descriptions.d7739229-1732-41fc-9c31-d5d0c4a881b4: Major Thracian centre established around 2000 BC on the river Tonsus. Philip II of Macedon captured it; the town later bore the names Diospolis and Goloe in different historical periods.
descriptions.2bc26dce-7797-40a5-8a39-589e5dee1453: Olmeca-Xicalanca city inhabited 650-1350 AD whose palace murals depict battles and ceremonies in vivid polychrome -- among the finest surviving pre-Columbian frescoes. Now a World Heritage Site.
descriptions.749c6264-126b-4aca-ab5d-219cee168da3: Fort with Bronze Age origins near Tickenham in Somerset, occupied through the Roman period. The name may derive from Cador, an Arthurian figure -- though the fort long predates that tradition.
descriptions.831371bc-5719-4399-ac7b-d0defb2022b0: Hilltop fort at 250 metres near Bickleigh. Parliamentary forces camped here during the Civil War while besieging Bickleigh Castle below -- ancient earthworks repurposed for 17th-century warfare.
descriptions.d138a529-7499-4ed5-b039-5607886bce86: A hillfort linked to King Arthur's legendary Camelot since the medieval period. Excavations revealed a massive timber hall and a 7.2-hectare ramparted plateau.
descriptions.574b24e0-9357-4d1a-a66b-556a0dfe6303: 200-metre hilltop near Yatton in North Somerset shared by Bronze Age barrows, a scheduled Iron Age fort, and a Roman villa -- three distinct periods of occupation layered on one summit.
descriptions.da4f66f6-683b-4655-a694-279361b05529: A Roman road that ran 160 km from the Humber Estuary to the River Tyne. Its exact course is still debated, though evidence exists on parts of the proposed route.
descriptions.9ceb5947-c91f-4a1f-8c8f-6a67dbb88de2: Phoenician colony from the 7th century BC on an Atlantic peninsula, settled for nearly 3,000 years without interruption. By the 18th century it was western Europe's dominant Atlantic trading port.
descriptions.93d28b0d-2eba-440b-97a0-2bf291232dd5: Univallate oval fort above the River Lynher in Cornwall, measuring roughly 275 by 170 metres and enclosing 2.5 hectares. Owned by the National Trust and a scheduled ancient monument.
descriptions.92d26614-c2fb-4b94-9342-99a5bd2407ab: Triangular multivallate fort in the suburbs of Cardiff, built on a previously occupied Neolithic site. At over 13 hectares, it ranks as the largest hilltop fortress in the south of the country.
descriptions.2851ba0a-1403-47b9-a605-deb3735046ca: Small fort of unknown date at 413 metres on the slopes of Tal-y-Fan in Conwy County, never excavated. The name means "Small Fort" -- beyond position and outline, little is recorded.
descriptions.84ec7925-84a6-434c-847f-bf3bf9294cff: Circular stone inner wall 3.6 metres thick enclosing a 61-metre space near Sancreed on the Penwith peninsula. The summit commands a 360-degree panorama of the southern Cornish coast.
descriptions.1baa447b-94b2-4081-9a54-f699005efcc5: Named for the chieftain Caradoc who led resistance against Rome. Two separate Shropshire hillforts bear his name -- historians have never agreed which was the site of his final stand.
descriptions.5b103764-5dfc-42b8-8d6b-6617495f7230: Second hilltop fort near Clun named after Caradoc, 26 km from its namesake near Church Stretton. Both contend for the title of the chieftain's last stand against Roman conquest.
descriptions.5e5354ff-e651-496a-a9bb-cf779d3cc501: Early hillfort north of Corwen with a large stone rampart, a guard chamber in the north-east entrance, and a deep defensive ditch. The westward and northward entrances remain visible.
descriptions.c10a35c7-ca6a-49ad-b620-7467aaca6b61: Narrow ridge fort at 365 metres in Gwynedd, elongated to 216 metres along its spine with steep slopes on every side. Natural terrain largely eliminated the need for elaborate artificial defences.
descriptions.2a87862a-98dc-4cbd-8d8e-89f7c1368e63: A Roman and medieval site with a double row of pentangular banks and marshy ditches. Based on similar sites, it may date to the 2nd century BC.
descriptions.81a36a2c-1d00-4f39-b7bb-951fb3c2ed5b: A hilltop with an ancient earthwork enclosure of undetermined age. Traces of a 1st-century AD Roman fort lie below the hill, adding another layer to the site.
descriptions.5d5061d0-c447-4438-a520-b40c7a04f657: Fort on the summit of Holyhead Mountain in Anglesey overlooking the Irish Sea. The exposed rocky position suits a watchtower; some researchers link it to a Roman-era signal station.
descriptions.ce7db300-8777-425d-917a-2f6d9f325b58: Roman city at the base of Mount Hermon, built around 20 BC near a cave venerated as the birthplace of the god Pan. The site is also one of the four headwater sources of the Jordan River.
descriptions.6799d014-2963-4be7-954d-6a50ebbdcbc4: Circular 7-hectare fort dated 500-300 BC within Windsor Forest. The ditch reaches 4 metres deep with an internal rampart 2 metres high -- well-preserved beneath dense woodland.
descriptions.210925a1-b043-4a19-80c5-7ec9ade6d940: A multivallate hillfort with multiple defensive rings on an irregular promontory. The entrance gap on the east side may be the original Iron Age way in.
descriptions.9cd5b89c-3734-4dc0-9181-a23eaaffac23: Palatial Maya hilltop complex near San Ignacio, inhabited from 1200 BC. 34 structures including pyramids and plazas span from the Preclassic through the Terminal Classic -- over 2,000 years of use.
descriptions.8fed20ca-19ed-4876-b286-0fb23e0fbc90: The largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, with 120 earthen mounds across 6 square miles. Monks Mound, at 30 metres high, is the largest earthwork in the Americas.
descriptions.9da5ad49-9327-44f5-bcbf-80deb823aabd: Medieval city in a meander of the Lot River with Roman walls, a Romanesque cathedral, and the Valentre bridge -- a 14th-century fortified World Heritage structure with three intact towers.
descriptions.c59b8485-583b-4c64-8d5b-61e046ed3437: A hilltop ritual site reused for 4,000 years, from Neolithic henges to Bronze Age burials to Iron Age rituals. In its day, it rivalled the Standing Stones of Stenness.
descriptions.ed1d1f31-ac7d-4a73-8591-8219c2417c79: Broch near Loch Alsh with walls 4.5 metres thick. Located close to the celebrated Glenelg brochs Dun Telve and Dun Troddan — a cluster of the best-preserved dry-stone towers in the Highlands.
descriptions.b2943cf3-26cd-437e-bdc6-0232105b38b6: Saxon Shore fort at Caister-on-Sea built around 200 AD — the Gariannonum of Roman records. Perimeter walls 4–5 metres thick enclosed 3.5 hectares until abandonment around 370–390 AD.
descriptions.f1c3510d-e477-440e-9755-4953f31da767: A Neolithic dolmen whose name means "Roland's Tomb" -- legend says his horse carried his body back from battle and buried him under this stone. The tomb predates the myth.
descriptions.bc28c81f-db22-46a5-bc4e-18cb8c2ecbec: Vast Maya lowland city that rivalled Tikal as a regional superpower during the Classic period. Soft limestone construction spans a site with evidence from the Preclassic through Postclassic periods.
descriptions.e6e02f02-3df6-44e3-ada1-7f41b60617a5: An ancient town on the Via Appia with Samnite-era tuff walls and a pre-Roman necropolis. Shaft tombs lined with stone slabs descend into the ground.
descriptions.fe7d7ee7-ca93-4cf5-93d8-0cc80564ccd8: Roman town at Tadcaster named Calcaria -- Latin for "lime kilns" -- reflecting the Magnesian Limestone quarried here. A river crossing waystation on a key road through Roman Britannia.
descriptions.1e9f3df5-ebe4-465a-8b98-28772e417358: An Aurunci city captured by Rome in 335 BC, which then became a key Roman base in southern campaigns. After 335, Cales minted its own silver and bronze coins.
descriptions.4fb5bdfa-4ff6-4897-a54c-7533e2bd2308: An Iron Age oppidum that became the walled Roman town of Calleva Atrebatum. The capital of the Atrebates tribe sits at a major crossroads of southern Roman roads.
descriptions.83cbd9c5-1962-4f95-8f49-eeb525af234f: The twelfth fort on Hadrian's Wall, guarding an important approach from the Bewcastle area. It sat on a high bluff commanding the Cambeck Valley.
descriptions.995d7504-5526-4e4e-96d5-a03ba4470425: Ancient city on three levels: hilltop acropolis with a temple, a covered 6th-century BC reservoir, and a stoa built directly over it -- water engineering and worship layered on one ridge.
descriptions.38a93ff8-af94-41d3-bc8a-7a60e529440a: A Roman road from Colchester to Silchester via St Albans, connecting three major towns. It crossed the Thames by bridge near Cookham.
descriptions.d49017eb-8e45-45af-a6d4-f90f3d35f3e3: The first capital of Roman Britain, originally a Celtic tribal stronghold named for the war god Camulos. A legionary fortress became a colonia, then was sacked by Boudica in 60 AD.
descriptions.bf81babd-58bf-4bac-b5e9-fac36c10c95c: A pyramid with a circular base aligned to the spring and fall equinoxes. Built by the Otomi people between the 6th and 9th centuries AD.
descriptions.5b879809-9fb8-4e48-bd31-dbdff455de20: The best-preserved Tartessian site, dating to at least the 6th century BC. The building was expanded and finally deliberately burned, sealing its contents in ash.
descriptions.49b5ec85-112e-4ba8-a8c7-62cf48f745ae: Maya city at its 7th-century peak, whose palace contains hundreds of rooms with 6-metre arched ceilings. Wealth came from jade trade, not conquest -- rulers grew rich without warfare.
descriptions.f3470fb3-320f-4660-b9e0-ed338741f464: The site of Hannibal's greatest victory: in 216 BC he encircled and destroyed a Roman army of 80,000. The battle remains a textbook example of double envelopment.
descriptions.6a199307-b761-4214-82da-2dbd4c89832c: A Bronze and Iron Age hillfort that is roughly square with a single rampart enclosing 5 hectares. Cliff erosion on the north side has eaten into the defences.
descriptions.ae05ab0c-a8a4-44e2-86db-92801a7da5a3: Large settlement in Catalonia occupied from the 6th century BC to 50 BC. Over six centuries, housing evolved from simple clustered dwellings into complex rectangular stone structures.
descriptions.dac7cdd2-495d-4410-b711-9d633c27c090: 1st-century BC aqueduct supplying ancient Seville from a spring near Alcala de Guadaira. Renovated by the Almohads in the 12th century, it remained operational until demolition in 1912.
descriptions.8fbbcbd3-8f18-471d-8515-0960e2e093b7: Aqueducts built by the Nazca 1,500 years ago that are still in use today. The puquio system taps underground water through spiral stone-lined shafts visible from above.
descriptions.885bbbdb-2583-4bc7-8be9-91b978cedcf3: An Aztlan-culture petroglyph panel about 4 metres long depicting fertility symbols: rain clouds, snail shells, and skulls facing east toward the dawn.
descriptions.577f2ec4-3dc0-4d10-9425-39f1cb654009: The ruins of a Roman city of Veton origin that became a municipality under Emperor Vespasian. Little survives above ground of this once-thriving town.
descriptions.28c704d5-c448-4d9a-81da-47fc3d0b7f57: A rock shelter with life-sized limestone animal sculptures from 13,000 BC. A human burial was found among the Magdalenian carvings of horses and bison.
descriptions.306dfb7e-3a81-4a74-9a84-e53e6147d58b: A Neolithic dolmen transformed into a chapel dedicated to Sao Dinis in the 17th century. The ancient stone tomb became the altar of a Christian place of worship.
descriptions.4df0cef0-d57b-417b-a0e3-c949b0811685: An ancient settlement occupied from the Chalcolithic through the Roman era. Thracian religious buildings from the 6th-5th century BC preceded 2nd-3rd century Roman ruins.
descriptions.1c0b4493-7302-4c4b-a126-a91e9b27305e: Double-ditched hilltop fort above the River Wye in Herefordshire, enclosing 4 hectares. The name derives from Celtic words meaning "lookout" and "flat-topped ridge."
descriptions.9c128b05-d7c1-45f8-873d-bc5f96d04751: Talayotic settlement on Mallorca, 12 km from Llucmajor, with stone towers and a layout unique to the Balearic Islands. Among the most extensively excavated sites of this type in the archipelago.
descriptions.5639ccb8-8d69-4268-b4f1-5d52245214da: A historical region of deep valleys and rock formations carved into homes, chapels, and entire underground cities. Derinkuyu alone could shelter 20,000 people.
descriptions.d40299c9-9bec-4a9c-b737-819cfbe769f7: An Iron Age enclosure on a hilltop 185 m above Devon's coast. Flint tools and a carved stone face found here point to Neolithic activity at this overlook site some 4,000 years before the hillfort.
descriptions.c65a0d07-5679-41e8-9049-df5b74c8e6a8: Major Classic-period Maya centre and regional political hub in the lowlands. Monumental architecture was constructed from the 2nd through 9th centuries AD across a densely occupied landscape.
descriptions.3807e5f9-2923-473d-930a-cc11b2b1138d: A prehistoric monument of 223 standing stones, menhirs, and burial cists in the Syunik highlands. Often called a local "Stonehenge" for its scale and mystery.
descriptions.ac5771c5-ceb8-4605-bbce-3c613919d2c8: The oldest city in the Americas, dating to 3000 BC -- contemporaneous with ancient Egypt's pyramids. No weapons or fortifications have been found, suggesting a peaceful society.
descriptions.d8f00889-db62-46af-a113-5365b4cdadba: Roman milefortlets extending Hadrian's Wall defences along the Cumbrian coast. These small fortifications guarded the shore beyond where the Wall itself ended.
descriptions.a4955f7b-3996-4477-9540-891364da6c71: A 137-km Roman-era ditch running along the western Fens edge. Whether it functioned as a canal, a drainage channel, or a territorial boundary remains actively debated among archaeologists.
descriptions.c52fd25f-8ddf-4d21-a875-f5602d15b623: An ancient ridgetop observatory dating to 200 BC with an astronomical structure 34 metres long. The drystone buildings include a priest's dwelling and ceremonial platform.
descriptions.241df2d5-69c9-47e0-9df3-105a26a4d141: A rocky promontory defended by vertical cliffs on all sides but one, where a massive prehistoric embankment blocks the approach. Its exact date and purpose remain unknown.
descriptions.56ba3b1c-2d33-465b-b4d0-85fb987fbdc2: Originally a Tartessian-Turdetani settlement, later Phoenician, Carthaginian, and Roman. The Necropolis contains hundreds of tombs spanning nearly a millennium.
descriptions.b539ba9e-5d7e-4ce8-a9ff-943ac3247297: Over 3,000 standing stones hewn from local granite -- the largest such collection in the world. Erected by pre-Celtic people, their purpose remains one of archaeology's mysteries.
descriptions.33f2b3eb-5fe2-444d-8168-807b81e17f2b: Neolithic tor enclosure at Redruth occupied 3700-3400 BC, with stone walls and an earth bank securing the summit. Evidence of organised violence makes it among the earliest fortified sites known.
descriptions.14737fca-a885-4a87-aece-42a835e94beb: A Neolithic or Bronze Age cairn on a summit in the Carneddau mountains of Snowdonia. The cairn sits on the final top of a long northern mountain spur.
descriptions.c7994816-1b61-4c2b-a82b-513380825948: An Iron Age village with a fogou (underground passage) whose function is still debated. Stone huts replaced timber ones around 200 BC and remained in use for centuries.
descriptions.37065cce-99dd-4055-bd92-4906840149e6: A hill covered in megaliths, including a stone circle, with local legend of a Devil-presided wrestling match. Two miners allegedly saw the spectacle and prayed it away.
descriptions.dea9db29-e9cc-4ebc-b01b-e6f3028fbd4f: Broch on the eastern shore near Golspie in Sutherland, visible beside the A9 road. The entrance passage leads to a guard cell; stairway remains survive within the wall thickness.
descriptions.58e730c7-6ec4-44a4-97e8-d2f75d9a1c9e: Rock outcrops of spotted dolerite -- the same stone type as the bluestones at Stonehenge, 250 km away. Whether the stones were quarried here or carried by glaciers is debated.
descriptions.1531d4a1-bb24-4727-9b25-f2089088acaf: A Roman legionary fortress and Pannonian fleet headquarters from 50 AD, later capital of a province. It lies halfway between modern Vienna and Bratislava on the Danube.
descriptions.0ecacadb-c9da-490b-95ef-4b220c386d3d: A 4th-century Roman villa with three main buildings and a mill, set beside the River Guadarrama. It lies near a Roman road in the hinterland of ancient Toledo.
descriptions.3c579791-33d8-46bd-90da-1551035cc419: Auxiliary fort on Hadrian Wall called Brocolitia -- a Celtic place-name likely meaning "badger holes." Outside the fort walls stood a well-preserved temple to the god Mithras.
descriptions.eecda91b-c255-4362-a7ed-1beac2c13869: A 5,000-year-old Neolithic dolmen with a 4-metre capstone resting on smaller stones. It was originally earth-covered, but time has stripped the mound away.
descriptions.2adae6b7-2156-4080-aaa0-921dd7f8a9c9: A 5,000-year-old dolmen where legend says Saint Samson placed the capstone with his little finger. The 4.7-metre capstone rests on three of its six remaining supports.
descriptions.b97f1e4c-09df-4190-aed5-22bfeb4a45cc: 16-stone axial circle 8 metres in diameter, two stone rows, and a relocated ogham stone -- the full megalithic repertoire on a single County Cork site. The central slab may have served as an altar.
descriptions.ed3e4264-7d20-4bbc-ba73-2d11563f2006: Oval hillfort crowning a Lake District summit at 690 metres, where only wall foundations survive. The fort was destroyed during the Roman conquest, and the ruins were left exposed.
