descriptions.b06e5cec-35e1-409c-aff9-ed4bfcd30556: At the height of Dilmun civilization between 3200 and 330 BC, an estimated 100,000 burial mounds covered this island — among the densest concentrations of funerary monuments on Earth.
descriptions.eb482c92-0104-4243-8ae6-0316f0bdec37: Settled from around 5000 BC, this Thessaly site has both Neolithic and Mycenaean layers. Symbols on a tablet dated to 5260 BC rank among the oldest candidate writing marks found in Europe.
descriptions.a38ebb14-4f7b-459e-9ca4-0cbc15d16a32: A rocky hillock near Beddgelert, rising 76 meters above the Glaslyn valley, with stone ramparts from an 800 BC fort. Arthurian legend places Merlin here and two battling dragons beneath its pool.
descriptions.057ed947-18f5-45f5-b4c6-6bc1e29264d7: About 337 meters long and 160 meters wide, this Herefordshire fort overlooks the confluence of the Wye and Lugg rivers from a spur of Dinedor Hill. Its out-turned east entrance is still visible.
descriptions.62a60a9e-24f1-40ac-a678-a7c0a6d91ce1: A late Iron Age village with Roman pot sherds repaired with iron clamps — people mended pots rather than replace them. Bones were made into tools and instruments.
descriptions.253204e7-0000-4ca2-aa8b-80d9b51c0685: Ancient Roman ruins behind enormous walls that still stand near their original height. The town has been continuously inhabited since 6000 BC.
descriptions.4e78a6c5-1811-46d3-8e62-8c613ec3afbe: A 4th-century retirement palace for Emperor Diocletian that now forms half of a living city. Apartments, shops, and cafes fill rooms the emperor once walked.
descriptions.9f746d42-3cd0-4dfa-a05d-096a6bb8afd6: This 7th-century BC paved trackway at Corinth hauled boats overland across the isthmus, bypassing the Peloponnese. Aristophanes coined "fast as a Corinthian" because of it.
descriptions.3580059c-c673-4cc3-823e-8c43982d1597: A sacred city at the foot of Mount Olympus, home to the great Macedonian sanctuary of Zeus. Alexander the Great offered sacrifices here before heading east.
descriptions.a52e274f-3e08-44b5-a03f-1d564fede9a2: The monumental main gate of Classical Athens, built in 478 BC. The Great Panathenaea procession — the city's most important festival — began here.
descriptions.b11e591e-1f4c-4850-a7af-b5a13bc499cc: A Neolithic lakeshore settlement on an artificial island, 5600–5000 BC. A wooden tablet found here bears symbols that may predate all known writing systems.
descriptions.a5232aa9-627c-444a-8ac7-82c5b79c3f2d: Ancient Roman ruins adapted to a mountain setting: a theatre, two forums, and temples. The paved Harsh forum square is entered through a monumental arch.
descriptions.5d97461b-02b7-4227-8918-bc6c80a531ac: Hominin remains dating to 1.8 million years ago make this the earliest known evidence of human ancestors outside Africa. Five skulls found here show surprising anatomical variety.
descriptions.01704ebd-c0b1-4c2b-bdd0-7ffb3b6b4370: At 15 meters tall, this is the largest tumulus on Rügen — the biggest of all prehistoric mounds on that island. Legend says a giant dropped a load of earth while trying to fill a nearby ford.
descriptions.97a2bde9-0352-465a-94ca-745bcec77e7d: A Cucuteni-Trypillian settlement from the 4th millennium BC covering 2.5 square kilometers near Uman. Aerial photography revealed city blocks and streets; peak population estimated at 16,200.
descriptions.d24b6616-bd08-4edc-b385-cd5200383e9b: A Roman road named after a 15th-century doctor — "gate" comes from the Scandinavian word for road. It connected two forts across the Peak District.
descriptions.3ca796ab-fbcc-4d93-9991-e17bcb558587: At 114 meters, Dodman Point is the highest headland on the south Cornwall coast. A granite cross erected in 1896 for navigators and Christian service sits atop the ancient promontory earthworks.
descriptions.5a04d6f3-c82d-4c82-b1e9-3d70bff135ae: At this oracle, priests interpreted Zeus by listening to a sacred oak tree. Herodotus traced it to the 2nd millennium BC — making it the oldest Hellenic oracle, second in prestige only to Delphi.
descriptions.ee6608f3-f192-4c43-ab41-1f7ad3c9507d: A 12-meter shaft cave with finds from Roman to early medieval periods. Human and animal remains accumulated in its depths over centuries.
descriptions.1b48aaf6-bd3f-4ec5-81d3-8e308de6e308: This 3500–2800 BC dolmen was destroyed in the 17th or 18th century, its stones scattered across fields. Moved 500 meters south and reconstructed in 1977 in its current location near Bergen.
descriptions.d760f193-0c0a-46fe-9af2-517846bf9171: Romans extracted gold here from the 1st to 3rd century AD using hushing — releasing stored water to strip hillsides — and purpose-built aqueducts. The only gold mines outside the Dolgellau gold-belt.
descriptions.37d877c3-c4ce-4c4d-8326-1e249306a0b2: Set on a hilltop with the River Culm curving around a flat northern promontory, this Devon fort had water on three sides forming a natural moat. The hill rises to 128 meters at its peak.
descriptions.d54c4f7c-3a1c-4797-a850-c3ca8e716541: A 90-hectare site spanning the Bronze Age to the 5th century AD. Its limestone ridge was a natural fortress for over 1,500 years of continuous use.
descriptions.dfe76079-9794-4c48-beef-d80ad9728849: A small stone circle with cairns spanning 3300–900 BC. Part of a tradition of stone circle construction spread across Britain, Ireland, and Brittany.
descriptions.27452e11-1d7b-44cd-85fe-d6893f11baa8: A Neolithic dolmen converted into a Christian chapel — a prehistoric tomb repurposed for worship. Two religions share one structure across 5,000 years.
descriptions.bb9dc8f4-100f-4159-99e6-e44c79bc8e57: Eight granite slabs form a polygonal chamber capped by a 4.5 x 3.5 m slab. One of the oldest and largest dolmens in Galicia, it still retains two stones of the original entrance corridor.
descriptions.0b994bf5-92ed-4592-a7f7-1a3d343cefd6: Built around 3000 BC near Saumur, this dolmen is the tallest and most voluminous of its country's 4,500 examples. No other dolmen in the region matches it in height or volume.
descriptions.4200b0d7-2aae-4e07-acf3-a342b0c468ac: A 4th-millennium BC passage tomb in a province holding roughly 200 megalithic monuments — among the densest concentrations of passage tombs anywhere in the western peninsula.
descriptions.8627799e-bfb9-4667-bbc6-d30ebdd99703: A 43-meter passage grave ending in a small chamber roofed with a single slab. The corridor narrows steadily — you enter standing and finish crouching.
descriptions.1758f6e8-4518-43fb-a14a-1ce52caca683: Built in the late 4th or early 3rd millennium BC near the Dolmen de Menga, this passage tomb was constructed by the same community that raised its larger neighbour just 70 metres away.
descriptions.485c3c0c-31f0-45a7-a06b-797c4c021466: Dating from 3750–3650 BC, this megalithic tumulus near Antequera was built with 32 stones — the largest weighing about 180 tonnes — moved without wheels or metal tools.
descriptions.f9385d18-0ee4-4c3a-a5a4-1855be105f86: A 20-meter V-shaped passage grave with decorated slabs. One of around 200 Neolithic burial sites in its province, it sits under a 75-meter mound.
descriptions.3f512971-679b-4f40-8f5e-1467424ce605: A dolmen near the Dolmen de Menga, built in the same era. Stone slabs form a narrow corridor tomb contrasting with Menga's massive open chamber.
descriptions.ff70aa7e-7371-4ffd-b673-175fd0c56ab4: A dolmen with three orthostats capped by a large slab at 1,020 meters altitude. At 3000 BC, Neolithic people hauled megaliths to mountaintop burial sites.
descriptions.1ff140bb-47dc-44c9-93bb-c47dda258591: Built around 2900 BC near Guarda, this dolmen stands in a rural landscape on the western bank of the Ribeira do Carapito. It formed part of a cluster of three dolmens in the same area.
descriptions.6f1d245f-a27d-479a-b2cc-8c9c0c85ec5f: A megalithic tomb from 4000–3000 BC with upright megaliths supporting a massive capstone. The classic dolmen form found across the Mediterranean.
descriptions.0c055192-decb-4a45-a0a6-19726d9f8477: Constructed between 3000 and 2500 BC in the Mangualde valley, this dolmen was later identified as a Beaker monument — reused by successive generations as a communal burial over centuries.
descriptions.adaf3933-e799-422f-92a4-29462e57df50: Built from around 150 granite orthostats in the Valdecañas reservoir near Peraleda de la Mata, this megalithic circle sits underwater most of the year — only emerging during severe droughts.
descriptions.ab03fa75-bbdc-46a2-ba55-25e2f5edd5c4: 32 megaliths form a chamber 27.5 meters long and 3.5 meters high near Antequera, dating from 3750–3650 BC. The heaviest stone weighs 180 tonnes — moved and raised without metal tools.
descriptions.a023ea22-2689-4ec1-9b56-6b6f7ed023b0: A Neolithic tomb with a roof supported by a 2.2-meter quartzite pillar at its center. Most dolmens rely on wall stones alone — this central column is unusual.
descriptions.b0b49640-6fb4-4cb1-b875-01dc81298e34: Over 200 dolmens on one island, from 4000–3000 BC. Each consists of uprights supporting a capstone — simple but enduring monuments to the Neolithic dead.
descriptions.8230ee02-ce60-4b34-b0cd-3beca70274fb: The only oval stone circle of its type in the country, dated to the 8th–6th century BC. Rough-hewn volcanic blocks form a unique outlier with no parallels among known local monuments.
descriptions.b18df6d2-0093-4398-9f14-01360c5dad48: A 4th-century AD fortified hilltop between two river gorges. Fortifications take advantage of the natural defense where the rivers converge.
descriptions.2e46252e-2205-4aed-92ee-38eeb5758399: Pottery from around 6000 BC found in this karst cave places it at the edge of the region's earliest occupation. Underground, it links to the Baradla cave system across the border into Hungary.
descriptions.0784c790-17b2-4450-9a95-286c1d9ef2f2: Pre-Nuragic rock-cut tombs called "Houses of the Fairies," carved 3400–2700 BC. Their interiors mimic actual houses, complete with doors and carved hearths.
descriptions.b672af27-ee37-4815-bd7c-f1a5e09f2413: A 3rd-century AD Roman house with lavish mosaic floors, built after Goths wrecked the city in 250 AD. The mosaics were a statement of defiant reconstruction.
descriptions.70a0244e-de85-46e2-9515-c7ca202868b9: A 1st-century BC Roman town house with mosaic floors. An 11th-century Muslim cemetery was later built directly on top of its ruins.
descriptions.b65e6760-1af4-46fd-8193-e053efd9428a: A 200-hectare tell with the most extensive Punic river port in the Mediterranean. Layers span the 3rd millennium BC through Phoenician, Punic, and Roman eras.
descriptions.f5ca382a-3725-4cbb-961a-6afbf5c21507: A Neolithic court tomb from 4000–2000 BC. Court tombs have an open courtyard of stone slabs — a gathering space for the living to honor the dead.
descriptions.a7afa2f1-87c5-4fa8-ab8f-0e86d714a8f8: A small Roman town on the Fosse Way — the largest of five defended towns on that road. It was forgotten entirely until modern archaeology revealed it.
descriptions.0a8f4bd4-8115-4b64-b20c-0014b2458106: A pair of Neolithic cursuses built end to end stretch 10 km across the chalk of Cranborne Chase — the Gussage Cursus to the south predating the Pentridge Cursus to the north. Built around 3300 BC.
descriptions.84d9c1fb-6f17-4a2e-84a5-5cb05ed6adf2: Twelve km south of Jubail, this site yielded the earliest Ubaid-style pottery in the region, dated to the late 6th–early 5th millennium BC. It links Gulf coast communities to Mesopotamian trade.
descriptions.18f993a6-2922-432f-b795-4ef914cffcd4: A Maya city founded in 629 AD by Tikal's dynasty to control trade routes. By 648 AD it betrayed Tikal and allied with the rival superpower Calakmul.
descriptions.e8d4bfaa-7f9f-440a-9fc9-7e5bb12f5e6e: A Roman-era sand quarry that became an archaeological site. Pottery and a Roman well reveal a substantial settlement nobody expected to find in a sand pit.
descriptions.867e1487-3a96-4974-ae74-eaf5448927b9: Spanning Numidian, Punic, and Roman occupation from the 5th century BC, this hillside holds a 3,500-seat theatre, a Saturn temple, and a Byzantine fort built from salvaged Roman masonry.
descriptions.6290ca43-4ceb-458c-a59c-cbe0053be3c1: At 340 meters on an eastern Quantock spur, this fort and its associated round barrow overlook the Bristol Channel. Both are on the Heritage at Risk Register due to vehicle damage and erosion.
descriptions.d74c1ef8-f9bc-4feb-8f8f-4aab984e4602: The third major tomb of Brú na Bóinne alongside Newgrange and Knowth, this passage tomb from around 3200 BC was stripped and left largely as a ruin. Its cairn is 85 meters across and 15 meters high.
descriptions.aaf549ca-d5c7-47da-a42a-76d0806d21e9: A 542-meter cave packed with cave bear fossils from 65,000–31,000 years ago. Medieval people mistook the massive bones for dragon remains — hence the name.
descriptions.2f93c277-9023-4fbd-9b56-dc2c4f18c1f6: A natural chalk hill with a bare patch where legend says Saint George killed the dragon. No grass grows on that spot — supposedly poisoned by the dragon's blood.
descriptions.f70384d7-00ec-45ba-b086-bf1aba816f84: A post-Minoan city near Neapoli that flourished in the 8th–6th century BC. Its stone walls bear the oldest known inscribed legal code — predating all classical-era law codes.
descriptions.c82e8c63-783d-4d7b-aead-69052b6a04a2: Three Bronze Age stone rows on Dartmoor, each ending with a menhir. The tallest reaches 4.3 meters — the largest standing stone on all of Dartmoor.
descriptions.e3243ed6-c53d-465c-83f4-e33f68b7510b: A small axial stone circle also known as "The Druid's Altar." Seventeen sandstone uprights originally formed a tight ring, of which 13 survive.
descriptions.aaeff3cd-427c-4c89-83d6-c884495c0380: A stone circle built around 2000 BC with an adjacent cairn and alignment. The full complex was designed as a unified ceremonial site, not added piecemeal.
descriptions.f9d17ed5-eb41-4332-a2c1-42d7d9b57a56: A nearly 20-meter Roman monument originally clad in marble, erected in 9 BC for the general Drusus. Roman troops built it as a cenotaph after his sudden death.
descriptions.03a7a357-12a8-40f9-ae6a-9cef78135fd3: A Roman port at the closest point to continental Europe. It grew into the gateway between Britain and Gaul — an essential cross-channel hub.
descriptions.b07c4d65-158e-4e9d-9817-f39161b7516d: Five weathered stones deeply grooved by millennia of rain. Originally seven, two sockets were found empty in the 1890s — the missing stones never recovered.
descriptions.90a0c184-5830-45a7-a5ab-f82191dc0c23: A chain of Iron Age earthworks stretching across Dorset. Each fort guarded a section of the landscape in what appears to be a coordinated defensive line.
descriptions.d13b661b-37ac-4ccb-bc4e-83b0bdd1da9c: Dating to roughly 3300 BC, this Great Wold Valley barrow is the largest round barrow in Britain — the dominant mound among four known as the Great Barrows of East Yorkshire.
descriptions.b8f4c5f4-c567-4605-9f3d-9475d2db6362: A burial site where a rectangular stone coffin was found during Japanese-era rule. Giant stone piles and artifacts date to the 2nd millennium BC.
descriptions.4a42b149-b113-4896-a907-24b21f8b36ec: Eight bright white quartzite stones set in an oval, the largest over 12 tons. The striking white stone makes this circle visible from a great distance.
descriptions.f54b9147-3f56-4070-9ad5-365b19e3b4f3: An ancient oasis city whose Akkadian name was Adummatu. Its ruins sit within an oasis that has sustained settlement since at least the 10th century BC.
descriptions.08886555-0ddd-40e1-bfe7-0322a41079ea: A 5-metre stone-and-mud wall surrounding the ancient oasis city, dated to the early centuries AD. It still traces the perimeter of the old settlement in the Al-Jawf province.
descriptions.24672b8a-ed91-4729-b39f-52220f827cd2: Perched 250 metres above the River Otter, this National Trust hillfort is crowned by a distinctive clump of beech trees visible for miles. Its earthworks rival those of nearby Hembury Fort.
descriptions.8d5976d1-7cf9-4f7c-aeac-f47bacd89805: A rare D-shaped "semi-broch" from 115 BC — a hybrid between a dun and a broch found almost nowhere else. Its unusual shape still puzzles archaeologists.
descriptions.1877a303-0731-4ad3-9814-2b852ff93242: An Iron Age drystone tower with 4-metre-thick walls and no mortar. Brochs like this are unique to the Highlands — over 500 were built, but none exist anywhere else on Earth.
descriptions.1db1cb71-0431-46ec-ab93-39338844dbab: This drystone broch on the Isle of Lewis still reaches 9 metres on its east side. Occupation raised the floor level so high over time that the building eventually fell out of use.
descriptions.c70dabb7-6915-4def-961f-14f0f7d8e30b: A 5-hectare Iron Age hillfort guarded by a single earthen bank. A Bronze Age barrow nearby was later reshaped into a Norman beacon mound.
descriptions.9cf1ec14-dd93-4270-897f-158203e91758: Its drystone walls rise to nearly 7 metres above the doorway, crowned by a massive triangular lintel stone. External diameter: 14.5 metres, built entirely without mortar from local Sutherland stone.
descriptions.b4666064-903d-4db2-a282-38897ac4c1a1: A 2nd-century AD broch with an internal diameter of nearly 10 metres and walls over 3.5 metres thick. A guard cell is built into the wall beside the entrance.
descriptions.bdba33af-64d6-4a74-90f3-4ecf9e512c83: A D-shaped semi-broch sharing a valley with two full brochs, Dun Telve and Dun Troddan. Its half-circular design suggests a transitional building form between duns and brochs.
descriptions.9fe61c60-5565-4dfd-99c8-3b51f0396dfd: A sprawling Aksumite mansion from the 4th–6th century with evidence of a hypocaust heating system. Locals call it the Palace of the Queen of Sheba.
descriptions.34c9266e-b55c-4f29-9e6e-eeb547ecfd50: 17.4 metres across externally, 10.5 metres internally — walls still standing over 2 metres around most of the circumference. A scarcement ledge inside once supported an upper timber floor.
descriptions.5d3974ac-5df3-4f32-9d62-634921bdaf5d: Bronze Age burial cairns placed at the highest point on Exmoor, 519 metres up. The builders carried stones to the summit to mark their dead at the peak of the landscape.
descriptions.c1fce6e2-c6ef-4f9b-89c5-41809188c6ea: A 1st-century AD broch on Tiree with walls 4.5 metres thick — nearly half the building's total diameter. Occupation debris spans centuries of continuous use.
descriptions.379931c0-89c4-4e2a-9c73-ec2472542070: Later fortified in the Middle Ages as Clan MacKinnon's seat for several centuries, this Strathaird hillfort dates originally to around the 1st century AD.
descriptions.52258395-f830-4181-bccb-8d5e37d2e440: Still standing over 10 metres tall, this 18.3-metre-diameter broch has a hollow double wall with an internal staircase. Companion broch Dun Troddan stands 500 metres away in Gleann Beag.
descriptions.3d4fbf16-e80f-42c3-853c-4a22206dee24: Rising 7.5 metres from a rock platform in Gleann Beag, this broch retains its scarcement ledge and a staircase between hollow double walls. Companion broch Dun Telve stands 500 metres northwest.
descriptions.9ca635c0-2df8-4a4a-ba1e-815f1fd7796b: An oval-shaped broch from 150 BC that originally stood on a freshwater lake island. Walls survive 4.5 metres high, and the sea now laps at its foundations.
descriptions.50ff0925-cbf5-482a-ae11-524226477cc7: A single rampart crowns a sandy hill at 93 metres — no ditch was ever dug, and the earthwork appears to have been abandoned mid-construction. What threat it was meant to counter remains unknown.
descriptions.8a8f5011-1b32-4b49-b7bd-afd2a0ca81f5: Settlement on this lake island began around 5000 BC and continued for thousands of years. Stone-built architectural complexes here rank among the earliest known in Europe.
descriptions.269e2820-acf1-4974-b75f-3c0460482ade: A 3rd-millennium BC temple with architecture unlike anything in Mesopotamia or the Indus Valley. Nobody knows which god it served — the dedication remains a mystery.
descriptions.337335d1-0648-4be3-8c44-97958477f6a9: A 14th-century BC ziggurat devoted to the Babylonian god Enlil, built by King Kurigalzu I. Its mudbrick core still rises above the flat Mesopotamian plain after 3,400 years.
descriptions.f0531983-dafb-4e80-8465-89bdc6860d27: A Roman town founded around 70 AD that grew into the capital of the Durotriges tribe. It featured a 4th-century town house with elaborate mosaics still visible today.
descriptions.27226cef-1c90-46cc-ac31-6b568c7f6c8a: A 32,000-square-metre Iron Age settlement dating to 100 BC — 70 years older than Roman Silchester. It may be the first planned town in Britain.
descriptions.ecc0e85d-51c0-47a0-a63f-a427b1f94b01: A Roman city that became the tribal capital of the Cantiaci and featured a large religious precinct. It eventually grew into modern Canterbury.
descriptions.7ec11470-fc03-404c-a2bc-db2f6507bb4a: Founded by Greek colonists from Corinth in the 7th century BC and later known as Dyrrachium. It served as the starting point of the Via Egnatia to Byzantium.
descriptions.89bb7456-d47b-4771-8d89-a14827233844: A massive Neolithic henge from 2500 BC, 3 km from Stonehenge — the second-largest such enclosure in Britain. Thousands of pig bones suggest enormous seasonal feasts.
descriptions.cc8c8638-cb77-4b61-a248-5c0f8e19cb66: An Assyrian capital with 24-metre-thick city walls, abandoned after King Sargon II died in battle. The entire city was built from scratch and deserted within a generation.
descriptions.6fbb5965-dc39-45db-8f09-3c0f24a8b487: A Neolithic tomb carved from a single massive sandstone boulder — the only rock-cut tomb in Britain. A huge stone block once sealed the entrance from inside.
descriptions.86c101ad-fcdb-413a-8aec-6aad2d1574e7: A fortified Cimmerian port city from the Bilozerka culture, 1250–925 BC. Ongoing excavations in the Mykolaiv park district continue to reveal its Late Bronze Age layout.
descriptions.cb0a55c2-48c5-4340-afb2-a5c0d5eec70b: A 1st–3rd century town of ancient Iberia with four palaces and Roman-style hypocaust baths. Its floor mosaics rank among the finest in the Caucasus.
descriptions.184adda6-1c21-4798-aa04-7c35670a2588: A major Maya city with temples named for their carvings: the Temple of the Captives, the Temple of the Owl. Its Peten-style architecture links it to Guatemala's lowlands.
descriptions.5cb68be0-593f-4b27-97f7-417a9314ef27: A Maya city occupied for thousands of years, famous for the Temple of the Seven Dolls. On each equinox, the sun rises directly through the temple's central doorway.
descriptions.cdd96b01-efff-4896-acca-a97484a9f87c: The Corieltauvi tribe — migrants from mainland Europe — built the Salt Road below Shilton Hill to move salt across Leicestershire, then settled the hill above it.
descriptions.c070b6b0-3fd2-4d6c-acbe-105539188253: Homo heidelbergensis fossils 500,000 years old make this the oldest human-remains site in the country. Butchered animal bones here are among the earliest proof of hunting by early humans in Europe.
descriptions.70947922-0b34-4e73-b6b0-8a13f2ff3806: A 3.5-kilometre earthen wall from the 1st century BC along the Han River, oval in plan and leaning east. Researchers identify it as Wiryeseong, the fortified early capital of the Baekje kingdom.
descriptions.5f8ce412-3bb0-4aa3-aff3-cd1d825273a6: Crude stone walls built without mortar stretching across hills for hundreds of metres. Nobody knows who built them or why — their origin remains one of the region's oldest mysteries.
descriptions.baf13030-1578-4edc-a351-ca627828a326: Nearly 1,000 monumental stone statues carved by the Rapa Nui people, some weighing over 80 tonnes. They were walked upright across the island using ropes and rocking motion.
descriptions.1ddc9784-b651-43df-84b7-0900f2bb67c5: A Bronze Age funerary naveta built with Cyclopean masonry — massive stones fitted without mortar. Navetas held collective burials and are unique to Menorca.
descriptions.d55baca6-8a56-4a3b-8323-f5399e331666: A 2nd-century AD gate on the main road to Byzantium, completely rebuilt in the 4th century with twin towers. The gate complex grew into a fortified quarter of its own.
descriptions.1cce02f8-8133-4c7a-aa65-b770587bc389: A univallate Iron Age hillfort enclosure on Exmoor, 1.8 km from Minehead. Later reoccupied as a medieval farmstead, the single rampart is its only surviving defensive feature.
descriptions.d9dc6883-3762-4abc-9dca-736e3292f527: A Neolithic settlement from 4500 BC in a valley of immense historical weight. Julius Caesar, the Saxons, and the Normans all made landfall near this same spot.
descriptions.19df2778-fb6e-4298-be94-c98d979a5f9a: The largest Roman town in northern Britain and a provincial capital. Two emperors died here: Septimius Severus in 211 AD and Constantius Chlorus in 306 AD.
descriptions.398c3ef8-56c3-4640-a28a-ebaa8a36df33: A downland spur in Wiltshire holds an enclosed Iron Age settlement and field system; the outer enclosure measures 700 by 400 metres. Roman-era layers sit above, preserving two superimposed cultures.
descriptions.9e34acd6-6cb0-44f1-bf20-97d250838359: A 142-hectare ancient woodland hiding Bronze Age rock carvings with cup-and-ring marks. The woods were used for charcoal production for millennia.
descriptions.ba0d3686-bd38-407f-b92d-c64505ba689b: Philip II of Macedon seized this city-state on the Malian Gulf and transferred it to the Malians in 342 BC. It later fell to the Aetolian League around 235 BC before passing to Rome.
descriptions.e5efe12c-25a8-423f-8974-98fc23e299e9: A 4th-century BC covered walkway at Olympia, named for the sevenfold echo its colonnade produced. Spectators gathered here during the ancient Olympic Games.
descriptions.64403aa0-d335-4c7a-84e9-02ee76b80254: The largest and most complex Iron Age hillfort in Cheshire, expanded in the 1st century AD. The Romans slighted it, but the Saxons rebuilt it as a burh in 914 AD.
descriptions.3324d203-1f5a-4b13-b6d0-c23382ac8d3c: 28 metres across and unusually large for a southern location, this 2nd-century broch near Duns was once called "Woden's Hall." Its current name recalls the legend of Red Ettin, the three-headed giant.
descriptions.1e7621c6-9b8c-4137-add7-4813f52a1e83: A Maya city occupied from 400 BC to 1500 AD with a main temple rising 40 metres. Engineers built an intricate canal system to manage seasonal flooding.
descriptions.1b0139f7-0c1f-4e6b-b64a-a176296a8185: A 13th-century BC Hittite sacred spring shrine with carved reliefs of gods and solar discs. The monument channeled water through a central collection system.
descriptions.3debd642-ff96-4840-bff2-9d8faced25cd: A prehistoric hillfort with triple ramparts enclosing Bronze Age burial mounds inside its walls. The barrows predate the fort by centuries.
descriptions.ecea9050-b22b-475c-ad05-7f7f53d34194: A 1370 BC Bronze Age burial so well preserved it revealed a young woman's wool clothing, bronze belt disc, and a birch-bark bucket of fermented honey drink.
descriptions.945482c9-9445-4622-add2-2a6334ccbd5b: A 95-kilometre Roman aqueduct built in 80 AD, flowing entirely by gravity through underground channels. Some stretches included bridges up to 1,400 metres long.
descriptions.0ed79845-f651-4c52-85cd-7f96bab43d4e: A four-stone alignment from 1700 BC stretching east to west. Tradition holds it marks the grave of Scéine, wife of the leader of the Milesian invasion.
descriptions.09327f42-d9bb-438f-8e78-ebba2c24fa42: A sacred cave used from the Neolithic through Roman times to worship Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth. A central stalagmite resembles a standing female figure.
descriptions.d8256f75-7b93-49b5-8910-801bd1591397: A 4th-century Elder Futhark runestone stands on a grave mound above the Valdres valley, protected under glass. Nearby cairns form the broader Gardberg burial complex.
descriptions.71b04ac9-3273-4928-b38b-d830e7610755: An Iron Age ringfort rebuilt across centuries — from defensive shelter to Medieval cavalry garrison. The only one of 19 Prehistoric forts on the island to be fully excavated.
descriptions.480f44f7-ad94-4ea5-bad8-fde912fa692b: A burial ground spanning from the Stone Age to the Iron Age, with passage graves, cairns, and standing stones all on one site. Over 5,000 years of death rituals in one field.
descriptions.b6995309-c325-413b-8630-441f16d0020d: A Maya kingdom with an extraordinary tomb found in the side of the largest pyramid, its original plaster still intact. The buried king, Ukit Kan Lek Tok', ruled at the city's peak.
descriptions.0255f640-58e0-4f86-b5e7-620bae889794: A Roman town founded on a small island connected to the mainland by a narrow isthmus. Its bath floors are paved with mosaics, and a small basilica sits on a circular base.
descriptions.cfd8864a-f9c2-47e8-aab1-5dbe86522c38: The name-giving site of a Bronze Age civilization (2200–1300 BC) that spread across southeastern Iberia. El Argar people traded sophisticated ceramics across the Mediterranean.
descriptions.bf30fac5-d015-46c4-b340-74e5614ce274: An Olmec site from 1100–800 BC famous for two pairs of monumental sculptures found intact and undisturbed. Twin figures sit between crouching jaguars.
descriptions.37999fa3-d22d-4c51-a2f5-fa0dd9d82942: Part of the Cotzumalhuapa zone, occupied from around 1000 BC. A stela here bears a Long Count date from the late pre-Classic era — one of the earliest such dates outside the core Maya lowlands.
descriptions.8fe59448-2356-47b1-810a-d31c76a580e3: A Moche temple complex where the Lady of Cao was found — a tattooed female ruler buried with war clubs and gold, challenging assumptions about gender and power.
descriptions.a5e50c3b-02dc-4f60-b94f-9f7cbd2a016e: A pre-Columbian burial site from 700–1000 AD containing chiefs buried with gold breastplates and emeralds. The graves revealed a hierarchical chiefdom society.
descriptions.86d06431-4ed1-4f2f-9814-7ed808c78968: A pyramid-like Wari mausoleum discovered undisturbed in 2013 with 60 burials, including three elite women. Over 1,000 artifacts were interred with them.
descriptions.52fe4aef-2fab-4d5b-9a5c-19b7f491a7fb: A 4-hectare site inhabited since the Iron Age, with its best-known phase in Late Antiquity (5th–7th century). Finds include gold coins and Visigothic pottery.
descriptions.c1ab9ac7-d0cb-46b3-9d7c-3d6c19be5a48: Ruins of a Maya ceremonial center from 800 AD — among the oldest monuments on Cozumel. Spanish conquistadors and later American WW2 troops both damaged the site.
descriptions.9b213431-295d-4e12-abff-00a0fb676fe4: The largest Maya city in the Pasión River region, occupied from 400 BC. After centuries of decline, it was revived by outsiders who left non-Maya artistic styles on its stelae.
descriptions.58bdf3b7-f210-49b4-bc02-f060c120737a: A sacred pyramid venerated continuously from 300 BC to 1632 AD by Chupícuaro, Teotihuacanos, Toltecs, Chichimeca, Otomi, and Purépecha. Few sites were holy to so many cultures.
descriptions.c1c984e7-1391-4153-b140-f9bcd446d759: Ionian colonists settled here around 600 BC; Carthaginians and Romans followed. The Lady of Elche bust — a pre-Roman masterpiece — was found at nearby L'Alcúdia.
descriptions.939c26ea-76be-40b5-b295-770e056ec82b: Saka burial mounds from the 6th–4th century BC yielding gold harness fittings, pendants, and chains in the Scythian Animal Style. A golden trove from the steppe nomads.
descriptions.75dccc9d-fb68-40a9-aa2e-e58a47067580: Cave temples hewn from solid basalt, mostly dedicated to Shiva, with sculptures blending Hindu and Buddhist iconography. The rock-cut reliefs date from the 2nd century BC.
descriptions.1906c7eb-b1d4-40a9-b50f-b6dbfe8a5e4f: The sanctuary in Athens where the Eleusinian Mysteries began their annual procession to Eleusis. Initiates were forbidden on pain of death from revealing what they experienced.
descriptions.c1fe860b-f047-431e-8384-489fa1686f50: Home of the Eleusinian Mysteries — the ancient world's most sacred secret rites, performed for nearly 2,000 years. Revealing the rituals was punishable by death.
descriptions.882c38f5-5b59-47b8-b6df-27f6d07b7abe: A 3rd-century BC corbel arch bridge: 3.95-metre span, opening cut in unmortared limestone as an isosceles triangle 1.84 metres high. Remarkably large for a false-arch structure.
descriptions.214ae628-b465-4a07-850b-2a491f421081: A Roman village that grew around a crossroads of the highway to Tongeren. Germanic raiders ravaged it in the late 2nd century, yet settlers rebuilt and carried on.
descriptions.21db0c59-87b1-4d2f-839c-c42543bd56c0: A sandstone hilltop carved with channels, basins, and figures by three successive cultures: Chané, Inca, and Spanish. The largest carved rock in the Americas.
descriptions.62e7aef7-f914-4080-ae06-b4c347600d6d: Built entirely of stone blocks in 238 AD, this oval amphitheatre seats 35,000 — the third-largest in the Roman world. Constructed on flat ground with no earthen banking, it stands almost fully intact.
descriptions.a71d8ba8-3ca0-4845-a519-609b286b4eb3: A site spanning millennia with prehistoric settlements, 18th Dynasty rock-cut tombs, temples, and Coptic monastery walls all layered together.
descriptions.e286fd8d-fb39-4196-be34-c32545c512b0: A Maya city that peaked in the 3rd century BC with some of the largest pyramids ever built in the Maya world. It was abandoned, reoccupied, and abandoned again.
descriptions.fce614a8-8697-45d3-9574-4b092231b0bd: A cave harboring the 18,700-year-old "Red Lady" — a woman whose bones were coated in red ochre after death. She was placed beside a massive engraved stone block.
descriptions.4e2c28ed-7ff1-4e9c-9e59-e33b24783af4: A Megalithic animal sculpture from the 4th millennium BC — a verraco, a type of stone beast unique to central Iberia. Locals say it's a bear; scholars say it might be a boar.
descriptions.64d602b0-c9e8-4313-aa2b-a96ed1d7cf5f: 58 hectares in the Chillón Valley, occupied 3500–1800 BC — before pottery existed in the region. Its scale rivals Caral and Aspero as a major pre-ceramic center.
descriptions.76174b71-0f02-43bd-9655-c4a489e54aa5: A petroglyph site with at least 465 carved rocks and boulders spread across a volcanic landscape. The carvings span over a thousand years of indigenous expression.
descriptions.95c9c8c1-e8ed-43b3-a87b-b79715442dbd: The largest Maya site in the upper river valley, straddling a national border, surrounded by rare perennial streams. Named "the watering basin" for its unusual water abundance.
descriptions.61fa29b3-fa75-4a3d-8d71-983b632773fb: 47 structures on the southeast edge of Cancún, with traces of post-Classic mural paintings. Now hemmed in by resort hotels, it is the largest Maya site on the island.
descriptions.f4931c71-9e14-4bdc-ad9d-88bf763b6985: A Middle Paleolithic site where Neanderthals camped for thousands of years. In 2014, the oldest known human coprolites were found here — direct evidence of Neanderthal diet.
descriptions.a808b0ee-786e-4677-92d6-1eb5a15e297a: A 2nd-century Roman villa whose owner is known by name: Caius Valerius Avitus, a local magistrate. Its mosaics and wall paintings survived in exceptional condition.
descriptions.fbe56df2-9a50-4b70-a012-f2e666d2f2f9: A major Classic Veracruz city that flourished 600–1200 AD with temples, palaces, and at least 17 ballcourts — more than any other Mesoamerican city.
descriptions.c5761cbc-32e4-48b1-97de-a33bca256831: A 15th-century temple to Tepoztēcatl, the Aztec god of pulque — a fermented agave drink. Pilgrims traveled from as far as Guatemala to worship here.
descriptions.d76c57ad-59ef-4f80-b20f-11ee50570934: Occupied 200 BC–1531 AD, this Zacatecas hilltop city ran a pre-Columbian industrial zone producing copper and ceramics. Shaft-tomb shell beads and Teotihuacan-motif earflaps were recovered here.
descriptions.006294ae-548b-40ac-9271-03a017df7217: A sizeable Maya city from 350 BC buried in dense virgin rainforest, accessible only by mule trail. Its pyramids and causeways remain largely unexcavated.
descriptions.44def22f-dca7-4075-a555-d64821a0d882: A 7th-century Maya city whose ruler Bahlam Ajaw conquered Comalcalco in 649 AD. Its monuments bear the inscription that fueled the 2012 "end of the world" media frenzy.
descriptions.e35c15c4-4ae7-4e7a-9f7c-e46e9561d0a0: Misnamed "Barrows" — this is an unfinished hillfort enclosing 3.5 hectares, bank begun but no ditch dug. A polished stone axe reveals Neolithic activity long before the Iron Age builders.
descriptions.cd7ea2bb-47eb-4ef4-9af0-4ba7f961d861: Pausanias saw a bronze goat at Delphi dedicated by this city, shown suckling the mythical twins Phylacis and Phylander. Its harbor Syia lay 60 stadia south on Crete's coast.
descriptions.a9a3d2fe-0f58-4627-a34d-124e0190d7e8: A Maya city 20 km from Tikal with a 45-metre temple crowned by a massive stucco sun-god mask. The mask was painted blood-red and once blazed in the sunset light.
descriptions.2a4f816f-71bb-43b5-be29-9239c432fc4f: Two ruined circles on Bodmin Moor, just 2.5 metres apart, each 23 metres across. Both have an exceptionally large stone to the southeast — the same deliberate placement in each ring.
descriptions.5179583f-6f4a-4fdb-bf98-f2c28a8f1228: Coastal erosion has consumed most of this promontory fort; a fraction of the eastern ramparts cling to a 150-metre clifftop. What survived is scheduled — what was lost is gone forever.
descriptions.0be01d6a-9e01-4002-8242-00c108968d5d: A Roman copper mine from the 2nd–3rd century with a carved stone inscription still in the tunnel. The only direct evidence of Roman underground mining in Central Europe.
descriptions.933ba591-a21a-47d0-93f0-49083c295395: Settled around 6000 BC — fresh water, fertile land, and a natural harbour drew the first inhabitants. Excavations from 1952 traced Neolithic layers below later occupation on southeast Chios.
descriptions.60d47079-a36e-4bfa-95e0-6636f9bc8ba4: Founded by Phocaean colonists in 575 BC; Roman occupation followed Hannibal's 218 BC campaign. Its exposed coast eventually left it open to raiders and it was abandoned in the Early Middle Ages.
descriptions.696624d4-3f88-4175-a4cd-fd145d00174a: The world's earliest known public museum, dating to 530 BC. Curated by Princess Ennigaldi, daughter of the last Babylonian king, near the Ziggurat of Ur.
descriptions.1a01ebc7-570b-4f83-8b09-86ab7a57390f: Capital of the Celto-Ligurian Salyes confederation, settled around 175 BC. Stone pillars with niches for displaying severed enemy heads were found in the sanctuary.
descriptions.4a371dbd-51ba-4336-a154-6152070b2023: A Roman road station from 14 BC where the Via Claudia crossed the ancient salt road from Salzburg. About 80 soldiers guarded this strategic intersection.
descriptions.3e012d60-1be3-49b9-83a2-7e1edeab0d77: Home to a 4th-century BC theatre where a coin dropped on stage can be heard in the back row of 14,000 seats. Also the ancient world's premier healing center.
descriptions.e50d493f-6f6c-4c30-8cab-5e86077ef361: A Roman city on a promontory above the Guadiela, replacing a Celtiberian settlement on the opposite bank. During the Sertorian War of the 1st century BC, the site functioned as a military camp.
descriptions.c93f25d4-5aa3-46f9-a672-71a2000ce517: A landscape dense with Neolithic megaliths from 4500 BC: the Kerzerho alignments, plus the Crucuno, Mané-Croch, and Mané-Bras dolmens all cluster nearby.
descriptions.28d68bb8-00cb-4f82-9ec2-f1b651b50c7d: An Urartian fortress founded in 782 BC by King Argishti I, with a cuneiform inscription recording the exact year of its founding. It served as both military stronghold and royal capital.
descriptions.dcb2c5f2-682f-483b-8904-88d3b6fe6119: A 421 BC Ionic temple on the Acropolis with the famous Caryatid porch — six marble maidens serving as columns. It housed Athena's sacred olive-wood statue.
descriptions.be26197d-61ab-4221-83d9-d43be9976e33: A town devastated by Philip V of Macedon during the Second Macedonian War in 198 BC. The Roman army camped here on its march toward the decisive Battle of Cynoscephalae.
descriptions.c2628a93-7c87-4a98-8d13-8301f7063403: A 140-metre-long burial mound extended over centuries, completed around 3300 BC. Part of the Locmariaquer megalithic complex, one of Europe's great Neolithic sites.
descriptions.df073013-30ac-4f4b-a420-d44829a5a723: A 3500 BC site with two stone circles — the southern one now submerged beneath the sea. Rising waters since the Neolithic have swallowed half the monument.
descriptions.cbe321a4-0b00-4c6e-9773-f006757e637a: A Roman road linking Gloucester, Cirencester, and Silchester — connecting legionary bases to major ports. Much of the original route is still traceable in the modern landscape.
descriptions.9a95f005-3bee-4270-a718-5aad8b971a5b: An ancient Sicilian mountaintop city famous across the Mediterranean for its temple of Aphrodite Erycina. Roman generals made pilgrimages here before battle.
descriptions.c96274da-bdec-445d-a79f-2a43c0688421: A cave with Paleolithic rock art and human traces stretching back 50,000 years. Neanderthal hunter-gatherers were its first occupants, followed by modern humans.
descriptions.cdde29e6-99d8-4bcd-9460-ac9c09713c0e: A 12th-century BC rock relief carved 8.5 metres up inside a cave, showing a royal family worshipping before a fire stand. Later hands added new figures centuries apart.
descriptions.277970ce-65f8-403a-8e20-dbcadac0f214: A sandstone outcrop with human activity dating to 6000 BC and a Bronze Age enclosure at its 242-metre summit. People have been drawn to this vantage point for 8,000 years.
descriptions.804f7b48-464b-40a2-b08d-0cd9c435096b: 16 Corinthian columns of the Temple of Zeus Lepsinos still stand — raised under Hadrian, among the best-preserved classical temples in the region. The city dates to the 6th century BC.
descriptions.540037f8-f9af-4776-b2fa-b82b4e9a80f0: A cross-border site on the Franco-German frontier, settled from 8000 BC through the Roman period. A Celtic princess's grave on the German side yielded gold jewelry of exceptional craftsmanship.
descriptions.7f4207f8-30df-4aa9-850e-6873fcab2bb3: A Neolithic chambered cairn 60 metres long and 25 metres wide, of the Severn-Cotswold type. These trapezoid mounds with internal stone chambers were built for collective burial.
descriptions.daf2b273-b9a9-4fe9-bd71-b76ff56e7671: A stone circle of twelve sarsen megaliths near Avebury, now reduced to a single standing stone. It measured 37 metres across when complete.
descriptions.8541ba4b-43ff-4428-b155-8e12fb96dafc: A Romano-Celtic temple with column capitals sculpted as heads of the Sun and Moon. Rich finds of glass, coins, and terracotta antefixes indicate a wealthy sanctuary.
descriptions.ba3cbac4-815f-4e9c-85d7-4118d4e23499: A Roman sanctuary at 1,550 metres elevation with temples, freestanding columns, altars, and rock-cut tombs. One of the highest-altitude Roman temple complexes in the Levant.
descriptions.933a2371-d810-463c-8799-33ba1731e463: Walls 15 metres high, at least 2,500 years of occupation, and a position linking Persia to India on the Silk Road. The citadel's origins predate written records of the city it guards.
descriptions.ec47336a-5eeb-4b59-b60c-9ef6d1901934: A Roman temple on open heathland anchored the largest known Roman-era settlement in Surrey. Excavations in 1848 recovered coins, pottery, and a priest's scepter from the surrounding site.
descriptions.373ccffa-991d-4455-b116-19957b288a28: Two 1st-century Roman marching camps flanking Dere Street, the military road from York into Scotland. Troops camped here during campaigns against northern tribes.
descriptions.f28a2d38-f5a9-49f2-83c8-53bb4c61cae4: A Roman castellum built in 4–5 AD where the Vecht branched off from the Rhine. It guarded the waterway leading to Lake Flevo, precursor of the Zuiderzee.
descriptions.a001babf-8527-44af-ab0c-14fb1016f3a6: A Roman fortress on the Rhine frontier, built by order of Tiberius around 5 AD and maintained for centuries. It anchored the northern edge of the Roman Empire.
descriptions.d5c4fc5c-f8ad-4b97-b2fd-087311f733c8: Dung and mud piled up over generations raised this mound above the Weser estuary marshes. By the 3rd century AD it held 300 people, 450 cattle, and 26 longhouses.
descriptions.fd2f475b-845a-42ec-8183-264673911980: A lake surrounded by moorland where Stone Age and Bronze Age pile dwellings were preserved in waterlogged sediment. The anaerobic conditions kept organic artifacts intact.
descriptions.21e1b481-d738-49de-a4ae-227bc73c55da: A Neolithic site spanning 5,200 years of habitation on a coastal plateau. Its layered deposits chronicle the full arc of prehistoric culture on the island.
descriptions.eaf2f471-84d2-4661-8781-6a81241b11fb: Around 68 stones form a slightly flattened ring on Bodmin Moor, measuring 46 by 43 metres. All but one are pink granite — the lone outlier is limestone, its origin still unexplained.
descriptions.decbad37-dc89-4adf-926b-19c94a17e50f: Active from the 7th century BC through the Roman period, this iron-smelting site in Burgundy ranks among the largest ferriers in Europe. Tons of slag remain scattered across the forested terrain.
descriptions.b3c4825c-79ff-48c7-bb38-015e73fc7ae2: The only Neolithic henge in West Yorkshire, with activity on the site from 3500 BC. Earlier circular monuments were built here before the henge itself took shape.
descriptions.8571f9c3-159d-4d6d-b33a-3e36fdabb5cf: A 3rd-century temple to Mithras with the classic layout: a sunken central nave flanked by raised benches where initiates reclined during secret rituals.
descriptions.24826df9-4bc9-46f9-b6ba-113f20861186: A multivallate contour fort on a prominent hill west of Montgomery, overlooking the River Severn. Its ramparts extend across terrain that made it among the largest hillforts in the region.
descriptions.f23a32f2-4b00-4b17-9cfd-2f30f753276e: A sub-circular earthwork enclosing 6.4 hectares on a chalk ridge. Its purpose has never been fully determined — it may be a henge, a fort, or something else entirely.
descriptions.1ed00cd4-fec4-406f-af91-8c6bf79eeb3d: Megalithic standing stones from 3300 BC carved with human faces, swords, and armor — rare stone portraits produced at the dawn of the Bronze Age in the western Mediterranean.
descriptions.70ba6d0f-f026-4b29-9379-a9152ee1e271: Hurriedly built 440–390 BC in response to a real threat, not a status project. Excavations in 2011 found a mass burial of women and children sealed within the wall.
descriptions.d44c1dff-0bee-4500-befe-9b16ae420e23: An ancient Greek city from the 5th century BC whose later fortifications used enormous stone blocks. Byzantine churches were added a thousand years after the first walls went up.
descriptions.ae6974c3-4079-4ce3-a3a4-70e4984ea2d4: A cult site where war booty was ritually destroyed and thrown into water from 350–550 AD. Over 700 artifacts include weapons deliberately chopped into pieces.
descriptions.1ab97e76-933a-4dc5-a734-42f53c8c7667: A double stone circle now completely destroyed. Built between 3300 and 900 BC, it was part of the megalithic tradition that spread across Britain, Ireland, and Brittany.
descriptions.66be5990-dc1f-47f2-bc11-367354a63a14: The largest ancient theatre in Thessaly, seating 10,000 people. Built in the 3rd century BC under Philip V, it was used for six centuries before being converted into a market.
descriptions.5e0e44b0-b557-4ffe-9cc1-7db2d3e3ecfc: A 113-metre-wide gateway at Karnak — the largest pylon ever attempted — that was never finished. Mudbrick construction ramps still lean against the inside.
descriptions.c0dce315-a1ed-4be6-8dd2-df515e754875: The largest Roman residence north of the Alps, built around 75 AD — only 30 years after the Roman conquest of Britain. Its formal gardens were surrounded by mosaic-floored wings.
descriptions.e765ff49-b186-4cf0-b32a-94a3aa453de9: A 6-metre Iron Age boat carved from a single oak trunk, dating to 457–300 BC. Its bowed bow and slotted stern board show sophisticated woodworking for river transport.
descriptions.fffb6208-b675-47ff-8a0b-4d11f455b0ff: A row of Bronze Age bell barrows arranged in an almost straight line along a ridge. The largest stands 3.3 metres high — a burial monument visible for kilometres.
descriptions.4297c23a-44ec-49e3-a34f-7715a16d7620: A Neolithic chambered tomb over 20 metres across on Taddington Moor, with paved burial chambers. Human bones from at least twelve individuals were found inside.
descriptions.d686e433-d062-4546-818f-1df39fce0931: A Bronze Age causeway of 60,000 timbers stretching 1 km across fenland, built 3,500 years ago. A small artificial island partway across appears to have been a ritual center.
descriptions.95981699-02b0-4ab9-9ccc-cd9efc14f97a: A late Neolithic enclosure discovered beneath Thomas Hardy's house. Half was excavated during bypass construction; the rest still lies under the novelist's garden.
descriptions.4115430c-0702-4c66-81ba-a6f1b580633a: The third-largest Roman amphitheatre in the peninsula, measuring 147 by 117 metres. Built by the same architects as the Colosseum, its underground machinery rooms survive intact.
descriptions.d56cc124-8502-45b8-8fc6-b7dc59d02e43: The only Roman city in Styria, elevated to municipium status under Emperor Vespasian. It grew from a Celto-Roman settlement on the Mur river into a fully planned Roman town.
descriptions.648d388d-8532-4605-9345-1b656640455e: A 4.8-kilometre earthwork standing 7 metres high, built between 330 and 510 AD. Its ditch faces west, suggesting Saxon invaders built it as a frontier against the Britons.
descriptions.edfde098-e28e-4206-83d9-bb2846ba735d: A Roman fort built by Tiberius around 4 AD at the mouth of what is now the North Sea Canal. It started as a marching camp and was later enlarged into a permanent castrum.
descriptions.d6665022-2763-44cd-8963-d6fb7d4cfc52: Three Bronze Age burial mounds including a disc barrow described as "the finest in Hampshire" — 28 metres across, containing two smaller mounds within its perimeter ditch.
descriptions.3415ea00-bddf-4f1d-bed2-7ce85b6c5871: Over 2,500 years old and still crumbling into Worbarrow Bay — erosion has taken a large portion of this clifftop hillfort. What remains is scheduled; what falls is beyond recovery.
descriptions.e3fc8870-e13e-40bd-8d81-455b5e30b97b: Three Bronze Age cairns predate the hillfort that encloses them on "The Hill of Three Cairns." Concentric stone ramparts housed 100 to 400 people at the eastern edge of the Preseli Hills.
descriptions.58b67d2b-fb58-41b0-b7d3-16c36ca4507a: Crowning the second-highest peak in the Clwydian Range at 511 metres, this hillfort covers 10 hectares. Offa's Dyke Path passes around its western slopes.
descriptions.fc4bf634-d20e-4c83-b72a-5b3a69d9ed59: A Roman villa perched on a clifftop with views across the Channel to the French coast. Human activity at the site goes back thousands of years before the Romans arrived.
descriptions.9064eade-4e85-43d6-a640-653866a2a59d: A Neolithic dolmen called the Pierre-Levée — a "raised stone" — standing since around 3000 BC. Dolmens like this once numbered in thousands across western Europe.
descriptions.6be9a7f1-53c8-447b-8c63-d6cc40f2281e: A cave with over 200 polychrome paintings from 17,000 BC — bison, horses, and mammoths in full color. One of the last Ice Age painted caves still open to visitors.
descriptions.64258455-db31-45cb-a1af-85c46b92d0c1: A Bronze Age well temple with a keyhole-shaped entrance aligned so sunlight strikes the water on the summer solstice. Built from precisely squared basalt blocks.
descriptions.59f8faa5-2f0f-4278-9c2c-97c4adaa55b7: Three springs recorded by Pliny the Elder that frequently went dry while neighboring springs kept flowing. Romans considered their behavior a sacred omen.
descriptions.008ecaa5-ce9b-484d-9eb8-0f27659bc91d: A site in the Cholistan Desert where ceramics dating to 5000 BC were found — evidence of the ancient Hakra civilization that predates the Indus Valley cities.
descriptions.46bceb53-3c23-41a6-9659-b7a67035197a: An 18th-century star fort with geometric bastions designed to deflect cannon fire from every angle. Part of a network of fortifications defending a border town.
descriptions.77127fe3-8116-4567-9b04-aebbe719e5a7: City walls first built in antiquity, rebuilt by Byzantines, then expanded by Venetians in the 16th century. Parts of both the Byzantine and Venetian walls still stand.
descriptions.f4f0c9af-1941-4d22-9513-4ec574590a9d: London's defensive walls began in the 3rd century AD under the Romans. Sections of the original Roman stonework still survive beneath and between later Medieval additions.
descriptions.cecfe56c-84f1-4958-b40e-ebaf52ace4a9: Knights Hospitaller enlarged these crescent-shaped walls over 5th-century BC foundations. A wide moat and artillery bastions repelled multiple Ottoman sieges.
descriptions.e1eaffd0-4281-4033-ab91-45d2b54377a7: A castle bearing traces of four civilizations in its walls: Illyrian, Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman. Each rebuilt and expanded what the last had left behind.
descriptions.a451f6be-a506-41f6-9bf7-85d8c7c7ac8e: A fortress carved over 100 metres deep into a cliff face, with chambers, rooms, and silos for provisions. Rain collection and piped spring water sustained the garrison.
descriptions.fc9b4ac3-3e4a-42d0-96f1-81f37f246230: Roman baths converted from 2nd-century buildings, with the hot rooms facing south and cold rooms facing north to use the sun's heat. One of several bathhouses in the imperial capital.
descriptions.df0e220d-573f-4cfd-92a7-c65f4c690186: The northernmost Roman city on the European continent, established after the Batavian Revolt around 70 AD. Emperor Hadrian granted it market rights around 120 AD.
descriptions.337268d6-ceda-4830-914f-cd6782010223: An oval Iron Age bivallate hillfort covering 10.5 hectares with steep natural slopes on three sides. The double-banked defenses concentrated on the vulnerable north side.
descriptions.fad5c73f-8725-47d0-b13c-372fefba62ea: A citadel inhabited since the Bronze Age and likely the acropolis of the Punic-Roman city of Gaulos. It has been continuously fortified for over 3,000 years.
descriptions.c4ec860c-ddf4-40a3-95f6-1313b9c0dee2: Linking the River Trent to Lincoln, this Roman-era canal was refurbished by King Henry I in 1121 and remains navigable today. Built around 120 AD, it is the longest-serving canal in the country.
descriptions.041049ae-edd9-49a3-8233-1ea9b3382913: A Roman road running 300 km from Exeter to Lincoln that served as the western frontier of Roman Britain for its first decades. Much of its route is still used as modern roads.
descriptions.5d8cbd90-1826-4ab0-b44f-94574d7dccc4: A Roman granite fountain from the 1st century with Latin inscriptions dedicated to the pre-Roman gods Tongoenabiagus and Nabia. A water cult blending Roman and native worship.
descriptions.c8dc3d03-6c81-4ef7-a8f2-e2cb2d047359: A 100-room Minoan settlement from the Early Bronze Age perched atop a steep hill. Two weaving looms found among the ruins hint at a textile-producing community.
descriptions.3f51c197-fcd3-4c3e-8ba2-ba4a566ef45e: An eastern suburb of Hertford built on a site with Roman and Saxon finds. Occupation debris from the 1st through 4th centuries lay buried beneath a modern gravel pit.
descriptions.01b50bc7-3e36-494e-9a91-fc4d60323ada: A cave occupied from 38,000 BC to 3000 BC — 35,000 years of nearly continuous human use. Obsidian from the island of Melos shows its residents were making sea voyages by 11,000 BC.
descriptions.b587a652-f222-47e6-adc9-b6ba1fa62722: A 4.4-hectare univallate hillfort in the New Forest with steep natural slopes on the west and south sides. Its rampart was extended to enclose a natural spring that has reportedly never run dry.
descriptions.9bedafde-94b7-40d2-a064-4130c224d7ef: A roughly 5,000-year-old menhir resculpted into a Christian cross, reportedly by the missionary Willibrord. Niches for saint figures were chiselled into the ancient stone.
descriptions.ace74343-3a13-4391-bc13-46a9907f197f: A complex with a Roman villa, a shrine, an amphitheatre, and a cemetery spanning both Roman and Saxon burials. An unusually rich concentration of ritual activity in one place.
descriptions.486d74c5-e309-485a-8d06-a1d91c25e7e4: A town with 15th–16th century buildings that once formed part of a fortification, plus an old Roman bridge and ancient water supply well still visible nearby.
descriptions.632d47b7-53ec-4514-b39c-87dbe7f8a9ab: The acropolis of Larissa, continuously inhabited since the city's earliest settlement. Temples, a theatre, and Byzantine fortifications all share this single hilltop.
descriptions.56fae5c5-8114-48a8-8685-877e23c12688: A Roman settlement built during the Flavian dynasty specifically as a retirement community for soldiers after the Illyrian Wars. Abandoned in Late Antiquity.
descriptions.359860c8-9f39-49d7-8834-1651987c8c1e: A 320 BC funerary monument near the Dipylon Gate showing a warrior striding forward in full armor. Carved from expensive Pentelic marble, it stood 2.5 metres tall.
descriptions.e2fc0a30-cd29-473d-ad34-7e109b098cb7: Raised around 320 BC in Athens, this marble tomb for Demetria and Pamphile was among the last lavish grave stelae in the Kerameikos before a law banned such monuments.
descriptions.61c16e64-b3b7-4bf5-9617-b23ea650f89d: A 4th-century BC funerary stela unique for its naval iconography — a young hoplite sits with his shield, helmet, and ship's prow. Found in the port city of Piraeus.
descriptions.44996991-ef99-4593-a645-74bf63d9056a: An ancient wall stretching 4 km across the island of Fetlar, dividing it into two nearly equal halves. Its exact date and purpose remain unknown.
descriptions.6cc9e902-c82f-4b21-9f36-41c2b783cebc: Near Anundshögen — the ship-shaped burial mound of legendary King Anund, among Scandinavia's larger such monuments. Norse saga tradition ties this site to a king whose name recurs across the region.
descriptions.5a71ba67-536f-405f-8aa8-eb386bb98dff: Occupied for at least 44,000 years with rock art dating back 28,000 years — the oldest securely dated prehistoric art on the continent. Stone pillars support its natural roof.
descriptions.04c8399c-298d-41ab-bb53-f56beb9e45da: Twyn y Gaer crowns the summit of this Black Mountains ridge at 427 metres. The hillfort commands views over both the Grwyne Fawr valley to the east and the Vale of Ewyas to the west.
descriptions.036bb557-22b9-4ca9-92ca-a284cf1070cc: One of approximately 570 Iron Age hillforts in the region — a density of fortifications found almost nowhere else in Europe. Each community built its own defensive enclosure.
descriptions.41701276-d1e1-4068-b767-5b6173f6512c: A Minoan palace from around 1700 BC built on top of a much older settlement, then destroyed by an earthquake. Its east wing is the best-preserved section.
descriptions.f305da7f-3d56-4dd5-b370-e41712cdf7d2: Modern Galaxidi occupies the footprint of ancient Haleion. Mycenaean remains at the hill of Villa and earlier traces from the Early Helladic Period mark a very long span of occupation.
descriptions.e9f1550f-44ab-4661-b362-0abdb4f33e74: A dolmen with a 12-metre burial passage and an "oven door" entrance just 2 metres high and 1 metre wide. Three massive capstones cover the main 6-metre-long chamber.
descriptions.e8777e45-24e2-46bb-8171-1f94220727c0: A vast Roman villa built around 160 AD housing the largest collection of Roman mosaics in the region. It included private baths and a temple to Mithras.
descriptions.3963cd3e-5203-4506-a8a5-785aea857b71: An oval stone circle of about 40 large pink granite stones, every single one now fallen. One lone limestone block sits among the granite — deliberately chosen to be different.
descriptions.3e60d066-60c4-41a5-a114-26569645efce: Over 1,500 petroglyphs from the 4th–1st millennium BC punched into rock at high altitude. Local legend says this summit is where Noah's Ark came to rest and turned to stone.
descriptions.4e9fb2b3-94fe-4898-80c8-6678ac2d5903: The legendary seat of the Yngling kings from the 3rd century AD onward, famous across Scandinavia. Three massive royal burial mounds still dominate the landscape.
descriptions.9635c4e8-6385-4bdb-a952-c9f53a4b2403: Emperor Galerius named this 3rd-century palace complex Felix Romuliana after his mother. The 4-hectare UNESCO-listed site preserves temples, fortifications, and two nearby imperial mausolea.
descriptions.3d801ecb-4453-4ce3-85db-dce392c67c9d: Two Achaemenid cuneiform inscriptions in three languages carved into granite above a creek. Locals believed the carvings were a secret code to hidden treasure.
descriptions.c7328327-2d1b-4ffa-ae63-dca2ee6f688a: A Neolithic dolmen built between 3500 and 2800 BC by the Funnelbeaker culture. Three support stones hold up a 1-metre-thick capstone that has cracked down the middle.
descriptions.89c1b8db-9d47-4183-b46f-e43bf3d90ecf: A multilayer Bronze Age settlement from the second half of the 3rd millennium BC. Its material culture reveals the daily life of tribes in the Guruchay river basin.
descriptions.4235fa73-a58f-400b-a1f6-4998a8d2893f: Petroglyphs approximately 7,000 years old carved along a riverbed, depicting moose. Among the oldest rock carvings in Scandinavia.
descriptions.6f6c5cc0-b0ac-4222-bb04-747352eb83d1: The plaster casts of 13 people killed by Vesuvius in 79 AD, frozen mid-flight in a garden that was a vineyard before the eruption. A family with small children is among them.
descriptions.16e413ef-7b76-4fda-8f07-5cecf817071d: Occupied 1st century BC–11th century AD, this Skåne site yielded a Roman Iron Age grave with a runic-inscribed silver fibula. Excavations revealed house foundations, a grave field, and a shrine.
descriptions.83abc4c8-1cdf-4429-a0f7-c9cc76f5c373: An ancient community at a river crossing, settled since at least the 10th century. Its medieval church preserves a 1612 pulpit and altarpiece by Danish sculptor Jakob Kremberg.
descriptions.8793ca33-397e-47a5-a6bb-020802f49e7c: Over 170 round-house traces, 100 still visible on this Llŷn Peninsula hillfort. The lower rampart is the original defence; a second eastern rampart was added in the 6th or 7th century AD.
descriptions.696fa141-d76e-4882-ab59-75f8a0d46d47: The only standing Greco-Roman colonnaded building in the Caucasus, built as a temple to the sun god Mihr. Its Ionic columns follow a style originating in the 7th century BC.
descriptions.fb877d92-953a-4dba-af74-64ac1330e47e: A rare dual court tomb — two megalithic tombs sharing a single mound, each with its own ceremonial court. Once 28 metres long, its roof stones have all collapsed.
descriptions.3b4ceaf0-0e07-4f25-bf33-83728e8aa49c: A late Iron Age hillfort built to control the waterways below, overseeing traffic to Uppsala, Sigtuna, and Birka. A seat of local power at a maritime crossroads.
descriptions.f9cfc5f7-a6c8-4c6f-9d82-f30151a36d6c: The ceremonial entrance to Persepolis, flanked by monumental winged bulls with human heads to ward off evil. Every visitor to the empire had to pass through this single gate.
descriptions.c2e7a1e8-c56f-40e9-8516-79e0c6bdd747: A monumental Doric gateway to the Roman Agora in Athens, funded by Julius Caesar and Augustus in 11 BC. Four Pentelic marble columns frame the entrance to the marketplace.
descriptions.4dc60f9f-66cf-4a4a-9c47-bf24cc0d618d: A 10-tonne arch carved from a single stone block at Tiwanaku, with 48 figures flanking a central deity. The lintel's iconography has never been fully decoded.
descriptions.7ceced42-5339-4dc0-84da-5c11f6898879: A passage grave from around 4200 BC whose interior stones are covered in densely carved spirals, arcs, and concentric patterns. The most elaborately decorated megalithic tomb in Europe.
descriptions.d1dd3311-9974-4e6e-81ae-a7eed2775e72: Seven Gaya confederacy tumuli complexes, 1st–6th century AD, inscribed as a UNESCO site in 2023. Together they trace a federation's funerary evolution across five modern provinces.
descriptions.84c1ff70-a242-423d-96f8-694b1b7fcc67: A Paleolithic cave dwelling with over 17,000 animal bone fossils documenting the region's Ice Age fauna. Stone tools found here span tens of thousands of years.
descriptions.2f68e3c4-6af8-40f0-833e-00602e7fe639: A medieval monastery with churches and tombs carved directly into the mountainside — the peak of Caucasian rock-cut architecture. Founded in the 4th century.
descriptions.e2f7cf07-9034-4e60-82e1-b43f37fc91c1: A hilltop military camp from the 4th–5th century AD — the Migration Period, when the Roman frontier was collapsing. It commanded the exit of the Kinzig valley onto the Rhine plain.
descriptions.019d61e6-08f4-46d8-bb15-78141831d5cf: A reconstructed Iron Age settlement from around 400–600 AD. Post-glacial land rise has moved the shoreline 500 metres from where it was when the village was occupied.
descriptions.365696cd-688a-412c-bb9f-66ff88fc7f35: An Iron Age fortified camp at Bulstrode Park survives here. The builders chose a strategic position in the Chiltern foothills above the River Misbourne.
descriptions.f5e529ea-2e30-4c33-82fc-8ec450f86687: A Roman military camp on the Pannonian frontier, built in the 2nd century as part of the limes defense system. Abandoned in the 4th century when legions withdrew from the region.
descriptions.1ed19de1-b9da-4cfa-a1ec-16693f6cc090: Stone ship burials, Bronze Age barrows, and Viking Age graves share this Öland gravefield. Burial forms spanning two millennia make it among the largest funerary sites on the island.
descriptions.8b78f040-2e72-4754-b3e1-0b78a4e970c0: A village with Iron Age and Viking Age finds including a helmet fragment, showing occupation from roughly 500 to 1000 AD. Located just 2 km from the legendary royal seat at Lejre.
descriptions.07ca1c0c-550e-41ab-ab5d-5563fce29d90: Two megalithic temples built 3600–2500 BC, predating the pyramids of Egypt and Stonehenge. The earliest temple complex on these islands, built from coralline and globigerina limestone.
descriptions.87b7df7d-023f-43ce-b644-4c12394a8f9f: A local spring fed these Roman baths — likely the reason they were sited here. The tepidarium, frigidarium, and caldarium all survive intact, uncovered during works to cap the spring.
descriptions.ebbad3eb-877c-4c7f-b6bf-66723f7b49e6: A 144-metre cave containing bones of animals stranded when the island was cut off from the mainland at the end of the Ice Age. Dwarf elephants and hippos became extinct here.
descriptions.919ca5f2-4d3b-474a-b7f5-1b706473797c: The only surviving Early-Christian catacombs in Gozo — a unique Roman burial site that has drawn scholarly attention for centuries.
descriptions.dd6ec46e-813f-458a-a881-a5673ea8b839: A cave complex next to mysterious prehistoric cart ruts carved into bedrock. Families reportedly lived as troglodytes in these caves until 1835.
descriptions.88deb44a-3ffd-401d-b9e0-54b0ec05fd89: Dating 4000–2000 BC, this Sindh desert mound is an early Indus Valley site that predates the mature urban phases at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. It lies in Johi Tehsil, Dadu District.
descriptions.6cc8d849-0080-41c6-8082-b713db44f82b: Sea cliffs 15–25 metres high defend three sides of this St Mary's promontory fort; three banks and ditches guard the landward approach. The rocky headland covers 0.4 hectares.
descriptions.c2b44932-6d84-476e-899c-02c744fcadd8: Two standing stones at the foot of Black Combe, the taller bearing a single cup mark and the smaller three cup-and-ring marks. Their original purpose is lost to time.
descriptions.78123025-5f8c-433a-9623-a60ea4105600: Collective burial tombs built by the Nuragic civilization during the Bronze Age. Over 800 of these "Giants' Tombs" have been found across the island.
descriptions.e0d56737-6459-4329-9ef5-1a46e8d75f10: A henge monument from 2700 BC with a 180-metre-diameter enclosure surrounded by a 3.5-metre-high earthwork bank. A megalithic dolmen sits off-center inside the ring.
descriptions.80770c65-0744-4dc3-a883-01bbd832e00f: A Neolithic oval barrow with an Early Bronze Age round barrow built on top of one end — two burial monuments from different eras fused into one mound. Part of the Arbor Low complex.
descriptions.bfe0f23d-1880-4931-b22a-ee60aa5cd018: A key stronghold of the early Piast dynasty from 940 AD, alongside Poznań and Gniezno. It began as a small 9th-century keep on a lake peninsula.
descriptions.9c35081a-a345-4545-962d-d3aeeb2f2b0c: Celtic burial mounds and sacred groves in a forest along the Roman Via Julia route from Augsburg to Salzburg. A church bell here dates to 1356.
descriptions.5e53212a-df01-4e4e-b9d0-fde511c2ec55: A hill with both Ordovician fossils 450 million years old and a Neolithic standing stone from roughly 4000 BC. Deep time and human time share the same summit.
descriptions.2a44dd94-7af2-4cee-9816-c54a2edafa9f: A Dacian town in ancient Moesia, part of a network of fortified settlements that resisted Roman expansion. Little survives but its name, recorded in ancient geography.
descriptions.9fc45c45-7f83-424d-8d9e-a18d14bb5526: A burial ground for the royal family of Khufu, builder of the Great Pyramid, dating to 2589–2566 BC. Mastaba tombs of queens, princes, and court officials cluster here.
descriptions.eff62515-9b70-43cc-afe6-c803dd4b5bc3: Three pyramids, the Great Sphinx, and a workers' village, all built between 2600 and 2500 BC. The Great Pyramid was the tallest structure on Earth for 3,800 years.
descriptions.e5cd6a5f-2b31-4e32-9b1b-258cfa87acf3: A Roman fort and naval base whose bathhouse walls still stand 4 metres high — the tallest surviving Roman structure in the northern frontier zone.
descriptions.f32a3584-270b-43a7-9c12-859bb6214b11: A megalithic complex with a wedge tomb, two stone circles, and paired stone alignments all clustered together. A single fallen slab hints at a once-larger monument.
descriptions.44748390-06eb-4452-bb1c-dd3dba36ce2a: A wealthy Celto-Ligurian city that expanded under Greek then Roman influence, abandoned after 260 AD. Hillwash buried it for centuries, preserving what later settlements would have destroyed.
descriptions.37507863-e875-4192-a739-b06980f79e1b: A town mentioned in Homer's Catalogue of Ships alongside Boebe and Iolcus. After Homer, its name vanishes entirely from the historical record.
descriptions.bcefdb51-0003-46f4-806a-9bfca2b630e1: An oval cairn surrounded by 30 kerb stones, some carved with concentric rings and spirals. The carvings connect it to the wider megalithic art tradition of Britain and Ireland.
descriptions.9f3c5cb7-92a4-4ae6-b8c2-3235b723516f: An Iron Age village built on a man-made island of timber and clay in 250 BC — the best-preserved prehistoric village ever found in Britain.
descriptions.dba260ef-3c25-4731-ac13-7eb55eb3db90: A life-size sandstone warrior in a leaf-crown headdress came from a burial mound here — a late Hallstatt princely seat with unprecedented evidence for Celtic sculpture and monumental building.
descriptions.bbde3c09-ac95-4fe7-b9d9-1be1fd6452fb: A Roman fort from 48 AD at a key Severn crossing, it became a colonia for retired legionaries in 97 AD. It grew into Gloucester — the name derived from the settlement's Latin title.
descriptions.0931e87d-b91d-4632-91af-e85c5bdfb2f2: Petroglyphs of moose carved approximately 5,000 years ago, first described in 1685. The carvings were made when the site was near the Stone Age shoreline.
descriptions.13b5bbe7-ff6b-4a1e-a8f5-d17ed3fee4f6: A coastal city with Bronze Age origins from the 15th century BC, later the frontier town of the Messapii. Multiple invasions — Iapyges, Romans, Ostrogoths — reshaped it over millennia.
descriptions.d953e9b3-de33-4c7d-9357-bbc5d94d2a16: Massive carved stone pillars erected in the 10th–8th millennium BC by people who hadn't invented farming yet. The oldest known monumental architecture on Earth.
descriptions.aaa12d23-d666-4a40-9f3c-17d861f4e143: Rock carvings spanning 20,000 years — from Upper Paleolithic hunting scenes to medieval camel caravans. A visual timeline of human culture etched into stone.
descriptions.9794f4c4-12b0-47a7-b454-a6611d441795: Hundreds of stone dolmens here served as grave markers and ritual sites during the 1st millennium BC Megalithic Culture. The peninsula holds over 35,000 dolmens — roughly 40% of the world's total.
descriptions.62baaf4c-8ad4-4bf4-b0e0-e5587c5a64a1: A bowl barrow hidden in a copse atop a chalk knoll 60 metres above the Hertfordshire-Cambridgeshire border. The mound was built for visibility; the concealing trees are a later addition.
descriptions.935c0e07-0e4c-4bf9-a2ea-0113c70a3e3c: A chain of chalk hills southeast of Cambridge named for a giant from legend, hurled from a cliff by Brutus of Troy. A Neolithic causewayed enclosure from around 3300 BC crowns the ridge.
descriptions.8b0b4ce8-ce4c-4dad-95b0-a342973aea43: A Neolithic great dolmen from the Funnelbeaker culture, built between 3500 and 2800 BC. Only one of the two original capstones survives on its six supporting uprights.
descriptions.c35b1649-9442-4195-9604-4481ce65ffbf: The main gate of Diocletian's Palace, built in the 4th century AD with elaborate decoration befitting an emperor's entrance. It was sealed in the Middle Ages and reopened in modern times.
descriptions.18911cb2-dff1-4d14-9110-de55c40706c0: A Roman signal station stood here — part of a coastal watchtower chain monitoring seaborne raids along the Yorkshire coast. The hamlet lies within the North York Moors National Park.
descriptions.ca012875-d72b-4d00-99a7-0246f1769a32: A 20-hectare island in Lake Prespa covered in ancient walls, medieval churches, and dense snake colonies — earning the nickname "Snake Island." It opened to tourism in August 2008.
descriptions.f04199e9-626c-4eda-bccf-0395ef21d332: A Bronze Age earthwork 175 metres across from the Urnfield culture (1200–800 BC). It is linked to a widespread solar cult that gripped Central Europe during this period.
descriptions.f91d645f-29ad-439d-83eb-fdf0531d93cc: An archaeological site where up to 1,500 caves were carved into conglomerate rock at multiple levels. Only 500 remain; the rest have eroded away with no conservation efforts.
descriptions.ff7fc6c8-04f1-4988-954c-99c9b9f113e4: Mentioned by Pliny the Elder and linked to the myth of Medea, this Roman Black Sea fortress dates from the early centuries AD. Gold, silver, and jeweled artifacts were recovered from its layers.
descriptions.0047ae41-af8e-44e1-b196-4035f5860554: A fortress city guarding the only two mountain passes into Thessaly from the north. Whoever held Gonnus controlled access to the Thessalian plain.
descriptions.a3648096-b2ce-4f81-b704-59a1875012e1: A 3-metre standing stone from around 3300 BC on a windswept plateau. The menhir shares the landscape with rare heathland species including adders and Cornish heath.
descriptions.509a6c79-4fa7-4055-b77b-1604880da8da: An Iron Age earthwork with two concentric banks and ditches encircling two leveled hut platforms. Small but strategic, it sits within what is now a national nature reserve.
descriptions.27e87200-26a0-4b11-bc12-8b7229bd8828: A planned ancient city with a regular street grid covering most of a hill — a rare example of systematic urban planning in the early Aegean world.
descriptions.a85f5309-ddd4-445e-b447-75f1cb48c76b: Roman capital of Crete and Cyrenaica, and home of the Gortyn Code — carved around 450 BC into a curved stone wall, the oldest complete surviving law code from antiquity.
descriptions.5e30b705-2163-47c0-bd65-3316be1806c9: A site with traces of human activity from the Stone Age through the Bronze and Iron Ages into antiquity. A medieval motte-and-bailey castle later crowned the site.
descriptions.8862f0da-6584-4963-911f-a88c454dc321: A Neolithic circular enclosure from 4900 BC — the oldest and best-known solar observatory in Central Europe. Its gates align with sunrise and sunset on the winter solstice.
descriptions.0e4e4bfd-6702-4adc-b6be-c2e47764cfef: A cave harboring 14,700-year-old human remains, including skulls fashioned into drinking cups. Britain's oldest complete skeleton, Cheddar Man, was found here.
descriptions.277be4f6-02bc-4dd4-b1a2-1898e529faf9: A Minoan town with narrow streets and a small palace, occupied from 2800 to 1200 BC. The modern name comes from the many hollow vessels found scattered across the site.
descriptions.630f8251-632b-4924-8ec9-3cacec046732: A 3rd–10th-century town with a Byzantine coin of Emperor Anastasius I among its finds. Researchers link it to the summer residence of Caucasus Albania's rulers and the medieval town of Aluen.
descriptions.355d25f2-d08d-44d5-8462-0238791d5c92: A portal tomb whose enormous granite capstone has slipped from its original position. Known locally as Pat Kearney's Big Stone, it once stood balanced on upright slabs.
descriptions.4bde4866-94ec-41c2-a7c5-d38e3a2280ea: Caves with 120,000 years of continuous occupation — from Neanderthals to early modern humans. Thousands of fossils document the full transition between the two species.
descriptions.e41063b2-f544-4093-a5a2-65a5757c9d57: The largest early Neolithic settlement in the South Caucasus, spanning 1.5 hectares and standing 8 metres tall. Its people were among the first farmers in the region.
descriptions.b4357b01-a483-4b2b-b667-68e0a6e6f500: A prehistoric mound site in Vojvodina's Kikinda municipality, inscribed on the Cultural Heritage list in 1991. Its layered deposits hold evidence of some of the region's earliest settled communities.
descriptions.9737ca03-ad30-46d2-8740-3dec20bed1ea: A site with possible evidence of human presence spanning 300,000 years. A mysterious script found on a temple altar predates any previously known writing in the region.
descriptions.5d1b5446-41d9-46db-98c9-ac4d1996a3c1: The largest stone circle on the island, with its biggest stone weighing 40 tonnes and standing over 4 metres high. A second, smaller circle lies just to the northeast.
descriptions.d1fb1d89-fc92-428f-9156-0b462f50569f: A stone city from 900–1470 AD hidden in the Andean cloud forests, currently closed to visitors. Circular stone buildings are decorated with mosaic-like relief carvings.
descriptions.ad73de2d-5176-4436-a2fb-4b75c81fb234: A cave containing remains of three distinct prehistoric cultures stacked in its layers. The oldest pottery fragments, found 2.5 metres deep, date to around 6000 BC.
descriptions.c0319301-7c5f-42bc-9af0-808880e776c2: A prehistoric refuge hillfort in the Harz mountains with rampart-and-ditch defenses. Legend claims it as the ancestral seat of the counts of Stolberg.
descriptions.1c4dc9a8-49e5-451f-9b50-af0f1d7ed3f6: A 16th-century BC royal cemetery with six shaft graves yielding gold death masks, weapons, and jewelry. Originally outside the citadel walls, later enclosed within them.
descriptions.a6712eba-ba7a-4047-8462-0f4ae9343373: An earlier royal cemetery than Grave Circle A, dating to the 17th–16th century BC. Its 28-metre-diameter enclosure held both shaft graves and simple pit burials side by side.
descriptions.cd37791b-f83e-42ab-8cf4-94767b4b6571: Iron Age burial mounds from the 6th century BC containing elite wagon burials with gold jewelry and imported Greek and Etruscan luxury goods.
descriptions.d78596fc-387d-4b43-b183-296bfeb4e0c3: At least 21 carved limestone headstones from the shaft graves of Mycenae, dating to 1600–1500 BC. Twelve bear relief carvings of chariot scenes and hunting.
descriptions.e0c96c85-50ef-4c9d-80f9-3f191dca4170: A marble stele from 394 BC showing a mounted warrior striking down a fallen enemy. It marks the tomb of Dexileos, an Athenian cavalryman killed fighting Sparta.
descriptions.80e5c917-0d44-4443-b183-3d03daa36bab: Over 300 small stone cairns cluster on this hilltop near Llanvair Discoed, built around 2000 BC. At 273 metres, the summit looks out over the Caldicot Levels and the Severn estuary.
descriptions.e7a05b23-e2a6-4970-8ba1-b350168b9a00: A farming parish dating back nearly 2,000 years with a prehistoric hillfort crowning Pulpit Hill. After the Roman conquest, a villa was built in the lowland below.
