descriptions.891ad351-7985-4c16-b6a6-830c26bc268f: The largest late-antique Early-Christian basilica in the region, built in the mid-4th century AD. Its marble-decorated interior with mosaic floors survived beneath later construction.
descriptions.378fe0dc-2d2d-4d91-abcf-4955b7c45230: The earliest known public water tank, built in the 3rd millennium BC. It measures 12 by 7 metres and was waterproofed with bitumen — remarkably advanced engineering for its era.
descriptions.e33ae2af-e4d5-45e3-af05-426849f0dad0: A Roman fort planted here around 44 AD where Ermine Street crossed the River Gwash. The village name itself — Great Casterton — derives from ceaster, the Latin-rooted word for a Roman site.
descriptions.80260626-f0b7-4a1a-95e4-5f26bcfe1ecd: A megalithic tomb from the 4th–3rd millennium BC built by semi-nomadic communities of the ancient Alentejo region. It stands isolated in an area of forested brush.
descriptions.d3d33b4f-7d75-4ce6-962d-386834c72cab: Funnelbeaker-culture great dolmen, 3500–2800 BC, on the Jasmund peninsula — trapezoidal mound oriented northeast-southwest. Two capstones originally; one survives. The Baltic is under 500 metres away.
descriptions.557a6dcf-0a4a-4b76-8fed-e8f89cd2b19e: Built 4000-3000 BC near Évora, with uprights up to 8 metres tall — the tallest megalithic stones on the peninsula. It is the largest dolmen of its type in the southwest.
descriptions.925b8dc7-7932-426d-af72-bcb406bb6f12: A 583-kilometre footpath crossing the country from coast to coast along ancient chalk ridges. Parts of this route have been walked for over 5,000 years.
descriptions.8f256d92-11a1-4310-90e2-be5cebfc350e: A 411-metre-long effigy mound shaped like an uncoiling serpent — the largest serpent effigy in the world. It was built on the rim of an ancient meteorite crater in Adams County, Ohio.
descriptions.4599daa4-93cc-4c55-872c-41e9c7875a59: Carved from the Giza bedrock around 2558–2532 BC, this limestone sphinx is 73 metres long and 20 metres tall. The oldest monumental sculpture of its age, it represents the pharaoh Khafre.
descriptions.c221d864-3e29-4789-a581-f52f3c3cf096: Sarsen stones scattered around a spring that may be the remains of a Neolithic monument — or stones collected by 18th-century farmers. The truth is still debated.
descriptions.1de7069f-5fdd-48f3-b48c-45b926248224: A Roman villa built on a hillside between 150 and 200 AD, then enlarged in the late 3rd century. Its bath suite and mosaic floors reflect two centuries of country luxury.
descriptions.d9c15346-2c71-4268-adce-937a32aa8afd: A village with both a Roman villa and a medieval motte-and-bailey castle as scheduled monuments. Roman and Norman power left their marks just metres apart.
descriptions.4ab1bd6e-a7fd-41c3-b341-9959d77d5a6e: A step pyramid built by King Ur-Nammu around 2100 BC, measuring 64 metres long and originally over 30 metres tall. It crumbled, and Nabonidus restored it 1,500 years later.
descriptions.54559aae-1d96-48f0-a2c0-9790d7ee7c20: The largest Iron Age gravefield in Bohuslän with 220 graves from the Migration Period (400–500 AD). Finds include glass beads and bone combs from the age of great migrations.
descriptions.e244d46c-a958-4c42-a154-5ed1ae613600: A 5th-century BC Greek theatre whose stone was quarried by the Spanish under Charles V to build fortifications. Centuries of reuse slowly dismantled the original structure.
descriptions.52bd1b99-5377-4a93-903d-cf99738b9926: A museum built inside a Romanesque church that stands on a Gallo-Roman necropolis. A hidden 6th-century crypt lies beneath the nave — layers of the dead beneath the living.
descriptions.bc4228ff-3afd-4efa-a458-65d0636135df: Two Neolithic chambered cairns about 5,000 years old — among the oldest standing structures in the Highlands. Narrow passages lead to central burial chambers.
descriptions.96938167-cc5f-44fa-b3fd-2ab39fad89a7: A pair of stone circles on Dartmoor, each 33 metres across and less than 5 metres apart, aligned almost exactly north to south. The name means "grey sheep" — the stones' silhouette.
descriptions.c4bfc499-08d9-4cd2-ac3f-91ddaa743710: A Neolithic flint mining complex with over 400 shafts dug between 2600 and 2300 BC. Miners descended 12 metres underground with antler picks to reach the best flint seams.
descriptions.80ea9e97-d2ed-46f6-b1db-293dfd277039: A multi-enclosure hillfort in Grimsbury Wood with a spring at its heart that has reportedly never run dry. The southern rampart was extended specifically to enclose that water source.
descriptions.e5051a8b-714a-4878-869d-6190e20380cd: A linear earthwork stretching nearly 10 km, built by the Catuvellauni tribe as a defense against the Romans. Today only fragments survive among suburban streets.
descriptions.46c1cbdc-32d7-45ab-90b9-f4886d67c45a: A Late Bronze Age settlement from 1300 BC with 24 stone hut circles enclosed by a massive granite wall. Named after the Anglo-Saxon war god Grim.
descriptions.5f77f387-c246-4943-821e-259e4d4f50ab: The country's largest long barrow — 100 metres long, encircled by 134 large stones. Three burial chambers lie within, two of which have been open since antiquity.
descriptions.774a99e0-e8f7-4881-aa6e-94462da0c52d: A massive tumulus from around 600 BC built by the Kalenderberg culture, a branch of the Hallstatt tradition. The town's name literally means "large steep hill."
descriptions.9bbea428-26aa-4cb9-a9c8-d3f8f059972d: A reconstructed 9th-century Slavic castle on a lake peninsula with a circular rampart 50 metres across. The reconstruction recreates reed-thatched longhouses and palisade walls.
descriptions.568aa67b-d4a2-46f0-91d8-ac0c0e820b75: A limestone cave that may contain the earliest evidence of Homo sapiens in Europe. Two teeth found here were initially attributed to Neanderthals, then reclassified as modern human.
descriptions.afac29e1-ce20-4266-8f23-7bb05390ac64: A nearly 1-kilometre Roman tunnel bored through volcanic tuff in 38–36 BC to connect Lake Avernus to Cumae. It was wide enough for two wagons to pass side by side.
descriptions.010a33fa-5687-40f7-8dfd-a0042d78eab7: Red starburst marks appear 14 metres into this Apulian cave. A woven basket of barley grains — a ritual offering — and earthenware vessels collecting ceiling water were also found.
descriptions.6c73072e-f130-4458-a612-e68ad3465ce4: A cave with over 150 Paleolithic engravings of bison, horses, and mammoths from around 23,000 BC. At least five human skeletons were placed in bear hibernation hollows.
descriptions.d7e1cd9a-7861-459a-8454-5631dbbadf8b: A cave containing 12,000-year-old Paleolithic engravings, accessible only through a basement room. The entrance is not disclosed to the public — it remains on private land.
descriptions.e7623642-d009-4d1f-8f0e-fa03a89be90e: An 8-kilometre cave with chambers large enough to be called "cathedrals," used by humans since 5000 BC. One of the longest caves in the Pyrenees.
descriptions.19ed3a0f-09e5-4844-ae5d-9d50bea1371b: Cave murals from 1200–900 BC deep underground — the earliest sophisticated painted art in Mesoamerica. The only known example of non-Maya deep cave art on the continent.
descriptions.b6aab229-8793-40ad-a697-c8dbf6e331bf: Ramparts still standing 3.2 metres high ring this univallate hillfort in Wiltshire. Excavations revealed five human skeletons buried within the earthwork walls themselves.
descriptions.5a4f7d76-c0d1-45ba-9e61-4c1fab2eff51: A stone circle on Burley Moor that may actually be a ring cairn — the distinction is still debated. Large cairns including the Skirtful of Stones lie nearby.
descriptions.1825d8d7-d419-457c-b575-94478e05c127: Lucanian settlers occupied this site in the 6th century BC; the Romans founded a formal city here in the 3rd century BC. Its forum, theatre, and amphitheatre survive in excellent condition.
descriptions.edd32f27-211d-4f83-ba97-a37d6654bf33: A 2-kilometre cave with Maya paintings from the Preclassic era or earlier — human faces painted in negative, geometric shapes, and animal figures on the walls.
descriptions.cc277657-9ec6-4579-8c7e-678abf1c4a37: One of the island's largest collections of megaliths, with tall stones standing among trees on high ground. Once over 60 stones; many have fallen or been removed.
descriptions.4598fdbb-4025-4bb3-955f-cdd68dae05ba: A Paleolithic red-ochre mining site, part of the Rydno Archaeological Reserve. Several hundred former workshop sites spread across the region from Skarżysko-Kamienna to Wąchock.
descriptions.aae646d9-5b3a-4a7c-9754-6d5ce4a0a9de: A pre-Columbian city occupied from 1000 BC to 1400 AD with stone-paved roads and aqueducts that still carry water today. Only a fraction of the site has been excavated.
descriptions.662d37b5-2ade-44f2-8ba6-3c6df5524bf8: A cave with bones of woolly mammoth, rhinoceros, and reindeer alongside Neanderthal flint tools. Human use spans from the Middle Paleolithic through the Upper Paleolithic.
descriptions.7c5f9b35-8195-4121-83b7-f2192a87e1fb: A field of fallen Aksumite stelae from the 4th–6th century AD, across the road from a large mansion. The monoliths once stood upright as grave markers for Aksumite royalty.
descriptions.ad30767a-8eb8-4ec1-a174-45f1e7399c05: An Iron Age site yielding vast gold treasures and evidence of a likely royal palace from the 3rd–6th century AD. The name itself means "Home of the Gods."
descriptions.d1a6a883-779d-47eb-8496-78fbb360ddd6: Human remains carbon-dated to 10,610 BC found here; use continued from 8000 BC onward. Cultivated beans and peppers from this cave document early plant domestication in the Americas.
descriptions.3b65586c-f850-4b57-b11d-199a8c77ed86: A 2nd-century Kushan stupa built of rough stone and mud on a hilltop summit. Gold coins of kings Vima Kadphises and Huvishka were found sealed inside.
descriptions.c88af005-464d-4b81-857b-d94db6b3e45a: A mountain city so well fortified that Alexander the Great chose not to besiege it. The theatre, tombs, and city walls cling to steep cliffs at high altitude.
descriptions.158bcd5a-1203-4ddf-a640-d86ee5c47e66: Buddhist caves from the 3rd–2nd century BC that may pre-date the famous Ajanta and Ellora caves. Stupas, viharas, and a chaitya hall are carved into the rock.
descriptions.8a66f7db-94df-45d9-919f-760b966192be: A megalithic site built atop an extinct volcano. Carbon dating has produced controversial results suggesting construction 9,000 to 20,000 years ago — a claim hotly debated.
descriptions.ece8c6c5-0934-4817-b30d-cc3c0e27899e: A headland shaped like a gurnard fish holds a promontory fort on Penwith's north coast. Pottery from 1100 BC marks the earliest occupation, with use continuing well into the Roman period.
descriptions.27330a46-8900-4b3b-9094-1910364284bf: Cliff-face caves carved into a valley wall near Dongmenying, Yanqing, formed dwellings for a fortified community. The identity of the builders and the reason for abandonment remain unknown.
descriptions.d661105f-26e9-4cea-b868-20c58ee3c52c: The ruins of the Silla Kingdom spanning the 2nd to 10th century AD — temples, palaces, and pagodas spread across a landscape sometimes called the world's largest outdoor museum.
descriptions.71e7014b-7bc3-4c1b-9f10-884e4805c6e8: The 4th-century BC training grounds at Delphi where athletes prepared for the Pythian Games. A covered running track and palaestra with baths served competitors and spectators.
descriptions.753a8b5b-669c-4062-b935-93e619291597: Named in Homer's Iliad and confirmed by Livy as one day's march from Phalanna. Between the Titaresius and Peneius rivers, it controlled the plains approaching the Vale of Tempe.
descriptions.ccaa2834-9ed2-4ae3-91e1-cf85e846d76d: A Roman fort along Dere Street, the military highway from York into Scotland. An altar found here records the name of a consular beneficiary stationed at the garrison.
descriptions.49cd7035-b70c-4991-b776-e5ae204ad8c5: A Neolithic dolmen measuring 3.25 by 2.95 metres and a tumulus nearby — both listed as historical monuments. The dolmen is known locally as the Dolmen des Bignes.
descriptions.43486bc0-4ffa-4420-ba63-482ebf306e8b: A Greco-Buddhist site where 23,000 sculptures blending Greek and Buddhist art were excavated. Civil war destroyed nearly all of it — one of archaeology's greatest losses.
descriptions.3ea6db8c-1b6a-4880-a954-b929302e8260: A late-antique defensive wall stretching 1.6 km across a valley to block invaders. Only 336 metres survive, with rooms for defenders built into its western face.
descriptions.d9436555-2b92-49fd-b4d7-605aeda17684: A city founded by Emperor Hadrian and later rebuilt by Justinian, who renamed it after himself. A small Roman theatre and Byzantine fortress ruins mark the site.
descriptions.d93c6643-5381-4887-84f6-3445ea0edef5: A triumphal arch of white marble built in 130 AD for Emperor Hadrian, standing 8 metres tall. Three passage arches are decorated with floral rosettes above granite pillars.
descriptions.f7a88213-58c1-4ee4-b791-4babfa0cd67a: A stone wall stretching 117 km coast to coast, begun in 122 AD. Forts, milecastles, and turrets garrisoned the entire length of the Roman frontier.
descriptions.360a4afb-9c39-427b-bed1-9b0201a59ae5: A 135-kilometre national trail following the Roman frontier wall from coast to coast. Part of the "Frontiers of the Roman Empire" World Heritage Site.
descriptions.833d2de9-5bc4-425d-b5a5-111d742c8f0d: A 345-metre-long cave with Paleolithic deposits and a narrow, high entrance 40 metres above the river. It served as both a prehistoric shelter and a later hiding place for rebels.
descriptions.b367310b-a211-40b3-b376-80e9da0fdd32: A compact Neolithic dolmen from 3400 BC with four uprights, a roof slab, and a threshold stone. Small in size but perfectly preserved on its island setting.
descriptions.fffac2f9-3115-47be-9830-f5969cce734b: A 1000 BC burial mound 7 metres high and 45 metres across — Scandinavia's most gold-rich Bronze Age grave. The mound was built of turf over a cairn, once at the sea's edge.
descriptions.31cb23a8-36ad-4fdc-8fe8-cfca39285d66: A megalithic temple complex from 3600–3200 BC built of soft Globigerina limestone. Millennia of weathering have severely eroded its surfaces, giving it a melted appearance.
descriptions.a2ceca93-fe33-44a6-abe3-de8c41424997: A fortified Minoan building with 37 rooms opening onto a central court. Its fortification walls are notable because so few Minoan settlements had visible military defenses.
descriptions.bbfd5685-5e03-4a18-8625-9435c4cf8e7b: A Minoan settlement with a "Royal Villa" near the palace of Phaistos. It yielded the famous Harvester Vase and a trove of Linear A tablets that remain undeciphered.
descriptions.84894867-d7b1-49b7-a1e7-398e73a725f2: Four Neo-Assyrian bas-reliefs from 704–681 BC carved into a cliff face, each showing a procession of nine figures — the king before the great gods of Assyria.
descriptions.bb3b9abe-cc92-4e02-b56f-45531e8d9666: An Iron Age village continuously occupied for 500 years, with entrance graves, field systems, and standing stones also on site. A rare intact prehistoric landscape.
descriptions.14f64a8d-97b4-4d86-9b1f-187a126febb8: A Roman municipium covering 3 square kilometres with a square ground plan, founded in the 1st century AD. The site was closed for protection after recent excavations.
descriptions.569f53de-6821-4597-b4f3-f695504b9d60: The largest surviving fogou in Cornwall — an underground dry-stone passage from the Iron Age whose original purpose remains a mystery. Storage, shelter, or ritual? Nobody knows.
descriptions.544c05a7-3614-43b8-bf63-a158622e5fdb: A Neolithic underground temple hewn from living rock on three levels, holding the remains of over 7,000 people. The "Oracle Room" produces eerie acoustic resonance.
descriptions.ef037940-91c4-4abe-907e-540c8ca22b05: Positioned at 185 metres on a pass between two hilltops near Halwell in Devon, this fort controlled movement through the natural gap. Bank and ditch encircle the pass summit.
descriptions.5e710f8a-fc74-40b6-ab42-424a3ded4713: Wedged between Southampton Water and the River Hamble, this promontory fort commanded both waterways. Henry VIII later chose the same spot for one of his Device Forts — St Andrews Castle.
descriptions.e50a076d-5550-4c47-a49b-aced289dd4e0: A Neolithic hilltop with paired causewayed enclosures from around 3500 BC, later converted into an Iron Age hillfort. Skeletons with arrowheads suggest violent attack.
descriptions.970633a9-5402-4221-af0e-1fefc6c8a427: 85 hectares of earthworks on Ham Hill — the largest enclosed hillfort in the country, and the only one with a pub inside its ramparts. Occupation spans the Mesolithic through the Medieval period.
descriptions.d6ca1bdf-173c-4659-b1fc-c9fb7259c5a3: Ham Hill's golden hamstone — quarried here since Roman times — has built much of Somerset's vernacular architecture. The hill itself is also a geological SSSI, a nature reserve, and a country park.
descriptions.9212f10a-d866-4d70-bb38-0cbffc49a2c5: Roman baths from the Flavian Dynasty (69–96 AD) fed by natural hot springs in the Aurès Mountains. The thermal waters still flow after nearly 2,000 years.
descriptions.082935cc-6367-40a7-86e5-dd01e0be5b1c: A ring of stones at 207 metres on a Dorset downland ridge — either a Bronze Age stone circle or kerbstones from a lost round barrow. Archaeologists still debate which explanation fits the evidence.
descriptions.d70e4239-42cb-4c8d-8def-f4bffb35d38f: A settlement site that yielded over 12,000 bird bones, documenting species driven to extinction by the first Polynesian settlers. Nearly 10,000 bones were from shearwaters alone.
descriptions.7fdaa528-53ef-44f1-81b0-c2112c2c1fdd: The name-giving site of the Harappan civilization, with ruins of a fortified Bronze Age city from around 2500 BC. At its peak, the Indus Valley civilization rivaled Egypt and Mesopotamia.
descriptions.4cdbbcf7-6cdf-4295-be70-8f77b1e92bf4: A Roman fort built on a mountain pass between 120 and 138 AD, garrisoned by troops from the Dalmatian coast. A parade ground leveled into the steep hillside still survives.
descriptions.d7c375d0-6ddc-42ed-a3d4-f128c3c1d89f: Dating to 3000 BC, this Funnelbeaker dolmen near Keitum was moved stone by stone in 1954 when an airport displaced it. Of roughly 600 such graves once on this island, half survive.
descriptions.174016a6-75a8-416d-b0e5-e316b4f96330: Three Bronze Age standing stones give the village of Trellech its name — "three stones" in the local language. The tallest exceeds 4 metres; local legend credits a giant with placing them.
descriptions.85a15fe0-fbb8-4072-b73a-7345fbe6f9dc: A Neolithic flint mine with about 245 shafts and pits covering 8 hectares. Miners dug up to 6 metres deep using antler picks to extract flint for polished stone axes.
descriptions.c06cb387-e065-4bcd-bbbe-a6b9d1a4082d: From Seaton in Devon to Dover in Kent, with finds dated to 600–450 BC and use stretching back to the Stone Age. Its eastern segment was rebranded the Pilgrims' Way in the 19th century.
descriptions.eb752f57-8327-43bc-b6c4-98fa1f0a7ac2: The only Neolithic gallery grave of its type in the entire region, dating to about 3000 BC. Two sandstone-slab chambers were built into the slope of the Hartberg.
descriptions.3d7dc21f-40f1-4ca1-883c-769a1856c578: Occupied in the 1st century BC, with naturally steep slopes scarped to near-vertical at the crest. The hillfort encloses 2.4 heavily wooded hectares above Hascombe village.
descriptions.20f27e8d-091e-41c2-9640-936e5833178c: A Bronze Age hoard from 1700 BC found inside a large bronze cauldron: two Hallstatt swords, bronze buckets, and twelve large circular bronze plates with iron fittings.
descriptions.7e33b1ac-bb32-4b6c-b070-2c4fdcaf19fb: The Hittite imperial capital with over 6 km of walls, decorated gateways with relief-carved lions and sphinxes, and a massive royal citadel. A Bronze Age superpower's seat of government.
descriptions.109fcdea-c114-4143-87ac-77c4c9c20f16: Hittite imperial capital from the 19th century BC, on a site settled since the 6th millennium BC. Modern identification restored knowledge of an empire whose existence had been entirely forgotten.
descriptions.261ab0dd-0674-4864-9162-87b179787403: A rock forest at 4,200 metres altitude with archaeological remains including rock paintings. Towering natural stone formations create a surreal landscape of corridors and chambers.
descriptions.eef7317f-a250-434f-b34d-7933fd546da7: A Late Bronze Age hilltop enclosure from 1100–900 BC, 350 metres wide, surrounded by two concentric ditches. A massive timber structure once stood inside the inner enclosure.
descriptions.41bb2c5e-4eb3-4bdf-8d1e-6ea497c44b26: A Celtic hillfort from the 4th century BC with a partially reconstructed wooden palisade and a Druid-style sanctuary. A medieval wooden castle was later built on the same hill.
descriptions.29074533-09e3-4f7b-9d43-dbffbf8a0a32: Roughly 130 metres above the Axe Estuary near Axmouth, this hillfort commands clear sightlines over land and sea. The earthworks follow a prominent hillside above the river mouth.
descriptions.cc06fd9c-ce49-49ae-bfb1-4b3b6d05a0bc: A pre-Aksumite obelisk bearing the oldest known example of the Ge'ez script — the ancestor of the writing system still used in the Horn of Africa today.
descriptions.9a941093-043f-4287-b188-aebddd81df62: A pair of Neolithic barrows of the Cotswold-Severn type, one of which was completely excavated. The excavation revealed the full construction sequence of a 5,000-year-old burial mound.
descriptions.88b99e63-3075-4fef-9d90-91a8c1f7e62b: An ancient Illyrian city that served as the capital of the Daesitiates tribe. Today only a basilica and some grave tombs remain of what was once an "Inhabited Castle."
descriptions.ab20e4ad-f101-4b3d-84fb-c0710060c941: A massive sarsen stone standing 4.7 metres high outside the Stonehenge earthwork, leaning nearly 27 degrees to the southwest. It aligns with the midsummer sunrise.
descriptions.2e974e22-9f31-4d6c-a258-0195f444f533: A circular ditch surrounding the Heel Stone at Stonehenge, about 1.2 metres deep. Whether the ditch and the stone were planned together or built separately is still unknown.
descriptions.285a2a92-7213-48ca-b4d9-fd157697e096: Beneath this Roman bathhouse town lay a Michelsberg ditch from 4400 BC — a rare find in the Low Countries. The 1997 Schelsberg dig produced almost no regional parallels for this period.
descriptions.47eb07cd-5c1c-4c0e-88c0-484d3b3411a1: The Nabataean kingdom's second city after Petra, with 131 monumental rock-cut tombs from the 1st century AD. Many still bear carved inscriptions in their original paint.
descriptions.287a5d74-480a-4c9e-a1d8-7c9ad96e31ec: The largest Celtic oppidum in mainland Europe, spanning 1,600 hectares of fortified plateau. Its massive earthwork ditches enclosed an entire community in the 2nd century BC.
descriptions.df6aa58a-16ff-416f-9112-75f8e2ea5c11: A 2.5 km Celtic ringwall from 500 BC, built as a Murus Gallicus with timber-laced stonework. It was deliberately demolished shortly after construction -- no one knows why.
descriptions.a228ae71-4a7e-4fb5-b773-cee87ffc946b: A 4th-century Roman triumphal arch that once had four massive arched openings. Only one arch survives, standing alone as a gateway to nowhere.
descriptions.7726fc99-c992-490d-a1ee-85e4755975fe: A Celtic oppidum ringed by 10 km of ramparts with six gates, protecting both sides of a deep ravine. Agricultural tools and coins show a thriving Iron Age economy.
descriptions.dfed1a81-7d54-4f3b-b1ab-e2be649acc2f: A double-walled Celtic hill fort from the 4th century BC, reused as a Roman sacred precinct and medieval monastery. Four thousand years of continuous ritual use.
descriptions.cb95c838-ea7e-485c-8c7f-4f00427c04e1: A trading hub from 200 AD, five centuries older than nearby Birka. Its workshops yielded a Buddha statue, an Irish crozier, and Coptic ladles from Egypt.
descriptions.1f34f490-a5ef-462d-961e-e4bbd8eb5422: A Hellenistic theatre from the 4th century BC, later expanded by the Romans. Carved into limestone in a city that was a center of Aphrodite worship for centuries.
descriptions.be150a09-409e-4594-b576-c3999e31227b: The largest structure in the sacred city of Dion, this 3rd-century BC theatre seated thousands at the foot of Mount Olympus. It still hosts summer performances today.
descriptions.3bcff938-2352-4ea8-872f-3655fb444c87: Badly botched in the 19th century, this 3400 BC Portesham Hill dolmen had its stones haphazardly re-erected. The burial chamber originally sat at the end of a 24-metre mound.
descriptions.5908e9f0-9f7f-43ee-8fd8-7ac446fd46c7: A Greek colony of Syracuse in the 4th century BC. Its ruins were still visible to Renaissance travelers before vanishing under farmland.
descriptions.ce525bf9-3005-4e2b-9985-ae0037cff99f: An Iron Age cliff fort where natural sandstone cliffs form a semicircular defense on two sides. Double ramparts and a sand-and-rubble wall protected the rest.
descriptions.786c39f1-9944-4733-93c5-4d465f5f7767: Occupied from the 5th millennium BC through the Roman invasion -- over 4,000 years of use. Its Neolithic causewayed enclosure is among the earliest in Britain.
descriptions.e1037d75-2eb6-4076-b28c-86f8159320ab: Triple ramparts enclosed nearly 3 hectares on this Dartmoor promontory, 178 metres above the valley where the River Dart and Holy Brook converge. Natural water boundaries guard every approach.
descriptions.296ed0f4-1ad0-4929-b019-196c80e547be: A prehistoric petroglyph carved with an intricate swastika-like maze pattern unique in rock art. Its meaning and the identity of its makers remain unknown.
descriptions.ae519f45-f80c-4464-8f76-e9d986803c34: Two massive quartz-rich boulders over 4 metres tall with a collapsed capstone between them. This Neolithic dolmen dates to the 5th millennium BC.
descriptions.6f3193fc-ec11-4999-baf1-2dfa1695b2ec: Called Hen Gaer — Old Castle — this compact hillfort near Ceredigion is smaller than a typical tribal fortification. Its single rampart, cut from solid rock, stands 12 metres wide and 4 metres high.
descriptions.b38b0f66-79cb-40db-9881-215e01196d2b: Occupied since the 3rd millennium BC, this headland served as a major Iron Age port trading with Gaul. Purple dye production here rivaled Mediterranean workshops.
descriptions.b67a72ea-cdd7-4feb-9847-aee79adcd9be: Stone Age settlement traces along this river valley include a rare Acheulean hand axe -- a tool type spanning over a million years of human evolution.
descriptions.0017f6df-44e0-4b24-ac21-0565406e1210: Established 432 BC between the Agri and Sinni rivers, this Magna Graecia city hosted the 272 BC treaty with Rome. The Tabulae Heracleenses — bronze tablets of Roman land law — were found here.
descriptions.9116c105-f7ac-4f02-8ea4-b724c68c9464: Founded by Philip II near modern Bitola, this ancient city became an Episcopal seat on the Via Egnatia. Its 5th-6th century floor mosaics rank with the finest in the Balkans.
descriptions.6846c284-a6af-4a0a-86ea-0d59f0b1e498: Wedged between Carthaginian and Hellenic spheres at the Platani River mouth, this Sicilian city changed hands from the 6th century BC. Theatre and residential quarters remain partially intact.
descriptions.dc51894b-cc2c-4d5d-81ae-955eb846326f: A Thracian-Macedonian city with tunnels, arches, and a studio for ceramic masks for an unknown ancient theatre. Its street grid follows Hippodamian planning.
descriptions.4c40a3eb-e009-4b8b-b507-18053a6538a1: A 6th-century BC Greek sanctuary to Hera with carved metopes depicting myths. The river has shifted the coastline 2 km since the temple was built.
descriptions.a12d37a7-29a7-40d8-947d-68b69ae30eb1: The greatest sanctuary in the Argolid, dedicated to Hera from 800 BC. Its builders imitated Mycenaean Cyclopean masonry -- a style already 500 years old.
descriptions.9d9d94a0-f338-4392-860f-983c29fabb16: A sanctuary of Hera from the 9th century BC with an L-shaped stoa, a large cistern, and dining rooms. Its unusual temple design has no close parallels.
descriptions.7be75434-ab13-4f9b-883d-3897bb86cb47: Home to the first gigantic free-standing Ionic temple ever built, in the 8th century BC. It was rebuilt three times, each larger than the last.
descriptions.feb1899e-d74e-4f5f-b22e-1fe3ff5c1f8e: Buried by Vesuvius in 79 AD under 20 metres of volcanic material -- far deeper than Pompeii. The extreme heat carbonized wooden furniture, food, and entire libraries.
descriptions.fdc3a783-3b1a-473a-bf22-8510308e0054: Herod built this desert fortress on a man-made mountain, then had himself buried inside it. The palace, bathhouse, and his tomb all survive within the cone-shaped hill.
descriptions.e7c32c5c-3f26-483a-9d49-75ad5003c44b: A Roman settlement with stone buildings and a quayside cut into bedrock. Industrial furnaces from the 1st century show it was a manufacturing hub, not just a town.
descriptions.aba8058b-c938-4e75-ac3f-79ce2777e95f: A shrine to the infant hero Opheltes, whose mythic death may have inspired the founding of the Nemean Games. Cult activity here dates to the 6th century BC.
descriptions.05d4e028-3cd3-46e8-ad35-aaaf70a3077c: A 380 BC Lycian tomb whose wall was covered in 152 carved stone panels depicting Greek myths. The entire frieze was removed to Vienna in 1882.
descriptions.e6ec727e-8e27-4885-b2bb-a9aadd8f17c9: A Neolithic ritual center from 5300 BC with scattered remains of over 1,000 people from distant communities. The bones show signs of systematic defleshing.
descriptions.fadd9ef3-4d6a-4a8b-8b2a-250388ee531d: Mud-brick walls in Mediterranean style on a 7th–5th century BC Danube hillfort — 2,500 years before such construction was standard north of the Alps. A major early Celtic center.
descriptions.f5893102-13b9-44a0-bc87-8348f7da115c: The oldest known stone fortification north of the Alps, dating to the 9th century BC. It guarded a Bronze Age copper and tin trade route through the mountains.
descriptions.fcc36c87-27e6-48cb-a701-c0188e545c6e: Ravensburgh Castle, an Iron Age fort near this village, enclosed 9 hectares with massive double ditches. Roman silver coins hint at continued use after the conquest.
descriptions.197ce800-a003-49e9-b797-3e029f766520: A 14-metre Roman tower from the 2nd century AD with a circular body on a square base. Seljuk and Ottoman-era repairs are visible in the upper stonework.
descriptions.4ce83e01-a19d-40d0-a739-d6b571b9e824: Built over a Phrygian cult center of the goddess Cybele, this Greco-Roman city sits atop hot springs that create surreal white travertine terraces.
descriptions.b612f959-939d-44be-852b-86e9b34ee902: Hidden in woodland on a narrow ridge, this univallate fort covers 3 hectares with an 8-metre-wide ditch. Roman silver coins found inside suggest use extended well beyond the Iron Age.
descriptions.4063671e-4cb4-405c-b5af-f7d0e9bd922b: A Bronze Age site from 1000 BC overlaid by an Anglo-Saxon cemetery. Glass vessels and gold jewelry from the graves reveal far-reaching trade networks.
descriptions.1da76491-5256-486f-b67e-ff6f762c46b5: An Iron Age cliff fort being eaten alive by coastal erosion. Pre-Roman, Roman, and Dark Age pottery all found at the same crumbling site.
descriptions.7b8f41e0-5e48-4247-8fc4-33863cb2af59: A Roman road that crosses a summit at 828 metres -- the highest Roman road in all of the country. It connected forts at Brougham and Ambleside.
descriptions.f4388f7e-a59e-45a0-bf56-44a5f75a4ff5: A Bronze Age site with tombs and a reconstructed 12-metre tower tomb from the Umm al-Nar culture. 3,000-year-old fingerprints survive on a wall.
descriptions.19bf579e-21fe-47f0-80b0-20e1fa747a8b: Two linear banks and ditches cut off the headland locals call 'the sleeping elephant.' This coastal promontory fort at Ilfracombe commands views across the Bristol Channel.
descriptions.5c4b2afd-f915-4625-a841-790460fddef5: Founded in 648 BC as the first Greek colony on Sicily's north coast, at the frontier of Carthaginian territory. The Battle of Himera in 480 BC changed Western history.
descriptions.58d2d752-30cc-4f22-b2d5-ff27a4b395d1: Two funerary hypogea from 2300 BC with chambers carved into rock and megalithic stone-slab corridors. Among the oldest rock-cut tombs on the Balearic Islands.
descriptions.60bee552-5606-4c54-806c-c6e69f03229d: A fortified Bronze Age settlement inhabited almost continuously from the Neolithic to Ottoman times. Iron-processing remains include grinders, furnaces, and slag heaps.
descriptions.3d166b88-6f0c-4634-8eb0-03abf17decb6: A Thracian town that became one of three top Roman cities in its province. Known by four different names across its history, including Diocletianopolis.
descriptions.51e6e482-0301-4200-9719-17e8b548a8db: Once a Punic trading post then a Roman base, this site stacks Phoenician, Roman, palaeochristian, and Byzantine remains. The nearby Kbor er Roumia — a royal Berber mausoleum — looms over all.
descriptions.e8ef9219-a255-457a-8f69-f365b1741038: An open-air museum with reconstructed Bronze Age longhouses where livestock and humans shared a single roof. A burial hut and pit-house complete the village.
descriptions.5ca2f8d6-0077-4fe6-9034-18308bb4a4d1: An ellipse of 38 to 40 dolerite stones, this is the only intact survivor of up to five circles that once stood on the Shropshire-Powys border. The others were destroyed or buried over the centuries.
descriptions.456ddcd7-75de-4626-b009-3172c196249d: Rectangular rather than round, this Bronze Age barrow on Beeley Moor breaks the standard burial mold. Built with 13 stones, only five survive on this exposed moorland edge.
descriptions.6bb8492b-2731-4f5a-8b48-4eb6b3b851f8: A Celtic chieftain buried in 530 BC on a 3-metre bronze couch with gold shoes and a gold torc. The 60-metre burial mound had shrunk to 1 metre before excavation.
descriptions.138608de-dc36-4805-b2eb-23e47359b1b9: A Maya city with facades shaped as giant stone masks of the god Itzamna, whose gaping jaws form the doorways. Pure Chenes-style architecture from around 800 AD.
descriptions.87dcefc2-025d-458b-9418-16e4bac7d17f: A 22-hectare Iron Age fort that the Romans stormed around 44 AD, then built their own fort inside. Ballista bolt holes in hut floors mark the assault.
descriptions.f0b786ae-17e0-4ce1-bfdc-c9184e5473a3: A 40,000-year-old ivory lion-headed figurine — the Löwenmensch — was carved from mammoth tusk in this Swabian Jura cave. It ranks among the earliest figurative sculptures ever recovered.
descriptions.7968021c-6036-45f7-96ee-2b8e198a8040: Perched at the southern tip of a coastal sandy spit, this fort is enclosed by tidal wetlands and dunes. Access on foot is nearly impossible — only a distant bird hide offers a view.
descriptions.13ef0bad-6c23-44d4-a5b6-d47ff146c84d: This square hillfort, 6th century BC, has inturned entrance gates and a single bank-and-ditch perimeter. Bronze axes from a millennium earlier show the hilltop was long in use.
descriptions.df612ef7-118e-442d-a451-e39062607faf: Straddling the Herefordshire-Worcestershire border at 242 metres, this fort spans two Malvern Hills summits. Its earthwork ramparts commanded wide corridors across the surrounding valley landscape.
descriptions.99add2bd-b314-4bb9-885b-95f407b3b44e: A wooded Surrey hillfort at 261 metres, dated to the late Iron Age on pottery evidence. Later research pushed the occupation back earlier than first thought.
descriptions.9705b676-7ba1-465f-aebd-a21f346de5a1: Iron Age stone huts with walls so thick they rival medieval construction. The site spans from the Bronze Age into the Roman period with no clear break.
descriptions.b797259e-3000-4217-b0cb-b5ace91112ea: Prehistoric timber piles from 1523 BC mark a lake crossing rebuilt as a bridge for 3,500 years. The current wooden footbridge continues the tradition.
descriptions.532df28e-27f6-4391-8167-bc139f303b3b: At 3,500 metres in the Ancash Callejón de Huaylas, this Wari-culture site has never been fully mapped. Its extent across the highland terrain remains incompletely documented.
descriptions.fc43c928-7377-4cc6-b0cc-2cd8941f4c08: Known as 'The Seven Stones of Hordron,' this Moscar Moor circle originally held around 26 stones — now seven visible, three concealed. The surviving ring measures roughly 16 metres across.
descriptions.b803b66a-768d-4040-bdac-6176611241da: Type-site of the Horgen culture, 3500–2850 BC, on the south bank of Lake Zurich. Its crude, undecorated pottery links it to the Seine-Oise-Marne culture of northern France.
descriptions.b987ab73-469a-4c3a-9c38-bfe90d05db82: A Roman villa whose large floor mosaic was found by laborers in 1797. The mosaics remained in situ for 130 years before being moved to a museum.
descriptions.bdc47035-70e0-4126-b9f0-698d294c7cc9: A Roman walled town not on any major road -- the River Bain was its main highway. A section of the ancient walls still stands after nearly 2,000 years.
descriptions.37cf1fab-1b40-486a-88ab-c480d323c995: A Bronze Age through Urartian fortress with unique architecture spanning over 2,000 years. Potters' kilns and storage vessels reveal a self-sufficient citadel.
descriptions.4b3024e4-d801-49ab-b0c4-d496090cee40: A Roman temple from 20 BC, likely built by Herod to honor Emperor Augustus. The 363 AD Galilee earthquake leveled it; a Byzantine chapel rose on its ruins.
descriptions.0025b0ba-fd74-4c08-96e3-acc17956aa44: Ruins of a large Jewish village from the Roman-Byzantine period, with an ancient synagogue and mausoleum. It may be the lost town of Teqoa of Galilee.
descriptions.ba2e2b75-be17-4c77-9f6c-b0cd4d282aa5: A 3rd-century AD Roman temple perched on a hill in the Beqaa Valley. Part of a complex blending Roman imperial religion with local Phoenician traditions.
descriptions.5b182764-5cd3-4a91-92ae-5cdcc2d6f245: A megalithic tomb from 3500 BC in the Forest of Broceliande, steeped in Arthurian legend. Local tradition calls it the fairy Viviane's prison for Merlin.
descriptions.3b04e370-3686-477d-a5c1-f1a6f7123c5f: A medieval village built atop Bronze Age farmland on Dartmoor. Abandoned around the 14th century, its stone longhouse foundations stand at 340 metres elevation.
descriptions.d2a5b201-c0b4-4e6e-a59a-7ada41de0099: A 4th-century Roman villa with mosaic floors so exceptional they are considered unique in all of ancient art. Only three rooms have been excavated so far.
descriptions.b25ebe2e-145f-403c-8f6a-e26cdb57050e: A Roman villa with 556 square metres of mosaic floors depicting Dionysus, hunting scenes, and mythology. A Hellenistic pebble mosaic lies hidden beneath.
descriptions.5e73f7ad-ee05-4eaa-bea0-bb66eb0abe9d: After the 62 AD earthquake damaged Pompeii, the owner converted this grand estate into rental apartments and a public bath. Buried by Vesuvius 17 years later.
descriptions.0865287a-1a0b-497a-aabb-de0131b3da61: A Pompeii house with frescoes of the Iliad and Trojan cycle, all in a unified Fourth Style. Named after a prince who attended the 1898 excavation ceremony.
descriptions.41fe2b17-a443-443d-be09-9c643fd4b05c: One of the richest houses in Pompeii, with private baths, a fish pond, and two atria. Built in 250 BC, it grew for three centuries before Vesuvius froze it.
descriptions.469a11d9-f643-4a16-a4d5-bd02ffa78850: One of Pompeii's oldest houses, with parts dating to the 4th century BC. Its long evolution provides key evidence about how elite Roman homes developed over time.
descriptions.45ac8925-95ec-476a-9a36-9bbb650add84: Latte stone pillars quarried 1.2 km away, from a site occupied as early as 10,000 BC. Only one pillar still stands upright after centuries of earthquakes.
descriptions.5b0337e9-12a4-4a14-a059-56a6602b3489: Among the largest houses in Pompeii, with private baths, a swimming pool, and two atria. A remodeling around 15 AD added the bath complex before the eruption.
descriptions.5752ff6c-ce00-4b78-aad7-f80a4d61c4e7: The grandest house in Republican Pompeii, covering an entire city block. Its Alexander Mosaic depicts the clash between Alexander the Great and Darius III.
descriptions.4014b1e9-bf5f-42b9-bb06-c7e940b84be5: Named for wall paintings inscribed with Greek epigrams, this Pompeii house was created by merging two older dwellings. Over twenty painted panels decorated its rooms.
descriptions.58a5a5b2-735a-4fda-bf2d-52e723fd86bc: Part of Roman Volubilis, this house preserves a floor mosaic of Bacchus and Ariadne. The city thrived as a Roman outpost at the edge of the Sahara.
descriptions.8484a13c-bf95-4bbd-bb4b-62d5033a4db8: A Pompeii house decorated entirely in the Fourth Style from a single period -- a rarity, since most houses mix styles from different centuries.
descriptions.f59ecbfb-c882-4ae2-8f30-8e979f49b266: Built around 300 BC and renovated in the early imperial period, this Pompeii house has a grand classical atrium with fine frescoes and proportions that impressed 19th-century excavators.
descriptions.3f08e508-839c-4735-bc93-7a1f2296e354: Created by merging two Samnite houses, this Pompeii dwelling features a mosaic fountain adorned with shells at the rear of its double-atrium layout.
descriptions.fa363304-5e02-42f3-b0f6-f38e44c57ebd: Named after ancient surgical instruments found inside, this Pompeii house has a sturdy ashlar facade of Sarno stone. Modest in size but built to last.
descriptions.655898a6-3d5c-40f3-8411-e6b3b185f11f: A two-story Early Bronze Age building from 2500 BC with baked clay roof tiles -- among the earliest tiled roofs in the world. The tiles gave it its modern name.
descriptions.0675d36c-5ce2-40a3-867c-4d2e14069fc6: Famous for its "Cave Canem" (beware of dog) mosaic and over twenty mythological wall panels. It inspired a pivotal scene in a 19th-century novel about Pompeii.
descriptions.61d7e44d-2cf4-4b54-84e6-7f1bc9cf911e: Owned by two wealthy freedmen -- former slaves turned rich merchants. Wall frescoes completed after the 62 AD earthquake are among Pompeii's best preserved.
descriptions.2726f1bb-9af6-4f23-af79-fc0f789a5ddc: Built in stone around 124 AD, this auxiliary fort on Hadrian's Wall housed up to 800 infantry. Its communal latrines — stone benches over a flushing sewer — survive in remarkable condition.
descriptions.0f91c646-480e-43af-a2c1-cb417fd10e89: A prehistoric mound 54 metres wide containing Bronze Age barrows and tumuli. Today the hill hosts annual free-speech rallies on Constitution Day.
descriptions.de97fdf7-80cc-425c-9c5b-b26b03310155: Post holes, hearths, and charred hazelnut shells mark this Northumberland cliff camp, dated to 7600 BC. Structural evidence points to repeated seasonal occupation over many generations.
descriptions.82c9fb95-c776-4450-bb5c-93a70fdcb056: A cave pit 60 metres deep holds a mastodon skeleton alongside a human skull dated to around 13,000 years ago. The remains rank among the earliest human fossils found in the Americas.
descriptions.d765c593-eb36-4978-b73f-534333b85bda: An adobe platform pyramid about 36 metres square, with occupations from the Moche period through the Inca conquest. Built from rammed earth and sun-dried brick.
descriptions.96235e5c-656a-41c4-8017-902d9353d2b6: A Moche adobe temple from 100-700 AD with polychrome murals on every surface. Six building phases are stacked inside, each with its own painted walls.
descriptions.b0b4e4d6-ef79-4b2d-ad6b-62532b5ba54d: An adobe temple whose walls are carved with dragon and rainbow friezes in relief. Two ramps connect its levels, flanked by figures that gave the temple its name.
descriptions.22415177-5658-4973-ab15-ddad22663cde: An adobe pyramid built from an estimated 143 million bricks in eight construction phases by 450 AD. Once the largest adobe structure in the Americas.
descriptions.2c437fa8-96cf-4451-b949-7e5c09889802: A Chimu adobe palace from around 900 AD with three terraces covered in zoomorphic and geometric friezes. Linked to the capital Chan Chan during the empire's rise.
descriptions.db227639-34b4-45db-817c-95092b4a916a: An adobe pyramid now surrounded by a modern city district. A rare surviving Inca-period huaca hidden in plain sight among residential streets.
descriptions.58aaa531-5cb7-409c-b0a4-755faf668c9e: A truncated Ichma-culture pyramid rebuilt over centuries, creating layers of patios, corridors, and enclosures. Each era left its own architectural stamp.
descriptions.e21d32e0-beba-4e70-9a7f-2a56cf70a476: A mound of ash, stones, textiles, and shells with occupation from 12,500 BC. Some of the oldest known woven textiles in the Americas come from this site.
descriptions.9066c343-918a-45ca-b449-b3642e924c2b: A seven-tiered adobe pyramid built by the Lima culture around 200-700 AD. Elite clergy who governed surrounding valleys used it for religious ceremonies.
descriptions.612ff287-3919-4ae9-bb6b-50ea7548b64b: Mountain ruins at 4,150 metres elevation, one of countless unnamed Andean sites still waiting for systematic study. Its builders and purpose remain undocumented.
descriptions.3f5089f0-0b0d-45c8-908c-9155de71c6b3: An early Postclassic city built on leveled terraces at 2,850 metres. Structures include a palace, an altar, and a wall, rich in ancestral Otomi traditions.
descriptions.ff4dc88e-bebe-4b88-90d3-6697bffc9107: An Inca-period site in the remote Cusco highlands, perched on the banks of the Luq'umayu river. Its purpose and builders remain poorly documented.
descriptions.62ea668a-68e5-41fe-93ed-3429127d6b4c: A Purepecha ceremonial center from 1200 AD that functioned until the Spanish conquest in 1536. Evidence of 10,000 years of habitation surrounds the site.
descriptions.4a4e2c30-8a8f-4b7d-8e7c-c0e837b94760: Modeled on Cusco itself -- one of six "New Cuscos" the Incas built across their empire. Over 4,000 buildings spread across 2 square kilometres of plateau.
descriptions.a744c90a-9a6a-4c23-ae16-ce84becaaa9a: Cave paintings roughly 13,000 years old share this Hidalgo site with a three-bodied Teotihuacan-style pyramid. The complex spans nearly 15 millennia of continuous human presence.
descriptions.23286e8a-3777-4e5f-b554-33c75c736633: Capital of the Wari Empire from 400–1000 AD, this city 22 km from Ayacucho covered a larger area than any earlier Andean urban center. Its stone and mudbrick buildings were painted red and white.
descriptions.58175827-2670-44ef-8eda-609467be08f1: The mountain towering 260 metres above Machu Picchu, with Inca temples and terraces on its peak. The steep trail to the summit is a sacred ascent.
descriptions.8d114f26-1360-4e96-a34a-cbe4415edb71: An Inca royal estate at 3,650 metres overlooking the Sacred Valley. Known as "Little Cuzco," it was built by Emperor Viracocha around 1420 AD.
descriptions.f21ef7bb-7a5b-4877-83cd-e7fb1b45e080: At the mouth of the Odiel and Tinto rivers, this Phoenician colony dates to the 9th century BC. Bronze Age copper trading through its harbor made it a metallurgical hub centuries before Rome.
descriptions.7e97d2a5-3f87-44fc-9ad0-f0d5a2d84cab: A rocky butte used by the Hohokam from around 1100 AD, with fifty bedrock mortars ground into exposed granite. A natural spring nearby drew early settlers.
descriptions.f7d0fdbc-8e4f-488c-879a-774eff5dfb4e: An ancient Turdetani town absorbed into Roman Hispania. Purported ancient coins turned out to be forgeries, making its early history harder to trace.
descriptions.316b3d27-1295-41ce-a5c0-3b9c8251647e: Covering 1.5 square kilometres in Xitun District, this Neolithic site has settlement layers from the 2nd millennium BC. A Tunghai University student uncovered it during fieldwork in 2002.
descriptions.66ca3d59-0402-4261-97cb-c5e5be3faac7: An Inca-period waystation along the trail network near Machu Picchu, above the Vilcanota River. Connected to the nearby citadel of Patallacta.
descriptions.5ae9fc36-4419-4e08-aa2d-a7653a46cafe: A mountain venerated as a sacred peak, with an archaeological site on its summit at 3,645 metres. Panoramic views span the Cotahuasi Canyon below.
descriptions.23da7867-1a59-4764-959a-ac94d81ef769: Set on a 15-metre hill near Bagenkop harbour and dating to 3300–3200 BC, this Funnelbeaker passage grave has a chamber and a separate lateral passageway — a form more common in Germany.
descriptions.8e54d502-a3b0-4738-8fdf-c74e6d10d03c: Neolithic settlement remains and a later hillfort share this Northumberland summit near Wooler. In 1402, a pitched battle between two rival armies was fought across the same ridge.
descriptions.4fa6f0c5-4a44-4540-8d37-bf10446429bd: A village on Dartmoor occupied in two phases: Bronze Age (1700-1000 BC) and the Medieval Warm Period. Climate shifts drove both abandonments.
descriptions.80c6aaab-af57-422f-9648-a47c7c51d09b: A village near the Heuneburg, one of Europe's most important Celtic centers from 600-400 BC. Burial mounds nearby held elite Hallstatt-culture chieftains.
descriptions.116de084-cd63-4ec0-aeca-4702b91b1bdb: The fifth fort on Hadrian's Wall, garrisoned by Roman cavalry. Coins, tombstones, sandals, and a spear point have surfaced from beneath the modern village.
descriptions.dfab4856-d41f-4228-a94a-e32822c59a0f: Built 7th–4th centuries BC near Northampton, this fort's wooden rampart burned hot enough to vitrify the stone beneath. The deep surrounding ditch has survived to the present day.
descriptions.3af2d2bf-8e21-4e12-83a7-5b1bffc3d5db: A 3rd-millennium BC Orkney-Cromarty chambered cairn on Eday, overlooking Calf Sound. Its three separate stalled inner compartments make it a rare tripartite example of the type.
descriptions.99e7c866-2d43-4ae6-abb7-3d174f4990ab: Set on a granite tor in Lustleigh Cleave, this oval fort exploits natural rock outcrops as primary defenses. From the summit, the line of sight reaches Haytor, Bowerman's Nose, and Hamel Down.
descriptions.7c94cfe0-8dc8-4286-acf4-dc994bd79853: A small univallate Iron Age enclosure perched 260 metres above two river valleys. Its slight earthworks suggest it was more farmstead than fortress.
descriptions.40de3b34-3c4e-4bbe-9074-d61fafac3154: 2nd century AD. A 134 by 85 metre temenos walled with cyclopean blocks rivals Baalbek in scale. Zeus and Baal merged here — a Roman deity wearing a Semitic mask.
descriptions.b7310da2-7ca9-4cb7-b6ec-90b372c8c985: Bronze Age hypogeum from 1700–1500 BC cut into Mallorcan limestone. Oval and rectangular chambers with benches and niches once held copper daggers, flint knives, and impressed ceramics.
descriptions.75fdea5d-2f5f-4191-81d4-096ddd468da5: A Bronze Age funerary hypogeum from 1700-1400 BC, emptied centuries ago and reused as cattle shelter. A rare vertical stone doorway still blocks the entrance.
descriptions.f69c8107-a8fe-45ae-a8d8-d5ab8e618e33: The Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak: 5,000 square metres, 134 columns in 16 rows. The two central rows rise 24 metres, topped with open papyrus capitals.
descriptions.abddd18e-797b-42ca-88b6-a588daf5f8f3: A Roman road running southwest to northeast, one of only four roads given the King's protection under medieval law. It connected the Fosse Way to Yorkshire.
descriptions.9adffc6f-a7ef-4809-96db-60b43fe3bf33: One of Britain's oldest trackways, following chalk hills from Norfolk to Wiltshire. Parts of the route may predate Roman roads by thousands of years.
descriptions.069e0320-14f7-497f-8239-4ffb969049c1: The cave where, according to myth, the titan Rhea hid the infant Zeus from Cronus. Votive offerings span from the 4th millennium BC to Roman times.
descriptions.d515d518-5298-42f0-8da8-5f484e8bcdee: Ruins of the Lycian city Idebessos, with a necropolis, Greek theatre, baths, and two early Christian churches. Founded around 168 BC.
descriptions.605268ea-e84d-4336-ad4b-647fa273e687: A village with a Roman fortlet or signal station on the hilltop above the church. The tiny garrison watched over the surrounding countryside.
descriptions.ceee8f24-5956-418d-b668-7f3e3e56a3f6: Recorded in the Tabula Peutingeriana between Stena and Tauriana, this town was sacked by Thracian king Sitalces in 429 BC during his southward campaign. Little else is historically documented.
descriptions.007eaa85-a68d-4310-8cc5-23fcfe7407c6: A 30-metre Roman column from 250 AD crowned with Jupiter and Ganymede. This cloth-merchant family's burial monument is the tallest surviving Roman pillar tomb.
descriptions.fcf4c04e-fd5a-43b3-881b-47802ea4f924: A Purepecha astronomical observatory and ceremonial center used until the Spanish conquest. Only 10% has been excavated due to limited funding.
descriptions.55727fad-d494-42c3-9463-dc8c1b54d331: A river valley where warriors sacrificed captured weapons for centuries. One deposit held 300 spear points inscribed with the runic name "Wagnijo."
descriptions.75f41466-f8d7-41b5-9d11-b1df05619c1d: Seven Roman-era house and temple tombs, some two stories high, at a wealthy summer resort. A mosaic floor depicts the sea god alongside a Greek inscription.
descriptions.b92a0687-5b6e-4598-942b-648938b6ebb6: On the Isla de la Luna in Lake Titicaca, this site dates to 1000–1500 AD — later than the better-known Chinkana on the larger Isla del Sol. Its name hints at a funerary function.
descriptions.6eec508c-8458-4758-aba2-5745dd9fe089: An Inca complex along mountain ridges above the Sacred Valley, with agricultural terraces, watchtowers, guard posts, and a major ceremonial center.
descriptions.4eca65e2-3dcc-4b23-874e-24696be9374f: In Cañete Province at altitude in the Lima highlands, this site bears a Quechua name meaning 'Inca house.' Its structures date to the imperial period, 1438–1530 AD.
descriptions.cec9a976-68e0-40a5-96ee-6dfd3786f069: An Inca temple with 80+ carved stone phalluses protruding from the earth inside a walled enclosure. A major center of power during the Inca period.
descriptions.31ba0428-1f43-411a-8473-0f1ade121091: Traces of two paleo-Eskimo cultures named after this fjord survive from 2400 BC. They built elliptical dwellings in one of Earth's most extreme climates.
descriptions.4bbe3ea8-22be-4609-bb4c-e5b13e3d4934: The largest known Inca ruins in the country, centered on an elliptical Temple of the Sun built around a massive rock. Mortarless stone-fitting rivals Cusco.
descriptions.d3afcf00-2741-44b9-b1de-db4cadb77e65: A gneiss rock formation covered in basalt stones carved with hundreds of symbols and glyphs. Many remain undeciphered to this day.
descriptions.5d0819e0-a352-4ea1-9d64-067da2e428f9: Built 1460–1470 as an Inca stronghold with 17 buildings and round silos, it stored the largest corn stockpiles in South America — grain distributed as far as Ecuador.
descriptions.6421a997-1446-4e19-8f3c-6e62eaf20aa2: An Inca administrative centre at 3,804 m, set against volcano Sara Sara and lake Parinaqucha. Built between 1438–1530 to govern one of the empire's most remote highland provinces.
descriptions.ef1f631d-1676-4b3a-bde4-7de221f892fb: At 3,804 metres in Huaytará Province, this Inca palace sits roughly 25 km from the town of Huaytará. Its high-altitude masonry dates to the imperial period, 1438–1530 AD.
descriptions.5d386393-99ab-4824-bc51-773f3126615b: In San Sebastián district on the outskirts of Cusco, this Inca site dates to 1438–1530 AD. Its proximity to the capital reflects the dense imperial infrastructure layered around the city.
descriptions.88897642-cf8a-48c2-a9a4-ebb0408a8804: Two Bronze Age entrance graves on a steep slope overlooking the sea, dating to 2500-1000 BC. The larger measures 8 metres in diameter with a long entrance passage.
descriptions.9347c4bf-5d34-4773-955d-af52852ce469: An Inca ritual stone with mathematically precise cuts aligned to the cardinal points. It tracked the sun's movement to control agricultural cycles.
descriptions.9c827589-5230-48e4-bf6b-fb7dee9e7c35: The Sun Gate of Machu Picchu -- once the main checkpoint for entering the sacred city. The stone steps controlled all access to the sanctuary.
descriptions.280f2b7d-4978-4352-896d-bcbb03837d3e: An archaeological site at 3,126 metres beside Lake Pumaqucha. Its name means "where the sun is tied" in Quechua, hinting at astronomical functions.
descriptions.aa24106a-9784-4f51-81a8-1f6b0c6dbab9: Lying in Pisac District within the Sacred Valley, this Inca site was part of the network controlling the fertile Urubamba corridor. Formal documentation of its structures remains sparse.
descriptions.a791798d-8ed0-4134-bd0d-de1deaef99a1: The mythic port where Jason launched the Argo with fifty demigods to seek the Golden Fleece. The city's Bronze Age roots run deep beneath modern settlement.
descriptions.32e69e53-2a3c-4e9b-9622-5606d0ddefbc: A Bronze Age through Iron Age fort on an isolated cone-shaped mountain. Massive ramparts with multiple rings of defense protected the flattened summit.
descriptions.006d81d8-1000-4954-9eb9-9ed2ba8187e5: A square Roman fort with four corner towers and three additional towers, from the 3rd century AD. Interior spa remains suggest it was more than just a garrison.
descriptions.f1322de6-8682-4d01-b0ae-7fbab9cc5864: The only gate of Diocletian's Palace in continuous use for 1,700 years. Its L-shaped entryway, secured by heavy doors at both ends, is a textbook Roman design.
descriptions.a7e1060c-e0e3-4fe0-a4ff-4737611a2203: An Iron Age cemetery with over 200 graves, yielding artifacts from the Celtic and Hellenistic periods. Finds are now in the national museum.
descriptions.9f328a68-b73d-4fd9-bc44-a78d3cae960c: Originally a legionary fortress for the Second Augustan Legion around 55 AD. 70% of the Roman wall survives as the base of the medieval city walls.
descriptions.a938f9bc-4f40-497d-8f2f-2ab44a0a2d1c: A 500-tonne megalith carved from a single tuff block, of unknown age. Surrounded on three sides by uncut bedrock, it measures 5.7 by 6.4 metres.
descriptions.15f3ae9f-86e9-4198-97c9-e67b42c034dc: Babylon's eighth gate, built by Nebuchadnezzar II around 575 BC and covered in blue-glazed bricks with golden bulls and dragons in relief.
descriptions.6e696e62-f344-4f80-8460-275fd591249b: An ancient mountain settlement with cisterns, wineries, and olive presses built in polygonal masonry. A three-nave basilica shows later Byzantine reuse.
descriptions.7d1856ba-e68a-4b0a-b3d9-1da34299a6d0: A pre-Columbian city on a mountain ridge with over 100 large buildings and running water. In extent and age it surpasses Machu Picchu.
descriptions.7bdca82b-3519-44ef-9229-ee59f43c179c: Inhabited since 2200 BC with over 80 ruins and Inca terraces on its rocky slopes. Inca mythology holds this island as the birthplace of the sun itself.
descriptions.36778e23-1b9f-4094-a1cb-d3e1272e8d35: This 450 by 198 metre Gulf Coast island yielded hundreds of pre-Hispanic figurines in excavations. In the Postclassic period it served as a ritual sacrifice site near the port of Veracruz.
descriptions.b2035589-d46f-496f-9736-15d2251bca4a: Capital of the Kowoj Maya, built across three islands in a lake. Occupied from 350 BC to 1200 AD, the largest Postclassic site in the Peten Basin.
descriptions.c65e3fb2-4e1d-43ca-8dab-1e751019985e: A ringfort with 95 houses inside a 300-metre limestone wall with nine gates, built around 200 AD. Never permanently occupied -- only used occasionally.
descriptions.3dbd5144-7f81-4aca-a88b-527f1928b0f3: A 4th–3rd century BC Saka burial mound, 6 m high and 60 m around, yielded a silver cup with an undeciphered inscription. The script links this steppe kurgan to Central Asian writing traditions.
descriptions.bee4acb0-48cb-4541-b051-f01996c7170b: A sanctuary of Poseidon from the 7th century BC, famous for the Isthmian Games. It sat on the key land route connecting Athens to the Peloponnese.
descriptions.6de0d66c-8252-46f9-9f71-dd6210234681: Caves used from 78,000 BC, yielding a Neanderthal jawbone, bone flutes, and cave paintings. Stone tools span the Aurignacian through Magdalenian periods.
descriptions.25f7db49-7e78-4dc6-8f6c-392fa067820d: A Roman fort and town on Dere Street where coins, tombstones, and even sandals have surfaced. The modern village church stands on the former Roman town center.
descriptions.c8a346a9-bed2-4420-83db-3a6fcca051e4: Founded in 206 BC by Scipio for Italian veterans, this city later produced two Roman emperors: Trajan and Hadrian. Its amphitheater seated 25,000.
descriptions.31b8b0fa-4110-4e2a-b53e-fe2667876579: A Roman buttress dam system of two structures from the 2nd-4th century AD. Engineering solutions for water control in arid terrain.
descriptions.39b42857-adb4-4cfc-ae7e-c3b2672bbc63: Augustus settled Actium veterans here between 33 and 25 BC, building a colonia atop a preexisting Berber town. Only three Roman coloniae existed in Mauretania Tingitana — this was among them.
descriptions.11581c9f-5cbd-46e3-b010-246ae355a3a2: One of three veteran colonies in the region, founded atop a 4th-century BC Berber village. Its forum, basilica, and baths follow classic Roman civic planning.
descriptions.0d938cf2-c77d-4741-83cb-c3413761d2c1: A village on the ancient Icknield Way, claimed to be Britain's oldest road. The Upper and Lower Icknield routes converge here, though the claim is debated.
descriptions.cce286a3-5ba9-4724-b465-6df5835eebc0: A hillfort 3 km south of Leominster, this is among the cluster of small defensive enclosures that dotted the Welsh Marches during the 1st millennium BC. Its earthworks are scheduled.
descriptions.a7bb511e-92d8-4199-aa70-425d4e88b4cc: A Roman villa complex near Pirovac in Dalmatia with basilica, baptistery, and the Church of Saint Martin. The villa dates to the early centuries of Roman settlement on the Adriatic coast.
descriptions.f5def4fa-8b29-49bc-badc-5415a75f79b9: A Maya port on the isthmus between two lakes, active from 1000 BC to 1700 AD. Identified as Saklamakhal, a Kowoj Maya capital with over 150 structures.
descriptions.386cadca-23fc-463a-ba46-c016494086ba: Capital of a Maya kingdom in the upper Mopan Valley. Occupied from the Late Preclassic through the Terminal Classic with hieroglyphic stairways.
descriptions.aee27c1c-f426-4334-8e86-95dd2bf5c270: A Classic Maya city with temple pyramids, a ballcourt, two acropolis complexes, and vaulted palaces. Twelve stelae and four altars chronicle its history.
descriptions.1f020df7-29e0-4b61-aecc-80e294e7b59d: Called "The City of Hills," its five massive Mayan pyramids were long mistaken for natural hills by locals. Human settlement here began around 550 AD.
descriptions.816d2414-5cf6-457c-9a41-e5ec77d63e72: A late Pre-Classic city with 80-130 mounds in eight groups, likely Mixe-Zoque. Its carved stelae link Olmec traditions to early Maya art.
descriptions.7ccaad38-8cfb-401e-a938-e2c792914b75: Petroglyphs of horned bison, standing figures, and a wild cat with a curling tail carved into red sandstone. Some carvings date to 7000 BC.
descriptions.cb4e0159-7d70-4981-900a-908015803e7b: Slightly trapezoidal and roughly 70 metres long, this unchambered long barrow near Boughton Aluph was built in the Early Neolithic. No burial chamber was found — it is solid earthen fill.
descriptions.e93e16aa-f555-4ad7-8ede-d8120fdf29a1: A history museum in a protected old pharmacy building, housing archaeological objects and over 1,500 photographic records spanning from prehistory to 1950.
descriptions.77935222-436a-4bf7-9337-e7a3d86f74ba: A coastal settlement with traces dating to the 3rd century BC. Its favorable climate and sheltered peninsula between two bays drew early settlers.
descriptions.c932b4f9-283e-4756-b9aa-cc5491aaddf8: An Ottoman gate from 1538 with an L-shaped entryway secured by heavy doors. A breach was later cut in the wall for a German emperor's triumphal entry.
descriptions.8325d125-ed63-4a02-8c93-1e2a6683f5e1: One of Europe's best-preserved mithraea, this underground temple to the sun god Mithra imitates a cave. It is now protected inside a glass-walled cage.
descriptions.8a42154e-7081-481f-ad77-49e7a02b2c98: Built in 1836 at the Peshawar entrance to the Khyber Pass, this fort guards a mountain corridor between Central Asia and the subcontinent. It was constructed under the Sikh Khalsa Sarkar.
descriptions.3858c6d1-29e2-4bfa-99b5-cf015969646e: A temple near Taxila famous for its Ionic columns and Greek-style layout with naos, pronaos, and opisthodomos. A solid wall replaced the usual rear colonnade.
descriptions.38d80f05-0d81-48f5-9b96-dfcf85493532: Shetland's most layered site runs from 2500 BC through the 17th century — Bronze Age, Iron Age, Pictish, Norse, and Medieval phases stacked in sequence. No site in Britain compresses so many eras.
descriptions.93370dfd-9467-4c8b-9dc7-dca5faa812ac: A UNESCO-listed limestone cave with speleothems spanning geological epochs. Archaeological layers from the 13th century BC show early human use of the karst system.
descriptions.561cf2b3-18e0-495b-a3bf-bdf521ca22eb: A 2nd-century AD Buddhist monastery with a main stupa, 27 smaller stupas, and 59 chapels depicting scenes from the Buddha's life. Set on a hilltop at Taxila.
descriptions.3d5ee71b-22cf-4781-9432-e4f275543a7d: A Roman enclosure with V-shaped ditches and a revetted defensive bank. A greyware vessel from the 2nd-4th century confirms military use of the site.
descriptions.50a67cd0-367e-4f97-ac04-4e4cbbd7b1e6: Thirteen pre-Islamic Berber royal mausoleums from Late Antiquity, built on hilltops and plundered for centuries. Their builders remain a mystery.
descriptions.086aa9b8-6e6e-492d-baf2-a829b5eb0f6c: A hillfort from around 700 BC was later overbuilt by a Roman-era stone settlement with an attached field system on this Northumberland moorland. Two occupations share the same defensible ground.
descriptions.c6d9487d-d138-4d73-beb1-5735e50da048: Site of a massive 703 BC aqueduct of over two million dressed stones with waterproof cement. It may be the world's oldest, predating Roman aqueducts by five centuries.
descriptions.40a33fe3-d4c6-4eda-ab0e-45bac8de7bdb: A 9-metre Roman wall from 125-130 AD with two large arched openings, beside excavated public bath foundations. One of the tallest standing Roman walls in Britain.
descriptions.66004bcf-8b17-4b3b-8dd0-ab55d21a1bd3: The highest mud mound in its district, where the Jhukar culture was identified. This post-Harappan phase overlaps with the Indus Valley Civilization.
descriptions.01f3d961-e2cf-4a3d-bc36-7e9976efe93e: A settlement at 4,115 metres with the earliest evidence of reduced mobility in the Lake Titicaca Basin, from 3400-1600 BC. Three pithouses were excavated.
descriptions.6ebfa164-e396-45a5-82fb-2e1cb9fe841a: Cut into the Ramgarh hills, these caves hold Brahmi-script inscriptions in Magadhi and coloured frescoes dated to the 3rd–1st century BC. The inscriptions are non-religious — rare for the period.
descriptions.0d70773f-7235-4afe-bfef-75ec938701b3: A Romano-Celtic temple active from around 69 AD to the late 4th century. Excavations revealed ritual deposits of bird skeletons paired with coins.
descriptions.cbc93ea2-6ae5-4be6-a320-254960a60ab7: The largest Iron Age grave field in the Nordic countries, with 660 graves including stone ships and stone circles. Active from 500 BC to 500 AD.
descriptions.b7319c81-70e7-4c3b-9b06-b39bf9cc7dd0: Two crosses carved into the wall flank the inner doorway of this 4th-century AD church near the Gulf coast. Physical evidence of Christian practice this early and this far east is extremely scarce.
descriptions.4154f90b-74f1-49d4-bdab-caa7bb1322fb: A Gallo-Roman city built atop a Celtic temple, serving as the Diablintes' capital. Its public buildings trace the spread of Roman urban planning into Gaul.
descriptions.6cb8a98b-4816-4879-9de7-84095b4c0989: A soapstone outcrop covered in ancient curvilinear carvings and petroglyphs. The designs are unique to this region and their meaning is still debated.
descriptions.7bf8ea0c-3669-41e5-9108-82a696f36664: Founded during the Cantabrian Wars (29-19 BC) as a Roman symbol of domination. Named after Julius Caesar, it was the most important city in Cantabrian territory.
descriptions.5d64e4f8-8a98-4cf7-a97b-c353d6029e84: Near Chilham in Kent, this unchambered long barrow from the fourth millennium BC survives in ruin. Built by early farming communities shortly after pastoralism arrived from continental Europe.
descriptions.4087ca78-09fc-458f-aae5-81e9aaaa2e9f: A Samnite city destroyed during the Social War, then resettled with Roman colonists. Its forum, temple, and basilica are open as an archaeological park.
descriptions.30728ed9-125f-4fba-80de-20fa17d2b02b: A Maya city in the Puuc region already inhabited by the 3rd century BC. Most visible architecture is from the 7th-11th centuries, linked to Uxmal by a raised road.
descriptions.beb52434-00b6-44e3-970b-a6d3a25fabba: Seven Buddhist caves carved into a mountainside with vihara-style architecture from the 1st-2nd century AD. The rock-cut chambers follow monastic layouts.
descriptions.105d50fa-5e1b-487e-af70-ff4f6224cd50: Polygonal Hellenistic walls form retaining walls for an ancient theatre at this Lycian city. Remains include a stadium, baths, agora, and temples — most surviving structures date to the Roman era.
descriptions.6791baaf-bb36-462b-a497-e704e23251ac: Built in 1601, this castle was deliberately modest for one of the richest feudal domains. Destroyed by fire in 1874 and never rebuilt -- only moats and walls remain.
descriptions.c04b9633-ab16-45bf-b36b-18f83096f46f: Built by the Commagene civilization in the 1st–2nd century AD, this castle includes a bazaar, mosque, dungeon, and waterways. Its layered construction spans the Roman and later periods.
descriptions.8838f1fa-2c3c-44b6-a554-75e34ae61ee9: A 4th-century Buddhist stupa where excavations revealed both Indian and Arab coins. This mix suggests Buddhism thrived alongside early Islamic-era trade.
descriptions.f489bb40-cfed-4692-8e6c-ed036791e55a: A Nubian temple relocated in the 1960s to escape rising Nile waters. Originally dedicated to Mandulis, with inscriptions in both hieroglyphic and Meroitic scripts.
descriptions.cc5d001f-1ebf-44b8-a478-bfb78ec2d8d8: A temple site in continuous ritual use from the Bronze Age to the Roman period. Excavations revealed unbroken worship sequences spanning two millennia.
descriptions.72fc10c1-c363-4476-a9fe-56ddfdfc8cc2: A sanctuary of Poseidon where the orator Demosthenes chose poison over surrender to the Macedonians. Cult activity dates to the 6th century BC.
descriptions.f56ab010-efda-4068-a979-f935d9ab521f: At Taxila, this Buddhist establishment contains the largest vihara monastery in northern India. An inscription records the enshrinement of relics as a Sarvastivadin gift, dated to 77 AD.
descriptions.3911fbf9-3c1c-4620-a197-10ccbb9e20f7: The likely site of the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD, where Germanic warriors destroyed three Roman legions. Thousands of artifacts confirm the location.
descriptions.5d8a914c-d69d-409c-9713-588113811da5: A museum at the site where three Roman legions were annihilated in 9 AD. The gap between hill and bog formed a perfect ambush for Germanic warriors.
descriptions.6a9e7467-7a1e-47e2-ac16-7c1a60cb2f98: A 4th-century BC Greek colony on the Crimean coast, divided into walled sections with a tower at each center. It changed hands between colonists and local kingdoms.
descriptions.3cc112fa-e1fc-420a-8089-1a9db46cddbf: High in the Psiloriti Range above Phaistos, this Minoan sacred cave yielded the finest examples of Middle Minoan polychrome pottery known. The ware type takes its name from the village and cave.
descriptions.9b5751dd-d54e-4e8a-b4c0-7b4dc2a863c7: A 40-tonne granite megalith, 3.6 m long, carved into a smiling turtle face. When or why it was made is unknown. Legend holds that if it ever faces west, all of Japan will turn to mud.
descriptions.eb5e398b-2ae0-4cd2-b2d5-431ea8c0b7c7: The largest burial tumulus in the Balkans, growing from 40 graves in the Late Bronze Age to 200 in the Early Iron Age. Active from 3000-700 BC and linked to over 200 tumuli in the region.
descriptions.8c9a882c-1a6c-44e0-a68c-4d2d2a647cde: A Minoan cemetery in southern Crete active from the 4th to 2nd millennium BC. The tholos tombs held elite burials with rich grave goods.
descriptions.29556c62-1823-4aa0-9873-12121d2cf630: One of the greatest Mesoamerican sites, occupied from 1500 BC to 1200 AD. Most of it now lies buried beneath a modern capital city.
descriptions.941b3241-8cc0-408b-a1be-2ee5cd8ad6f7: Petroglyphs on sandstone blocks up to 12 metres high, from the Upper Paleolithic to medieval times. The oldest images may be over 20,000 years old.
descriptions.5fe20684-2090-41cf-8154-c2a50a0b9602: Located in Espinar Province at altitude in the Cusco Region, this Inca-period site remains largely undocumented. Its structures and function have not been subject to systematic study.
descriptions.2f0e58ba-3b2f-4f39-828f-b5d4935121b3: 109 Buddhist caves carved into basalt, 1st c. BCE–10th c. AD. Rock-cut channels fed rainwater into cisterns above the cells. Inscriptions in Brahmi, Devanagari, and Pahlavi script cover the walls.
descriptions.c0667188-d786-40ea-8afd-1257c58e2dae: Built by Kushan king Kanishka in the 2nd century AD near Peshawar, this stupa housed Buddhist relics. Among the tallest structures of its era, it drew pilgrims from across Asia.
descriptions.943f68a1-7483-4fe7-beb9-d114c2092d5a: Founded in the 3rd century BC around a sinkhole 142 metres long, 95 metres wide, and 50 metres deep. Four basilicas were built around its rim — the chasm treated as sacred for centuries.
descriptions.e8b4caf8-9818-4121-ba50-93bada5fa215: A Celtic settlement from the 4th century BC that grew into a major urban center. The site's name derives from Turkish words meaning "black ring" -- a warning.
descriptions.3696e872-ce24-42c2-b632-fe7b034171df: T-shaped pillars and animorphic figures from the 9th millennium BC, close to Gobekli Tepe. Part of a cluster of pre-agricultural monumental sites now being uncovered.
descriptions.f294fd21-7428-4c73-9810-dae8ff8ee546: Hellenistic in origin and rebuilt through early Byzantine times, this limestone settlement has seven surviving houses — four single-storey, three two-storey. A Roman road runs through the site.
descriptions.c42910ee-2da6-4aff-8346-b4b2fe875e4f: A funerary monument for a Commagene queen and two princesses, from 30-20 BC. A column topped by an eagle bears Greek honorific inscriptions.
descriptions.acee0988-8506-40f4-81e7-63c6216ea43b: A Seleucid fortress from the 2nd century BC on rock so steep that locals warn against climbing without a guide. Never developed for visitors.
descriptions.2297e801-c762-4bb9-9e88-102c65e301a1: An open-air museum in the ruins of an ancient fortification. The site preserves monumental architecture from the frontier of several ancient civilizations.
descriptions.8ca3f6a9-2b4a-461e-8f64-84b43eb87201: A Minoan refuge at 1,100 metres, occupied after the Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BC. Its dramatic clifftop setting has been compared to Machu Picchu.
descriptions.6bb12b0e-f96b-4243-a96f-395cc7c5d317: Ancient Buddhist rock-cut caves with large windows carved into a hillside to light the interiors. The complex spans the 2nd century BC to the 5th century AD.
descriptions.14c0c237-0ece-4124-ada8-8ec56b431b08: A vast temple complex built over 2,000 years, from 1971 BC to the Ptolemaic era. Its Hypostyle Hall has 134 columns across 5,000 square metres.
descriptions.e2dbb087-8f25-4726-967a-e1054d4be16c: An ancient Greek city-kingdom founded by Phoenicians. Its most famous resident, Zeno of Citium (born c. 334 BC), founded Stoic philosophy.
descriptions.2ff6f6ff-dada-465c-ad3b-6db67b57a31b: A stone-tool production site on an island separated from the mainland 10,000 years ago. Evidence of habitation abounds, but no people were found at contact.
descriptions.b26650f3-6208-486d-a9e8-92e52baf1158: Limestone caves in the Katlang Valley expanded from Kushan to Shahi periods. Rare bronze coins found nearby hint at an independent local polity within Gandhara — a reading the evidence supports.
descriptions.50ec8479-7493-4e04-9606-ac49aab0964a: Ancient Cillium, a Roman settlement with a theatre carved from a hillside, a triumphal arch, and the three-story Mausoleum of the Flavii.
descriptions.70efdd32-f351-43cc-9347-6cbe0dc0614c: The largest ancient tumulus ever found in its country, dwarfing Philip II's tomb at Vergina. A 4th-century BC Macedonian burial mound of staggering scale.
descriptions.9072416f-69c6-4c4a-a5d3-6981eb899114: Rectangular — 60 by 35 metres — with 7-metre-wide walls and six gateways, this 2000 BC stone enclosure near Pattijoki is the largest of forty such 'Giant's Churches' in this region.
descriptions.7ef5997f-b5ec-4559-9611-8016a7191f0a: A 4th-century Roman refuge fort built after Germanic tribes overran the frontier. Townspeople fled here during raids behind hilltop walls.
descriptions.b19343e4-3110-4343-8ce8-2f085db85001: An ancient Carian city with a 5,000-seat theatre, six excavated temples, and rock-cut tombs lining the cliffs outside. Byzantine walls crown the acropolis.
descriptions.0849cdd5-5b9a-40c2-9aa9-f58c1ac32b22: A fortified Cretan peak settlement at 713 metres from the 12th-7th century BC. A refuge after the Bronze Age collapse, overlooking the Gulf of Mirabello.
descriptions.7d356160-ee86-4110-974a-2c77e02eb710: A "Dark Age" settlement in the Cretan foothills, mostly dating to after Minoan civilization fell. Houses cluster on a terraced hillside above the sea.
descriptions.60ef45e0-fd0e-414c-a000-22ddccdd332b: Home to the only known Roman villa or high-status farmhouse in the entire county. Bronze Age remains from the 12th century BC underlie the Roman layers.
descriptions.93a36090-1dd8-43e4-8da1-79782cb01b96: A five-stone axial circle from the Bronze Age, with tall portal stones aligned north-south. Set on bogland overlooking a deep mountain valley.
descriptions.09100b6c-e7a9-4332-afca-8d5c44e31015: An ancient port town on the Isthmus of Corinth, active since the 6th century BC. Its harbour moles remain visible beneath the modern shoreline.
descriptions.cc003c29-1af3-4d7c-a025-cd9c457524d1: Radiocarbon dating places this hillfort's occupation at 400–100 BC, with earlier pre-fort activity beneath the ramparts. The scheduled site sits beside the A39, roughly 3 km east of Wadebridge.
descriptions.ee2d3797-494f-4588-98e8-23d6d76622c6: Seven hillforts survive in Cheshire, and this promontory fort is among them. Used briefly in the 1st millennium BC, its only recovered artifact is a bronze palstave found in the 19th century.
descriptions.61d2ef8c-e4a4-4dca-b7e7-36d58f391b60: Iron Age cliff castle on a north Cornwall headland: 170 by 160 metres of earth-and-stone ramparts with an external rock-cut ditch. Mesolithic flint flakes beneath it predate the fort by millennia.
descriptions.5235f9f1-cfe9-4631-bb35-0cba709f093d: A Roman vicus founded c. 40 AD on Lake Zurich's shore, 300 by 200 metres. A walled temple precinct held two Gallo-Roman temples and a fire altar. Occupied continuously for over 2,000 years.
descriptions.0989a7d5-9fa2-447d-a774-5f5b8351fd27: A 2.5 km avenue of paired standing stones from 2200 BC, linking Avebury to The Sanctuary. Around 100 pairs originally lined this Neolithic processional route.
descriptions.e6f95365-5042-4815-9275-e0e5f295c8e6: Rock carvings along the route to Hunza Valley. Little is documented about them, making these among the region's least-studied archaeological features.
descriptions.931ddb0f-7236-4315-ac59-8cc677dd5aa7: A cave system occupied for at least 500,000 years -- one of the longest records of human presence in Britain. Both a geological and archaeological treasure.
descriptions.bc936eb9-20d2-4d52-9637-cca891a4b6e8: A possible Iron Age through Roman fortress on a plateau. A single rampart and ditch enclosed 1.6 hectares of what is now dense woodland.
descriptions.294968f3-036b-44ff-b704-91593648927d: A Late Neolithic open settlement from the 5th millennium BC -- the only significant unfortified settlement of its period in the Cyclades.
descriptions.24018f0c-73bc-4af8-bf08-bd05b74c2c9f: Athens' potters' quarter northwest of the Acropolis gave the world the word 'ceramic.' Monumental funerary sculptures lined the Sacred Way through its cemetery — among the finest of antiquity.
