descriptions.b42c7181-73fa-48c8-8916-a6fe7b4b74b1: Nine stone circles and one double circle in the Nianija district, with a unique V-shaped "bifid" stone — the only one found across the entire region.
descriptions.ac5c3d55-1122-4aad-bcee-90a514c56f4b: Founded 2,600 years ago as the colony Pantikapaion on the Kerch Peninsula, this city has been occupied ever since. A major World War II battle was fought across its ancient streets.
descriptions.f292ac8c-041c-4740-906c-af202af10489: Seat of the ancient D'mt kingdom, with stelae up to 14 metres tall inscribed in Ge'ez script. Dating from around 500 BC, it predates the Aksumite empire.
descriptions.7bb92044-9831-42cc-9909-f4532dceb21d: A Roman villa whose only above-ground survival is a mausoleum. Geophysical surveys found more buildings, but the full layout remains unknown.
descriptions.f192960b-ae02-4b86-9469-99c61a2b2842: Evidence of metalworking from the 1st millennium BC -- among the earliest in Southeast Asia. Excavations revealed copper-smelting tools and daily-life artifacts.
descriptions.d8dbc474-410c-4a59-8add-61fb14ede6a7: A 400-100 BC port at the crossroads of the South China Sea and Bay of Bengal. Glass beads, stone ornaments, and metal tools reveal pan-Asian trade networks.
descriptions.75c57d9d-cc2d-41dc-9937-ab8939869594: A mountain at nearly 4,810 metres near Lake Titicaca, with a prehispanic site on its slopes. Declared a national cultural heritage landmark.
descriptions.ff1c4702-9115-43fc-b64f-15a9729bc6d9: In Kharkhorin, this museum holds artifacts from Karakorum spanning the Upper Paleolithic through the 14th century. The collection includes Hunnu, Uyghur, Liao, and Rouran material.
descriptions.f1710818-b1bc-401e-95ca-cae1bb55ada8: Occupied from the 7th to 4th millennia BC, this Neolithic settlement of round stone houses became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998. Burials were placed beneath the house floors.
descriptions.6e1f996c-be31-4337-bd80-7a94b03a3d05: Paleolithic cave paintings of stags, buffalo, elephants, and ostriches span from walls to ceiling. Overlapping images create layers spanning thousands of years.
descriptions.e2030e0e-b33e-410c-b8df-8ccd76b8af03: An island continuously inhabited for 5,000 years, from the Neolithic through the Cossack era. It played a pivotal role in Zaporozhian Cossack history.
descriptions.16d71206-b1bd-4575-85b9-14567a8c1c4e: A Scythian-era hillfort from the 6th century BC covering 31 hectares. Rampart, scarp, berm, and moat ringed the entire plateau in formidable layers of defense.
descriptions.f13da15c-a8df-4b8b-9346-4b0c529a3a26: A Neolithic settlement from 3500-3100 BC that overturned views of Stone Age life in the far north. People here were not nomads -- they lived in permanent villages.
descriptions.c75b6409-59b2-4675-a402-796d4b2ba6fb: Twin portal dolmens with a massive capstone spanning 6 metres -- among the largest portal tombs in the country. Built by Neolithic farming communities.
descriptions.d7b854ff-65ad-4131-a67a-a570af61d9e8: Within an 18th-century National Trust estate near Exeter, a hillfort from the 1st millennium BC lies concealed on a steep wooded slope. Visitors walk the garden above ancient defenses unknowingly.
descriptions.25a909ba-518e-4651-90cf-ef9e49a1a7f5: Over 800 ancient monuments within 10 km, with 150 from prehistory. The densest concentration of Neolithic and Bronze Age remains in mainland Britain.
descriptions.43bb69c7-5c0e-4b99-baed-f23b921b0ca4: A wedge tomb with two chambers on a mountainside, originally covered by a stone cairn. Part of a cluster of prehistoric monuments in the Dublin Mountains.
descriptions.d966ae3d-201a-4028-89f2-50e5df35ae00: A portal tomb with a massive granite capstone on two portal stones, aligned toward the summer solstice sunrise. A rare door-stone blocks the entrance.
descriptions.40393153-89d4-4178-b9aa-88bbe09c956a: Dated on ceramics to the late Iron Age, this hillfort near Painswick has been quarried and partly converted to a golf course. Significant stretches of the ramparts survive the disturbance.
descriptions.775deb7e-4de9-46c9-936c-9de468d21192: A Copper Age burial mound that rises over 5 metres above the flat Banat plain. One of the highest points in the region, despite being entirely man-made.
descriptions.66cebfd5-9c0d-4116-bb94-c6f8dcda9b84: A rectangular enclosure of 56 standing stones on Bodmin Moor, from 4300-3300 BC. Its interior fills with water, and the original ground level remains unknown.
descriptions.19dcdb91-8d2c-43a7-acae-e7d709c576fe: A Neolithic henge 90 metres in diameter, 400 metres from Mayburgh Henge. Named after King Arthur, though it predates the legend by thousands of years.
descriptions.2c780872-8603-4ff7-b740-147b3cd5f22f: A 21-metre 4th-century obelisk in the ancient city of Axum. Decorated with a false door at its base and window-like carvings on all sides.
descriptions.59aaf6d8-4d0d-424b-bfba-cadddf848c1c: Dated on ceramics to around 100 BC, this multivallate Hampshire fort was reoccupied in the 13th–14th century. Medieval pottery sits alongside Iron Age ceramics in the same excavated levels.
descriptions.0b8a8edd-8a60-4758-985c-bf354de4a985: A Neolithic earthwork from 4500-2500 BC that has never been excavated. It may be a Saxon boundary ditch, but its true age and purpose remain unknown.
descriptions.aa56465b-1a9e-45b2-abec-b50be3796d8f: A museum on the site where Richard III's remains were found in 2012 beneath a parking lot. DNA confirmed the identity of the lost medieval king.
descriptions.e406449f-9274-4ab6-ba10-0d4ea77fa7af: At the south-western Mendip Hills edge near Wells, this hilltop enclosure has two or three interlinked sub-enclosures with an attached field system. It may predate the city now spread below it.
descriptions.21cb78e1-9265-49c9-a9e3-1daf14962c19: Double banks flank this Somerset hillfort 1 km east of Wiveliscombe, the inner wall rising 2.5 metres. A hoard of 1,139 coins buried in a pot 30 cm deep was found alongside Neolithic arrowheads.
descriptions.c17fcb7a-b41f-406c-9799-e42fa9443371: A Neolithic burial chamber with a 4-metre capstone on two upright stones at a cliff edge. A third upright has fallen over the millennia.
descriptions.09fcbc60-19c1-4742-a69d-3cb7afe19443: The largest stone circle in its county, with eighteen sarsen stones in an egg-shaped oval 27 metres across. It has never been formally excavated.
descriptions.c0bca5b2-b29b-4810-bebe-9b7615778a1f: Occupying the east end of a 1.6 km ridge above Bristol, this fort is now public open space managed as part of the Blaise Castle Estate. Ancient ramparts survive beneath the parkland surface.
descriptions.d2b862c0-44e2-422f-9c17-5548b3c74a7f: A Roman villa discovered during 1947 housing construction. Visitors can see the only exposed Roman mosaic pavement in the entire city.
descriptions.1d4dd1f5-e841-4c8c-9761-2d4ad3eec155: A stone circle dismantled by a farmer in the 18th century for gatepost material. In 1925, a local doctor "restored" the 11 stones to approximate positions.
descriptions.86ea97f7-ef72-4599-8d68-152db475d12f: An Early-Byzantine settlement with the earliest preserved house church after Dura-Europos, dating to the early 4th century. One of the "Dead Cities" of the region.
descriptions.b3180c5d-77b8-4144-a69c-8503ce6c06f4: A Roman cavalry camp called Bravoniacum where coins, tombstones, sandals, and a spear point have surfaced. The village still follows the Roman street plan.
descriptions.411cacb0-6312-4465-81f2-76417d209c17: A 334-metre hilltop with Bronze Age barrows, medieval tin mines, and a 19th-century chimney. Layers of industry spanning 4,000 years on one summit.
descriptions.47c37ef9-98ee-41d8-879b-e78db06295da: A city-kingdom from the 13th century BC. Its most famous son, Zeno of Citium (born c. 334 BC), founded Stoicism -- one of antiquity's most influential philosophies.
descriptions.ba33abc5-f266-4b9c-85f1-cd691699b271: A Neolithic chambered long barrow from around 4000 BC. Three uprights support a capstone in an H-shaped formation -- hallmark of the Medway Megaliths.
descriptions.7e503bd7-1d82-4054-b481-6be171a77611: A Maya city from 550-880 AD so well-preserved that archaeologists compare it to Pompeii. Abandoned intact around 880 AD for reasons still debated.
descriptions.600e2f90-b845-4def-a440-10a45e1da307: A forest with 37 Slavic burial mounds 4-10 metres high, spanning from the late Stone Age to the 11th century. Pagan rites continued here for millennia.
descriptions.b44da255-c03d-4304-b7c8-f9e7e8093720: Dating to 3500–2800 BC on Møn near Klekkende, this passage grave has a chamber and connecting passage. Its kerbstones are among the tallest at any comparable Neolithic monument.
descriptions.5b36f014-cb4a-4c2f-84b3-80996c503702: An early medieval settlement near the Oder River with three archaeological sites from the 5th-10th century. The area was part of the earliest foundations of the state.
descriptions.b5af43a8-181e-47d2-8a3c-0bfdbd445b5e: A 4th-century gateway added through Hadrian's Wall where a burn flows beneath via a culvert. One of the rare later additions that pierced the wall.
descriptions.fd9e31aa-e71d-4cf1-81ff-4104b7df8465: At the rim of the Vale of Pewsey, this causewayed enclosure from around 3700 BC has ditches broken by characteristic gaps. Whether settlement, meeting place, or ritual site remains debated.
descriptions.87cc7367-7c4d-4b5b-ae73-9cf41c550e9c: A Neolithic farmstead from 3700-2800 BC that may be the oldest preserved stone house in northern Europe. Two thick-walled buildings with low doorways face the sea.
descriptions.274600b9-31f5-45ce-96da-b0f326977dd5: Inhabited since the Stone Age, with a Roman military camp called Burnum from the 1st century BC. The medieval fortress dominates the landscape above the river.
descriptions.ef7d92df-a76b-4c2c-8160-32ad83100a71: Stones on Knockmany Hill's summit are carved with spirals and concentric circles — rare megalithic art in a monument dated to 3000 BC. A concrete shelter built in 1959 now protects the carved slabs.
descriptions.0ac27bb1-9767-4302-bcfc-0480349aaf1b: A Neolithic cist tomb from 3000-2500 BC with a capstone carried from a nearby river. The burial chamber sits on a small ridge in a city park.
descriptions.38a50d38-0077-4957-ae63-27f5375858d7: A 3,500-year-old complex with a recumbent stone circle, a radial cairn, and two portal stones aligned north-south on blanket bogland above a deep valley.
descriptions.84270114-d8f9-4f10-9ed3-bd0f86c35038: Queen Maeve's Cairn crowns a 327-metre hill west of Sligo — never opened, sealed 5,000 years ago. At over 55 metres in diameter, it covers a presumed Neolithic passage tomb.
descriptions.e0e45b1f-a762-481b-a278-cfa82c003518: A passage tomb aligned so that winter solstice sunset shines along the passageway. Scattered quartz may have once formed a gleaming white facade.
descriptions.c8af8070-bdd2-46a4-b651-a87fadb09bfe: Enclosing 1.6 hectares with a single ditch and inner rampart in Hampshire, this fort sits where Grim's Ditch — a mysterious linear earthwork — also runs. Their relationship remains unexplained.
descriptions.4028c95c-7e75-4787-9b90-ebe102696748: Roughly rectangular with a south-south-east entrance, this Wiltshire univallate hillfort has been read as a defensive cattle enclosure linked to Roman-era settlements — an unusual dual function.
descriptions.c345810f-7f8d-4845-88c7-64c652fa34d1: The Palace of Minos -- a labyrinthine complex that served as Minoan religious and administrative center. Occupied from 8000 BC, it inspired the Minotaur myth.
descriptions.6972abd9-37c7-4fc4-8588-3af3510975b6: Excavated in 1934, the stalled chamber held 29 people — 17 skulls lined the walls in a row. The bones of 36 red deer were stacked alongside them on a ledge above Eynhallow Sound.
descriptions.94ab84bf-c1f7-450a-a178-827834d34fd7: Roughly 90 metres above the River Caen near Braunton, this fort occupies a promontory with water on one side. Its small footprint makes it among Devon's lesser-documented prehistoric sites.
descriptions.5a04c048-e207-42fe-9d26-b39a0217bf09: A henge complex where a ruined Norman church stands inside a Neolithic earthwork ring from 4500 BC. The sacred geometry was echoed by medieval builders.
descriptions.57ad1380-8a82-42e8-8b2c-03f952ba7bdf: A 3200 BC passage tomb ringed by 17 satellite tombs, with the largest collection of megalithic art in Europe. Part of the Bru na Boinne World Heritage Site.
descriptions.e514dc13-8bd1-443b-8137-94ff173d32b8: Built 1554–1556. Legend says a thunderbolt struck it because 90,000 Buddha images surpassed his father's temple of 80,000. Hidden under jungle until the 1980s.
descriptions.e81d1a12-99bd-4878-bbb8-9c1e95efdf3b: A Maya city known for its Temple of the Masks -- a pyramid flanked by giant stucco faces from around 500 AD. Nearly 200 mounds remain unexcavated in the jungle.
descriptions.69ca7503-8a89-4ca9-ba2a-957af7a86955: A Bronze Age megalithic observatory with stone markers tracking the sun's position. NASA ranked it among the world's most significant ancient observatories.
descriptions.0dfe8664-4fa5-4be3-8c2e-bded5978b236: A Minoan harbour town for Phaistos, active from 3100-1100 BC. After the Bronze Age collapse, a post-Minoan sanctuary was built directly over the ruins.
descriptions.c66b25a2-35e6-4d6f-a8bb-683a473f86ca: A 4th-century BC winery with about 500 square metres of floor space, used for a century before fire destroyed it. The remains reveal ancient grape-pressing methods.
descriptions.3a391842-b266-467f-8ea2-c1c01fe236af: Sixteen rock-cut cells in the Ramgarh hills, dating to the late centuries BC. The caves are counted as the earliest Buddhist rock-cut establishments from the western Deccan.
descriptions.8a3a0f0e-6656-4b50-92ff-7f02f9f1548e: The largest passage grave on its island, with a 10-metre chamber and a 7.5-metre passage. Investigation began in 1839 when a merchant went treasure hunting.
descriptions.4d5e5614-2bef-4d1c-85be-8fbe423bac32: At 12.5 metres, this Lolland passage grave has the longest chamber in the country. Its surrounding kerbstones are among the tallest at any comparable Neolithic monument, dating to around 3200 BC.
descriptions.69b83929-86e2-4a3e-8e0d-2418db5192ed: A Paleolithic site from 78,000 BC -- a seasonal hunting camp on a lakeshore. Two birch-pitch pieces found here are among the oldest synthetic materials ever made.
descriptions.c086510a-dc65-4f32-ae34-f86578bd7cdf: Megalithic temples from 3700-2500 BC overlooking the Grand Harbour. Originally three temple complexes, but only one survives today.
descriptions.b0fed6c8-fd75-44e0-b57b-65ed6215f46d: A Cucuteni-Trypillia mega-settlement from 3200-2700 BC covering 120 hectares. One of 2,440 proto-cities from this culture found across the region.
descriptions.37c35150-d91b-44bb-a039-48783357de8e: Lead and silver were mined here under direct imperial control from Trajan onward — one of Rome's largest mining operations outside Iberia, producing an estimated 5,500 tons of silver.
descriptions.c207499d-5adf-4758-a902-09c031c6aad8: A pre-Harappan coastal site dating to 4000 BC on the Arabian Sea. It predates the Indus Valley Civilization and likely served as one of its earliest harbors.
descriptions.9ee5d047-1345-405a-a689-4624365e0104: A fortified settlement from 3300 BC that was a forerunner of the Indus Civilization. The citadel sits on a 12-metre mound above the surrounding plains.
descriptions.98cb1e3f-2eab-4bd0-9cda-8bd61abcacb6: An 18th-century fort on a 33.5-metre hill directly above a pre-Harappan site from 2500-2800 BC. Two civilizations, separated by millennia, sharing one hilltop.
descriptions.5baef468-20dd-4e38-90ea-e209fc29e508: A temple complex with six periods of continuous occupation from 3000-1800 BC. Its pottery links to the later Chavin culture through stirrup spouts and stampings.
descriptions.e10052fd-e1f4-4452-a811-c601472efbd5: Circular stone-lined pits found in Minoan palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, and Mallia. Named after round bread for their shape, their purpose remains debated.
descriptions.72d00882-cac4-420f-8105-e1a0f7999340: A Prepalatial Minoan cemetery with three tholos tombs 10 metres in diameter. These circular tombs held elite burials with decorated grave goods.
descriptions.9983bdce-9f35-47a3-a570-4021cfa41b97: A city-kingdom founded by Greek settlers from Argos, perched on a cliff 100 metres above the coast. An earthquake in 365 AD destroyed it entirely.
descriptions.d66ae4dc-8aaa-4934-b332-5d8eda991bc8: A Roman city with massive triangular walls, 17 U-shaped towers, and two gates. Its defensive scale suggests a major strategic position in Late Antiquity.
descriptions.ce1d8e3d-924e-4667-9ba6-9e32a3fac6d3: Occupying a hilltop in Loznica district, this Roman town's ancient name — Gensis — has never been confirmed. Below the walls, a harbour operated on the river Drina.
descriptions.06f6a014-f2c1-423a-8944-17c81374fd02: Late Pleistocene burials from a former lakeshore, with over 22 individuals. Among the most robust early skeletal remains found on the continent.
descriptions.be7c5289-b6ed-4ed5-95cc-e6d2520f497c: A cave used since the Lower Paleolithic, marking an early migration route from Africa to Europe via the Balkans -- before the Gibraltar route.
descriptions.3a5d5834-888a-458f-8a4b-66c709340688: A Roman metallurgical center active from 280-380 AD, dated precisely by Diocletian-era coins. The entire complex was destroyed by fire in the late 4th century.
descriptions.c80bf1e4-215a-440d-9e2e-848c40348037: The largest known recovery of Neanderthal skeletal remains from any Upper Pleistocene site worldwide. The collapsed cave shelter preserves a rich fossil record.
descriptions.7aa50e78-6ede-4901-b2a3-155f842ca0e2: A Roman quarry worked around 200 AD by the 22nd Legion. Soldiers left inscriptions and carvings in the sandstone they extracted from this forested hillside.
descriptions.4e158e46-2cf3-422f-b0da-6868bedb431e: One of Europe's largest prehistoric flint mines, active from 3900-1600 BC. Underground shafts cut through Jurassic limestone in a complex rivaling Grime's Graves.
descriptions.88c417e9-5131-401f-8187-1da8cc344b0f: In the historic Lubusz Land near the German border, this village lends its name to the adjacent Krzesin Landscape Park. Prehistoric settlement evidence underpins its archaeological classification.
descriptions.a5d9e9a7-9fd2-4a0f-a3ae-7dd78fba429b: Founded in 1690 by the Kounta from Ouadane deep in the Saharan interior, these ruins represent a documented historical settlement in a sparsely recorded stretch of the desert.
descriptions.4b0717fa-0f03-4d1c-87d0-7add7d34e6f0: A 3rd-century Roman castle from the reign of Constantine I, in the ancient province of Mauritania Caesarean. Built to control the inland territory.
descriptions.043fd021-51f4-4365-9a86-366d834f6ab0: A megalithic burial site with 69 monuments including hood stones, stone circles, and umbrella-shaped Kudakkal tombs from around 2000 BC.
descriptions.38aefc7c-1eb9-42d2-bd76-8d6b70847e35: A walled Chachapoya city from the 6th century AD with 421 circular stone buildings. Some walls stand 2 metres high with carved friezes of faces and patterns.
descriptions.a0b08567-cd34-467a-bd6d-428196261423: Twenty towns spread across 20,000 square kilometres at the Xingu headwaters housed close to 50,000 people. This Amazon complex was occupied from around 550 to 1650 AD.
descriptions.a25065ea-a21b-47b6-8218-916a24943461: Founded c. 300 BC by Chandragupta Maurya, first emperor of India. Excavations show it served as the mint of the Mauryan Empire — coins of the dynasty were struck in this Punjabi town.
descriptions.7830c6d4-496b-4799-9ef5-637ff48bd1fd: Six Elamite rock reliefs from the 8th-6th century BC in a gorge, showing processions, animal sacrifice, and music alongside cuneiform inscriptions.
descriptions.071a0b3f-a648-4b63-825e-a2031db6e69d: Uncovered in 1830, this stone-built Scythian royal kurgan near Kerch was the first of its type brought to light in modern times. Gold earrings with Nike figurines are now held at the Hermitage.
descriptions.a0f7b1be-f78f-49af-8fb4-a58cf9ba7bf4: Home to the earliest record of a definitively Indo-European language -- Hittite, from the 20th century BC. An Assyrian trading colony thrived at its base.
descriptions.d6ea97bd-2ddb-4065-961a-1e2c8d6a2a3b: A Kura-Araxes settlement from 3500-2400 BC with circular brick buildings. Cultural layers reach 7-10 metres deep -- evidence of long continuous habitation.
descriptions.20326ef3-6536-4849-a23b-64640d569867: A Neolithic settlement with cultural layers 22 metres deep, spanning from 12,000 to 4500 BC. The earliest 9 metres belong to the Neolithic Age alone.
descriptions.0f1ec894-b1b1-40e9-9e00-bd193b316484: A Maya city from 600-1050 AD with a palace, altar, and a round structure that may be an oven. About 300 structures spread across a 6 km site.
descriptions.c639cf64-349d-4c56-899d-b5606ee1afac: A Kushan-era Buddhist stupa and monastery from the 2nd century AD on a hill overlooking the ancient Indo-Greek city of Sirkap at Taxila.
descriptions.24951d4a-ac38-4098-8f55-6e10e5a59c35: The largest Bronze Age burial cairn in its country, 36 metres wide and 4 metres high. Legend says a king lies within, but the grave has never been opened.
descriptions.facb2c7f-777a-4eb0-8036-731853847f07: In Huamanguilla District of Huanta Province in the Ayacucho highlands, this Inca-period site lacks systematic documentation. Its structures and function have not been formally studied.
descriptions.cb2aa656-31dd-41f5-915c-f946d5bbfefd: An Andean religious center from 1000 BC with complex stone architecture and sculptures. Its builders maintained links with the influential Chavin culture.
descriptions.796f3d0c-638a-4722-92e2-2de70c61b67f: An Inca temple with zoomorphic carvings of snakes and toads on a limestone outcrop. Located within the archaeological park of Sacsayhuaman near Cusco.
descriptions.2f8f4a6f-2480-49a1-ae22-23ad1102f77d: One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, and the historical capital of the Kingdom of Colchis -- the legendary land of the Golden Fleece.
descriptions.8a90c0c4-3388-441f-b312-33ba8e8f44fa: A Cucuteni-Trypillia proto-city from 3600-3200 BC covering 150 hectares. One of 2,440 such mega-settlements discovered across the region.
descriptions.ac628dfb-ee59-4329-84dd-d5358e0adeb3: Ruins of the Lycian city Cyaneae, with rock tombs, inscriptions, and chamber tombs across the acropolis. A compact but richly layered ancient site.
descriptions.e9e6da5f-9c61-444a-aa39-6a2a690813b7: A small Postclassic Maya plaza from 950-1539 AD, set against a mountainside with broad stairways. Nineteen structures cluster in six architectural groups.
descriptions.78c3716d-79fb-46aa-82df-3a26d8ffd414: A site of the El Argar culture (2200-1500 BC), which controlled territory the size of Belgium. An exceptionally rich female burial hints at women holding power.
descriptions.d5a977c8-ba4b-42b7-904b-40c867ece178: A Maya city from 600-830 AD caught in the war between Tikal and Calakmul. Two centuries of warfare so depleted the population that the area was abandoned.
descriptions.9e2b99df-4b4c-41cb-80d3-879a5812e7ed: Built in 313 AD on the site where Crispina was beheaded in 305 for refusing to honor Roman gods. One of Africa's largest Roman basilicas, it drew pilgrims for centuries.
descriptions.5b596888-09d0-4c39-9749-228f50945bfb: The largest wedge tomb in the country, dating from 2300 BC. Three massive capstones cover a divided burial chamber with three buttress stones at the rear.
descriptions.042c8c7f-1ec1-485a-ba0b-3ab847320ee7: A Maya ceremonial center from 862 AD in the Puuc Hills, with a 120-metre palace and an elaborate arch gateway linking buildings via a ceremonial road.
descriptions.5003c338-1646-4bd1-8c28-67827b3d8ff6: Sacred to Carians and Mysians, this 4th-century BC site in the Mugla uplands preserves traces of cult activity. Almost no written sources survive to describe what rituals were performed here.
descriptions.3bee62b6-a82c-4191-86a1-24aad78dab71: The Inca capital of the Chincha kingdom — the Incas built their administrative complex into an already-functioning city rather than razing and replacing it.
descriptions.b5c58acf-f910-4eba-ac18-7c80dc812de2: A dolmen group with nine large stones forming a polygonal burial chamber and a two-part corridor. A communal funerary site from the 3rd millennium BC.
descriptions.d82e4a95-00dd-4c1d-8e94-dd201f72e331: A rock shelter with a carved animal frieze from 13,000 BC depicting rhinoceros, deer, and aurochs. Among the oldest sculptured friezes in western Europe.
descriptions.5e1bd6c1-43bd-4a34-a7ae-7ea240f9f7b2: This cave yielded the first recognized Neanderthal burial, found in 1908. The carefully placed skeleton changed our understanding of Neanderthal behavior.
descriptions.2eb96a66-8c29-4a38-a704-7d5c6d153a31: A 40-ton Olmec colossal head carved from local basalt, 3.4 metres high and roughly spherical. The fifteenth such head discovered, it appears to be unfinished.
descriptions.1010b3bf-a7d5-4e2c-9f70-8212a2cd1699: A 7th-century Maya court whose ancient name was Sak-Nikte', 'White Flower.' For decades, its stunning limestone reliefs appeared on the black market before anyone knew where they came from.
descriptions.c053a09d-ff4f-4277-9776-5c246cdfca79: A Roman town built along Watling Street in the 1st century AD. Iron Age remains beneath it suggest people lived here long before the legions arrived.
descriptions.c6bd2d66-f54d-4d02-8b14-041414043cf3: At 10.5 hectares, Ladle Hill's fort was never finished. Unexcavated but sharply defined, its interrupted ditches reveal the step-by-step construction method Iron Age builders used.
descriptions.90923e91-3e29-4568-aa2e-989de43d2a0f: A cave occupied 70,000 years ago where seven Neanderthals were buried, including infants and a fetus. One of the strongest cases for Neanderthal burial rituals.
descriptions.a38c611d-9801-4b23-b965-fbe0f5d4af24: A menhir dating to around 3000 BC, one of many Neolithic standing stones in Normandy. These solitary megaliths may have served as territorial markers or astronomical sightlines.
descriptions.4dc7086c-f261-4f38-85f2-10a20eeda1bc: A Paleolithic cave system with over 500 art figures, 40 hand stencils, and 4,000 fossils. A sealed chamber preserves a campsite floor untouched for 16,000 years.
descriptions.ca329810-35cd-431c-9313-0b53a706b325: A Maya city built across a network of islands and lakes, occupied from 300 to 1400 AD. Its watery setting made it a natural fortress for over a thousand years.
descriptions.ec4f5013-86b2-45a2-af61-d69b8f863d74: A Roman fort built around 74 AD during the campaign against the Brigantes tribe. The civilian settlement that grew around it became the town of Castleford.
descriptions.29d6fc00-4e39-4707-bea6-237454b055fb: A 4th-century BC sanctuary to Hecate — goddess of crossroads and magic — in ancient Caria. The ruins of her temple here are among the best-preserved devoted to that deity.
descriptions.90816aee-0043-4edf-9b7b-965b3734b678: A Gallo-Roman pottery factory that mass-produced signature red tableware from the 1st to 3rd century AD. Its ceramics have been found across the entire western Roman Empire.
descriptions.e2a08d7d-4038-4738-9702-4eb316357521: Occupied around 35,000 BC, this cave near Châtelperron sits at the boundary between Neanderthal and modern human toolmaking traditions. Its artifacts define the Châtelperronian culture.
descriptions.68677772-b461-49a3-bf2b-376e2b0e970b: A dry lake holding the continent's oldest human remains, dating to 48,000 BC. Mungo Lady is also the earliest known ritual cremation anywhere on Earth.
descriptions.10096963-03a9-4698-82b9-8c6386759359: A lake whose Greek name means 'ancient outlet,' connected to the Black Sea by a narrow channel. Artifacts from the ancient kingdom of Colchis have been recovered from its waters.
descriptions.7008f483-697f-4f0b-b2c4-5b234d28d4c7: A conical mound from around 3000 BC with a lower section that resembles a planned town. It dates to the same era as the great Indus Valley cities.
descriptions.97bdea94-4c2b-4508-83c3-777aaa16de29: Eleven churches carved top-down from solid volcanic rock between the 7th and 13th centuries. Each was sculpted from a single block, roof to foundation, with no blocks added.
descriptions.c050afab-2a46-4cbc-b795-b180b1d8172d: A Maya city occupied for over 3,000 years, from 1600 BC through the Spanish colonial era. Its Mask Temple features a 4-metre stone face of a ruler wearing a crocodile headdress.
descriptions.72396ba8-bfa7-46e1-8abe-e06c76dbe570: A cave with 15,000-year-old engravings showing detailed human faces with individual features. These realistic portraits challenged the idea that Ice Age art was only abstract.
descriptions.e9a63a95-86fb-4708-9041-0a7a74f2051d: A fort from the 1st millennium BC, later adapted in the Roman period. The same strategic hilltop hosted a post-Medieval fair and a telegraph station centuries after that.
descriptions.a0f583a3-f913-4c6a-9300-68f005b06999: A Zapotec settlement occupied from 700 BC to 750 AD, with 197 mounds across 117 hectares. Stucco friezes depict a ruling couple with elaborate headdresses and name glyphs.
descriptions.b43e7f32-5f59-4370-9cf0-43c3f159e4e3: A Maya satellite city between the giants El Mirador and El Tintal, occupied from 250 to 830 AD. Extensive looting has stripped many of its structures bare.
descriptions.6adb5ed9-34b6-4985-8d4f-ece2fcdd31e4: A Roman fort founded around 80 AD, rebuilt multiple times over four centuries. Its garrison helped defend the northwest coast against Irish Sea raiders.
descriptions.b2a3365d-ad8d-45e9-a5b2-be3a0c9f5782: Seven Neolithic tombs from 3500-2800 BC, built by the Funnelbeaker culture. Three are encircled by stones forming rectangles, and one has a lone 'guardian' stone.
descriptions.39f7cab4-e0d9-4c15-a4a0-8fccd461ba3b: A fort guarding a river mouth, built in 1621 and upgraded through the 19th century. It repelled the last seaborne invasion of the country in 1667.
descriptions.cdd84f55-f2c9-41a9-8f15-72e6e3f4e69d: A 6th-century BC oasis mentioned in the Bible as the land of Ishmael's descendants. Babylonian king Nabonidus lived here for ten years, abandoning his own capital.
descriptions.c63b0df7-79e5-4734-bb99-b17ccd8f54eb: A Neolithic stone tool factory from 4000-3500 BC, high in the mountains. Axes made from its volcanic tuff were traded across the entire island, hundreds of miles away.
descriptions.90e093d7-8495-4671-b99b-6dd14344b1cf: The largest Bronze Age burial mound in its country, originally 175 metres long. Legend says a giant was buried here so tall that no normal mound could contain him.
descriptions.bc89e53c-a9e6-465e-9cc9-4a6f844b9589: Occupied 38,000 years ago during the Pleistocene, when sea levels were far lower. Stone tools from this rock shelter in Krabi document early human presence across the region.
descriptions.8b90f9f0-db52-4d17-a699-e70fc6e5c2ae: An alignment of 77 standing stones from around 5000 BC. Local legend says they were a drunken wedding party turned to stone for mistreating a stranger.
descriptions.4eba8602-4117-47ee-9c24-7e0ab06ef999: A 4500 BC dolmen with a capstone 5.5 metres long balanced on three uprights. It collapsed in an 1815 storm and was re-erected, but now stands shorter than the original.
descriptions.e3330c2d-88f8-4101-88f0-4b174cb1bbf8: A palatial Roman villa expanded over four centuries, from the 1st to the 5th century AD. Its mosaic floors depict Achilles and Odysseus in vivid polychrome detail.
descriptions.cfe7373f-ccbd-42a0-88db-bc19fe33d950: A 1.92-metre standing stone from around 3000 BC with petroglyphs carved into its surface. Its base was cut, so the original stone was likely even taller.
descriptions.6a519122-e346-405f-8d4a-71f33d1eadc5: Built in the 3rd century AD, this gravity dam channeled the Farlón stream — a tributary of the Aguasvivas and ultimately the Ebro — for irrigation across the arid Teruel landscape.
descriptions.78da2ae0-bbc4-41f1-a5d0-5671e83d51e7: A Minoan fresco fragment from 1450 BC showing a woman with red lips and a sacral knot at her neck. She was nicknamed 'La Parisienne' for her striking resemblance to a modern portrait.
descriptions.756eef96-c792-4ecc-a998-b0eb2ee70e93: Near Lapford lies Bury Barton, where a large pre-Flavian Roman fort was succeeded by a smaller one and abandoned within decades — rapid military turnover marking a shifting frontier strategy.
descriptions.7cfb8a17-e0c7-4062-be2a-f79777dacf94: An archaeological site on the high Altiplano plateau. Settlements this remote and elevated show how pre-Columbian cultures adapted to some of the harshest terrain on Earth.
descriptions.9949dec1-5552-40ad-b5b5-fb9c29bff468: A hilltop citadel occupied from 300 to 1200 AD whose builders remain debated. A massive stone stairway climbs the terraced site, and a votive pyramid holds racks of human bones.
descriptions.2d48d802-42b6-4d45-95ac-54edd7eece15: An Iron Age contour hillfort that follows the natural curves of a hill spur. Only one gateway pierced its ramparts, making it easy to defend with a handful of warriors.
descriptions.e7f9d07d-60a4-4ec3-8ae7-45da301da233: The acropolis of ancient Argos, fortified from the Bronze Age through the Venetian era. A Byzantine-Venetian castle sits directly above foundations dating to the 1st millennium BC.
descriptions.1284cb97-6d86-411c-9643-1dc93c1dd47d: A Neolithic gallery grave from 3000 BC built from over 40 massive stones. Its corridor is four times longer than wide, aligned northwest-southeast with the winter solstice sunrise.
descriptions.ceeaa7d2-cb81-4e17-9c3d-abcfe8bccd20: Domed ruins of 4th-century Roman baths near San Pedro de Alcántara. Octagonal pools fed by lead pipes show sophisticated hydraulics — the settlement may have ended in an earthquake.
descriptions.9b639757-cc79-496b-9748-69594f98c109: Over 600 paintings from 17,000 BC cover this cave's walls with horses, bulls, and stags in vivid mineral pigments. The cave was sealed in 1963 because visitors' breath was destroying the art.
descriptions.123386c5-0ca7-4674-8b92-e878815ea662: This Ávila hilltop lent its name to two cultures: Cogotas I (pre-Celtic Bronze Age) and Cogotas II (Celtic Iron Age). Its decorated pottery style is unlike anything else in Iberia.
descriptions.3e876321-b41c-4322-8d13-159b4dbfe7ef: A Huastec city from 1000-1250 AD, now surrounded by a modern metropolis. The Huastec were the only Maya-speaking people who settled far north of the Maya heartland.
descriptions.5a2b16a7-5636-40c9-8875-124de3041d9b: A coastal temple complex from 1800 BC, built before ceramics were even in use. Its massive platform mounds face the Pacific, oriented toward the sea that sustained its builders.
descriptions.f12d3b76-a0e0-44e6-94cb-5dedd8203b90: A set of petroglyphs carved into beach rocks by the Pacific shore, dating to the 9th-10th century AD. Waves have eroded some, making each visit slightly different from the last.
descriptions.c81634b0-969c-484b-aa1f-5b5926e05fd3: The largest open-pit gold mine in the entire Roman Empire, active in the 1st century AD. Romans used 'ruina montium' — channeling water to collapse entire mountainsides and expose gold.
descriptions.f4a3f373-d1c2-4e4c-a1ea-875809fa90b0: A 5th-century residential compound for Maya elites, once linked to Copan's Grand Plaza by a raised causeway. Life-sized stone figures in feathered headdresses adorn the main structure.
descriptions.397a788d-849d-43ea-89dd-4dba1ced2526: A Roman road built under Augustus around 12 BC to push military access through the Alps. Cyclopean stone substructures are still visible, carved directly from cliff faces.
descriptions.d59ece30-3681-4056-ac17-068b36088e96: A 600-metre mesa rising sheer from the plains, used as a natural fortress across multiple eras. Only a single narrow passage leads to the top of this flat-topped stone plateau.
descriptions.b0c061fd-8644-433e-a61c-9b20fd960c26: A lakeside deposit on Lake Neuchâtel dating from roughly 450 BC to the late Iron Age. Artifacts pulled from the water define Celtic material culture across a zone stretching from Ireland to Anatolia.
descriptions.331d86ab-697d-411b-b61b-6af1875c7e1c: Over 500 standing stones from around 5000 BC spread across two municipalities in Huelva. This 5th–4th millennium BC complex rivals the largest megalithic concentrations in Europe.
descriptions.588e9b03-5d4a-44cd-a6f4-f1de7c8ff3aa: An Upper Paleolithic rock shelter from 12,000 BC, famed for Magdalenian art including carved figurines. Part of a UNESCO cluster of Ice Age sites along a single river valley.
descriptions.474c3e7d-ee4a-4c29-a62e-9ef87ca12ea0: A Roman legionary base on the Danube frontier, headquarters of the Legio II Italica for 400 years. At its peak, the fort and civilian town housed thousands along the empire's edge.
descriptions.1c899f53-4414-4954-821d-9119802aa39a: A 5th-century BC colony of Sybaris, built at the mouth of a river that once marked the border between Lucania and Bruttium. When Sybaris fell, its refugees fled here.
descriptions.d65e157b-14d2-422d-9735-bdb060b24b7d: A 5th-century BC princely chariot burial with exceptional gold jewelry and an ornate Greek bronze cauldron. The cauldron's rim features the Greek river god Achelous — found far from the Mediterranean.
descriptions.362a06f8-98cf-4cf4-be47-8ea8dd6bbc65: Founded around 900 BC, La Venta became the dominant Olmec ceremonial center. Its 34-metre clay pyramid and basalt heads weighing up to 40 tonnes were shaped without metal tools.
descriptions.44c520ac-00bf-4bb6-a11a-8875c559b10e: A small lookout turret built on Hadrian's Wall shortly after 122 AD. It was dismantled under Septimius Severus and later rebuilt using reclaimed stone.
descriptions.8be0203c-2703-42bd-947d-f0d46b916b71: A harbour town of ancient Gortyna that housed a famous healing temple of Asclepius. Pilgrims traveled here seeking cures, sleeping in the temple to receive divine dreams.
descriptions.21c82bf9-ef46-4b65-86c7-d4f10001159e: A city with roots in the Bronze Age, perched at the edge of vast marshlands. Phoenician and Tartessian traders both used this strategic river crossing from at least 1000 BC.
descriptions.1876d7d8-2561-4f0b-8278-f89293aecbb7: An Iron Age enclosure roughly 65 metres across, perched on a promontory above a stream. Its small size suggests it was more a defended farmstead than a military fort.
descriptions.ec838509-a1e6-4f6a-b216-3f1791c16d67: A striking tripod dolmen from 3000 BC with a massive capstone balanced on three slender uprights. It looks impossibly top-heavy, yet has stood for 5,000 years.
descriptions.6c736688-98d7-4c57-bf53-1f4367950131: A Neolithic flint mine producing a prized caramel-coloured stone traded across Europe. Finished tools from this quarry have turned up as far away as the Netherlands and the Pyrenees.
descriptions.af9036d8-9a13-4107-b22d-b5c088006d91: A castle built in 1537 by Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent to defend against Venetian naval attacks. Ali Pasha of Ioannina later besieged it, burning the surrounding village.
descriptions.bddad876-e487-4c8c-a0ff-8b84b0dfbef4: A natural tunnel large enough for a modern road to pass through. Inhabited for 30,000 years, the Grotte du Mas d'Azil lent its name to the Azilian culture bridging the Ice Age.
descriptions.73106998-2108-42c6-8b07-3a1c79783968: In 1908 a complete Neanderthal skeleton surfaced at this Dordogne rock shelter. The Mousterian tool culture — named after Le Moustier — spans Neanderthal populations across Europe and Asia.
descriptions.7c40fd0e-0b13-4b8a-979c-96f11452525f: A Chalcolithic village from around 3500 BC where cruciform stone figurines were carved. Reconstructed roundhouses on site show how early Cypriots lived 5,500 years ago.
descriptions.3e72d2be-c025-439b-88f6-6b8a90260a77: A harbour town since the 3rd millennium BC that became one of Gortyn's two ports. Its sanctuary of Asclepius, built around 400 BC, drew the sick seeking miraculous cures.
descriptions.2dcaaefa-e48b-4eab-993e-982418c3c8eb: Founded as a Roman legionary camp around 29 BC, its very name derives from 'Legio' — the Latin word for legion. Roman walls still encircle parts of the medieval city center.
descriptions.e20a253e-63e2-4423-9852-c05615206f93: A Mesolithic settlement from 9500 BC with trapezoidal buildings and eerie fish-human stone sculptures. It may represent one of the first planned villages in European prehistory.
descriptions.56b27be6-0aca-42b7-806b-1e0a096262c5: Capital of ancient Triphylia, built around two citadels 7,400 metres from the sea. Lepreum fought bitterly against Elis for independence and allied with Sparta against its neighbor.
descriptions.159db30a-1599-4425-8134-e0d08d164a95: A collapsed cave just 800 metres from Lascaux containing Neanderthal remains that may be deliberate burials. Bear bones arranged around the body hint at ritual activity 70,000 years ago.
descriptions.4739673e-66ac-454f-b7de-76e270f1e110: An ancient settlement on the route between Argos and the southern Peloponnese, occupied for 3,000 years. In myth, the nearby lake was home to the Hydra slain by Heracles.
descriptions.c292f83a-933b-40e3-a658-ad7aa6c19d33: Over 600 engravings of horses, mammoths, and reindeer — made roughly 13,000 years ago — fill two galleries here. Their density helped prove Cro-Magnons produced sophisticated art.
descriptions.05d60350-c231-4179-851b-380505d30a87: An unexcavated Iron Age settlement on a steep hilltop, enclosed by a single rampart around 1.2 hectares. Its secrets remain entirely underground, never formally dug.
descriptions.74bda98e-3c30-4945-926c-4563ccfbf13f: A two-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge from the reign of Augustus, standing 27 metres high. Known locally as the 'Devil's Bridge' — people assumed only supernatural power could build it.
descriptions.fc247379-6a08-4cca-bd66-ff2c661e6c00: A small circular ringfort, or 'round,' with a single entrance and enclosing bank. Hundreds of these compact defensive homesteads dot the Cornish landscape from the Iron Age onward.
descriptions.dc6fddb9-eb1c-4df0-81af-44b517857f7a: A layered site spanning Phoenician, Roman, early Christian, and Byzantine periods. Twelve centuries of continuous occupation left ruins from four distinct civilizations stacked together.
descriptions.4c7f0732-59f2-45dc-a19e-484c410769a3: The sanctuary of Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis, with temples to all three deities from the 6th century BC. A trilingual inscription found here cracked the code of the Lycian language.
descriptions.e427d7bf-01bd-4238-b972-b0ff62511a9e: A 'princely' grave from 1940 BC with a timber chamber under a massive earth mound. Gold jewelry and bronze weapons mark it as one of the richest Bronze Age burials in Central Europe.
descriptions.533ef43f-8c4a-47bf-bdeb-d6662ae50e68: An Iron Age water burial site where about 100 individuals were placed in a spring over three centuries. The waterlogged environment preserved bones that normally dissolve in acidic Nordic soils.
descriptions.2cce98a2-9851-42c7-9e9e-47f39b12be9c: At 279 metres, the hillfort crowns the highest point in Dorset. Its original bank and ditch survive despite centuries of activity on the summit.
descriptions.07892a09-1ce0-440e-8300-9f097e3be591: A stronghold of the Labeatai with Illyrian-construction walls from the late 4th century BC. In 1444, Skanderbeg convened the League of Lezhë here — uniting lords against the Ottomans.
descriptions.52ebea62-0e4b-4307-a6f5-03d06c3335f0: The 'Stone of Destiny' on the Hill of Tara, used to crown the High Kings. Legend says the stone would roar when touched by the rightful king.
descriptions.bad314d6-47c3-457f-ab77-9600fe9b04d2: Over 30,000 clay tablets assembled by Assyria's last great king in the 7th century BC. This collection preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh — the oldest known work of literature.
descriptions.21f76b39-07bd-40cc-8506-116019eac196: A 2nd-century BC mausoleum standing 21 metres tall, divided into three tiers atop a five-step pedestal. Only three examples of this Numidian royal architectural form survive anywhere.
descriptions.3f4f1ffc-6f45-40a2-a2ca-779889d2258b: A Sicilian coastal settlement where Phoenician traders operated from the 12th century BC. Greeks later built a fortified station here, and it became a key battleground in the Punic Wars.
descriptions.142c0275-1a5c-47dd-a562-c6874cafa728: A Late Bronze Age and Early Iron Age univallate hillfort covering 3 hectares near the Ridgeway, first occupied around 800 BC. Historians have proposed it as Mons Badonicus — linked to King Arthur.
descriptions.34d5b282-ab84-430a-90eb-6347f007fd2e: In 180 BC, Rome forcibly transplanted 47,000 Ligurian tribespeople to Samnium. The territory they occupied — the Ligures Baebiani — became a distinct settled community within the Roman state.
descriptions.86066b6b-c86e-48ad-90b7-9099ca1e5e58: A 550-km frontier of forts, walls, and ditches marking the Roman Empire's border with unconquered Germanic tribes. It ran from the Rhine to the Danube for nearly 200 years.
descriptions.bd1de8bd-0eba-46c3-9657-acfb494f9ca3: The most northerly point of Hadrian's Wall, and thus the most northerly point of the Roman Empire. The wall ditch here was never finished — the builders hit solid limestone and gave up.
descriptions.463b8850-768f-423c-8927-94718dc1893b: A Viking and pre-Viking burial site with nearly 700 graves, many marked by stones set in ship-shaped outlines. Sand drifts buried and preserved the entire cemetery for centuries.
descriptions.c17927cb-4b63-4fa0-9c64-b72a65decaaa: One of the three ancient city-states of Rhodes, founded according to myth by Danaus. Its dramatic acropolis holds a temple to Athena Lindia rebuilt after a fire in 342 BC.
descriptions.a32abe1a-9378-40b5-93e7-4f0564fb7a53: A Roman legionary fortress promoted to 'colonia' — the highest status a Roman city could hold. Its sewerage system, with drains large enough to walk through, still runs beneath the modern city.
descriptions.035aa343-1776-4667-8162-4f295287f6cc: Founded in 328 AD in Hangzhou, this Chan Buddhist temple's surrounding cliffs hold hundreds of carved Buddha images. It ranks among the wealthiest Buddhist institutions in the country.
descriptions.9a9a0dca-52c8-44c2-94f6-adb655db17dd: Rock-cut burial niches from 600-500 BC decorated with carved lion reliefs. The lions were guardians of the dead, part of 2,600 years of continuous settlement at this oasis.
descriptions.75f2454d-5538-42ea-87b2-ba091dec3df6: Timber post-holes at this Buxton site date to around 5000 BC, preserving rectangular Neolithic buildings. Charred grain here is among the earliest direct evidence of farming in the north.
descriptions.a6492846-5963-4307-8ffc-ea06bb554b1e: A wedge tomb from the late Neolithic, one of about 400 scattered across the island. Wedge tombs narrow from front to back and typically face the setting sun.
descriptions.9b11a285-235d-4a00-832c-b3b90509e409: A harbour town of ancient Elyrus that flourished from the Classical period through Late Antiquity. Its sanctuary of Asclepius drew pilgrims to this remote southern coast.
descriptions.68181f11-04ab-4bfb-aedb-0c7bc0ebb2f8: The central monument in the Carrowmore passage tomb cluster, standing apart from over 60 surrounding satellite tombs. Its massive roofstone may weigh over 70 tonnes.
descriptions.c1be61fc-2a9b-43c8-aa1e-dd41864e2f0f: A Roman colony founded in 194 BC that ancient writers dismissed as unsuccessful. Yet excavation shows a thriving town that lasted until the 4th century AD.
descriptions.1ac6809e-58ee-4d7e-ad3b-d3c53f3b59b4: At its height, Littlecote grew to 60 rooms with two bath suites and underfloor heating. Its Orpheus mosaic — found in Berkshire — ranks among the finest surviving Romano-period floor art.
descriptions.a0d4a5ea-fb2c-435c-a8b0-a6e12143b007: A ruined Neolithic chambered barrow from around 4000 BC, now a jumbled pile of massive sarsen stones. Locals call it the 'Countless Stones' because legend says you can never count them twice the same.
descriptions.70c04f92-593e-467b-8568-b585e1cdb58f: A small circle of kerb stones that once surrounded a Bronze Age cairn. One stone bears rare spiral and concentric ring carvings — a type of art more common in Ireland than here.
descriptions.789a9fa1-5e23-4631-912d-75ce1726bf89: A fort from the 1st millennium BC, later reshaped in the Roman period. William Tyndale lived nearby in the early 16th century while translating the Bible into the vernacular for the first time.
descriptions.7c97de3a-0401-4cd9-892a-79450990b3ce: A stone circle at 2,188 metres elevation on an Alpine pass between two countries. Hannibal may have crossed this very pass with his elephants in 218 BC.
descriptions.92313299-3bb1-45c2-aa95-eb147b0269ba: An Iron Age farmstead from around 800 BC that became a model for understanding how ordinary people lived in prehistoric Britain. Its grain storage pits reveal a sophisticated agricultural system.
descriptions.d812b71d-59b6-4313-a4a4-830ceea2f17b: The remains of a possible Bronze Age stone circle near a Dorset village. Only a few stones survive, making its original form a matter of archaeological debate.
descriptions.b3b5da82-1302-4f67-841c-28b51e578976: A mountain with archaeological ruins at nearly 4,800 metres elevation, venerated by locals as an 'apu' — a sacred mountain spirit. Andean peoples still make offerings here.
descriptions.ad570ccb-8234-4813-985f-807a1ef9b882: A village surrounded by Neolithic and Bronze Age monuments — standing stones, burial chambers, and hut circles. Few places pack so many prehistoric remains into such a small area.
descriptions.3209dfdf-ca19-45aa-b3a1-29815b5f5726: Known as Bwrdd Arthur — 'Arthur's Table' — this coastal promontory on Anglesey has a flat-topped summit ringed by Iron Age earthworks. A Medieval church to St. Michael stands below.
descriptions.0ec71a0c-1f82-4890-a9a8-8238461f9bc0: Vast pre-Columbian earthworks including mounds, raised fields, and causeways spread across the savanna. These engineered landscapes supported a large, well-organized society for thousands of years.
descriptions.f5e7956b-9aa4-47b0-b88a-3ed159f451d1: A Medieval castle built directly on top of a much older Iron Age promontory fort. The hilltop has been fortified for over 2,000 years, commanding a river estuary.
descriptions.28163f7d-d85a-4fa6-ba08-c33cd62b1da8: An Inca complex along the trail to Machu Picchu, serving as a rest stop and ceremonial waystation. Its buildings are oriented to align with Machu Picchu's sun temple across the valley.
descriptions.6be27ced-3d16-4603-8957-845c16d7bd8a: Settled since the Bronze Age, the city of Iltirta stood here long before Rome arrived. Its inhabitants fought Hannibal, then later received municipium status under Roman rule.
descriptions.539b56ad-5705-40c1-848b-767710247e7c: A Neolithic burial chamber capped by a massive roof slab estimated at 25 tonnes. Inside, the remains of 15 to 30 people were found — a communal tomb used over generations.
descriptions.3e634b8b-68d6-4601-80d9-f795a6fa217f: Ancient Edeta — capital of Edetania — lies beneath modern Llíria. Decorated pottery from its ruins depicts warriors, musicians, and dancers: the richest visual record of pre-Roman life in the region.
descriptions.7a0bddc9-582a-470b-a568-ecda06e46d8d: A single rampart enclosing about 3 hectares on the north side of the Tanat valley. The inturned gateway forced attackers into a narrow, vulnerable passage — a standard hillfort trap.
descriptions.a42d9ff4-6d8d-4cb2-bb1d-64b1c66cb290: A lake where over 150 Iron Age metal objects were thrown as offerings between 300 BC and 100 AD. The hoard includes weapons, chariot fittings, and slave chains from across Celtic Britain.
descriptions.00d1c243-0301-4212-a7dd-27a82bdc3fa0: A reservoir where a hoard of Bronze and Iron Age weapons was found during construction work. The mix of bronze and iron pieces dates it to the exact transition between the two ages.
descriptions.0cd58c95-e8da-453a-9ac4-ecaeeda843cc: The Grand Menhir Brisé at Locmariaquer stood 20 metres tall — the largest stone Neolithic people ever erected. It toppled into four pieces and has remained unraised ever since.
descriptions.8718faea-a442-445c-b369-c8572ec0be7e: An Indus Valley civilization site from the late period, near the banks of the Indus River. Artifacts here parallel those at Chanhu-daro and other late Harappan settlements.
descriptions.75e685c6-e246-425d-8a2b-e1bf69d6af19: A 3rd-century Roman temple to the mystery god Mithras, discovered during construction in 1954. The entire building was relocated stone by stone to allow modern development above it.
descriptions.ea02d8ad-f52d-4b24-9d4e-9dfe5bf4f44e: A 71-km Roman road that crossed the North Downs and ran straight across what is now a forest. Sections of the original agger — the raised road surface — survive as woodland paths.
descriptions.0da526f9-499d-4d15-a0ea-a45093fc4970: A defensive wall first built around 200 AD that enclosed Roman London for over 1,500 years. Fragments still stand in the modern city, some incorporated into medieval and later buildings.
descriptions.e9217b6f-c6c8-4798-a514-1e2751cf936b: An unchambered Neolithic long barrow built by pastoralists in the 4th millennium BC. Unlike chambered tombs, these sealed the dead permanently with no way to reopen them.
descriptions.b656d341-6132-4601-a0d3-386e7e725b6f: A Bronze Age landscape and Medieval structure uncovered during housing construction in 2013. Decorated tile foundations had lain completely unknown just below the surface.
descriptions.230087f0-20a3-4efb-a2d1-ebff696208d8: A 72-metre-tall hill figure holding two staves, cut into a chalk slope. Its age is fiercely debated — estimates range from the Iron Age to the 16th century AD.
descriptions.08afcd57-156b-4ab2-b53a-8e274c7a0324: The third-largest stone circle in its country, an oval of 59 stones measuring 106 metres across. Long Meg herself stands apart, her face carved with spirals and rings.
descriptions.4bc8c850-b194-4d4a-b0a4-40f8c4ef762a: Tens of thousands of Buddhist statues carved into limestone cliffs over six centuries, starting in 493 AD. The largest Buddha stands 17 metres tall with earlobes reaching its shoulders.
descriptions.255f657f-15e7-4eee-b9d9-7a30ce68d130: This Dere Street fort in County Durham was garrisoned by the Twentieth Legion. An inscription slab naming them was later reused as building material — history recycled by soldiers.
descriptions.3962491a-58ec-4e7c-a1be-3c456f9818a6: A 2.3-metre limestone standing stone with natural holes worn through it. Folklore says passing a child through the holes could cure rickets and other ailments.
descriptions.924cc0ad-a5ee-4200-84b1-8d41fc60d1ff: Just 40 metres across, this hilltop enclosure in West Somerset was too small for a garrison — more likely a homestead for a single extended family. Its earthworks survive as a scheduled monument.
descriptions.9aab078b-ef81-43a1-8169-235e5b22dd34: Twenty-four enormous artificial caverns carved from sandstone over 2,000 years ago. No historical record mentions them — farmers stumbled on them in 1992 while draining a pond.
descriptions.45958d56-72b2-44e3-ada0-c7030f469445: The largest Roman mosaic yet found in Somerset came from an eight-room villa. A mechanical digger in 2001 struck coloured stone cubes just centimetres below a farmer's field, exposing the floor.
descriptions.333616b7-4363-4251-9d94-397160f5d560: A Roman town with extensive remains including an aqueduct, thermal baths, and a forum. Its location on the road between Zaragoza and Pamplona made it a hub of trade and transport.
descriptions.bbe632de-a422-458f-8379-bef7ed34d4ef: A ceremonial center built from 300 BC with a unique design: stepped circular pyramids surrounded by ring-shaped platforms. This concentric layout is unlike any other Mesoamerican architecture.
descriptions.df850648-a8ae-40c9-9b63-e1545d6746f2: A Chalcolithic walled settlement from around 3000 BC that supported roughly 1,000 people. Triple walls, a dozen forts, and a necropolis of over 80 tholos tombs protected this copper-working community.
descriptions.6b703aad-2def-4538-8acf-b3ff22972f76: A cluster of 4th-millennium BC passage tombs spread across a hilltop range, decorated with rare megalithic art. At the equinox, sunlight enters one cairn and illuminates carvings on its back wall.
descriptions.ba7e3421-2f30-4f00-91e4-52d989e50000: Dating to around 500 BC, this 4-hectare fort sits inside Epping Forest. Its earthwork banks were reinforced by a wooden palisade, and the ditch appears to have been deliberately flooded.
descriptions.f9e7abcd-b8a2-4844-8145-4a29f19568e2: A forest clearing with about 50 upright megaliths, many over 2.5 metres tall. These Bronze Age stones once numbered far more — neighboring sites have lost theirs to farm clearance.
descriptions.a25850c8-b73b-4eed-9eff-8fc6dc28ff73: An ancient Maya city occupied from 400 BC to 950 AD, now reduced to artificial mounds. Much of the ancient stonework was demolished and reused as road fill in modern times.
descriptions.0d9dc1e0-d65e-4507-be51-4c2220ba8de3: A fortified early Christian bishop's seat from the Byzantine era, found during railway construction. Its mosaics and basilica reveal the wealth of provincial Christianity in Late Antiquity.
descriptions.7ef3f356-b352-48ea-b5f0-04dd2a0e958a: A Roman military camp built over an earlier Celtic settlement on the shore of a lake. It grew into a thriving town and eventually became the modern city of Lausanne.
descriptions.d2575f3f-5a83-4e7a-8e7c-d3325602aee5: A Late Classic Maya city from 730-890 AD built entirely of dry-laid stone blocks with no mortar. Its unusual black slate construction sets it apart from every other Maya site.
descriptions.c5c4cc93-5ab1-40f1-8b8f-b42255fea0c5: A sanctuary to the goddess Angitia, whose worshippers were famed as snake-handlers and herbalists. Legend says they could cure venomous bites using mountain herbs and incantations.
descriptions.cfd35d85-208d-4cab-ade6-118647969036: The westernmost gate of London's Roman wall, rebuilt several times before its demolition in 1760. Its name survives in Ludgate Hill, the street leading to St. Paul's Cathedral.
descriptions.e0ffa4e7-7b44-473d-af17-99abdfbef90e: Dating to around 4100 BC, this Wiltshire long barrow is one of many burial mounds in the region from early farming communities. The mound, on level ground, is orientated west-east.
descriptions.cb3fa612-c066-4646-ba63-ec80fa8c57c2: Founded in 43 BC as a Roman colony, Lugdunum served as capital of all three Gallic provinces. Two Roman emperors — Claudius and Caracalla — were born here.
descriptions.25e70d58-3211-47c3-8dc5-b4023cc2a7eb: Occupied from 80 AD to the 5th century, Lullingstone Villa spans pagan cult room to house church. Chi-rho wall paintings here are rare physical evidence of 4th-century Christianity in Roman Britain.
descriptions.7e18e007-0d87-4a66-92fc-1fae8937c8c7: Capital to nine successive dynasties and eastern terminus of the Silk Road, Luoyang has been a major urban center since the 11th century BC. Buddhism reached here before spreading further east.
descriptions.ee29e9ee-2892-4487-b318-0c0fc88f9a25: The only purpose-built brothel identified in Pompeii, frozen by Vesuvius in 79 AD. Erotic frescoes above each doorway served as a menu of services for visiting clients.
descriptions.77c38659-cde8-4de5-9c1a-5a2d4d2125eb: The Gallo-Roman predecessor of Paris, founded by the Parisii tribe at a key river crossing. Its amphitheatre, baths, and forum lie beneath the modern city's streets.
descriptions.c97527d0-4640-4b04-9bd6-132fcb6fd17d: A massive temple complex from 1400 BC dedicated not to a god but to the rejuvenation of kingship itself. A mosque built inside it during the Medieval period is still in active use today.
descriptions.442dd9ec-8c4a-45ef-9370-6b5c01ecbd47: Called 'the oldest city in the world' by the ancient writer Pausanias. Its sanctuary to the goddess Despoina held a colossal sculpture whose drapery depicted real animals and musical instruments.
descriptions.74e0a41e-6437-4691-b430-35a076358628: A Roman healing temple to the god Nodens, built inside an older Iron Age hillfort. J.R.R. Tolkien studied its inscriptions — the name 'Nodens' may have inspired 'Numenor.'
descriptions.d6d67a37-3efa-44d4-9340-004a07a52ea8: A coin dropped at center stage of the Theatre of Epidaurus carries clearly to the top row — 60 rows back. The 4th-century BC theatre nearby remains the most acoustically precise of antiquity.
descriptions.6c689af9-749f-4272-aa69-d1634dd8e4d5: A 52-metre-long Neolithic barrow with a 1.8-metre standing stone placed just 9 metres away. The pairing of barrow and menhir suggests a deliberate ritual connection between them.
descriptions.dfc745b9-b361-4d9e-9f95-90bb2237c66d: A 60,000-year-old open-air site where the remains of at least nine woolly mammoths were found alongside Neanderthal stone tools. It may be the clearest evidence of Neanderthal mammoth hunting.
descriptions.7b747114-5587-42b6-816a-b701f791bd19: The ruins of an ancient city with remarkably intact two- and three-storey building facades lining its agora. Temples, baths, and a necropolis fill the surrounding landscape.
descriptions.e1edddb2-56c8-498b-b926-78642bc312e2: A fortified Late Bronze Age settlement built on a peninsula around 1200 BC. Evidence of metalworking and trade suggests it was established by Mycenaean colonists fleeing upheaval back home.
descriptions.f7ed0deb-1206-4b70-b798-80ad7d442261: A Roman river crossing called Trajectum ad Mosam that grew into a medieval religious center. Neanderthal remains found here push the area's human occupation back tens of thousands of years.
descriptions.505bd44a-9fec-4324-a414-4ee080bf37fa: Two Macedonian barrel-vaulted tombs from the 4th century BC, discovered during clay extraction. These elite burials reflect the wealth of Macedonia at the height of its power.
descriptions.211bbc3a-1c61-4c8c-b5c2-0e49e027c18a: Two Macedonian tombs at the site of ancient Pydna, where Alexander the Great's dynasty ended in 168 BC. Tomb A, the larger one, was found intact with its grave goods undisturbed.
descriptions.37808e2a-8837-485c-9b69-f103a2be79b4: A Roman market building buried beneath a medieval church. The structure sits atop an even older Greek agora — three layers of commerce stacked over 2,000 years.
descriptions.9f5be838-53ab-48d8-9a1a-ac9597a87777: Pompeii's food market on the Forum, still being repaired from a 62 AD earthquake when Vesuvius buried it in 79 AD. Fish scales and sea urchin spines were found embedded in the floor.
descriptions.9711aeef-a3b2-45ad-8f2c-6c8f033eb9ec: A Roman market whose columns are riddled with holes bored by marine molluscs — proof that volcanic ground movement submerged and re-raised the building multiple times over centuries.
descriptions.02e075bc-19b7-4522-92ff-c07f230b5678: A Maya city from 550-830 AD in a remote jungle region. Its carved stelae record royal histories and alliances, including ties to the powerful Calakmul dynasty.
descriptions.811c92cf-dd96-4a75-89b0-e808cb12d882: Six stone circles on a single moor, some built from granite boulders and others from tall red sandstone pillars. The mix of materials suggests different builders over different centuries.
descriptions.888edebd-abcc-4eb9-a513-947ddcbe5453: An Inca site at 3,850 metres elevation with 14 terraces and partial buildings. Located near Chinchero, it may have served as an agricultural storage complex for nearby Inca estates.
descriptions.4f366f34-983c-42e1-a89d-7e8f5f77cdce: A 15th-century Inca citadel at 2,430 metres, built from polished dry-stone walls without mortar. Its Intihuatana stone was precisely carved to track the sun through the solstices.
descriptions.2fe3e1da-dcae-4014-a4d9-8b3132952546: An archaeological site with wall ruins perched on a hill above a river. Settlements like this across the high Andes demonstrate how pre-Inca peoples fortified natural terrain.
descriptions.ab077874-2a7f-4add-adec-8cb42e9e9561: The Nabataean kingdom's southernmost city after Petra, with over 100 monumental tombs carved into sandstone. Inscriptions here appear in four scripts — Nabataean, Lihyanite, Dadanitic, and Latin.
descriptions.f8c28568-017a-4b61-903c-bed2ba67bce0: Cliff dwellings built inside natural caves by the Paquime culture between 950 and 1060 AD. Entire multi-room homes were constructed within rock overhangs high above the valley floor.
descriptions.203fbf02-196b-4853-8504-d35a34085345: A cylindrical drum topped by a cone, built for a Numidian king between 300 and 200 BC near Batna. This mausoleum near Aurasius Mons is among the oldest royal funerary monuments in North Africa.
descriptions.bb724fd3-aa84-4a86-a22f-2a6f5e267797: An Iron Age cliff castle near Land's End, one of only two fortified sites in its county where early Iron Age pottery has been found. A stone rampart blocks the only landward approach.
descriptions.c50a5a61-0ce6-4e28-a525-b19a21140a30: A diamond-shaped standing stone 3.7 metres tall and 2.8 metres wide, carved from local red sandstone conglomerate. Its age and purpose remain unknown — it stands alone on open moorland.
descriptions.e77b33be-0bb1-48e2-9da7-4d2503f28134: A Mendips hillfort that marked a post-Roman frontier between Brittonic Celts and West Saxons. The nearby Wansdyke earthwork formed the visible boundary of that contested zone.
descriptions.7a9ec11e-65bd-4030-bf21-499f9cac6168: A Neolithic cairn from 2800 BC aligned so the midwinter sunset illuminates its back wall. Vikings broke in centuries later and carved the largest collection of Norse runes in existence.
descriptions.c5f853ae-ee16-4da1-9f17-f3ff66205f61: Dating to around 250 BC, Maes Knoll covers 8 hectares with a rampart rising 14 metres. The Wansdyke — a post-Roman frontier bank — meets the fort at its eastern edge.
descriptions.e790a37d-2265-48ad-8e62-67fb72ec73c7: The largest Hallstatt-period tumulus in Central Europe, dated by tree rings to exactly 616 BC. Over 100 secondary burials surround the central Celtic prince's grave.
descriptions.d1bb188e-07a5-4b2d-9624-65a918e88435: A Roman fort predating Hadrian's Wall itself, originally built for the Stanegate road. Unusually, the Wall's defensive ditch curves around it rather than running through it.
descriptions.bd3f6a4e-0452-448a-8674-b8a87c0e63e8: A cave with prehistoric paintings spanning thousands of years, drawn in bat guano. The images include a solar calendar, dancing figures, and hunting scenes of striking expressiveness.
descriptions.191e7642-eef6-476a-bdf1-4672f400a083: A Buddhist monastery of rock-cut caves carved from solid black basalt. Part of a cluster of about 200 caves in the surrounding hills, all from the Hinayana phase of Buddhism.
descriptions.14bd22eb-e75c-436b-bd18-85d9b31d28fc: Built directly over a Neolithic causewayed enclosure at Dunstable — two defensive systems separated by 3,000 years sharing the same plateau. A disused chalk quarry flanks its northwest side.
descriptions.cea5eebe-1a8a-4132-8867-12102672ecc0: Occupied from around 600 BC until the Roman conquest, this Cheshire hillfort is only seven in a county where such sites are scarce — a rarity reflecting the region's distinctive geology.
descriptions.39a50b0a-cc96-4e76-967c-fd1a1946aa2c: Multiple concentric ramparts added over centuries from around 600 BC enclose this site 2.6 km southwest of Dorchester. A Neolithic causewayed enclosure and 546-metre bank barrow preceded the fort.
descriptions.deea88d4-dfe2-42b2-bee6-a76f34f7d00b: Compact at 108 by 88 metres in Grinton, this settlement carries a name derived from an old term for a fortification held to be impregnable. Its Iron Age date is inferred from its earthwork form.
descriptions.5a91fe47-3207-443c-9eff-a1afd9e47481: A 32-km Roman road linking two forts and passing through some of the most remote terrain in the province. It connected the Hadrian's Wall garrison at Carvoran to supply bases further south.
descriptions.86d27903-d193-4c17-b760-072129d86c0b: The last fort at the western end of Hadrian's Wall, perched on a 15-metre sea cliff. It was the largest fort on the entire Wall, built over the eightieth milecastle position.
descriptions.c2d5c319-78e7-415e-8b15-a27b4bd30611: Dedicated around 4–7 AD, the Maison Carrée in Nîmes is among the most complete temples surviving in former imperial territory. Thomas Jefferson modeled the Virginia State Capitol directly on it.
descriptions.d85b55ee-afa3-423c-99d5-84149e5f8ee9: A long storage building from the age of Pericles, used to warehouse imported grain — mainly barley and wheat. It fed the Athenian navy based at the nearby port.
descriptions.edcaeefb-884f-4f74-b33c-1b3c44ed7c2d: A Minoan country house from around 1400 BC on the south-east coast of Crete. Pottery and tools recovered from the site show daily rural life well outside the grand palatial centers.
descriptions.af407cc1-1f93-4570-b93c-b38952a87fa0: Founded by Phoenicians around 770 BC, making it nearly 2,800 years old. Its Roman theatre, Moorish fortress, and Renaissance cathedral sit within steps of each other.
descriptions.ff53d37c-ab2b-4874-8ed8-a3336ccd12fc: A Late Minoan tholos tomb from around the 14th–13th century BC on 'Kafkala' hill near Maleme. Corbelled beehive vaults like this required each stone ring to be set smaller than the last.
descriptions.c5eb5ec1-0a24-41dd-9ca6-7ed721c29d3b: The third-largest Minoan palace complex, smaller than Knossos but with a unique circular kernos stone with 34 hollows. Each hollow may have held a different offering to the gods.
descriptions.e6eab365-fb0c-4851-94f9-8fcc35f1238d: The largest multi-period burial mound complex in the northern Black Sea region, with over 600 funeral sites. Burials span from the 4th millennium BC through the Medieval period.
descriptions.94fd509a-71e9-4a1e-b235-4eb91b1cacca: A former Nabataean caravan stop on the Incense Road that grew into a Byzantine city. Horse stables here could hold dozens of animals — vital for the desert trade route.
descriptions.eed2d08c-3d09-4d93-885a-0b0b2eb7126d: A Bronze Age hillfort from 1200 BC on a peak called 'Mother Hill.' Constant landslips on its eastern face earned it the name 'Shivering Mountain' and have been reshaping it for millennia.
descriptions.7cf71e81-b840-41ac-86e1-9d39eda3a2fb: A Roman fort founded around 79 AD at the junction of two major roads. The civilian town that grew around it eventually became the modern city of Manchester.
descriptions.56876b69-7222-4afd-8204-5f1f00bd0725: Two granite boulders near Øster Velling carry engraved geometric patterns from the Bronze Age — ships, sun discs, and other symbols. The stones were moved 50 metres from their original find spot.
descriptions.c1980a31-6a2b-4e83-ad99-8f36b6036ff2: A megalithic tomb from around 5000 BC with four side chambers and two dolmens built into a hillside. The remnants of a tumulus once covered the entire structure.
descriptions.d530ed2f-28b3-4802-a34a-555422ef0c43: An Early Bronze Age town on Euboea covering 50–80 hectares, with an estimated population of up to 15,000 around 2800–2200 BC. Few settlements of that era in the Aegean matched this scale.
descriptions.dd425ddf-0128-45e2-84dd-c442978149e3: A 2nd-century Buddhist stupa marking where, in the Jataka tales, Prince Sattva sacrificed himself to feed seven starving tiger cubs. Gold and bronze relics were found sealed inside.
descriptions.8382ce85-cfd3-485e-b738-58f21611091e: A medieval village formed along the King's Road, with eight estates by the 16th century. Recent excavations reveal daily life under Swedish rule in remarkable detail.
descriptions.fa579d23-36bc-469f-9351-2be5f11e180f: A Gandharan village near Rawalpindi dating to roughly 2,000 years ago, known for the nearby Manikyala Stupa. Local tradition holds the Buddha sacrificed part of his body here to feed seven tiger cubs.
descriptions.a055fb8a-0492-4a85-8660-f90db7efcc7a: Part of a cluster of about 200 Buddhist rock-cut caves in the surrounding hills. These Hinayana-phase monasteries were carved from solid rock to house monks in permanent retreat.
descriptions.2dfb1bee-9ec5-4eb6-b8b7-cfedbcb09744: A mud fortress built in 1797 to protect a harbor handling trade with Oman and Bahrain. The British captured it in 1839 and used it as a springboard to seize all of lower Sindh.
descriptions.ad4c7749-8844-4926-bed4-04ec7dd33543: Fourteen edicts of Emperor Ashoka carved into boulders in the 3rd century BC, written in Kharosthi script. They promote nonviolence — carved by a king who renounced war after its horrors.
descriptions.fd79f148-d931-42c7-8883-41732a93d209: A Wari-period archaeological site on a plain between two towns. The Wari empire was the first to unify much of the Andes, centuries before the Inca.
descriptions.3dd6b568-007f-4a95-877b-12324e031893: A site along the Qhapaq Nan, the Inca road system that stretched over 30,000 km across the Andes. Way stations like this kept the empire's relay messengers running.
descriptions.b1a2bdd2-590d-4a2f-8168-d398739c1661: A pre-Inca city built from around 400 AD, nicknamed 'Machu Picchu of the North.' Its circular galleries and monumental stone walls predate Inca construction by centuries.
descriptions.785bc662-62c6-43ad-a631-32d0a0a38842: A Roman capital city renamed by Emperor Trajan after his sister Marciana. Its excavated villas contain stunning mosaic floors that rank among the finest in the Balkans.
descriptions.4a59d4e4-c3b6-40bf-9153-302dd1f52595: A village atop several hundred Paleolithic industrial sites, now part of an archaeological reserve. Stone Age toolmakers came here for thousands of years to quarry local materials.
descriptions.ccf92317-4881-4850-a573-4ccd961772d5: The largest Neolithic henge enclosure yet found in the UK, built around 2200 BC. It sits exactly between Avebury and Stonehenge, raising questions about connections between the three.
descriptions.bebb7616-5341-4fd5-a69e-ee430e59c44f: A hilltop with a summit cairn whose surrounding peat has been dated to around 1500 BC. The uniformly aged peat suggests the cairn was built when the hilltop was freshly cleared.
descriptions.191945f6-3a8e-47bd-9a72-5ec74c14bef7: A Roman settlement on the Fosse Way whose Celtic name means 'marly fort.' It grew from a military post into a small walled town that outlasted the empire by a century.
descriptions.be29b127-7a5f-48fe-b1f9-ad4f67fe9c55: A fortress so formidable that Queen Zenobia of Palmyra laid siege to it and failed to break through. She declared 'he who reaches Marid has indeed attained power.'
descriptions.7c20f481-787e-44b6-b7f3-973e8d87c6d4: One of the ten ancient city-kingdoms of the island, prosperous from copper and gold mining. Ptolemy I razed it in 312 BC and relocated its entire population to a new city.
descriptions.cd2e38bd-c70e-4813-8ccd-0a567ab6a7ca: A mountaintop site at 3,580 metres with cave paintings and stone burial towers called chullpas. These above-ground tombs let Andean peoples keep their ancestors visible on the landscape.
descriptions.5d8a7c0e-3d54-497b-a9dc-5c9cbee82670: A village where a Scordisci Celtic settlement was found. The Scordisci were a fierce Celtic tribe who raided as far south as Delphi before Rome subdued them.
descriptions.1f5cb852-dcc8-440d-9931-c5968dff6cc0: A 19-metre Neolithic mound from around 2400 BC, second in height only to nearby Silbury Hill. It was later used as a castle motte, hiding its prehistoric origins for centuries.
descriptions.9bae60a8-363b-4c0a-a470-87836fcc9158: A Mesolithic coastal settlement from around 8800 BC, the oldest known in the Aegean islands. Stone tools, tombs, and structures show permanent habitation millennia before farming arrived.
descriptions.6023d320-c3ba-406d-98ea-9bfcd0eaae61: A 100-metre gallery with Paleolithic art along its entire length, including bison, horses, and human figures. Ornamental shell beads found here were carried from the distant Atlantic coast.
descriptions.3b4f0f7c-3828-49a3-bd1a-5392e2a34731: A Roman town at the junction of roads connecting three modern countries. Its amphitheatre, temple, and baths served a garrison guarding the vital Alpine passes.
descriptions.f7847cdc-5030-4ccf-bcdc-df1a6e47fce3: A Neolithic enclosure that became the type-site for a whole category of prehistoric earthwork. Archaeologists named the 'Martin Down type' after this exact monument.
descriptions.af65dcac-14b8-4dcc-802f-183c9fbf5db8: A Roman fortlet on a cliff edge, positioned to watch for raiders crossing the channel. Its garrison of perhaps 60 soldiers monitored sea traffic from this remote coastal post.
descriptions.9b10cebe-56ec-42cd-9f05-fa9c679c2bce: Established around 122 AD on the Cumbrian coast beyond Hadrian's Wall, this fort yielded 17 Roman altar stones buried in ritual pits — a concentration unmatched at any comparable site.
descriptions.8a082425-b949-4e34-a37a-02238d6a2817: Herod the Great's fortress atop an isolated rock plateau in the desert. In 73 AD, 960 Jewish rebels held out against 10,000 Roman soldiers — then chose death over surrender.
descriptions.2e23ad32-b50b-4439-8260-fe854b891c5d: The tomb of King Massinissa, who unified the Numidian kingdoms and ruled for 54 years until his death at age 90. He allied with Rome to destroy Carthage in the Punic Wars.
descriptions.291542d5-8a09-4599-bd7a-715f45e432a1: Bronze Age rock carvings showing men raising axes and spears, footprints, and overlapping figures. The carvings were added over generations, each artist carving atop earlier work.
descriptions.616719a2-c7ee-4162-b6f6-da52b85dbc4a: A Roman castellum on the southern bank of the Oude Rijn, guarding the Limes Germanicus. No pre-Roman finds have appeared here — the garrison was the first human settlement on this spot.
descriptions.4c0798e4-c439-490e-a8b7-60a0bad11cfd: A Neolithic henge 85 metres across, later converted into a Roman amphitheatre and then refortified as an artillery position in the Civil War of the 1640s. Three civilizations reshaped the same ring.
descriptions.fa26417b-eb7c-49d0-aaf7-adcd4909e78a: Built 353-350 BC for a Persian satrap and his sister-wife, it was so magnificent it became one of the Seven Wonders. The word 'mausoleum' itself derives from his name: Mausolus.
descriptions.5b56e7e6-b135-441e-a9d8-90fa30b4cff3: A pyramid of exactly 1,994 stone blocks was built over this grave in 1994 — the number matching the year. It is claimed to hold the legendary founder of the first Korean kingdom.
descriptions.69e127d4-7ea5-44b8-8b0b-b1b7fb000531: A 2nd-century Roman mausoleum built beside the road from Zaragoza to Pamplona. Only a single sandstone wall survives, but it marks where a wealthy family chose to be remembered.
descriptions.f34e558e-26db-49b6-8f93-67be4a67b097: An archaeological site at 3,915 metres on the banks of the Apurimac River. Ruins at this altitude testify to Andean communities thriving in conditions most civilizations avoided.
descriptions.b4d35f13-0f0e-479e-84a1-e388dda01d4d: Near Paccaritambo in the Cusco region, close to the place the Inca considered the mythical origin of their civilization — the cave from which the first Inca ruler was said to have emerged.
descriptions.3635030a-59d7-4fcf-84b2-e22a000e6b7d: The last Maya capital of the Yucatan, ruling from the 1220s until its violent fall around 1440 AD. Over 4,000 structures housed 15,000 people within a defensive wall.
descriptions.c078b659-9020-4254-84f5-bd19690dea97: A henge built from river cobbles rather than dug earth — unique among all known henge monuments. A single massive standing stone remains inside, where once there were several.
descriptions.04982451-5603-41cb-957d-758925170c8e: The site of ancient Madauros, a Roman colony famed for its schools. The writer Apuleius, author of 'The Golden Ass' — the only surviving complete Roman novel — studied here.
