descriptions.dd38b86d-325f-4243-8f7e-3cb8c47beaae: A luxurious late Roman residence from the era of Constantine the Great, with a peristyle villa and private baths. Emperor Constantine was born in the nearby city of Naissus.
descriptions.c3c19561-b4fc-48a8-9fd4-187fdc27f42b: A large stone wheel of white limestone laid on a mountaintop, used for sacred ceremony and astronomical observation. Its 28 spokes may track lunar cycles across the year.
descriptions.274ff0f7-d0f7-4f66-8c73-43cf53c895e9: The mortuary temple of Ramesses III, with massive reliefs of his victory over the Sea Peoples around 1178 BC. These carvings are the primary record of one of antiquity's most mysterious invasions.
descriptions.095b09bf-61d4-4ac8-9c91-7b7eb9d11aa7: A village with Iron Age roots and a church restored from Norman-era foundations. Old timber-framed cottages and chalk rock buildings preserve centuries of continuous habitation.
descriptions.c59f1d6c-eb9e-44af-adcf-75944b64358d: The only known group of Neolithic megaliths in all of the eastern part of the country. Built from local sarsen stone, they stand isolated from any comparable monuments.
descriptions.64f6ea93-b037-4a95-95e2-010e339fb0ac: A portal tomb from around 3500 BC with a capstone estimated at 24 tonnes. A supporting portal collapsed, leaving the massive stone tilting at a dramatic angle.
descriptions.689a3324-ea93-4c8a-b1d4-c0907751c5da: A Chalcolithic necropolis from the 3rd millennium BC at the end of a once-navigable stretch of the Torre River. Corbelled passage tombs occupy a 10-hectare hillside in the Portimão municipality.
descriptions.250f2312-e906-4021-aaca-984096199937: Over 80 Neolithic tombs clustered in a single forest — the largest concentration of megalithic graves in Central Europe. The Funnelbeaker people built them between 3500 and 3000 BC.
descriptions.98b331ac-5d1a-47e1-b854-4343f9a3e07d: Defensive walls from the 4th century BC, originally 3.6 km long, 4 metres high, and 5 metres thick at the base. Only fragments survive of these massive fortifications.
descriptions.38325c7e-7878-4dc9-b9eb-318ac744d3c2: Up to 5,000 Neolithic tombs were once scattered across this region; over 1,000 survive today. The Funnelbeaker people built them in varying styles that differ from district to district.
descriptions.41109fda-7c50-4e94-8441-4e372e2623a5: Founded in the 8th century BC near modern Augusta, Megara Hyblaea itself founded Selinus — among the wealthiest cities on the island. Syracuse razed it in 483 BC, ending three centuries of existence.
descriptions.62f21f04-c668-474e-8548-69bbdbc35620: A treasury building at Olympia where the city-state of Megara stored its offerings to Zeus. Treasuries like this lined the sacred way, each city competing to display its wealth.
descriptions.2eae8fd6-d3d4-4764-a8bd-2d3a8f88ebbe: Settled by 7000 BC on the Kacchi Plain, Mehrgarh ranks among the world's earliest farming villages. Drill-bored teeth with filled cavities found here predate all other known examples of dental work.
descriptions.fbdc7958-5aa3-4197-89fa-77f2a84cc4c9: The first attempt at a straight-sided pyramid, built around 2620 BC. Its outer casing collapsed in antiquity, leaving a tower-like core rising from a mountain of rubble.
descriptions.b8abad34-a66f-4e08-85e9-9b069301128b: A Scythian burial mound from the 7th century BC near Kropyvnytskyi. A gold-sheathed iron sword from the 1763 excavation ranks among the earliest examples of Scythian animal-style metalwork.
descriptions.b50c4816-2378-425f-abae-fa19a9cbaf3c: A 4th-century BC Scythian kurgan that yielded an elaborate gold pectoral and a gilded gorytos — a combined bow-and-arrow case — despite partial looting before excavation.
descriptions.8dd71a06-99c7-40a8-830a-702aa493f331: Enclosing 5.6 hectares on the Wiltshire–Berkshire border, Membury Camp's circular earthworks are completely shrouded in mature woodland, rendering them nearly invisible from outside the tree line.
descriptions.931415bf-1cf2-4132-89ec-10b88eadf5d1: Positioned 204 metres above sea level near the village of Membury in Devon, this hillfort commands sightlines across both the Yarty and Axe valleys — key corridors through the landscape below.
descriptions.e14380ae-7474-4960-8aa2-0c4b85569cae: Three standing stones including a ring-shaped holed stone. Local tradition says crawling through the hole nine times against the sun cures back pain and rickets.
descriptions.041bcb70-5676-4ef5-bab2-07f2153098c0: A Mycenaean settlement near ancient Sparta, with a sanctuary to Menelaus and Helen of Troy. In myth, Helen was abducted from this very place, triggering the Trojan War.
descriptions.f634e2ff-366e-49f1-be74-ac930ba5bc02: The second-tallest standing stone in Brittany, over 9 metres high. Legend says it rose from the ground to separate two brothers about to kill each other.
descriptions.000ca7dc-d1c0-41b9-ae83-95608b6c0cb9: An 8.7-metre granite monolith weighing around 85 tonnes — the tallest menhir south of the Loire. Notches in the stone show how Neolithic builders shaped it before raising it upright.
descriptions.6c6bb00c-45f8-4d2e-8532-79e612ae267a: A granite standing stone from around 3000 BC, classified as a National Monument. Menhirs like this dot the Alentejo landscape, often near megalithic tombs.
descriptions.521ade1a-0eaf-442b-973d-ccae9e9fbb35: At 7 metres tall and roughly 18 tonnes, the largest fully human-carved menhir on the peninsula. Found fallen near Castelo de Vide, it was later re-erected on its hilltop in the Serra de São Mamede.
descriptions.53325d71-8fe8-404a-8995-f4b2dd9d7d13: A megalith known locally as Penedo Comprido — 'long boulder' — found on its side in 1969 and later re-erected. It stands near the border, part of a megalithic landscape spanning two countries.
descriptions.416634af-9655-4973-a39a-9e1a9e3f0f2c: A phallic granite menhir from the 5th millennium BC, standing 2.7 metres tall near the town of Nisa. Scholars regard it as the second oldest identified menhir in western Europe.
descriptions.77de5950-a4b5-4dd4-a22f-7541057867c9: A group of menhirs from the Late Neolithic that served as territorial markers or defined sacred spaces. Some bear carved symbols, and more keep appearing as excavations continue.
descriptions.a1428be8-db83-4d05-be49-9ee85ed77689: A cylindrical limestone obelisk from the Early Neolithic with a faint spiral engraving. It was once part of a group of nine; only two survive today.
descriptions.48bd1c07-897c-4699-9c14-73ce5b01fbd6: Around 200 BC a Celtic oppidum of 49 hectares rose on the Staffelberg above the Main valley. Ptolemy recorded it as Menosgada — 'town above the Main valley' — in his geographical writings.
descriptions.872b2d83-1e91-46b7-82b6-299b706487a1: A standing stone bearing an early Medieval inscription: 'Rialobranus son of Cunovalus.' The stone itself is far older — a Neolithic or Bronze Age megalith reused as a memorial centuries later.
descriptions.e8acbde6-7c73-409f-a4cb-6bb47736f4c7: A spa town built over Bronze Age origins, with traces of settlement from the 3rd millennium BC. The ice mummy Otzi was found in the mountains above, frozen for 5,300 years.
descriptions.f1d0560a-b652-41f8-bc17-649dca0a5b48: A national park sheltering the Vallée des Merveilles — over 40,000 Bronze Age rock engravings at 2,500 metres altitude. Cattle, weapons, and geometric shapes cover the rocks.
descriptions.5144ec8c-3071-4484-83d5-aded69094bb0: An Eneolithic temple and burial complex of four large stone kurgans. The site preserves rituals from the Copper Age, when the first metal tools were changing human society.
descriptions.db82031b-7d84-466a-b0c1-d1fdf9a1b801: Home to Camp de Bierre, a Neolithic site with a dry-stone wall 32 metres across and 7 metres high. Stone construction on this scale without mortar required extraordinary engineering.
descriptions.1803a375-2b6b-4335-b158-98a371ce8889: A Bronze Age landscape on Dartmoor with stone rows, a stone circle, standing stones, and burial cairns. The sheer density of monuments suggests this moorland held deep ritual significance.
descriptions.f0a1dcca-8eb4-4c5a-b2ef-d90160d13d79: A vast Buddhist complex with over 400 statues, monasteries, and stupas — with a 5,000-year-old Bronze Age site buried beneath it. A copper mine threatens to destroy the entire site.
descriptions.bc058dac-5a3f-45db-8959-ba1df10920c4: Thracian fortification walls at Mesembria predate the colony's 6th-century BC founding. Hellenistic remains include an acropolis, a temple of Apollo, and an agora on the Black Sea coast.
descriptions.5945ab7d-4240-4c77-8eba-3761949713f1: Founded in 369 BC after centuries of Spartan domination, with 9 km of defensive walls. Its stadium, theatre, and Asklepieion are among the best-preserved Classical ruins anywhere.
descriptions.7f9cea0c-abb9-41c8-b475-76703db262f3: A Magna Graecia colony from 700 BC where the philosopher Pythagoras spent his final years and died. Fifteen standing columns of its temple of Hera still rise from the coastal plain.
descriptions.25f1846e-dc7e-4faf-b794-eed92f0ab6c4: A temple to the Mother of the Gods in the Athenian Agora, converted from the old city council building. It also served as the official state archive — where Athens kept its laws and decrees.
descriptions.d48494e9-7b90-40ce-816d-4aa39a43ba59: An ancient city inhabited continuously since the Early Bronze Age, 5,000 years ago. A theatre, bath complex, and colonnaded streets reveal a prosperous Greco-Roman urban center.
descriptions.16e6a769-9879-458f-8f21-35e26549dc66: Strabo records Metropolis was formed by merging three small Thessalian towns, later expanded with settlements including Ithome. The city sat within a natural quadrangle of high ground.
descriptions.e8764512-a557-49a6-b4ca-1ec9452e9563: A fortress site with evidence of metal smelting dating to the 4th millennium BC — among the oldest metallurgy in the world. It was destroyed not by the Urartians, but likely by Scythian nomads.
descriptions.6f91fd7b-d4db-43d8-ab5c-3aef866d4430: A castle ruin in the region ancient sources called 'Rough Cilicia,' a coastline so rugged it sheltered pirates for centuries. The fortress controlled the approaches from the interior.
descriptions.ca9afd0a-cb8a-4056-9869-4e77b7ca0a68: A 7th-century BC castle built by the Luwian people, originally called Kirshu. Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions found here are among the latest known uses of this Bronze Age script.
descriptions.01d20059-dc53-4f51-8669-33dac18f46bb: A 15,000-year-old dwelling built entirely from mammoth bones — jaws, tusks, and skulls arranged in patterns. Four such structures were found, each using bones from dozens of mammoths.
descriptions.2da0bfc3-cc20-444a-bfa7-bf23642ecb0b: A Paleolithic settlement known for engraved mammoth-ivory bracelets with geometric patterns. Some researchers argue the marks are the earliest known attempt at musical notation.
descriptions.bbb89876-9bbf-47fa-853a-8ca7465f176e: A perfect circle of 600 post holes cut into limestone bedrock, 11.5 metres across. It is the only known prehistoric permanent structure carved directly into bedrock on the East Coast.
descriptions.98fa4a94-3073-41d6-aefc-c5df9ba24c87: Dating to around 190 BC on the Potohar plateau, Mian Khan sits at the foot of hills along a route northeast of Mardan city. It is regarded as the oldest village in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.
descriptions.c5851dba-f3f4-4aaf-a4a1-37bf6a56600b: A wood preserving archaeological features from the Bronze Age through the Roman period. Centuries of forest cover protected earthworks that would have been plowed flat in open fields.
descriptions.2ca81ca5-16b2-4bc5-ac27-d23549309bc8: A 17-metre Phrygian rock facade carved into a cliff face around 600 BC, covered in geometric patterns. Despite its name, it is not a tomb but a shrine to the mother goddess Cybele.
descriptions.3c47ded2-01b0-4789-bf6e-defb171ddd43: Originally called Perseuspolis, this Mycenaean citadel in Argolis was linked in myth to Perseus and Alcmena — mother of Heracles. Its ancient walls still stand in the eastern Peloponnese landscape.
descriptions.32429f3c-6e14-4015-900a-a9cd9fbb81eb: A 1775 folly castle built in the shape of a playing card's clubs symbol. Legend says the owner chose the design after winning the fortune to build it in a card game.
descriptions.5e0211cd-62e0-47c8-95f5-3085dbd75768: Perched between two creeks on a narrow Rousay promontory, Midhowe Broch is a dry-stone tower from the 1st millennium BC. Part of the associated settlement has already been lost to coastal erosion.
descriptions.f7625adc-de9a-4628-90d2-4200314e7f80: A 23-metre-long Neolithic tomb from 3500 BC, divided into 12 compartments by stone slabs. The remains of 25 people were found inside, laid out on stone shelves like a communal ossuary.
descriptions.776629fa-7b09-4af3-ad4c-3de6dff22753: Spanning two hilltops along the Malvern Hills, this fort from around 390 BC contained hut platforms for over 200 dwellings — a permanent community, not just a refuge in times of crisis.
descriptions.bab70593-9241-44a4-b704-4b0d70c399f9: Settled since the late Bronze Age around 1200 BC, Miholjanec's late Iron Age inhabitants were recorded as the bini populi — 'two peoples' — whose identity remains debated among scholars.
descriptions.6fa8cd4d-074f-4b88-9f98-95465b49c9ae: Settled from the Neolithic onward, Milazzo's strategic peninsula was fortified by successive powers for millennia. Homer's Odyssey may place Odysseus's encounter with the Cyclops near this bay.
descriptions.b394e9cc-950d-45f6-9506-947b61692668: Bisected by a minor road near Newton Abbot, Milber Down's fort sits 110 metres above sea level. A rare bronze stag figurine found here hints at ritual activity beyond military use.
descriptions.b78239e5-3b96-4537-9cab-b700c3d7335c: Small forts placed every Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall, each with gates to control passage through the frontier. Eighty milecastles spanned the wall's entire 117-km length.
descriptions.d91a6d50-451d-42b1-9276-35b97c52bf5d: Small rectangular forts placed at regular mile intervals along the western coastal extension of Hadrian's Wall. They extended the frontier's surveillance beyond the wall itself.
descriptions.53300097-052c-41d7-b5a8-52110f7c8130: A Roman supply road running just behind Hadrian's Wall, linking every fort, milecastle, and turret. It was added after the wall was built, connecting a chain of garrisons across 117 km.
descriptions.d8e43401-673e-4f9a-902b-90959d10cf93: A Chanka-period site perched at 3,500 metres on a mountaintop. The Chanka were fierce rivals of the Inca — their defeat in battle paved the way for the Inca Empire's expansion.
descriptions.c1be948a-70d7-466b-bc60-1e2a3dc88612: A village with an Iron Age cemetery now protected as a cultural park. The burial ground preserves funerary customs from a time when Celtic and Baltic cultures overlapped here.
descriptions.81ee931d-9549-4cdb-a508-d06ae8971ba4: An extinct volcano where Celts built a massive oppidum covering 49 hectares. The hilltop also harbors a cold-air phenomenon — pockets of permanently cold air trapped in rocky crevices.
descriptions.e74b1d0f-c8e8-46f2-97e6-54a05a4cf2f6: A hoard of two gold torcs, three bracelets, and a bronze rod found in a pottery vessel in 2000. Dated to 1150-800 BC, these are among the finest Bronze Age gold pieces found in the region.
descriptions.9fe8d7e0-6fa4-4ab3-86b5-b33f0a95fd86: A 28.5-metre carved stone pillar near Kabul, built during the Kushan Empire's Buddhist golden age. It was heavily damaged during the civil war and later destroyed entirely.
descriptions.ba633252-4119-4f23-b1b7-6bfb3f86f2fc: An underground chamber dug 6 metres into a large mound around 2,000 years ago. Narrow steps spiral down into a rock-cut space whose purpose — ritual, storage, or something else — remains unknown.
descriptions.efc5d816-988a-4e81-9cbb-29be23f75771: A 2nd-century shrine to the goddess Minerva carved into a quarry face. It is the only rock-cut Roman shrine in all of Western Europe that remains in its original location.
descriptions.f8f6d3e9-c012-4fac-a562-cfbb592a3263: The ceremonial heart of Minoan civilization, covering 14,000 square metres with over 1,300 rooms. In myth, King Minos kept the Minotaur in a labyrinth beneath these very halls.
descriptions.b3ba4215-08b7-49b2-a217-f7bbf7a7d02a: The main naval base of the entire Roman Empire, housing the Classis Misenensis fleet. From this harbor, Rome controlled the western Mediterranean for centuries.
descriptions.efc21020-1705-481f-8e85-a2b1539ea6a3: A network of parallel tracks carved into bare rock, known as 'cart ruts.' Their age ranges from Neolithic to Medieval estimates — no one agrees on who made them or why.
descriptions.88c87513-c453-4b72-9630-287bf1a186c3: Thirty stone uprights on dry heathland at 330 metres in southwest Shropshire. Local folklore tells of a fairy cow milked by a witch into a sieve — draining it dry and breaking the enchantment forever.
descriptions.674ac922-23ba-4632-a588-9f50fa1a103e: A Zapotec and Mixtec city whose name means 'Place of the Dead.' Its geometric stone mosaics — assembled without mortar from thousands of fitted pieces — are unmatched in Mesoamerica.
descriptions.0ed41363-8709-42cc-a676-7cb76e3440bf: The entrance to an ancient tomb at Mitla, the most sacred Zapotec burial site. Priests descended into underground chambers to inter rulers and communicate with the dead.
descriptions.152323b2-51d4-4c65-b66c-8d9bd34e5ba8: A Postclassic Maya city with over 120 structures across 15 groups, set between two river gorges. It held out against the Spanish until 1539, one of the last Maya cities to fall.
descriptions.c1f010f5-9a19-4070-8a1d-a3ddb408eac8: Three conjoined Neolithic temples from around 3600 BC, built from coralline limestone. The lowest temple is astronomically aligned — sunlight marks the equinoxes and solstices on its inner walls.
descriptions.14dd917b-b58e-45d6-9578-bc1cefd34728: A Minoan harbor settlement on what was once a peninsula, now an island due to rising seas. Its graves yielded gold jewelry dating to 2600 BC — the earliest gold work found on the island.
descriptions.b269e1ad-573d-4cd1-8bb2-581a74b5f565: At 455 metres on a prominent Clwydian peak, Moel Arthur sits 1.6 km from the hillfort of Penycloddiau — part of a chain of six forts overlooking the Vale of Clwyd to the west.
descriptions.8338f530-c53c-4284-95fa-66062a89b887: Limestone quarrying has consumed the northern half of this Clwydian fort. What survives on the ridge above Dyserth retains substantial defensive earthworks with views stretching to Snowdonia.
descriptions.ab1ccd8a-a3b1-4266-adf0-9c04b3e3b1f4: A ring of 41 stones with a central cist, likely a ring cairn rather than a true stone circle. An outlying stone to the north-northeast may mark a celestial alignment.
descriptions.8ae2a431-14b9-4900-9b54-e8832b52cea0: One of a chain of Iron Age hillforts running along a mountain range. Its ramparts follow the summit contours, creating a defended space visible from the valley floor below.
descriptions.c6ad2aac-55ba-4cce-92eb-86f9e72c8781: Set on a western spur of the Clwydian Range near Llanbedr, this fort belongs to a chain of six where each summit could signal to the next — a coordinated warning network across the ridgeline.
descriptions.931d37ed-0a6f-4048-80ca-279f35f251e9: Crowning a summit of Llantysilio Mountain northwest of Llangollen, this fort is part of a heritage scheme managing six Iron Age hillforts in the Clwydian Range as a single conservation landscape.
descriptions.1268a0fc-ad34-46f1-878c-4cb4402d9cfa: A well-preserved 7th-century BC hillfort where excavations revealed timber defensive structures and multiple phases of building. The fort evolved over centuries, rebuilt and expanded repeatedly.
descriptions.8d416cb3-e799-4990-96a9-50a70fde39c2: An Iron Age summit fort on a rocky peak with a stone rampart around a small enclosure. Its high prominence and rocky terrain made it naturally defensible with minimal construction.
descriptions.b8cd2d69-a83f-4bcc-bad2-999627bb0567: A 4th-century BC burial mound that yielded a stunning gold wreath, silver vessels, and a complete horse harness with silver fittings. One intact tomb held a chariot and a sacrificed horse.
descriptions.48bcd825-c682-4bf1-bd67-af12191f2046: A ruined Roman villa rustica from the 4th century AD, now a protected national monument. Its position between two rivers made it both a productive farm and a defensible compound.
descriptions.a7ce791d-67cb-4895-bb89-00d4f1dd868b: A 2nd-century Buddhist monastery near Taxila where monks lived close enough to the city to beg for food but remote enough for silent meditation. Carved stone heads of the Buddha were found here.
descriptions.aceee58f-9865-4095-8bff-bef66f5baa73: A temple complex from 1800 BC with massive mound platforms and human-sized sculpted heads depicting deities. Large crowds gathered here for ceremonies long before the Inca existed.
descriptions.d78800a3-e78d-4c72-90b0-069140ad9b02: A Minoan town destroyed at the same time as the Old Palaces around 1700 BC. Its destruction layer preserves a snapshot of daily life at the exact moment catastrophe struck.
descriptions.5987b6e6-6da5-4f79-8ca2-674bfc7b3be9: A Baekje kingdom earthen fortification with walls 2.7 km long and up to 7 metres high. It defended the ancient capital during a period of constant warfare between three rival kingdoms.
descriptions.b596bc7e-15ff-4dfd-b052-710626210123: A Bronze Age hillfort occupied from 1850 to 1450 BC, surrounded by massive stone walls with Mediterranean-style architecture. Its layout mirrors Mycenaean citadels across the Adriatic.
descriptions.430a3857-be99-4701-91e1-82c5432f0f77: A Maya site on the Pacific coastal plain of Escuintla with enormous earth constructions covering about 1 sq km. Its coastal position shows how far Maya influence reached beyond the highlands.
descriptions.27f27e7e-4224-4378-b0d2-ef22f88bd725: An ancient city at 900 metres elevation with both Greek and Punic cultural layers. Its hilltop position made it a contested prize during the wars between Greeks and Carthaginians in Sicily.
descriptions.f7a0a44f-651b-4dfa-a500-e1a57feb2c2f: A mountaintop leveled and plastered to create a massive plaza, capital of the Zapotec from 500 BC. The 'Danzantes' — carved stone slabs showing contorted figures — may depict slain war captives.
descriptions.364ea265-5078-4181-a4de-46b51309996e: An ancient hilltop settlement on three descending terraces, with both Greek and indigenous Sicilian artifacts. A dolmen on the mountainside predates the settlement by millennia.
descriptions.95bc3d88-46db-4ee3-a5a2-4d1d04a50488: A 5,000-year-old spiral temple built from adobe and rounded stones, as old as Caral. Its unique spiral ground plan is unlike any other known temple in the Americas.
descriptions.5c7bd8b5-b6c8-4efa-be21-c84bfecdc3c7: A small hill with Neolithic and Bronze Age layers, controlling a narrow passage between plain and lagoon. Its strategic position made it a natural chokepoint for thousands of years.
descriptions.87fec19f-7aa6-42e9-9aba-bfdf3c3938d6: A mountaintop site where a 6th-century BC tomb yielded an extraordinary bronze krater with griffin protomes. The vessel was imported from Greece, evidence of long-distance elite trade networks.
descriptions.ed05c23a-973b-4d69-923c-b2e7b1b97305: A military fortress first erected during a 1640 revolt, later used as a prison and execution site through the 20th century. It now serves as a museum overlooking the city and harbor.
descriptions.2d786593-6e3f-40a9-8113-8012f6c2d35e: A victory pillar at Delphi, originally built by Macedonia but seized and repurposed by Rome after the Battle of Pydna in 168 BC. The conqueror literally put his name on his enemy's monument.
descriptions.5f980f95-98cf-4390-ba82-5f6af9e51155: A stele at Delphi honoring King Prusias II of Bithynia, a ruler so unpopular that his own son murdered him to take the throne. His offering to Apollo did not save him.
descriptions.38a17d5e-fd25-457f-9286-dce01bc61696: A Maya city whose 6-year-old king was installed in 662 AD under the supervision of Calakmul's ruler. By 690 AD, rival Palenque had poached the same king's allegiance.
descriptions.9755c087-8b24-46e2-9785-b5ac6c91f3ea: Concentric circular terraces descend into natural depressions at Moray, built by the Inca with an integrated irrigation system. Temperature varies by up to 15°C between the terrace top and bottom.
descriptions.93dd77da-64ad-4947-96b3-8ead4d6c98c1: A hilltop where over 250 pits filled with dismembered human and animal remains were found, dating to around 100 BC. The scale of ritual deposition here is unprecedented in Celtic Europe.
descriptions.0beaf7bd-7e6d-44f2-8f4f-7c3050b5d2b4: Once the largest funerary complex in Thebes, now almost entirely destroyed by floods and stone quarrying. Only the Colossi of Memnon — two 18-metre seated statues — remain standing.
descriptions.3f27e34a-1817-4b2b-bc19-c3c17a7e6374: Three terraces carved into the Deir el-Bahari cliffs for pharaoh Hatshepsut, who reigned 1478–1458 BC. Her successor Thutmose III later methodically chiseled her name from every wall.
descriptions.a6573398-0692-48b2-8dd6-ef01c8c26e33: The mortuary temple pressed against the Great Pyramid, built for Pharaoh Khufu around 2520 BC. It housed the rituals that sustained the dead king's spirit for eternity.
descriptions.5c669408-503d-4479-90a9-4968a8a679b4: A 19th Dynasty temple dedicated to the worship of Osiris, god of the dead. Seti I began it; his son Ramesses II finished and expanded it after Seti's death.
descriptions.89dd3a0c-d36c-439d-8ccc-f005666e7ec9: A Phoenician city on San Pantaleo, connected to the mainland by a submerged causeway. The marble Motya Charioteer recovered here ranks among the finest sculptures from the 5th century BC.
descriptions.8019f2d1-7e7d-4651-bc79-226f3f7458b0: An Iron Age triangular earthwork with coursed stone ramparts. Its name comes from the medieval Monceaux family, though the fortification predates them by over two millennia.
descriptions.e2542533-42d1-450b-b96a-e3b9fe79086c: Excavated repeatedly since the 1870s, this 400 BC hillfort shows signs of a violent end. Roman-period sling stones and charred timbers point to a final assault around the time of the conquest.
descriptions.65881dcd-e524-404a-a931-3d69e7348c71: A Minoan peak sanctuary where a temple at nearby Anemospilia may hold evidence of human sacrifice. A skeleton was found on an altar when the building collapsed in an earthquake around 1700 BC.
descriptions.a88980f8-c949-4f48-94c6-0185f01a6862: A mountain sacred to Zeus where, according to ancient sources, human sacrifice was practiced and participants turned into wolves. Athletic games held here may predate the Olympics.
descriptions.55d6f958-6ee7-4a0a-9e3c-23bbdb63d571: A mountaintop ringed by colossal stone heads from toppled 9-metre statues, built as a royal tomb around 60 BC. The king who built it, Antiochus I, placed himself among the gods.
descriptions.dfd872f8-26e9-446d-936e-bdbcd978257a: Unrecognised until the 1930s, this Dorset superhenge once held timber posts forming a vast roofed structure — among the most ambitious prehistoric wooden buildings in northwest Europe.
descriptions.bcc037db-7637-44c9-8204-3ce6d4370653: An Aboriginal greenstone quarry known as Wil-im-ee moor-ring — 'axe place.' Axes from this quarry were traded across hundreds of kilometers through established exchange networks.
descriptions.e522ea1d-4166-429d-8cac-8d31f72b944b: An Early Iron Age hillfort that was occupied for only a brief period before being abandoned. In medieval times the site was reused as a moated settlement with fishponds.
descriptions.92a50129-08f7-47c2-903e-6d50c29c2bef: Built in the early 1st century AD during Augustus's reign, this gravity dam on the Huerva River created a reservoir to supply the colony of Caesaraugusta — the city now known as Zaragoza.
descriptions.9599cc2a-23cc-44e9-9e5c-420b3392ca10: A 2nd-century Buddhist stupa in Gilgit, high in the mountains at a crossroads of ancient trade routes. Buddhism once thrived in these valleys before Islam arrived.
descriptions.ff38d0f1-cb2f-4a71-ad13-e925af8488a7: Three 1.7-metre support stones in a U-shape hold a partly slipped capstone on Mulfra Hill, Cornwall. From the hilltop the sea is visible over the surrounding landscape — a prominent Neolithic marker.
descriptions.482a2a89-7c40-4f4d-a411-ab99de88b701: Barren hills where Late Paleolithic and Mesolithic stone tools have been found scattered across the surface. These finds push human presence in the area back tens of thousands of years.
descriptions.e364d6eb-f92a-44d7-80b2-025092a81561: A fort whose original construction may date to 1000-800 BC, rebuilt many times by successive rulers. British colonial forces destroyed it, leaving only fragments of its long history.
descriptions.addf400a-89eb-41a3-8a0e-90d928b7904e: A Bronze Age center of the Helmand culture with a 9-metre-tall occupation mound. Its monumental architecture and artifacts link it to the Indus Valley civilization to the east.
descriptions.30e889ff-9d4d-4e93-be13-5f47ca534a91: Copper and iron mines drew Rome to this Seville hillside between the 1st and 3rd centuries AD. The terraced sanctuary fuses Roman architectural conventions with local pre-Roman building traditions.
descriptions.3eee3fb1-0f33-4eb3-99b9-ddabd93495e5: At Findon, Iron Age roundhouses and later rectangular Romano-period buildings share the same ground. The shift in form marks the material transition from native to Roman domestic architecture.
descriptions.7356fc90-8d0c-4554-b51d-f6b65c926244: The world's densest concentration of rock art — over a million petroglyphs, some up to 40,000 years old. Images include extinct megafauna like the thylacine, carved while the animals still lived.
descriptions.f0b9b853-6515-43e1-86dd-bc8dc326fff4: Positioned 175 metres above the Axe valley near Musbury, this hillfort controlled movement through the river corridor below. Its earthwork banks remain visible despite the site's lack of excavation.
descriptions.761dfa49-30a6-4e09-a4c6-cb5294f3a98e: An anthropological museum housing Olmec, Totonac, and Huastec artifacts, some dating to 1300 BC. Its collection of colossal Olmec stone heads is among the finest anywhere.
descriptions.7b061e76-f20f-447d-9650-c334492b86dc: The largest and most visited museum in its country, housing artifacts from every major pre-Columbian civilization. The Aztec Sun Stone alone draws millions of visitors each year.
descriptions.ac202ead-509d-4093-9680-2a4f4e74e8ea: A museum built directly on top of a ruined Roman villa, displaying mosaics from the ancient city of Marcianopolis. The polychrome floors depict mythological scenes in vivid detail.
descriptions.b36ba7d0-962c-48cc-93c2-717890bb64e7: Bronze Age stilt houses that collapsed into a river after a catastrophic fire, preserving everything inside. Textiles, tools, and even food bowls with meals still in them survived intact.
descriptions.fe6b3da9-80c2-4692-a859-cd645550fabd: Nearly square in plan with 9 bastions, this castle in Mut was built over the area of the Roman city of Claudiopolis. A cylindrical inner keep at its core suggests earlier Byzantine-era construction.
descriptions.7e40873d-033a-4bef-ba20-f4109219a1b3: Occupied from 350 BC to around 1500 AD on the Yucatan's eastern coast, Muyil spans nearly 1,900 years of Maya habitation. Its 17-metre pyramid once overlooked lagoon trade routes to the coast.
descriptions.2448ad8b-9e65-4eb8-ac3a-ede7cfcfd8e0: The circular stone base of an Inca tower within the fortress of Sacsayhuaman. Three concentric walls once supported a tower used as a Temple of the Sun before the Spanish dismantled it.
descriptions.27fd971a-5ea6-42d0-94db-e4a45523f016: A hilltop archaeological site at 3,400 metres on the banks of the Watanay River. Pre-Inca and Inca remains dot the hills around Cusco, each one a piece of the empire's sacred landscape.
descriptions.40ce67f7-1961-49cd-beff-33c03f702a17: Its Lion Gate — two carved lions flanking the entrance — is Europe's oldest monumental sculpture, 13th century BC. At 274 metres above the Argive plain, it dominated Bronze Age power in the Aegean.
descriptions.7d4c324c-649f-4414-91d8-93409b8fb168: A Mycenaean fortress ten times larger than contemporary Athens or Tiryns, yet never mentioned in Homer. Its massive walls enclosed a drained lakebed that served as agricultural land.
descriptions.3b7fc9a8-a685-4e5b-9ae7-df7a0d530d2e: A Mycenaean citadel linked in myth to Perseus and Heracles' mother Alcmena. Massive Cyclopean walls — built from boulders so large later Greeks thought giants stacked them — still stand.
descriptions.c5a5ae3a-46fd-45e6-8d02-45abfdee24aa: A Mycenaean burial ground spanning 450 years, with chamber tombs cut into the hillside. Gold jewelry, bronze weapons, and pottery found inside chart the rise and fall of Mycenaean Patras.
descriptions.163dc5dd-513c-4dd2-9fd2-87a74fe1078a: Carningli — 'Mountain of the Angels' — rises 347 metres in the Preseli Hills, its summit ringed by Iron Age earthworks. St. Brynach reputedly climbed here in the 6th century AD to commune with angels.
descriptions.0c879c8d-da82-4297-be35-796650ca0765: Roman practice camp earthworks and a hillfort share this plateau above Libanus in the Brecon Beacons. Rectangular outlines left by Roman military drills remain legible in the ground today.
descriptions.2e8550b6-1358-471f-9be5-9957b2613c9d: The name Mynydd Maendy — stone house mountain in the old tongue — marks a hilltop Celtic hillfort near Gilfach Goch. A wind farm now shares the summit with its ancient ramparts.
descriptions.d06989b5-7687-4624-aa68-92b4a7eab35d: A Lycian city famous for its spectacular rock-cut tombs carved to resemble wooden houses. St. Nicholas — the historical Santa Claus — served as bishop here in the 4th century AD.
descriptions.a4bfb021-8b30-4a2c-8d13-ed70b474ab0f: Scythian settlement founded around 800 BC between the Dniester and Dnieper rivers. After a Kyivan Rus revival spanning 900-1250 AD, the Mongols reduced it to ruins.
descriptions.6c2319ca-2998-4408-a7d8-2939397c300e: A Minoan settlement occupied for 2,000 years, destroyed and rebuilt multiple times. A unique stone vat found here was used for fermenting wine — the earliest known winepress on the island.
descriptions.f4f03f57-9987-48a4-98c0-c165e8e907fe: Capital of Lesbos since the 11th century BC, once home to the poet Sappho. Its ancient dual harbors were linked by a 700-metre channel cut through the narrow isthmus between them.
descriptions.97b3cd09-f833-48ca-8273-8b76767fc245: A remote summit in Primorsky Krai ringed by megaliths of disputed origin. Scholars argue whether the formations are natural weathering or deliberate human construction.
descriptions.1d7c880b-80be-41b1-8be5-58d07a0e5dcd: Surviving the Preclassic collapse while most Mirador Basin centres fell, this Maya settlement remained active from 150 to 950 AD. Construction continued here long after neighbouring sites went dark.
descriptions.35e015d9-6ab6-4763-9873-0ff2560b9b91: A 1532 AD castle built with reddish clay walls instead of the usual white plaster. The unorthodox color made it unlike any other fortress of the era.
descriptions.0fc4e372-5add-4a40-a51c-371e161e8bf4: An ancient city also called Dionysopolis, where Greek refugees may have settled after fleeing the fall of Ai-Khanoum. Greek culture thrived deep in Central Asia.
descriptions.be53cb70-c063-415a-a127-4997d12c405e: Settled by 1400 BC in the Mirador Basin, Nakbe predates most Maya cities. Structure 1, its largest pyramid, towers over 45 metres — built before the Classic period even began.
descriptions.238793b3-c335-4dcf-8155-c9e2d4985e0d: Bronze Age rock carvings with drainage channels all directed toward a canyon. Some carvings double as grave markers, hinting at rituals involving flowing liquid.
descriptions.f506ffba-65ac-49ac-8b8d-93fc29db3cd7: A village and Bronze Age site with artifacts spanning thousands of years of continuous habitation. Its current population is exactly one person.
descriptions.b9609879-342b-4fae-8dd5-5f6a6ac155d1: A Talaiotic settlement from the 2nd millennium BC featuring a talaiot tower 12 metres across on the outside but only 6 inside. Walls this thick were built to last.
descriptions.99341592-6e5c-4676-8037-cf8b0b763128: Tunnels and caves carved from volcanic rock since 500 BC, running beneath the city and all the way to Vesuvius. Naples sits on a honeycomb of ancient underground networks.
descriptions.3569c20c-c279-4f19-ae36-9f52ddf16c6c: Four bas-reliefs carved into limestone in the 3rd century AD by early Sassanid kings. The carvings document the founding moments of the empire that would rival Rome.
descriptions.26b5802c-5fbf-4f3d-b872-7201bf027518: Occupied from about 500 BC to 950 AD with six triadic temple complexes and two ballcourts. Its carved stelae record centuries of dynastic wars and alliances in the Petén Basin.
descriptions.d43a692d-7387-4bd2-8dd8-dcd70a85398d: A Bronze Age settlement in the Mil plain with ceramics matching the nearby Uzarliktapa layers. The pottery links sites across the region into one cultural network.
descriptions.bc10d0af-75ab-4c01-8b2c-a00327d0bb80: An 1814 fort built entirely from brick, with no wood or iron used in its construction. It was designed to guard the gateway to the Thar Desert against Rajput incursions.
descriptions.313f4e35-e699-41d0-93a3-7fe924d194c5: A cave with an inverted V-shaped ceiling and a precision-cut false door carved into the rock face that leads nowhere. Tiwanaku-style niches suggest pre-Inca origins.
descriptions.3191f287-4b47-4d83-903f-9815001086ed: A Harappan-era settlement occupied from 3000 to 1900 BC, just 6 km from the even older site of Mehrgarh. Together they span 7,000 years of continuous civilization.
descriptions.9e551c56-dda2-492e-ae6d-fe6896fdce32: Boat-shaped megalithic tombs unique to Menorca, dating from 3300 to 2100 BC. Their corbelled walls create the profile of an upturned ship, which gives navetas their name.
descriptions.71b5fca6-6ce4-43f0-bddd-6b3c15ca3f0e: The largest naveta on Menorca, a 1200 BC boat-shaped tomb standing 4 metres high and 14 metres long. Inside, remains of over 100 individuals were found.
descriptions.36359f5c-4989-4417-8b4b-dc534b6dceea: Boat-shaped Bronze Age houses built on the Balearic Islands from 2500 to 1200 BC. Their massive dry-stone walls served as both living quarters and workshops.
descriptions.ec7f3fd8-9328-4a69-bf84-594f4fc2aa2a: A Roman auxiliary fort guarding a bend of the River Noe from the 1st to 4th century AD. A civilian settlement grew up around it, as happened at forts across Britannia.
descriptions.cf614eac-2835-4d18-9904-13b9c47c1ed2: Giant geoglyphs etched into the desert over 2,000 years ago, depicting animals, plants, and shapes. They can only be fully seen from the air, and their purpose remains unknown.
descriptions.3b2ac589-fc14-4d95-a457-9b2912e40b0b: Around 4000 BC, the Cucuteni-Trypillian culture built a mega-settlement here covering 260-300 hectares with over 1,200 structures. At that time, up to 17,000 people lived within its bounds.
descriptions.cc775c2a-7c42-4cb9-a9ac-0bc6e3fbc0ec: The traditional burial site of the prophet Samuel, with a mosque built atop Crusader-era ruins. Beneath it all lies a Mamluk crypt housing the tomb itself.
descriptions.1d36e739-d9a2-411a-b6a4-aac1cda794e6: A necropolis of 288 rock-cut tombs spanning two distinct phases: protohistoric and archaic. The sheer density of graves suggests this was a major regional burial ground.
descriptions.0453d752-2033-4aee-9e66-0f831ea1e38e: A complex of fourteen artificial caves used for burials from the Bronze Age through the Iron Age. Each cave was hand-cut into the rock as a communal tomb.
descriptions.64b35e06-02b1-40d7-8931-ab1eaca02649: Three late Neolithic collective tombs from around 3000 BC, dug directly into smooth limestone outcrops. The dead were buried communally, not individually.
descriptions.23242c3f-c221-4689-a166-af4f464f5c1b: An Italic necropolis from the 1st millennium BC. Burial practices of pre-Roman peoples here offer a rare window into how Italic tribes honored their dead.
descriptions.9789eadf-a133-43dc-9f8e-2d7f7818ecc2: Five stone burial cists from the 4th millennium BC, each surrounded by stone circles. The design closely parallels contemporary tombs across the Mediterranean.
descriptions.05133e1e-6d12-461c-a682-d8ac77d2550f: The highest concentration of menhirs in Sardinia, with two megalithic tombs and stone circles from the 4th millennium BC. Over 60 standing stones mark this funerary landscape.
descriptions.ff8e7afb-57c1-4656-9e28-1881ee99157f: The largest Punic necropolis in the entire Mediterranean, carved into a hill whose name means "little cavity." It served Carthaginian settlers from the 6th to 3rd century BC.
descriptions.a5e18e50-09ea-4878-b26a-6ce7590ddb6d: At Negrine, Roman Casae Nigrae was built atop ground occupied since the Capsian culture, dating to 8500 BC. Capsians left massive middens of ash, snail shells, and stone tools.
descriptions.0060e6c0-8388-4762-bf51-9a3f88807899: Spanning the 2nd century BC to the 6th century AD, this Kakheti site holds a monastery founded in the 500s that still functions. The ruins mark the region's shift from pagan antiquity to Christianity.
descriptions.7063f8dc-a347-4324-9930-6983ed9c997a: A 2nd-century fire temple variously identified as Zoroastrian, solar, or Manichean. It was destroyed in the 5th century, and its true religious identity is still debated.
descriptions.c76343df-e566-42b8-a0a8-5ce3060a46bd: A 4th-century BC temple of necromancy devoted to Hades and Persephone, where the living came to consult the dead. It may also have doubled as a fortified farmhouse.
descriptions.2c0b2769-f00d-418a-853b-f1bd62f245cb: Home of the Nemean Games, one of the four great Panhellenic athletic festivals. Here, legend says Heracles slew the invulnerable Nemean Lion.
descriptions.968704a0-f6a5-4665-905a-e709f72eb39f: A 4th-century BC bathing house for athletes at the sanctuary of Nemea. It sat beside the athletes' lodging and served competitors in the Panhellenic Games.
descriptions.2e86513c-ffc6-4f83-9f75-3d12862c7592: Three main stupas flanked by 56 smaller ones and a monastery, dating to the 2nd-3rd century AD. The Swat Valley was once the Buddhist kingdom of Uddiyana.
descriptions.7f7fe84f-3bf8-415b-af7b-c6c95333807a: Houses two of the oldest surviving buildings in the world, dating to the 6th millennium BC. Over 1,800 artifacts were found inside these Neolithic dwellings.
descriptions.c69e6b19-ea4d-4983-841b-4682f9963d04: Neolithic flint mines active from 4300 to 2200 BC, among the largest and earliest in northwestern Europe. UNESCO cited their remarkable diversity of extraction techniques.
descriptions.d3b11ebc-593d-4f1f-bf1d-6a55902d93a6: A settlement near Mount Olympus from the 1st millennium BC. Despite its proximity to the mythical home of the gods, almost nothing is known about its ancient inhabitants.
descriptions.9d6d7ffa-cd80-481b-8b57-9ad7d0042776: Capital of the Histri tribe, ruled by the legendary King Epulon. When Rome besieged it in 177 BC, the defenders chose mass suicide over surrender.
descriptions.a45b9287-fe45-43b0-a8d6-8c434e16e65b: An ancient city on the Black Sea inhabited for over 3,000 years. Its old town sits on a peninsula connected to the mainland by a narrow human-made isthmus.
descriptions.f23e6b6d-f14b-459e-ac2b-f1b7fd943fd0: On a narrow finger of land at Scat Ness, a 2nd-1st century BC promontory fort uses the sea itself as a defensive wall. The fort lies 1.6 km south of the Old Scatness archaeological complex.
descriptions.d2299791-da47-4124-9bf4-ade97912a1aa: Derventio's Roman fort on the Stanegate road stood about 1 km south of Hadrian's Wall. By the 12th century, a church had risen directly atop the fort's foundations.
descriptions.bb0df218-2b05-41e7-b496-73c458bae35f: The site of two Roman villas near Watling Street, the great Roman road from London to the northwest. One villa was at Whitehall Farm, the other nearby.
descriptions.c74cd952-80cb-41e0-831b-475a738d890d: Home to Lugbury Long Barrow, a chambered tomb from around 4100 BC where 28 skeletons were found. A Roman villa and a medieval castle also occupied this site.
descriptions.2d89e6d4-8fa0-4258-a70a-bc42ad3c47bf: Traces of human habitation here reach back to 13,000 BC, with the town sitting on the shore of the lake that shares its name. Settlement has continued on this site for over 150 centuries.
descriptions.04cdaa66-9cc6-4135-b4b6-ae0f3dbcef2d: A stratovolcano with a 1.5 km wide summit caldera containing two crater lakes. Aztec and earlier peoples left offerings in these lakes at over 4,200 metres elevation.
descriptions.9b397e71-c3d1-4a5e-8ec4-48aee7d136c4: An Iron Age or Medieval earthwork that partially crosses the Polden Hills. It was part of a larger defense scheme along with the nearby Ponter's Ball Dyke.
descriptions.7ff04b48-cfda-41a9-9ad0-8d84c58510f0: One of the original seven gates of Roman London's city wall, dating to the 3rd century AD. By the 12th century, parts of the gate had become a notorious prison.
descriptions.e4f22a09-abfb-43d9-a7af-e87c033ae455: A 3200 BC passage tomb older than Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids. On the winter solstice, sunlight pierces a roof box and illuminates the inner chamber.
descriptions.6d9aac40-25c6-4379-8cc8-175b1a33f894: A 3rd-century Roman arch in Lincoln that is still used by traffic today. It is the oldest arch in the UK that vehicles still drive through.
descriptions.8d0a101a-45fb-42a3-8106-6a609161e7f1: Built in 280 AD from local flint, chalk, and limestone, this farmhouse still stands near its original wall height. Its roof was massive limestone slabs, each pierced by a single nail hole.
descriptions.7054234a-ec07-477d-afe0-df191dbca303: More than 650 petroglyphs crowd a single 200-square-foot sandstone face, carved across 2,000 years by multiple cultures. Designs range from bighorn sheep to abstract forms spanning 1 to 1300 AD.
descriptions.06a1c527-b9cc-44f8-a8a2-7d9510d1c5b0: A sacred Aboriginal tabletop mountain with evidence of human habitation dating to 38,000 BC. The Djungan people consider it a powerful Dreaming place.
descriptions.2d28d660-358d-4f4b-a99c-57d5b7395bc4: A Mycenaean settlement that cultivated olives and terebinth for export during the Bronze Age. At its peak it had a royal-style megaron, though it was always smaller than Pylos.
descriptions.9b34941b-70ae-4be4-80a5-eefc3c470ce0: A Roman city founded by Trajan around 102 AD to celebrate his Dacian Wars victory. It reached its zenith under the Antonine dynasty and minted its own coins.
descriptions.00980091-cbe8-4838-acff-78d936585d4c: A Roman town founded by Trajan to mark his 105 AD victory, one of two such victory cities in the region. Its coins feature the full Greek name Nicopolis.
descriptions.ba0ce1ee-9848-4de1-9884-0e0bb37e2abd: Mammoth ivory carvings from nearby caves date to 35,000 BC — placing this area among the earliest sites of artistic expression in Europe. The figurines were cut from mammoth tusks.
descriptions.521164cc-282e-46aa-8204-9c06a9627697: Four Roman temples in the Bekaa Valley dating from the 1st to 3rd century AD. Two sit at the edge of the village; two more hide 2 km uphill in a place called Hosn.
descriptions.6069036e-08d0-48dc-b808-ba568efe707f: The oldest city in the country, with Roman military presence from the 1st century BC. It celebrated 2,000 years of continuous existence in 2005.
descriptions.ee0017b2-44f4-426d-8901-5842c832eb30: Dubbed the most Roman city outside Italy, it has the best-preserved Roman arena and the Maison Carree temple. Neolithic habitation dates to 4000 BC.
descriptions.0d2486f1-4650-4c10-9f4c-b25a3e345012: A Maya Classic Period site whose king once wore a headdress so elaborate it became the site's modern name: "Big Hat." A jade pendant found here is among the finest Maya jewelry.
descriptions.564bde41-2281-41fb-979e-9d75e413a845: A castle built by the Ayyubids and massively enlarged by the Mamluks, with walls of carefully squared stone. Pointed cross-arches roof the towers along the walls.
descriptions.45e548cc-858a-45cb-bc0e-a470c897a06c: An Assyrian capital from 1350 to 610 BC, rebuilt by Shalmaneser I and made magnificent by Ashurnasirpal II. Its palaces held the first botanical garden in recorded history.
descriptions.06a44374-50d9-4bc1-b747-41fa09e28eee: About 30 pre-Inca chullpa burial towers perched at 3,000 metres elevation. Chullpas were built so the dead could face the rising sun in an eternal vigil.
descriptions.8cb5f5de-c5c9-4605-9f7b-1412e4e330cc: A Kulli civilization settlement from the 3rd millennium BC built on a flat schist bed with a central platform. The Kulli culture may have derived from the earlier Harappan.
descriptions.2a4b62ce-c1d8-4def-ba57-ec8c77edb502: Ten millstone grit stones form a ring 10.8 metres across on Stanton Moor. A lone outlier called the King Stone stands to the southwest, watching over the circle.
descriptions.0688bc28-0762-4ebb-b7b4-770340c2ff18: Sixteen stones still ring this burial chamber on Dartmoor, though its cairn was robbed and its central cist — locally called a kistvaen — destroyed. The site is also known as the Seventeen Brothers.
descriptions.402f38a8-f484-49eb-99bb-d508093abbd3: A 108-metre-long Neolithic stone row of nine megaliths, also known in Cornish as Naw-voz, meaning "the nine sisters." Stones range from 0.8 to 1.4 metres tall.
descriptions.b373de6a-8294-4c8b-88e5-8b4bf920d359: The smallest stone circle on Bodmin Moor, just 15 metres across with eight granite stones and one in the center. Only two stones were still standing before its 1889 restoration.
descriptions.ad4967fa-1303-4b2c-822e-de70130f841b: A stone circle originally 13.7 metres across, now reduced from seven stones to four. Cup marks carved into one surviving stone hint at ritual significance lost to time.
descriptions.50f9ccc8-06b1-4283-af88-a6769d0b9083: Nine sarsen megaliths form a compact ring just 9 by 8 metres wide near Winterbourne Abbas. A small opening at the base of one stone — perhaps a symbolic threshold — gives it an air of ritual purpose.
descriptions.f166fc6f-310e-4ca1-8b61-edb98e2c7ec2: A city continuously inhabited for over 2,000 years, founded by Celts and later reborn as the Roman city of Naissus. Emperor Constantine the Great was born here in 272 AD.
descriptions.feb1725e-7ef0-464d-8659-17912cfa7a05: A Bronze Age fortress built with Cyclopean masonry on a hill, with a square plan, corner towers, and an internal cistern. It dates to 1725-1450 BC on the Karpas Peninsula.
descriptions.d8d9d536-918c-461f-a05f-4080c8660afa: The oldest archaeological site in the central part of the island, with habitation from around 4,000 years ago. Neolithic people here knew agriculture and lived in settled communities.
descriptions.5077f16f-1d87-4be3-a870-35f3e1cf55fe: The Riesenberg — a megalithic tomb of glacial erratic boulders — sits metres from the cliff edge above Tromper Wiek bay. It ranks among the largest stone graves in the northern Baltic region.
descriptions.f509d927-063b-4a03-b40a-624aadd6a2a4: Six architectural groups at this Early Classic Maya city were built during a single construction boom. Hieroglyphic texts link Noh Kah to the Snake Kingdom dynasty's government in the 5th century AD.
descriptions.db29dbfd-e56d-41ac-a815-161899b03f2b: A Maya pyramid built around 250 BC, largely destroyed in 2013 by contractors mining it for road gravel. Only the core of the once-massive structure survived.
descriptions.da470f76-02c7-479e-b4e5-809381183ab8: Over 200 burial mounds of the Xiongnu aristocracy, dated to the late centuries BC. One tomb belongs to Wuzhuliu, a historically documented Xiongnu ruler who died in 13 AD.
descriptions.a621b66e-1fda-41b4-9c34-d1a3e7486bd5: A 20-hectare fortress that served as a stronghold of the ancient kingdom of Colchis. Multiple layers of ruins span from the 4th century BC through the 6th century AD.
descriptions.ef162631-d359-4a8d-a69b-106be09f6b85: A bank and ditch defend a spur on Brown Clee Hill, from the late Bronze Age into the early Iron Age. The univallate fort sits at the plateau's western edge, overlooking the Shropshire Hills.
descriptions.719a16f0-0834-4e6a-962b-650b166c730c: A barrow cemetery visible from Stonehenge along the southern horizon, with burials from 2600 to 1600 BC. Over 40 round barrows line the crest of a low ridge.
descriptions.afa52222-ee6e-4b90-aae8-3078dae3ae71: Ploughed almost to nothing on its south and east sides, this univallate hillfort survives only within a small copse. Double banks and ditches there remain hidden under trees and undergrowth.
descriptions.a2c6e1bf-1538-43c4-ad4a-65a0186193a7: An Iron Age warrior buried with an exceptional set of grave goods, including a unique helmet. He was about 45, stood 1.72 metres tall, and was buried with full military honors.
descriptions.79d3bea7-47b0-4ca9-a969-a6d19775977c: A Roman villa that grew over four centuries into a luxurious estate with 19 mosaic floors. It eventually became a sprawling courtyard complex with housing for farmworkers.
descriptions.fd3adb91-4d43-4d62-ad03-d33615f0119c: The fort here bore the name Nemetostatio — road-station of the sacred groves — hinting at a pre-existing Druidic sanctuary. Romans crossed the River Taw at Newland Mill and built successive camps.
descriptions.befdcbb6-1a51-45eb-9ed3-30281f402bcf: A Bronze Age hill fort with a single circular rampart 250 metres in diameter. Three holloway entrances are flanked by linear banks extending from the perimeter.
descriptions.2e0236e5-ca62-49f1-8532-303463aba86b: A central passage and small chambers held human remains for thousands of years before the barrow was sealed in 1976. The mound measures 27 by 18 metres and dates to the 3rd millennium BC.
descriptions.28748d23-bf94-4025-83a1-22ad8a78a882: A 1st-century AD legionary fortress on the Danube, Novae later grew into a town in Moesia Inferior. It has been fully excavated and opened to the public — rare among limes forts.
descriptions.26f1208b-57b5-400e-a2b4-160d91fcf7de: Julius Caesar founded Colonia Iulia Equestris around 46-44 BC on land seized from the Helvetii. The colony settled cavalry veterans and anchored the military frontier.
descriptions.673d799c-45de-440d-9e65-df84ddf7ee95: Chichester's Roman predecessor, first a legionary winter fort in 43 AD for the invasion of Britain. The army left, and a proper Roman town grew in its place.
descriptions.d53238e1-cad3-4f42-bfb0-bf072e4aebd3: Granite and sandstone pyramids built over several centuries as tombs for Nubian kings and queens. They are steeper and smaller than their Egyptian counterparts.
descriptions.68e33bbf-a632-4b27-992e-ce0910417b48: A Bronze Age village on a plateau near the Ggantija megalithic temples, occupied from 1500 to 700 BC. Grain storage pits are among the few visible remains.
descriptions.1aabb9f3-327b-48d5-9fee-045f7ebd4f1f: A Celtiberian stronghold that held off Rome for 20 years. In 133 BC, Scipio Aemilianus built a siege wall around the entire city; the defenders starved rather than surrender.
descriptions.a777855f-56f5-4860-8707-d90dfb1f5053: Over 7,000 tower-fortresses built between 1900 and 730 BC dot Sardinia; archaeologists estimate 10,000 originally existed. No other region holds such a dense concentration of megalithic towers.
descriptions.75e58917-b363-45f5-8d87-a0b836856398: Bronze Age and Iron Age huts surround a roundhouse with a water basin — among the best-preserved examples in Sardinia. Melting slides here confirm major bronze-smelting activity.
descriptions.e3f62da6-9fdb-4011-9135-47f41c546ac7: A 7-hectare Nuragic village with a holy well, two megaron temples, an amphitheatre, and a labyrinth. Romans occupied it in the 2nd-3rd century AD, adding another cultural layer.
descriptions.e5bb0a42-df89-47d8-9ac4-669df257592a: A village hidden inside a massive cave on Monte Tiscali, with round and rectangular dwellings from the 1st millennium BC. It was reoccupied in the 1st century BC and used through the Middle Ages.
descriptions.dafc7527-c6c8-45c3-8c7d-4813d20a4dcf: An Inca archaeological site featuring a carved white rock known as Yurac Rumi. Carved rocks like this served as sacred shrines tied to Inca cosmology and landscape worship.
descriptions.f96b9c6e-f51d-4cb7-88b2-3015b25bd05c: The first Bronze Age site found in the country, with burials containing pottery filled with animal bones, beads, and spear points. No iron was found, helping date the site precisely.
descriptions.f12e6473-3c60-4196-a99d-0611be3bb2a3: An Iron Age sacred bog where defeated armies' weapons and ships were offered to the gods. Items were deliberately bent, broken, or hacked apart as ritual sacrifice.
descriptions.250714e7-df78-444d-bfc0-303dfd6a3a03: A hub of the Bosporan Kingdom since the 600s BC, Nymphaion stands on a rocky cape now 200 metres from the shoreline as erosion claims the ancient waterfront. Its ruins overlook the Cimmerian Bosporus.
descriptions.bd8def7d-14df-4ba8-902f-a2ba0d93fdd6: Built around 2800 BC and measuring 27 by 18 metres, Nympsfield holds multiple separate chambers. Curving walls frame the trapezoidal entrance to the mound.
descriptions.2caba95a-c797-4e59-bea2-959793b6c6fc: Settled around 500 BC as Nyrax by a Gallic tribe, the site was described by Hecataeus of Miletus ca. 500 BC — placing it among the first Celtic towns to appear in written records.
descriptions.e62c980a-351d-40c1-8297-05f52f72a59c: A 100-metre Roman bridge built as a double-decker: the bottom vault carried a brook, while arches on top connected two hills. It functioned as both bridge and tunnel.
descriptions.ae28d423-c02b-44be-b78d-7d65c99f3c3b: Roughly 30 barrows cluster near a Neolithic mound on Cranborne Chase, dating from 2500 to 800 BC. The earlier earthwork likely shaped where Bronze Age communities chose to inter their dead.
descriptions.c13dae70-fbe5-41bf-9679-57fd17343e4a: A Neolithic entrance grave on a steep slope, where excavation revealed a crouching male skeleton and Bronze Age cremation urns. It sits on the tiny island of Gugh in the Isles of Scilly.
descriptions.37008e3f-056c-43dc-81c2-74904cacdb4e: Hewn from a single granite block, this Aksumite stela stands among the tallest monoliths erected in antiquity. The obelisks at Axum date from the 4th century BC to the 10th century AD.
descriptions.a50cf939-77f1-489c-82f7-93b07b2bc5ae: A 160-tonne phonolite stela from the 4th century AD, decorated with false doors and window-like carvings. Metal frames once enclosed its semicircular top.
descriptions.8db3d247-e43b-4e08-ba47-b73dea0e3fd5: The second-largest ancient obelisk, carved from a single block of pink granite in 1457 BC. It stands 28.58 metres tall and weighs 343 tonnes.
descriptions.54dead1c-8dc0-4cdd-a581-47d2e033fdab: An Egyptian obelisk of Thutmose III, re-erected in Constantinople's Hippodrome by Emperor Theodosius I. It traveled from Aswan to Istanbul, surviving millennia and two empires.
descriptions.9b1fc275-41fd-4fbd-b88c-b4e05eb0b29d: The last survivor of four obelisks that once flanked the entrance to Karnak Temple. It stands 21.7 metres tall, weighs 143 tonnes, and carries three columns of inscriptions per side.
descriptions.871fbe6a-2eb0-4d28-b2bf-1a58d9e5766c: An ancient Black Sea port that was a Greek colony of Mesembria. The Romans named it Templum Iovis, Temple of Jupiter, reflecting its sacred significance.
descriptions.e7ee7c00-1b94-4ff8-832e-7af0323bd3aa: An Italic-Roman settlement with temples to Jupiter, Hercules, and a shrine to Ceres and Venus. Pilgrims, traders, and shepherds all stopped here to worship.
descriptions.7c762fd9-2ec5-4d25-a67b-f391837257af: A hamlet with a stone circle that underwent a major excavation in 1997. It revealed oak post circles from 2872 BC were replaced by stone circles centuries later.
descriptions.41aca9cf-1bfc-4ef6-90e2-3de22ff55604: A stone circle built in stages: first two concentric rings of oak posts around 2872 BC, then their removal and replacement with standing stones centuries later.
descriptions.2cabb7a1-0596-457c-b37f-c041440b4fe2: A stone Roman theatre built in 161 AD with a three-story facade and a wooden roof of Lebanese cedar. It seated 5,000 and still hosts concerts on the slopes of the Acropolis.
descriptions.df0881e1-4fd6-4d2d-b9de-ffdca718970c: A Roman-era council house that doubled as a theatre, built in the 2nd century AD. It went through four construction phases before being abandoned in the 4th century.
descriptions.3a28b216-d9f2-410d-a12e-050fc4759a98: A small 2nd-century AD Roman theatre, not to be confused with the large theatre next to it. A temporary wooden roof once shielded the audience from the elements.
descriptions.ff3a9a41-c6ee-459a-ad30-cced049e2dbb: A major Roman city on the Danube whose name comes from the Thracian word for "water." Ongoing excavations keep revealing new parts of this once-thriving settlement.
descriptions.9c7230d0-e962-4c5f-95c0-3b3ea8cf1b4c: Ploughing had badly damaged this 4th-millennium BC causewayed enclosure before Peter Drewett's 1976 excavation. Its ditches alone yielded roughly 7,000 pottery fragments.
descriptions.2f8e6a44-0802-497a-aeb5-5f680ebae88f: A city once known for having 365 churches, one for each day of the year. It sits on a lake so ancient and biodiverse it is sometimes called the European Galapagos.
descriptions.1c0baadb-054d-4ffc-be2a-9da571437fb2: A Lycian city near the Taurus, Oinoanda preserves a 65-metre Hellenistic wall of polygonal masonry. Stone pipe sections from a Roman aqueduct siphon remain visible on site.
descriptions.7e6261c5-5292-4019-8a1b-5860a37714f9: Overlooking the ancient crossing of the River Barle, this oval fort stretches 220 by 91 metres with bank, ditch, and rampart. It lies near the Devon border north of Dulverton.
descriptions.a2b988c2-368a-44ac-a95b-32d73d74a116: A 50-hectare multivallate fort west of Ightham — the largest Iron Age fort in southeast of the country. Sling stones hint at violence; wooden gates once barred the entrances.
descriptions.49967491-e345-4a3f-933b-37636fa18da3: Rock shelters occupied by Neanderthals around 50,000 years ago, where they made distinctive bout-coupe handaxes. These tools are a hallmark of the final Neanderthal cultures.
descriptions.9760e579-1005-4b8f-bf08-b9be81a716da: A group of six Neolithic burial mounds and dolmens from around 4100 BC. The largest dolmen was once 45 metres long; most of its external stones remain.
descriptions.2efa2892-86a4-46f7-bc3f-03c631621930: The first Parthenon, begun after the Battle of Marathon around 490 BC but never completed. Its massive limestone foundations still lie beneath the current Parthenon.
descriptions.c7bbe836-c8b3-4e74-ae95-08724e63b389: A Bronze Age through Urartian citadel set on two large hills. Nearby, Cyclopean forts at Ghak and Shvaghtapa form a network of ancient strongholds.
descriptions.58b9666f-7ff2-4be0-9843-7f1c2b43592c: Called the Stonehenge of the Iron Age, this hillfort's layered earthworks in north Shropshire date from 800 BC. The Mercians later incorporated it into Wat's Dyke during the early medieval period.
descriptions.d368515e-bbd0-4ad3-99d3-4288e2fa9545: The original site of Salisbury, inhabited from 3000 BC through the Middle Ages. It sits on a hilltop just 3 km from where Salisbury Cathedral would eventually rise.
descriptions.f7c6b78b-4d82-4443-bd30-ecda84f4bc6e: An archaeological layer cake: Iron Age broch, Pictish buildings, Viking remains, and Medieval structures, each generation building atop the last for thousands of years.
descriptions.50fdb577-af39-425e-a038-a0f8205f66fc: A 6th-century BC archaic limestone temple on the Acropolis that housed the xoanon, the sacred wooden cult image of Athena. Its foundations were only confirmed in 1886.
descriptions.a0f4690e-06d0-457b-92da-40207bfeec25: Bronze Age barrows from 2100-750 BC cluster inside a hillfort built ca. 600-300 BC and abandoned by 100 BC on a 66-hectare Hampshire ridge. Two eras of burial and defence overlap in the earthworks.
descriptions.cb100b64-537e-4105-802b-acf4d530254e: An Inca royal estate built by Emperor Pachacuti in the 15th century, with massive stone terraces and a ceremonial center. Its enormous wall blocks fit together without mortar.
descriptions.d2bfe5ff-6e7a-46ad-b9ae-69723cb08563: A commune with two archaeological sites, Cuntorba and Figa la Sarra. Little is known about these settlements beyond their existence on this Mediterranean island.
descriptions.9ba7c034-6aec-492e-b66e-4541ce3c987c: Home of the ancient Olympic Games for over 1,000 years, from the 8th century BC to the 4th century AD. Over 760 buildings once filled this sanctuary to Zeus.
descriptions.00f522ff-8e1b-4983-961c-ef6cb1ff27d1: Ruins of an ancient Lycian city, now part of a national park. Together with Phaselis and Idyros, it lines a stretch of coast rich in ancient harbor cities.
descriptions.04d8ce82-4fa3-4e48-88b7-bb41b354260c: Remains of the Lycian city of Olympus, founded no later than the 4th century BC. A wall and a sarcophagus inscription provide the earliest evidence of habitation.
descriptions.d5eb0b0d-1c74-4b14-aea9-a765f7a97379: Philip II of Macedon razed Olynthus in 348 BC after the city flourished from 432 BC. Its grid-plan streets across two flat-topped hills are an early landmark of urban design.
descriptions.976c20ca-6be3-4db6-843d-e4dd2d77a0c5: A sacred marble stone at Delphi marked the navel of the world: Zeus released two eagles from opposite ends of the Earth and they met here. It dates to the 2nd-1st millennium BC.
descriptions.12217bc1-adc7-4c12-ac37-3f690e02cfdc: Vesuvius buried Oplontis in 79 AD. Its two excavated villas contain extraordinary fresco cycles — Villa A's wall paintings rank among the finest surviving Roman frescoes anywhere.
descriptions.c9645011-82ed-4818-b2fd-0b3632713d1c: A Gallic hill town covering 20 hectares, Altimurium was founded in the 2nd century BC. By the 1st century BC, a 2 km perimeter wall enclosed the entire settlement.
descriptions.b4cf565e-e8fa-4f06-b2ca-68c9e7ff4d4f: A Gallic hill-town occupied continuously from the 6th century BC until Roman rule. It sat near the Via Domitia and the Canal du Midi, commanding fertile farmland in the valley below.
descriptions.1feef50a-659c-4a9b-bebe-d12b641036b1: One of six Iron Age oppida in the Vaunage valley, first occupied around 700 BC. Its inhabitants moved between nearby hilltop settlements as fortunes shifted.
descriptions.1c1c8f74-707b-4ad2-a0db-d7518b9138b6: One of six Iron Age hill forts in the Vaunage valley, occupied from 800 to 50 BC. Four distinct construction phases show a community that kept rebuilding itself.
descriptions.6125f2db-15e7-4770-aaa3-5616fa6cf623: An Iron Age hill-town built around 700 BC, not fully excavated until 1911. It has been a protected historical monument since 2004.
descriptions.f309bc3f-15a8-4f5d-afbb-7d2128b9c1f7: Founded in the 3rd century BC, this oppidum reached 380 hectares at its peak in the late 2nd century BC, housing up to 10,000 people. A 7.2 km wall enclosed a settlement of urban scale.
descriptions.2eeaa376-a489-4600-83cf-0318d19e9d4a: A Celtic oppidum on a volcanic basalt cone, its name literally meaning "stone castle." The twin peaks of Kleiner and Grosser Gleichberg are geological twins of volcanic origin.
descriptions.150e64a1-8d04-49fb-b4cb-49c8b2c2fc4f: A La Tene oppidum near Zurich from around 500 BC, with a 5th-century BC burial field later destroyed by railway construction. Excavations since the 1830s documented its scale and extent.
descriptions.ea2fba59-c9e4-4471-bb38-b07cd2d3845a: An Iron Age enclosed settlement in what is now Winchester, dug in the early 1st century BC. The later Roman town of Venta Belgarum was built right over its eastern end.
descriptions.fd07993c-983b-4d37-b01d-6ef8f8aeb7a6: A Roman theatre with its original back wall rising 37 metres — the most complete stage wall surviving anywhere — stands in this town. A triumphal arch from Augustus's reign also survives here.
descriptions.f8ec7ade-8db0-4be6-b75b-ce13fa8e0a70: A powerful Arcadian city from the 7th-6th century BC that minted its own currency. It began as a prehistoric settlement and grew into one of western Arcadia's dominant powers.
descriptions.ffd8b3fc-4127-4b2b-9df1-212aac377683: A city of the Minyans that became one of the wealthiest Bronze Age settlements in the region. Its 14th-13th century BC tholos tomb rivals the Treasury of Atreus at Mycenae.
descriptions.6d4a0330-a271-4d2d-a0c8-2a5f768e78af: An ancient Greek harbor that began as an Illyrian port in the 6th century BC and grew into an important Roman city. It straddled the border between ancient Epirus and Illyria.
descriptions.0a9380b3-247c-4564-b1da-0195ea84236f: A Scordisci village in the Vinkovci area, Orolik formed part of a La Tene network across the Vukovar-Syrmia region. It preserves the Iron Age cultural layer beneath a continuously inhabited village.
descriptions.0db1078f-012b-42ef-a9b4-e5e482c92767: A stone village of low, windowless, sod-covered buildings perched on the rim of the Rano Kau volcanic caldera. It was the center of the Birdman cult on Rapa Nui.
descriptions.a3fdb1d8-083b-4e8f-a170-5b98638d5b53: Built in 1583 by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, this castle was at the center of 16th-century wars that unified the country. It has been destroyed and rebuilt multiple times — the current tower dates from 1931.
descriptions.698f577f-cfce-45b6-b2a7-6ddeaa1f5923: A city on the Drava River with origins in the Neolithic. The earliest known inhabitants belonged to cultures that predate any written record of the region.
descriptions.7345ac3a-0fbd-4507-807b-a2f8a592c39d: A megalithic structure behind the Temple of Seti I at Abydos, built with enormous stone blocks. Its original purpose is unknown and has sparked centuries of debate.
descriptions.c4d4863e-2344-49aa-8699-457d71985c96: A shaft descending 30 metres below the Giza plateau to a flooded tomb chamber. Its second level held two granite sarcophagi, pottery, and bones dating to 1550-500 BC.
descriptions.f523b5df-b6a1-4dd9-ab12-59e22b0c7ea0: Nine or ten temples were built successively on one spot at Abydos from the 1st to the 26th Dynasty. Each new temple incorporated walls of the one before it.
descriptions.1a3eff28-12e9-441c-9e4d-ae763e52b867: Settled since 4000 BC, with Lengyel and Globular Amphora cultures among the first inhabitants. The city later became a hub of the country's oldest industrial basin and its historic metallurgy.
descriptions.cbca1610-17fd-49f8-9c3e-536db4f7c9ce: A 4th-century BC Thracian burial mound over 18 metres high, with six chambers covering 100 square metres. One chamber is carved from two solid granite blocks totaling 60 tonnes.
descriptions.90dac465-52f7-495a-ae8e-79953fa8d9b9: A Silk Road ghost city that commanded the crossroads connecting China, Europe, the Middle East, and Siberia. It thrived from the 1st to 15th century AD as a regional trade hub.
descriptions.37f08947-0576-48de-90ca-ef211b615619: A former royal capital for nearly 250 years until 1866. A monumental royal necropolis of successive sovereigns stretches across the top of a prominent mountain.
descriptions.cee33cc0-9de5-493c-b43b-82678a6b1d8b: A city known since Roman times for its hot springs, called the Burgas. It remains one of the European cities with the greatest thermal heritage.
descriptions.4248c931-9e5f-470d-94d5-545746b84336: An ancient settlement with layers spanning the 5th to 3rd millennium BC. It sat on the left bank of the Arpa River and was occupied for over 2,000 years.
descriptions.47fd6754-01a4-4aa9-aef6-c81ef7695e46: A 1st-century AD timber fort rebuilt in stone, Over Burrow stood in Roman-era Lancashire above the Lune valley. By the 18th century, Burrow Hall was built directly atop the buried fort.
descriptions.414416be-0a81-45f7-a572-216f39ee6a0d: A 1960 experiment in archaeology: an earthwork was deliberately built and buried with test objects. It is being excavated at intervals over 128 years to study how sites decay.
descriptions.f784a924-a2de-42ae-b530-4b292753fa8f: The start of the Ridgeway, one of Britain's oldest roads, likely in use since the Stone Age. Several scheduled barrows and ancient monuments cluster around this hill.
descriptions.02dbd963-d64f-4c40-a267-2ad5b2ea821a: Occupied from 600 BC to 1500 AD, this Maya site is famous for the Satunsat — a building designed as a labyrinth replicating a cave, with ventilation shafts aligned to celestial events.
descriptions.86400297-e0cd-42ec-b79d-aae00be16bfd: A fortified Moche and Chimu city from 600 to 1370 AD, protected by cliffs on two sides and a wall on the third. Brick serration patterns reveal the chronology of its construction.
descriptions.4cc8d5e7-e7f8-443e-b787-2a8529667d68: Inhabited for nearly 2,000 years from 900 BC, this southern Maya lowland site sits atop a partly artificial limestone acropolis. Its Maya name means stone set in earth.
descriptions.54c10788-8f83-470d-9a0b-6eb03f502572: Named after the creator god Pacha Kamaq, this oracle site drew pilgrims for 1,300 years from 200 to 1500 AD. Even the Inca incorporated this powerful deity into their pantheon.
descriptions.be92ce6c-0c0e-43da-b5b8-be9137f0e151: A pre-Inca astronomical observatory formed by a stone lintel atop two parallel blocks. It was used to track seasons, lunar cycles, and predict eclipses from a hilltop at Lake Titicaca.
descriptions.855cc936-929b-4e3f-87fa-cef41ed81ca0: A ceremonial center from 1200 to 500 BC built with cut and polished stone. A dozen related archaeological sites surround it in the northern highlands.
descriptions.360da20f-8f95-4ba9-83fc-49d4b193b679: Limestone caves with evidence of habitation from 11,000 BC to the 3rd century AD. The larger cave has nine chambers connected by narrow passages, with sinkholes letting in daylight.
descriptions.5c3a138c-7052-4cb4-a482-10df27239b2e: A small Bronze Age defended hilltop enclosure about 73 metres across. Its single surviving rampart stands 3 metres high on the outside but less than a metre inside.
descriptions.6eabe5c3-03f4-4155-8b7d-dbd5616f5d59: A Greek colony founded around 600 BC, famous for three Doric temples from 550-450 BC that are among the best preserved in the world. The city walls also remain largely intact.
descriptions.8d96a44c-dbe5-4d08-875f-fd67534ae9cb: Built in the late 3rd century AD and rebuilt twice, this Romano-Celtic temple gained an internal screen after 367 AD before being abandoned. Finds suggest a dedication to Mercury.
descriptions.30cf4488-c74c-42d8-8e21-a017ca0bf921: A city with many megalithic sites, including the "Four Highland Guards." It sits at the feet of Mount Dempo, a volcano and the highest peak in its province.
descriptions.09833bba-315b-4cd0-866b-a0918a9d3434: Over 45,000 finds fill this Apulian cave, including oat-harvesting evidence from 30,600 BC — the earliest documented cereal processing. Tools, human bones, and animal remains span the Paleolithic.
descriptions.cfcd2e8b-5e36-4a05-9bda-6893f5021ac6: About 800 petroglyphs pecked into basalt boulders covering a granite outcrop. It is the largest petroglyph site in the area, dwarfing the 40+ other recorded sites nearby.
descriptions.af919ba9-7fa1-4da0-bc15-443767ae8b66: A cave with animal engravings dating to 28,000-23,000 BC, among the oldest known examples of prehistoric art. Horses, ibexes, bovines, and mammoths are etched into the walls.
descriptions.4695356b-52be-4152-8707-b1db00ef4707: The Delphic gymnasium dates to the second half of the 4th century BC, the oldest surviving of its kind. Earthquakes and landslides have battered the palaestra more than any other part of the complex.
descriptions.bdf88679-e9b7-4344-a3ed-212184e26102: A tiny archipelago in the middle of the Adriatic, inhabited since the 6th millennium BC. It can only be reached by a chartered boat ride of several hours.
descriptions.6b3a880e-1257-4c36-a72f-33c1f2cbc671: A Minoan trading hub at the eastern tip of Crete, active since the 5th millennium BC. The nearby port of Itanos, mentioned in ancient texts, now lies metres below sea level.
descriptions.dc025c66-9391-4ad3-95d5-77a2006c529b: Sinagua cliff dwellings built from 1100 to 1400 AD in red sandstone cliffs. Pictographs on the rock walls predate the dwellings and include some from as early as 4000 BC.
descriptions.d1877f2c-7bdb-46ee-8368-950eacc0edd5: Augustus built this imperial palace on Capri's north shore, later modified by Tiberius. According to Tacitus, Tiberius maintained twelve villas on the island — this was among them.
descriptions.3f40b195-d3cf-422b-b903-9f3d68b62903: Chief town of the Vaccaei, recorded as Pallantia by Strabo and Ptolemy, this Celtiberian stronghold stood on the Carrion river — one of the first large urban centres of the northern interior plateau.
descriptions.9b2cd3fd-9171-4862-a9a2-a2efe7aa4817: Palenque flourished from 226 BC to 799 AD in Chiapas before abandonment. Its bas-reliefs and stucco friezes surpass those of any contemporary Maya city in artistic refinement.
descriptions.d2aa1553-52b5-4107-bcdd-38679e18421b: A town near Agrigento where numerous archaeological finds from Magna Graecia have surfaced. Greek colonists settled this coast in the 8th century BC.
descriptions.14ca23b2-2208-4930-99f7-632db64ca953: Founded by Pompey around 75 BC during the Sertorian Wars. Settlement traces go back to the late Bronze Age, but the Roman general's name stuck for two millennia.
descriptions.c365e1f8-e4bb-43f0-9c46-58497b709fae: Terraced pools of white travertine formed by thermal spring water cascading down a hillside. The adjacent ancient city of Hierapolis was built to exploit these hot springs.
descriptions.5f920699-7eb3-47f3-88b1-ba85d4aaa4b2: A site occupied by both the Moche and Inca civilizations, a rare overlap of two of the Andes' greatest cultures. Artifacts from both periods are found in the same complex.
descriptions.ca1f8a94-27e1-4318-b3d5-3db181795ffd: The first permanent European settlement on the Pacific coast, founded in 1519. It was destroyed in 1671 by the Welsh privateer Henry Morgan.
descriptions.db85cd62-288f-4142-9cad-f15532e4fe26: A 420 km stretch of Roman frontier fortifications along the Danube, defended from the time of Augustus to the 5th century AD. Forts lined the river at regular intervals.
descriptions.ddd6cdfa-6891-4f6f-932a-e276f2be47bd: Founded by Milesians in the late 7th or early 6th century BC on a hill above Crimea, Pantikapaion became the capital of the Bosporan Kingdom. Its name derives from the Scythian word for fish-path.
descriptions.ba020c96-afeb-452a-8dbc-faf14155c96c: A Neolithic dolmen where the remains of 56 people were found during excavation. Its massive capstone measures about 3 metres across and rests at ground level on one end.
descriptions.a208b264-39c4-4d7f-a52d-8e1e78a9e7e9: Ruins of an ancient walled city with a perimeter of 516 metres. Ancient artifacts and wall fragments have been found, but most of the site remains unexcavated.
descriptions.16818a72-af8e-4397-a814-36c1502b27d3: Derventio — the Roman fort at Papcastle — was first built in timber and later rebuilt in stone. The fort's name echoes the Celtic word for oak, preserving a trace of the pre-Roman landscape.
descriptions.edd175c5-eeb5-4cff-8c18-7ae518915cc4: A megalithic tomb whose name means "priestless church" or "popeless church." It was nearly destroyed in the 1860s when locals quarried it for building stone.
descriptions.8e116b0a-fbaa-4375-a211-ba18767ed1e5: At Old Paphos, a renowned sanctuary to Aphrodite stood on the mythical birthplace of the goddess since the 1st millennium BC. The sanctuary drew pilgrims from across the Mediterranean world.
