descriptions.07483ba4-e923-4b37-9fb6-e8f88ec9c3e5: Four elaborate Roman villas with stunning floor mosaics depicting scenes from Greek mythology. The House of Dionysos alone has over 500 square metres of mosaic floors.
descriptions.875c0673-36e1-4296-a7af-29637effcec3: Settlement began after 1130 AD; by 1350 the Mogollon culture was raising multi-storied adobe structures across this Chihuahuan desert site. Construction stopped abruptly around 1450 AD.
descriptions.9989d873-9183-41e1-aeda-d543deb038ce: A 181-metre-tall geoglyph cut into a coastal hillside, visible from 20 km out at sea. Dating to around 200 BC, its purpose and meaning are still debated.
descriptions.06b8aeb4-f8fd-4ec0-aa49-a450dd924df0: A Neolithic chambered tomb from the 3rd millennium BC with a trapezoidal stone cairn. It is classified as a Severn-Cotswold type, a style found across western Britain.
descriptions.3f498fbd-0cb5-4910-8740-a4e2128f3b7c: Perched on Bryn Ddiol — trackless hill — this hillfort sits 95 metres above sea level on a Carboniferous limestone plateau on Anglesey. Cliffs drop on three sides, leaving one approach to defend.
descriptions.943c2240-ce5a-4cff-bfd1-3bc33ad19ff1: A sacred well from the 11th century BC anchors this Nuragic site, with a meeting hut and enclosure alongside. About 200 metres away, a single-tower nuraghe and elongated structures complete it.
descriptions.665a152b-5e67-4110-b58e-7f1bce3b739c: A stone circle of 127 granite blocks up to 4 metres tall, dubbed the "Amazon Stonehenge." It was built by indigenous peoples for astronomical observations.
descriptions.4824e3bd-0240-4e21-9292-f49e7aa6b7ee: Occupied from 900 BC in the Peten Basin, Uaxactun features giant stucco masks at its ceremonial buildings. By the Late Formative period, multiple temple groups had risen across the site.
descriptions.f48403a7-03b2-4d2b-ad9f-1d8369a502c8: Capital of the Postclassic Mam kingdom before being conquered by the K'iche'. Its temple-pyramids show a mix of Mam and K'iche' architectural styles.
descriptions.fbd85388-fa8e-4136-be64-6ca2612effac: An open-air museum housing Olmec colossal heads, carved stone altars, and mosaic floors from the ancient city of La Venta. Three colossal heads with distinctive features are on display.
descriptions.417445b4-e0db-49ac-99db-fe236794e9ff: Completed in 15 years from 447 to 432 BC, the Parthenon was built as thanksgiving for victory over the Persians. Its sculptural program set the standard for classical art for centuries.
descriptions.c5747999-7851-403a-bc69-ab150fba0dd8: The westernmost fort of Roman Dacia, guarding the limes along the Marisus river. It sat in territory once held by the Sarmatian Iazyges.
descriptions.0248e2bc-e43e-4bb6-8435-b9f9cac52040: Founded around 550 BC by Cyrus the Great as the first capital of the Achaemenid Empire, Pasargadae covers 1.6 square kilometres. A stone mausoleum on site is widely identified as Cyrus's own tomb.
descriptions.7e2b3ee7-ffb0-40d3-ae9d-7c8044dd42d2: A city at the confluence of three rivers, once a Roman colony called Batavis. The Boii Celts established a settlement here after being driven north from Italy.
descriptions.7160623a-6bd3-4d1f-8a77-b3c30e6df919: The remains of Roman walls of Tarraco, originally running 3.5 km around the city. About 1.1 km survives, and its gate is still in use today.
descriptions.5e7bfc36-038c-43e0-825c-c6b55f0dd78c: An Inca site on the trail to Machu Picchu, at the confluence of the Cusichaca and Vilcanota rivers. It served as an administrative checkpoint on the route to the famous citadel.
descriptions.29245d49-3e8c-4c31-baf4-a3cdd54a8964: Ruins of the capital of Lycia, with a 6,000-seat theatre, Ionic colonnades, Hadrian's granary, and a lighthouse. Its harbor is now a swamp choked with sand.
descriptions.ae5fec13-59e9-433e-8579-9d6d1110f0b6: A Thracian city with a Temple of Asclepius on the hill of Hissarlaka. It received the name Ulpia Pautalia from Emperor Trajan and minted coins depicting its public buildings.
descriptions.01dee6c5-2bcd-4fe7-9126-755ea3c7a3f7: The oldest known submerged city in the world, about 5,000 years old. It has a nearly complete town plan with streets, buildings, and tombs visible underwater.
descriptions.6da4f22e-a5a5-49f2-abb2-b6576e131746: A Neolithic portal dolmen from 3500-2600 BC with a long burial mound. It sits on a north-facing ridge looking out over a tributary of the River Camel.
descriptions.548905c8-b859-40a8-9e6b-194e8b52bfe7: A fortified Gallic trading post active from the 6th to 3rd century BC. Three successive occupations have been identified, by a people called the Elisyces.
descriptions.8e8c9643-4dd3-4640-a5cf-11ad7766294e: Murals dated 25,000–16,000 BC line this Lot cave, extending over 2 km on two levels. About 1,200 metres remain open to the public — a rarity among prehistoric painted caves in the country.
descriptions.93af4a1c-5f49-4daf-a488-65d5be9a355a: A 74 km road through Norfolk and Suffolk follows a Roman-era route that writers have argued predates Roman arrival. Its name comes from the medieval word pedder — meaning a travelling merchant.
descriptions.0011452e-b306-49d7-92a2-4044cf1ca5ec: Neolithic petroglyphs of two animals, each carved with six legs to suggest motion. The figures are scratched into a solitary boulder and may depict running deer.
descriptions.8f8d1ce5-3527-4c35-925f-579e6dc51784: An ancient city that served as capital of Macedon and birthplace of Alexander the Great in 356 BC. Ruins span from the Neolithic through the Islamic period.
descriptions.63cbc133-6e22-46aa-b430-ac7da2e405cd: Capital of ancient Macedon and birthplace of both Philip II and Alexander the Great. It was the largest and richest Macedonian city of its era.
descriptions.33d852f7-c9bf-4846-8b3f-17e28e92e2a6: Pellana on the Eurotas river was identified by Theodore Spyropoulos as the Mycenaean capital of Laconia, predating Sparta as the dominant centre. The identification remains debated.
descriptions.061c9bb7-bfdf-402b-8a85-34376f18172e: Chief town of the Vestini on the Via Claudia Nova. It was the birthplace of Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, one of Rome's greatest generals under Emperor Nero.
descriptions.73be8eb3-140a-4646-8bfa-e7ec9d78c38c: Rock shelters with paintings, engravings, and a dolmen dating from the prehistoric era. Minerals, rocks, and fossils fill the surrounding mountain landscape.
descriptions.2069e069-c994-46e2-b8b8-f8f8dd01abd0: A 7th-century BC Iron Age hillfort controlling the middle of the Tera valley. It sits on the boundary between mountain highlands and the plateau below.
descriptions.bdd568d3-3a54-442a-9f8c-af7ac07bbaf0: A fogou, an underground stone passage unique to Cornwall, dating from the 1st millennium BC. Its purpose is debated: storage, refuge, or ritual space.
descriptions.0888887e-7cdb-44aa-8e48-36afb0198623: Double ramparts ring this large hillfort at the confluence of the River Ystwyth and Afon Rheidol, commanding the Cardigan Bay coast. The site dates from 800 BC to the Roman period.
descriptions.b69f338c-fb2b-4860-9935-61e93e27ddf3: Two Bronze Age standing stones, each about 3 metres tall but only 20 cm thick. They stand 3 metres apart like thin blades driven into the earth.
descriptions.48a6d6b8-7224-4edf-b20c-a6fba056d8fa: An oval hillfort measuring 74 by 48 metres and enclosing just 0.32 hectares, with up to five concentric ramparts on some sides. The tightly layered defences suggest multiple phases of construction.
descriptions.3ec1f730-53d8-4e3e-a932-c0cd91bb27a3: The largest and best-preserved Neolithic dolmen in the region, with seven stones including a massive capstone balanced on pointed uprights. It dates to the 4th millennium BC.
descriptions.7b7bb7e1-3497-4c6a-afd5-f42a743c466b: At 26 hectares, Penycloddiau is one of the largest hillforts in the region. In 2017, the Clwydian Range Archaeology Group recovered 4,000-year-old Bronze Age tools — far predating the Iron Age fort.
descriptions.532b3d3d-df65-40bd-8a8f-6f1112da97de: At 331 metres, the flat summit of Pen-y-crug overlooks the Usk valley on three sides. A rampart rings the entire hilltop; the name in the old tongue means top of the mound.
descriptions.19ec6c34-0d5d-4a55-9c8d-d0cdda84b9ad: A hillfort with defenses spanning the Bronze and Iron Ages, including two cairns and extensive prehistoric field systems nearby. The visible remains are mostly Iron Age.
descriptions.57e9b3c3-1d32-49dd-ad8c-49577ed78d06: A Roman-era castle built along the Via Egnatia, with walls once 12 metres high. The last resident was Demir Pasha during the Ottoman period.
descriptions.0bb4315b-c214-4c45-8417-e34e12b71ace: On chalky downland near Compton, this 5.7-hectare univallate hillfort shows signs of seasonal occupation. Grain storage pits and slag pits are the main archaeological traces found inside.
descriptions.0a0e276c-19cf-442b-9104-b27d57d09d1b: Ruins of an ancient city that became the Greek settlement of Perge in Pamphylia. A Hellenistic wall, theatre, stadium, and temple of Artemis have been uncovered.
descriptions.45c83a06-69a6-46f3-bb7a-eea482b9767c: Remains of a monumental altar built during the reign of King Eumenes II in the 2nd century BC. Its sculpted frieze depicting the Gigantomachy is a masterwork of Hellenistic art.
descriptions.908d6a9b-6032-4fd4-84c7-72896374778b: Cut into the steep hillside at Pergamon, this theatre seated 50,000 spectators — its raking angle among the sharpest of any surviving ancient theatre. The auditorium descends at a near-vertical pitch.
descriptions.d571a05b-ece2-4cee-b252-2590660bf26c: A Roman theatre in the ancient city of Perge, built in the 1st-2nd century AD with a capacity of 11,000. The structure served a thriving Pamphylian trade hub.
descriptions.97443726-74e9-40ac-b388-5daa15448ff1: The oldest known inland sedentary agricultural village in the Central Andes, dating to 3800-3000 BC. It documents the transition from foraging to farming.
descriptions.d50d2211-0fe2-4f1b-80fa-1f95e193be8a: The largest megalithic ensemble in the Balkans, built on a 470-metre hill from 5000 BC. A giant multi-story structure and monumental rock-cut architecture have been uncovered.
descriptions.e00a1e45-3c66-48f4-8cac-3169146aad21: Ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, raised on a walled platform from 515 to 330 BC. Its grand halls were occupied only seasonally, and its true function remains unclear.
descriptions.7446fda2-a380-40c3-bd00-5547f545a7f3: A collapsed Neolithic burial chamber whose status is disputed: some say it is just a large boulder in a field. Its 2.5-metre capstone rests on two collapsed uprights.
descriptions.2fb54462-31f6-441e-9b6c-64c6da84877b: A karst cave system where the Tanagro river flows underground. Pile dwellings from the Bronze Age were discovered inside, showing people once lived in the caves.
descriptions.f7f2dac5-0f0a-4cbd-8ac0-c2f1f42311ca: A cave occupied by Neanderthals until as late as 39,000 years ago, one of their last known habitats. It has been nicknamed the "last house of the Neanderthals."
descriptions.e810df47-1da8-4751-8fbc-5ff9bf0295d9: A Roman legionary fortress built to control routes during the wars against the Astures and Cantabrians. Its canabae civilian camp later grew into a proper Roman city.
descriptions.9058e3b7-8329-4b31-a263-226fe8361c08: A Celtic and Roman site from the 2nd century BC to the 4th century AD, with visible ruins of an oppidum and a fortified Roman village. Both Celtic and Roman layers survive.
descriptions.a06a95d0-35b4-44bb-a0c1-716cbf972b19: A trade capital carved into sandstone cliffs around 300 BC. Its Nabataean engineers mastered flash-flood control with dams, cisterns, and water conduits through the desert.
descriptions.53681595-1e58-4cec-99f3-0b3458769e26: A Minoan town with a palace-like building from 3100-1100 BC. The main structure was two stories tall and covered 2,800 square metres overlooking the Cretan sea.
descriptions.45e80c0e-3eaf-4f57-8461-a821ef3ea096: The largest fort on Hadrian's Wall, now completely buried beneath a suburb of Carlisle. It measured 180 by 210 metres and housed a full cavalry regiment of 1,000 riders.
descriptions.8c39badd-8113-4a71-a041-21d68f47bf58: An Alaskan beach with the highest concentration of petroglyphs in the southeast region. The site is about 8,000 years old, with at least 40 carvings found on boulders and bedrock.
descriptions.abcf3620-5667-441d-b2dc-dc5b23bd7fce: A provincial park with petroglyphs dating to at least the 10th century, depicting mythological sea creatures and human figures. They are sacred to the Coast Salish and Snuneymuxw.
descriptions.b801d712-8e04-4b96-86dd-cf1b4bb9db11: Over 3,500 petroglyphs on ancient migration routes, the largest rock art collection in the region. They depict animal domestication, sacrifice, and daily life from the Bronze Age onward.
descriptions.c3517388-2457-42fd-9cf8-f6a043021b1e: Founded by Celts, ruled by Rome, then home to Scordisci warriors. The Petrovaradin Fortress, built over these layers, became the historical anchor of a modern city.
descriptions.6c3149ff-3881-4a25-bd83-167325c511ce: A Minoan peak sanctuary where unique clay figurines of weasels and tortoises were found alongside the usual human and animal offerings. No other peak sanctuary has these.
descriptions.5f9051e0-639a-4d93-939b-f96b41fd35b1: A Roman fort founded in 70 AD that grew into the probable capital of the Parisi tribe. It marked the southern end of Cade's Road, a 160 km Roman highway heading north.
descriptions.f56eb08e-29e1-42dc-b238-4867b12ba88b: A Neolithic dolmen near Saint-Aquilin in the Dordogne, dated to around 2400 BC. Its name joins the Occitan peyre ('stone') and the word for brown, a nod to the mottled colour of the local rock.
descriptions.ef91e19e-db13-4475-b6a8-feb6f3298146: An open-air museum of reconstructed Neolithic and Bronze Age lake dwellings on Lake Constance. The stilt houses replicate how people lived over water from 4000 to 850 BC.
descriptions.fb563088-580b-4d87-8c51-8934659a5d31: A Minoan palace city from the 4th millennium BC, the second-largest on Crete after Knossos. The famous Phaistos Disc, with its undeciphered spiral script, was found here.
descriptions.3e9107fa-e54c-407c-aaa7-a6f198e48c0f: The largest ancient Greek city on the Taman peninsula, founded in 543 BC. It served as the eastern capital of the Bosporan Kingdom, a major crossroads between the Black Sea and the Caucasus.
descriptions.966f26e0-c2ae-4a0f-ac46-8a481ad80b19: A Lycian city with three harbors and a 24-metre-wide main street running through the center. Hadrian's Waterway Gate stands at the southern end, flanked by ruined shops.
descriptions.62c6ca1d-d37b-45b2-a773-15ce8bf69ea1: Philip II of Macedon renamed this settlement Philippopolis in the 4th century BC, and it later became capital of Roman Thrace. Signs of habitation on its territory date back to the 6th millennium BC.
descriptions.fb8c9056-7078-495a-81e0-4e3e0a0e24a5: A Minoan cemetery active from 2400 to 1200 BC with burial types ranging from tholos tombs to pit caves. It sits on a hill visible from the sacred peak of Mount Juktas.
descriptions.9e4fdcf5-98b1-4607-b412-e2348889b3b3: An ancient Thessalian city with evidence of habitation stretching back to the Stone Age. It is not mentioned by name until the 4th century BC despite its deep roots.
descriptions.d621bf90-9c67-405d-b7fc-d8efb7057f0b: A historical park where prehistoric rock paintings decorate unusual rock formations. Massive spires, balanced boulders, and natural platforms have attracted worship for millennia.
descriptions.722bf4c1-6dca-454a-9d27-89503114e75c: A small cave sacred to Pan and the nymphs, known as "Lamp Cave" for the many oil lamps found inside. It has been identified as the setting for a comedy by Menander.
descriptions.8493b619-147a-46d2-8fc8-0a10db2f08b9: A Colchian settlement on the coast at the confluence of two rivers, active from the 2nd millennium BC to the 2nd century AD. Its ancient name is lost to history.
descriptions.2981f5c9-7aa0-4ed2-bb1a-b5bb43ab1b75: Ruins of a Roman bridge built around 90 AD to carry Dere Street over the River Tees. The river has since shifted 90 metres, leaving the bridge stranded in a field.
descriptions.619ffc36-179c-4a12-859c-ed9fe626b204: A garrison on the Tees from about 70 AD to at least the early 5th century, Piercebridge had a bath house and vicus. Victorians plundered carved stones from the fort to build a nearby church.
descriptions.17b9fc46-bc88-42a8-9606-7d7bc0dac9d1: A Roman signal tower built on high ground above the Stanegate road in the early 2nd century AD. It was later absorbed into Hadrian's Wall, with a 2-metre fragment still standing.
descriptions.01ef71b0-4942-486e-bb0e-f13fffd9ebda: A Neolithic burial cairn 45 metres long with a single chamber of upright slabs capped by lintels. The chamber inside measured 4.5 metres long but less than a metre wide and high.
descriptions.efaa3f7a-4a10-4d40-84b7-e4a1a49e47c6: A large Wari culture ceremonial site from 550-1000 AD. It was never completed when the Wari abandoned it, leaving a partially built village frozen in construction.
descriptions.1ac14890-b87e-43e5-a108-57fc4c51c6b2: Natural rock pillars 150 to 300 metres high, formed during the Cambrian Period over 500 million years ago. Fossils from that era are embedded throughout the formation.
descriptions.a98dcb51-39c4-4ab9-b34e-1f10a9aa14d9: An ancient trackway dated to 600-450 BC but likely used since the Stone Age. Later generations called it the pilgrims' route from Winchester to Canterbury.
descriptions.5b4a848a-90b8-432e-9016-d931607218cd: An Inca archaeological site on the shores of Isla del Sol in Lake Titicaca. The island was the mythical birthplace of the Inca sun god Inti.
descriptions.bf3e61c6-0ecc-4223-949e-86afe1d8d2ac: A multivallate Durotrigian hillfort crowns a 277-metre hill in Dorset. Fourteen hut foundations found within suggest a sizable settled community on the summit.
descriptions.5025eee3-28ea-46d6-b2c3-dbb1f38a24d6: A Lycian city above the Xanthos valley, Pinara preserves rock tombs — including a royal tomb — carved in Cyclopean masonry. Inscriptions appear in both the Lycian alphabet and in Greek.
descriptions.8cecb38f-08cf-4a93-b350-9ccbb74109bb: An ancient Lycian city dating to the 15th century BC with temples, rock tombs, and a royal tomb. Its upper and lower acropolis overlook the ruins below.
descriptions.d9960a60-016d-4c3e-89ae-f3366abd45c7: An Inca site on a mountainside between two rivers, facing the town of Ollantaytambo. The structures served as storehouses perched dramatically above the valley floor.
descriptions.16d660a1-92c1-4853-ad87-7d6979ce47cd: A hill in the Malvern range, site of two possible Bronze Age round barrows. It sits between Jubilee Hill and Black Hill at 357 metres elevation.
descriptions.96395824-9c31-477a-bf51-13ecb5035d56: A Vaccaean city, part of an early Celtic society in northern Iberia. The Vaccaei were the first sedentary people of the Duero-Pisuerga valley.
descriptions.a1174754-0d0f-4d54-8802-e51658125770: The mound at Pirak rises 8 metres and covers 4.8 hectares in Balochistan. Occupation ran from 1800 to 800 BC near two related Indus-era sites along the Nari River.
descriptions.86cc95dc-f784-43c8-b31c-a68cade567c2: An Indus Valley port at the mouth of the Hub River, dating from 3300 to 1300 BC. It likely served as a key maritime trading post for the Harappan civilization.
descriptions.df70e98f-a1d1-4998-966a-d9a4ee2a945f: A temple complex with continuous occupation from 3000 BC to the Inca Empire. A fortress at over 3,800 metres above sea level guards the site's upper levels.
descriptions.c99e3f1e-85ab-47d3-ac5c-2f50e896417d: Built under Augustus to supply the Roman fleet at Misenum, this hillside cistern at Bacoli is comparable in scale to the Basilica Cistern in Istanbul. Its 48 pillars still stand in four rows.
descriptions.b0fdd6ca-3571-4452-9e64-9689ceb1445b: A 1,220-metre mountain with Norse farmsteads at its base that were part of the Western Settlement until about 1350 AD. Conflicts with the Inuit and climate change ended them.
descriptions.1ce162fb-4605-4313-b36f-1209718e7b1e: A 5th-century BC Greek trading post in Thrace that sustained intensive commerce with Thasos, Maroneia, and Apollonia. It flourished in the 4th century BC along the Maritsa.
descriptions.a3316d5c-ee94-49c8-a428-6355708a4d64: Fourteen rock-cut caves from the 3rd century BC mark Pitalkhora as a landmark of early monastic architecture. The caves rank among the earliest rock-cut monasteries in the subcontinent.
descriptions.3f7e973f-f972-4677-9d02-6ae0b6942fcd: Iron Age stone jars hewn from solid rock and scattered across a plain. Their size and purpose remain debated, but they likely served as funerary urns or food storage.
descriptions.7504a195-6a15-4b53-951a-c58d093163d0: A possible Iron Age earthwork that may actually be an animal enclosure, not a fort. Its position on a slope with a hill rising 50 metres above it weakens the defensive theory.
descriptions.f93fec72-80a3-4baa-9ced-5e93e6ef9cd3: A Maya site with the earliest urban remains in the Upper Usumacinta region, dating to 50-100 AD. It contains a unique ancient theatre designed for elite use.
descriptions.3208b51e-e296-4c28-af06-55f6869e507c: A 35-metre section of Hadrian's Wall showing where builders switched from Broad Wall to Narrow Wall mid-construction. The join is clearly visible in the stonework.
descriptions.a3c3f3e8-b249-4f70-bb03-8cd733213e76: A Celtic settlement dating to around 300 BC on the southern slopes of the Sandberg ridge near Platt. The Sandberg also preserves traces reaching back to the Neolithic period.
descriptions.412a1f97-7dfd-4624-b6ec-2813217f39bf: A 120-hectare Neolithic settlement of the Vinca culture, occupied from 5500 to 4700 BC. It was destroyed by a catastrophic fire and never rebuilt.
descriptions.0fe3f733-23a8-4bd4-a4c1-14a3caf010d2: Son Catlar, dating to 1700-1400 BC, is a Talayotic village encircled by a wall built in distinct phases. Vertical stones, plinths, and horizontal rows mark the different construction techniques.
descriptions.3b2e39f0-6ca3-4905-8a23-f118b7ae632a: A Talayotic village with a table sanctuary, necropolis of artificial burial caves, and stone-roofed rooms with columns. The "table" is a T-shaped stone unique to Menorca.
descriptions.f91af2e3-60fc-4c63-9622-05c4e3f4b1cd: A 6th-century BC quarry where tuff blocks for the Greek walls of Neapolis were cut. Alphabetical marks carved by ancient quarrymen are still visible on the rock faces.
descriptions.45ed4119-e8ac-4e56-8af5-0751b5f02c1b: A castle inhabited from the 5th century BC to the 10th century AD. The Romans called the nearby lake Lyhnidos, meaning "Lake of Light."
descriptions.e8ef0cd6-6f7b-4b96-905d-e3eb22423006: A town named after the cult of Apollo, who had a major temple here in pre-Roman times. Both the original village and its twin were destroyed by the 1631 eruption of Vesuvius.
descriptions.7a43d34c-2051-48b6-b598-d4482adb4623: Buried under 4 to 6 metres of volcanic ash in 79 AD, preserving a complete Roman city with bakeries, bathhouses, and graffiti frozen in place. Even bread was found in the ovens.
descriptions.e9d865b7-643e-4acd-89ac-e73c6182664c: A city in territory once held by the Astures, a Hispano-Celtic people conquered by Augustus. The area became one of the richest gold-mining regions of the Roman Empire.
descriptions.2f50d5d0-bcb3-4400-9cfc-bc0126ca2624: Guarding the north bank of the Tyne from the 2nd to 4th century AD, Pons Aelius sat on Hadrian's Wall at present-day Newcastle. Its name — Aelius's Bridge — honoured Emperor Hadrian's family name.
descriptions.096b583c-5131-43e1-b7e3-4ad0f66f8df8: A 1st-century BC Roman bridge on the Via Domitia, of which only one of its original eleven arches survives. In the Middle Ages, a chapel to St. Mary was added to the structure.
descriptions.e6b248f2-394d-44ea-8283-e9fad9ae5449: A bridge of the Roman aqueduct to Nimes, on the same system as the famous Pont du Gard. Its three segmental arches total 17 metres, with two now buried underground.
descriptions.8dec4979-434b-46dd-9468-f829d6d1e713: A bridge on Roman foundations with a 37.3-metre main span, rebuilt in Gothic style in 1283 and reconstructed again in 1965. A stone chapel sits on top of the arch.
descriptions.bed41f64-e2c3-4a2c-b06a-0a8971542dbf: A segmental arch spanning 15 metres carries this bridge across the Canal de la Robine through Narbonne. Shops and houses line it above — a survival seen at only a handful of bridges worldwide.
descriptions.5fc3dde6-5284-41ba-af51-d91420bd0299: Built around 19 BC, the Pont du Gard carries a Roman aqueduct 49 metres above the Gardon river on three tiers of limestone arches. The channel conveyed water over 50 km to Nemausus.
descriptions.863e756a-6e77-4d6d-82d1-d22640bec0f4: A Roman bridge in an isolated spot within a nature park, linking two ancient paved roads across a riverbank. Its simple stone arch has endured since the 1st century AD.
descriptions.dca491e4-5192-4fba-8ac2-d501cd6b138f: An ancient Roman bridge. That is nearly all that is recorded about it, but its stone arches still stand in the Braganca District after nearly 2,000 years.
descriptions.772fb4ca-70f0-4584-81e1-0cf5a887f9ab: A 2nd-century Roman bridge over the small River Coura, now part of the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage route. It has carried travelers for nearly two millennia.
descriptions.9ad825a0-4a22-4e24-a7dc-bc21b3cfbc28: A linear earthwork crossing a ridge between Glastonbury and West Pennard. Both ends vanish into moorland that was once impassable swamp, making it a natural barrier.
descriptions.1d9420cf-134e-42bd-93bd-9fb8c1910da3: Built in 103-105 AD to guard the southern end of Trajan's Bridge over the Danube, this fort protected a strategic river crossing on the Moesian frontier.
descriptions.59c0ea5b-ba27-4a21-afdf-b4ec1ab0aa69: A single-arch limestone bridge from 12 BC, Pont Flavien is the only surviving Roman bridge bounded by triumphal arches from the Augustan period. It carried the Via Julia Augusta across the Touloubre.
descriptions.27781284-7698-46ff-b6aa-096800327282: Founded by Milesians in the 7th century BC on the Southern Bug estuary, Pontic Olbia became a trading hub between the Black Sea and the northern steppe. Its ruins form a national research preserve.
descriptions.4d5292ae-6594-45be-a2cd-e2f7cac4c108: Monumental rock-carved tombs of the Pontic kings, 8 to 15 metres high, cut into a 272-metre-high limestone cliff. The royal tomb chambers are hewn deep into the stone.
descriptions.2feb8c8c-9dcb-4efb-abe3-9f402839dc57: A Roman stone bridge from 3 BC with openings in the columns to let floodwater pass through. It carried traffic on the Via Domitia until 2005, over 2,000 years after it was built.
descriptions.5b59aada-2931-4de8-aad0-cd97a35e7e0b: A Roman bridge with a main pier protected by triangular cutwaters of rectangular stone blocks. The paved roadway rises sharply to the main arch, then drops to the far bank.
descriptions.de3c2d9b-b7df-40c5-bfce-3f8521d9ad8f: Crossing Ibiza's only river, Pont Vell was the sole western approach into Santa Eularia des Riu until modern times. The bridge served as a military crossing before being restricted to pedestrians.
descriptions.2b2d0e62-5cbc-4427-be06-542064fb5076: Forty-four round barrows from around 1500 BC occupy low-lying ground near Winterbourne Abbas — unusual for a barrow cemetery, which typically sits on a ridge. The site lies near the head of a valley.
descriptions.db73b982-65ce-4782-a5ee-9f641a61a229: A stone circle on Exmoor, part of a tradition that spread across Britain, Ireland, and Brittany between 3300 and 900 BC. The purpose of these monuments remains unknown.
descriptions.d4714397-6e73-432d-add3-c01e22cb055f: A 2nd-century Roman double-arched city gate, one of ten that once ringed the city. It stands opposite the modern Citadel, which is built on the ancient capitol's foundations.
descriptions.c9755577-6815-411d-bb1e-f96330776818: A massive Roman city gate built in grey sandstone after 170 AD, with two four-story towers. Its name means "black gate" from the darkened color its stone acquired over the centuries.
descriptions.9b4f553e-24bf-4860-9790-4f8184426360: A 2nd-century Roman triumphal arch, 5.6 metres wide and 11.2 metres tall, at the southern end of the city's cardo. Both facades were decorated identically.
descriptions.a2110592-42cd-4a95-aa28-6338d4b7e835: A Roman-era gate drilled through solid rock for an aqueduct, later converted to a city gate in the Middle Ages. Vauban fortified it in 1546, and it has been a protected monument since 1944.
descriptions.10a8eb08-72a6-47ee-b53d-0f2e4fce865e: A promontory hillfort above the Calder valley near Whalley, built first as univallate and later expanded to multivallate. It overlooks the valley floor from a slight ridge to the northeast.
descriptions.1f66729b-c7e8-476a-b9cc-84b23a36074f: A cairn cemetery with at least six entrance graves from 2000-1500 BC, the largest surviving group of its kind. An ancient field system stretches across the northern section.
descriptions.f8e537ac-c6e0-49f5-9b2f-995be80ab401: An ancient burial landscape with the largest assembly of surviving entrance graves. The best-preserved is a Bronze Age granite tomb with a clearly defined entrance passage.
descriptions.baf89ae1-61ca-47d4-a5ee-9e4a02362803: A 72.6-metre portico with a double colonnade of 29 exterior and 15 interior columns. It was associated with the Aetolian League during their control of Delphi in the 3rd century BC.
descriptions.d569aff2-99e0-4964-b6a5-a197bea12cda: Iron Age earthworks consisting of a hill, a mound, and a rectangular enclosure connected by a zigzag causeway. They date to 395-205 BC and sit inside Hatfield Forest.
descriptions.d622c812-d34b-4e3d-8005-978fb0e51079: The best-preserved Roman fort north of the Alps, later converted into the medieval Portchester Castle. It was part of the Saxon Shore defenses protecting Roman Britain.
descriptions.99439beb-a299-4c62-a8b2-3eddd7fe395c: The first harbor built specifically for the Roman western naval fleet, named after Julius Caesar. Octavian constructed it as an urgent wartime base during the civil wars of 39 BC.
descriptions.2f217cc8-9aad-4f87-93fb-c8732fe85e39: A Roman Saxon Shore fort whose ruins are known locally as Stutfall Castle. The sea it once defended against has retreated, replaced by the drained marshland of Romney Marsh.
descriptions.a8333fc8-7376-4362-b1e5-194d7475ab02: An ancient road from Silchester to Old Sarum that may predate the Roman occupation of Britain. It formed part of a longer route between London and Exeter.
descriptions.dadbf949-f5cc-4313-9111-20224ebf9f43: A Roman vacation district where elite villas lined the coast from the 1st century BC. An imperial pleasure villa and the Tunnel of Sejanus can still be visited today.
descriptions.dde17f3b-8489-41f6-83e4-7cb23927e266: Evidence of habitation goes back to the Upper Paleolithic, with a cave called "La Porta" used by prehistoric hunters. Roman-era luxury villas were later built here.
descriptions.c7aa9aff-8f4d-4b04-8216-529deb2cd734: A hillfort with bank, ditch, and rampart just south of Vowchurch, Herefordshire. Beyond its location and scheduled monument status, little else has been documented about its history.
descriptions.190821d5-ac73-40cb-86cf-76a59a6cce72: A portal tomb from 4200-2900 BC with three standing stones supporting a heavy capstone. It is the best known of the approximately 172 dolmens scattered across the island.
descriptions.179f8253-8391-4278-b03c-c905df8f6818: Poundbury Hill holds Neolithic, Bronze Age, and Iron Age earthworks — plus a Roman aqueduct section and a Romano-Celtic cemetery. Human use of the hill spanned from prehistory to the 8th century AD.
descriptions.cd66f88c-ac89-4f7e-9ef8-4bf167df259a: A Nuragic sacred well built with perfectly squared limestone ashlars in the isodomic technique. It stands on the ruins of a pre-existing megaron temple.
descriptions.da488c94-540b-4fdc-8d3a-0d5aba57b372: A Greek colony founded around 531 BC by refugees fleeing the tyranny of Polycrates on Samos. It became a major Roman port and commercial center.
descriptions.3b1d4d7e-d27d-4910-90c2-2ac662cb304f: A Neolithic cave tomb and a Chalcolithic beehive tomb near the beach. The site represents a rare combination of two distinct prehistoric burial traditions in one place.
descriptions.0ae727b3-6355-47ad-9c47-2c5f01a3bc20: A Paleolithic cave with paintings of red dot patterns dating to around 16,000 BC. It also yielded an unusual collection of portable art on pebbles with abstract motifs.
descriptions.21bd525e-fe10-40dd-96be-32d3c8d36d26: A 9th-century Hindu temple complex dedicated to Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. Its tall, pointed towers are characteristic of Hindu temple architecture at its most dramatic.
descriptions.41705e94-8ffd-45f3-943e-df6fac317144: A 13th-14th century temple at Angkor Thom with a 33-metre causeway lined by seven-headed naga balustrades. A 3-metre Buddha statue sits in a shrine before the main entrance.
descriptions.5c8779da-b96e-44a7-b460-fa391205e10d: An Iron Age hilltop fortress in eastern Herzegovina with little historical data. The peak rises above the Dabarski polje and is surrounded by other unresearched monuments.
descriptions.74ef6000-7bfa-4e7c-a745-b29b55f35030: Open-air Paleolithic rock art dating to 22,000-20,000 years ago, the earliest in a span that reaches into the 20th century. A UNESCO site shared between two countries.
descriptions.4c650823-6f85-4e10-9976-61cf1369a9b9: Two Neolithic chamber tombs on Anglesey, the southern one capped by a stone measuring 4 by 3 metres. Both sit about 1 km northwest of Bodedern near Llyn Llywenan.
descriptions.8d403814-0068-4383-a553-17b0170336d0: A 240-metre hilltop on the northeast edge of Dartmoor, near two other hillforts — Cranbrook Castle and Wooston Castle — both within 2 km. The three overlook the Teign Valley from a single ridge.
descriptions.a1435e3d-4c9d-410e-992e-842f24dfba16: Four circular earthwork enclosures from 2500-2180 BC, each about 190 metres in diameter. Three stand in a nearly straight line, with the fourth offset by 350 metres.
descriptions.8b4d5105-2e39-465f-987d-78a543a5cfed: Two barrow cemeteries of the Bronze Age sitting at either end of a field near the Priddy Circles. Bowl barrows and bell barrows are both represented among the mounds.
descriptions.972ded7c-665e-4ca6-98cc-af4dff9ac8f3: Rebuilt in the 4th century BC on a new site, Priene was laid out on a strict grid across steep Ionian terraces. Its orthogonal streets are an early and clear expression of systematic urban design.
descriptions.e4631001-b923-4f36-be7f-c961f9e287ba: A celebrated Minoan fresco from 1550 BC Knossos, showing a figure in a lily crown. The painting was found in pieces; most of what you see today is reconstruction.
descriptions.93f7a2e9-2d34-4ac7-bb22-9327d1897648: A 7th-century BC temple with striking similarities to ancient Egyptian architecture, including an Egyptianised seated goddess. It sits halfway between Knossos and Gortyn.
descriptions.e7b1d5cc-4481-4f5e-a1b6-d759ce1bd666: A coastal settlement first occupied around 3000 BC, active through the Minoan Bronze Age and into the Classical period. It sits on a promontory with views of the Cretan sea.
descriptions.1cef72f4-b9d4-4180-b93a-10b0cbe1a234: An 80-metre-deep pit inside a hollow cone-shaped hill, 65 metres across at the top. Locals named it after Solomon, believing he imprisoned demons here. It hosted a Mannaean temple.
descriptions.ccf1b82b-6822-40ba-adf3-07913b155b7b: A Scordisci settlement from the late La Tene period, excavated as part of 1970s-80s rescue digs. It was part of a Celtic settlement network in the Vinkovci area.
descriptions.c010f54a-5ced-4bf6-973b-89fd6130cf14: A city with settlement traces from the 6th millennium BC, home to Neolithic Lengyel and Globular Amphora cultures. It later became an outpost of the Roman Empire.
descriptions.5ba97e90-56e7-4234-a617-bc0b4eeafa2b: A 1st-2nd century AD earth dam with a stone retaining wall, still in use today near Merida. The aqueduct it fed collapsed after Rome fell, but the dam outlasted the empire by nearly two millennia.
descriptions.9f99919a-d5d6-4384-994b-704ece327ab6: An ancient city in the territory of the Heraeum, the celebrated temple of Hera. In mythology, Prosymna and her sisters were wet-nurses to the goddess herself.
descriptions.3030e8d3-54a7-4014-ac0b-385aa42bed7b: An 18-hectare Roman provincial forum built starting in 73 AD by Emperor Vespasian. Its worship area is now occupied by the city's cathedral.
descriptions.1d2575fd-2c00-46cb-bdbe-08a006b52114: A village with two prehistoric tumuli and a 2nd-century AD Przeworsk culture settlement on a section of the ancient Amber Road connecting the Baltic Sea with the Roman Empire.
descriptions.b8bf4ddf-8b56-4544-adde-843e7577320f: A Minoan and Mycenaean island port from the 4th to 2nd millennium BC, with about 60 buildings ranged around its harbor. Cliffside stairs once connected the town to its wharf.
descriptions.f0054526-9c55-402b-904f-9f4fa40ebd79: A Minoan sacred cave associated with the birthplace of Zeus. Hesiod wrote that Rhea hid the infant god here, and votive offerings were left inside for over 2,000 years.
descriptions.51023eb3-d454-4077-a1c0-2fadb0cf79f6: One of the five cities of the Pentapolis of Cyrenaica, well preserved under sand. Its ruins reveal a planned rectangular city with a hippodrome, three theatres, and an amphitheatre.
descriptions.f921cb05-ab49-4bc9-b9a0-3dae48ee3e5a: The 4.2-square-kilometre site in the Lake Titicaca basin was the first large urban centre in the region, dating to 1800 BC. The Pukara culture is named for this site and its sculptural tradition.
descriptions.70aedb08-34af-45ae-9414-887ef9467e7e: A site with a prehistoric burial ground where tools from 2,400-2,700 years ago were found. A 10th-century defensive stronghold was located nearby.
descriptions.817ff7b7-a814-405a-a5af-0ef173f07045: A Roman arch bridge spanning the River Tagus, rebuilt multiple times since antiquity. It was the only entry to the city for pilgrims during the Middle Ages.
descriptions.43e8118f-ea04-4525-88a6-ed50a41bd240: The longest surviving bridge from the ancient world, stretching 790 metres with 60 spans. It was built by the Romans in the 2nd century AD and is still in use for pedestrians.
descriptions.7f087418-8568-4446-8100-5d163563ca83: A megalithic site with an ancient terraced pyramid and structures spanning from 2500 BC to the 16th century AD. Menhirs and dolmens from the 12th-16th centuries also stand here.
descriptions.7df3ac64-8a51-4a51-aeb0-7b99c1e9c196: A 35-hectare archaeological park with over 15 sites, including a Talayotic settlement dating to around 1300 BC. One site, Son Ferrandell, has Mycenaean pottery.
descriptions.1ee1e668-a44a-47f0-840a-c1d5e804ff2c: A 15th-century Inca fort of large walls, terraces, and staircases guarding the approaches to Cusco. Its position on the outer perimeter made it a sentinel for the Inca capital.
descriptions.edb4cd03-cbf2-412f-9861-bb88db0d2027: A mountain at 4,302 metres with an archaeological site declared a National Cultural Heritage. It lies north of the mountain and site of Intikancha.
descriptions.676dbe65-abbf-4e30-8e56-70cae048f1e0: The Pula Arena, a 1st-century AD amphitheatre seating up to 23,000, retains all four exterior towers intact — alone among surviving amphitheatres. The city has been inhabited since the 2nd century BC.
descriptions.7661e2ac-0a20-46be-9069-961b36db4ac7: A Roman amphitheatre built from 27 BC to 68 AD, the only one with all four side towers still intact. It ranks among the six largest surviving Roman arenas in the world.
descriptions.6582c043-0113-4fb9-a3d3-d3a2b0820a53: A quarry of red scoria inside a small extinct volcano on Rapa Nui. This red stone was carved into the pukao topknots placed on the famous moai statues.
descriptions.0294d74b-0e97-4509-913a-475e3c21e1a7: The most substantial surviving example of Punic architecture on the island, a tower incorporated into a private garden. Its exact age and purpose remain unknown.
descriptions.b5627c73-537c-4301-a6d1-9a3afb45faec: Six Punic-Roman towers on high ground, positioned to communicate visually with each other across the island. They served as a defensive network from the 3rd century BC.
descriptions.79132373-7a68-45e3-a174-3b1e429a12b3: Northernmost tip of the peninsula, where Phoenician salt fish factory ruins and a Phoenician port survive. A lighthouse raised in 1850 still operates on the same headland.
descriptions.234bd55f-9444-44e9-8fde-7e66c049561d: Inca administrative centre in Lima's Ate District, occupied 1438–1530 AD. The adjacent Huaquerones pyramids-with-ramps sector holds a vast Inca burial ground studied by modern archaeology.
descriptions.ba2e3e1a-f3d0-4c41-9508-946ceced696a: A Chachapoya archaeological site near Purum Llaqta. The Chachapoya, called "Warriors of the Clouds," built stone cities high in the Amazonian cloud forests.
descriptions.c8529ed4-208b-45d2-9e75-58a5c3022c82: Capital of ancient Gandhara from 1400 BC, later an Achaemenid regional capital. Alexander the Great's army passed through here during its march into the Indian subcontinent.
descriptions.ee30b751-ef8d-482a-a6cd-838eca0e563e: A Neolithic menhir called La Droite Pierre, raised around 3300 BC. Standing stones like this served as territorial markers visible for kilometres.
descriptions.94cc711b-1ce7-4f7d-867c-64d59c65c76d: An Inca city at 3,600 m altitude, nicknamed "The City Above the Clouds." Five ritual stone baths still channel water through carved channels.
descriptions.8b423740-32d5-47e6-80ed-c764f7be5af5: Inhabited since the 7th millennium BC, this was the Mycenaean kingdom of wise King Nestor from Homer's Odyssey. His palace was found nearby.
descriptions.c70a32fa-651a-4a64-b09b-abd2bcf0974a: A 4th-century fortress that became Goguryeo's capital in 427 AD. The move from the old fortress signalled a shift in Korean power southward.
descriptions.d47439dd-6349-4633-bf0b-eb97094ac743: A queen's pyramid from 2600 BC standing in the shadow of the Great Pyramid. It held the burial of one of Khufu's closest royal women.
descriptions.7eb461fd-4017-4ac9-8a0c-698b81b2ef41: The central of three queens' pyramids flanking the Great Pyramid, built around 2600 BC. Its owner remains debated among Egyptologists.
descriptions.95c0ba9a-11f1-4d7d-9cbc-c099c0a944cf: A 2600 BC queen's pyramid built for Henutsen, one of Khufu's wives. Even royalty got miniature versions next to the pharaoh's monument.
descriptions.3df64c15-9caf-430f-b6d0-82bd2b15ddd1: A satellite pyramid in the Khufu complex with a 21.75 m base and 13.8 m height. It likely housed the pharaoh's ka, his spiritual double.
descriptions.64c9b400-5cab-45f2-8662-03c24c4367ce: A 55 m pyramid built around 1991 BC by the founder of the Twelfth Dynasty. Its core reused blocks stripped from older Old Kingdom pyramids.
descriptions.9ef004b4-0fe9-48c5-9f93-d8476487bb6e: Built in the 19th century BC, this pyramid once sat beside a labyrinth so vast that ancient writers compared it to the one on Crete.
descriptions.872b05b1-618b-4618-b3ae-6c69f3177911: A marble-clad pyramid tomb built in Rome around 18 BC. At 36 m tall, it copied Egyptian style during Rome's obsession with all things pharaonic.
descriptions.ad346943-799d-4c32-8ee0-22593797f59f: The northernmost pyramid in the Nile Valley, built by Khufu's son around 2500 BC. It now stands mostly in ruins, heavily quarried for stone.
descriptions.e27fc6a0-7922-4807-81dd-61438b3e7e7c: The first pyramid built in South Saqqara, dating to the 25th century BC. Pharaoh Djedkare moved away from Abusir, breaking a dynastic pattern.
descriptions.2b2812a6-63d4-4985-b334-ebb80f2ddd90: The world's oldest monumental stone building, a six-tiered step pyramid from the 27th century BC. It launched the entire age of pyramid-building.
descriptions.5e55b918-e5c7-4224-aa90-f244416f696f: A limestone pyramid with trapezoidal masonry enclosing a 7 x 9 m room. Its exact age is disputed — estimates range from Bronze Age to Roman.
descriptions.89489dc6-0f27-48bc-9365-5c74725b46dc: The second-largest pyramid at Giza, tomb of Pharaoh Khafre who ruled 2558–2532 BC. Its summit still wears a cap of original limestone casing.
descriptions.0d1797ca-6a3a-41fc-acbd-73c94d84a285: A 25 x 25 m queen's pyramid at Abusir, built partly from Neferirkare's leftover limestone. Originally ~17 m tall, it now stands just 4 m — and its queen may have ruled as pharaoh.
descriptions.9fe4c3dc-03a7-4ba8-a87d-929b6129c4fd: An unfinished 25th-century BC pyramid abandoned when the pharaoh died too young. Its incomplete state reveals exactly how pyramids were built.
descriptions.75dac040-12f2-4c78-b989-33cd3f5f07a9: A small queen's pyramid built just 10 m south of Userkaf's own, dating to the 25th century BC. Queens got their own mini pyramid complexes.
descriptions.3f129351-f576-4b35-a9d1-5925e1101d01: The tallest pyramid at Abusir, built in the 25th century BC on the highest ground. It was originally planned as a step pyramid, then redesigned.
descriptions.14fab6bd-8c5b-4233-816b-a90169bcefea: Built for Pharaoh Pepi II in the 23rd century BC — 78.75 m base, 52.5 m tall. Last full pyramid complex in Egypt; its 400 m causeway and three queen's pyramids still stand at South Saqqara.
descriptions.70e08059-7e26-4fa2-885f-31bb426f182d: Fifth Dynasty pharaoh Sahure's pyramid at Abusir, built c. 2465 BC, features causeway walls bearing relief carvings — among the finest narrative art to survive from the Old Kingdom.
descriptions.019ea3e7-663b-4a60-863a-980007df6878: An unfinished step pyramid from 2645 BC, abandoned so early it was buried under sand. The sealed sarcophagus inside was found completely empty.
descriptions.9b3eed6b-54e2-4321-8e84-9b204819879a: A Twelfth Dynasty pyramid at el-Lisht built near his father's, around 1950 BC. Nine smaller satellite pyramids surround the main structure.
descriptions.b0e8cb34-7b53-4900-a440-cc3c3b9c62bf: The smallest Old Kingdom pyramid, from the 24th century BC. Its walls hold the Pyramid Texts — the oldest religious writings on Earth.
descriptions.eb760e32-f0d1-48f3-9fe8-486680efe0f4: Built around 2490 BC by the first Fifth Dynasty pharaoh, right next to Djoser's step pyramid. Its interior was carved from the living bedrock.
descriptions.fa130f14-d604-4a66-a620-15d48ada6a4d: Three satellite pyramids from 2600–2500 BC flanking the Great Pyramid's south side. Each held the burial of a queen or royal woman.
descriptions.faf09f30-a927-4d6b-9fd9-14e1ab1b7c81: An ancient city-state mentioned by Homer in the Iliad as ruled by Protesilaus. It sits on the Pagasaean Gulf, inhabited since the 6th millennium BC.
descriptions.e7c2dc58-a477-41c6-ad83-02fea34c8d56: Ruins of a 3rd-century BC Doric temple on Mount Oeta — where myth says Heracles built his own funeral pyre and ascended to Olympus.
descriptions.8884677a-dd9d-49db-b3b0-8e25bc63de63: An ancient town on Samos inhabited from the 4th millennium BC through Roman times. It holds a famous tunnel engineered to carry water through a mountain.
descriptions.c7bbc3a4-57b3-4778-8fe0-fe9bc7d96058: Sassanid-built in the 3rd century AD, this castle at Qatif was later refurbished by the Ottomans as a Persian Gulf military base. The complex once held eleven mosques and a keep.
descriptions.7959bac1-48f2-4648-b9fa-7b23847cd894: An Inca-era settlement in the Ayacucho highlands. Sites like this served as administrative nodes in an empire spanning 4,000 km without wheeled transport.
descriptions.e0ffb4ea-6cfd-461b-ac5d-87583a566362: A 2nd-century BC Hellenistic palace built by Hyrcanus, head of the powerful Tobiad family. Its remote location served as both refuge and statement.
descriptions.41070db5-8f7c-4d69-8652-cc2d4bfb8bf4: A temple with Old Kingdom-style architecture on an escarpment ledge, built from massive unworked stone blocks. No inscriptions reveal who built it.
descriptions.1c93058e-d647-4f04-8aba-297c20ad41f2: Named from Quechua for "zig-zag," this huaca 6 km northeast of Cusco was carved from bedrock. Channels cut into the rock directed ritual liquid offerings during Inca ceremonies.
descriptions.29924a49-a6ce-430e-a5f7-a048a20d7dca: A settlement south of Lake Titicaca linked to early Tiwanaku culture, dating from around 100 AD. The region produced some of the Andes' first cities.
descriptions.07ea80ce-863f-43b9-8f7e-d155a0182f4f: The first emperor's 38-year tomb project, begun when he was just 13. A 76 m mound hides an underground palace that has never been opened.
descriptions.941ec7f7-645f-4c87-9cc5-f156e7504054: Perched at 2,600 m on a 32 km² Rift Valley plateau, this pre-Aksumite city traded on the Adulis–Aksum route. Over 80% still unexcavated; rock art dates habitation to 5000 BC.
descriptions.9c1414b7-dda6-4bbc-ad6f-541dd811763d: Inca buildings cut into a granite cliff at 3,436 m altitude, used for both administration and religious ceremonies. The stonework hugs the rock face.
descriptions.5a301f69-7dc6-44e0-94a2-2e6e533ec6ec: Inhabited since 2200 BC by the Saqqaq, a Paleo-Eskimo people who thrived in Arctic conditions 2,000 years before the Inuit arrived.
descriptions.4a9b3802-1067-4f6b-a144-4c2ffe9619a4: The holiest Inca temple, dedicated to the sun god Inti. Its ashlar walls were so precise that the Spanish built a church directly on top of them.
descriptions.aba085f1-0a92-44a7-904a-5aac35c0aa40: A 3400 BC burial cairn that held the remains of 157 people. An Iron Age roundhouse was later built right into the ancient tomb around 700 BC.
descriptions.7e45bd64-0e85-4b03-9cb7-2b865ef867dd: Oval in plan with a counter-scarp and entrances at northeast and southwest, this Hampshire hillfort sits on a commanding hill. It overlies an earlier palisade enclosure.
descriptions.727fbd40-0d27-4a24-a2e7-0f0b43544b62: A dolerite quarry worked from 3500 to 1800 BC to produce polished stone axes. Its tools spread across Brittany and beyond for 1,700 years.
descriptions.d1720193-07a3-495c-ba7e-823426aa4f17: One of four altepetl forming the Tlaxcala confederation, occupied in the 16th century. Tlaxcala famously allied with Cortés against the Aztecs.
descriptions.c9a49774-6211-499c-b80c-9dbeec95b47c: Aboriginal rock art dating back 25,000 years depicting Quinkans — mythological spirit beings. The sandstone galleries hold thousands of paintings.
descriptions.b5974adf-ab54-406e-99a4-e7c29c6ca5ba: A pre-Inca highland settlement from around 1200 AD. Sites like this preserve the cultures that flourished before the Inca empire absorbed them.
descriptions.c34f1705-3a2e-490a-875c-8ece315c36c1: An Inca rest station between Sayaqmarka and Phuyupatamarka on the trail to Machu Picchu. It serviced travellers on the empire's mountain highway.
descriptions.657dbfe1-7b3f-4548-93c6-99be8674a6ff: Built around 3000 BC on Sanday in Orkney — modelled closely on Maeshowe — this Neolithic cairn contained skeletal remains of multiple individuals when first opened in 1867.
descriptions.31203a3c-220a-41a8-87ff-befc4263c8d4: The K'iche' Maya capital — "Place of Old Reeds" — held temple pyramids and a ballcourt when Spanish forces arrived in 1524. Pedro de Alvarado torched the city that year.
descriptions.35671923-e17a-4e2b-9333-bf31063c375b: A summit earthwork atop the Raddon Hills at 235 m elevation. Its strategic position made it a natural lookout point in the Iron Age landscape.
descriptions.026dfe16-5509-47f2-bede-504b006d704d: A Sassanian rock relief 4.9 m high and 6.5 m wide, carved into a cliff. Weathering and deliberate vandalism have largely destroyed the imagery.
descriptions.b8781f6d-d85e-4fba-82f2-afc6a1d1fb76: Occupying 2.6 hectares in West Northamptonshire, this bivallate hillfort dates at least to the 6th century BC. Its inner rampart rises 3 m above the enclosed area.
descriptions.c3ed760b-0027-4275-bed0-787ef5d7ef02: A Cornish headland where Iron Age inhabitants cut a ditch across the narrow land-neck, leaving a central causeway still visible. Round house platforms survive on the eastern section.
descriptions.3a86a102-9b92-4f11-8dcf-4230d3534858: A massive New Kingdom mortuary temple from 1186–1155 BC. Its reliefs depict the only known ancient account of a Sea Peoples invasion.
descriptions.f7dd4933-c591-4d4a-b900-22edb8cb2276: Among the best-preserved Gallo-Roman city walls in northern Gaul, built in the 3rd–4th century AD. The exact construction date remains unknown.
descriptions.ce033c02-864e-45aa-8b32-f233dda3e043: A 2nd-century AD Buddhist site spread across 4 sq km from the Gandhara civilization. It served as the centre of Buddhist learning for centuries.
descriptions.56c3e7d6-250a-457d-9c42-7d37ef47af3c: A volcanic crater that served as the quarry for 95% of the island's moai over 500 years. Hundreds of unfinished statues still lie embedded in its slopes.
descriptions.9cb2bfc1-76b9-4904-941d-0d3cc7f86d6a: A fort near Algiers anchored Rome's Nova Praetentura road in Mauretania Caesariensis. Under Hadrian, a civilian town named Rapidum grew alongside it and persisted into the 4th century.
descriptions.093a4419-157b-4562-8da5-6be601aabc2d: Perched at 3,480 m, 110 km from Cusco, this Inca site's Temple of Wiracocha had a 10-metre central wall — the tallest surviving Inca masonry — enclosed by a 4 km perimeter wall.
descriptions.c961d960-661c-4406-a645-4185684b4c89: Ruins of a Punic-Roman sanctuary on Gozo's southwest coast, dating from 1500 BC to the 4th century AD. The promontory site was used for millennia.
descriptions.cc8b3804-e27e-4dc3-b6bf-5ffeeaef0018: A Roman town that grew from a native settlement in the 1st century BC. Today it lies beneath modern Leicester — where Richard III's body was found.
descriptions.8ae0ddaa-c1bd-4796-9328-ae7e64812b07: A Moesian city founded in the 4th century BC on the Danube, later renamed Colonia Ulpia Traiana Ratiaria. It became a major Roman provincial capital.
descriptions.7b3f1698-60de-4e2f-98cc-f405bfa01478: A Roman fort and naval base whose bath house walls still stand 4 m high — among the tallest surviving Roman structures in the region.
descriptions.de46e3ac-0cc0-4466-81aa-0af7a0ac25af: A 2nd-century bath house with walls standing 4 m tall, originally part of a Roman fort. Patches of original pink plaster still cling to the stone.
descriptions.d3da22e7-2499-4573-80f1-32037b641d57: A Roman earthwork with two parallel banks 20 m apart and a channel between them. Its original length was over 550 metres; pottery sherds from the early Roman period date the construction.
descriptions.4c4c07a0-d94d-42fa-b1f2-a4f4ab3b8094: A village 50 km northwest of Niš, recorded in Roman times as Cametas. The name means "stake" locally, and the municipality retains visible remnants of its Roman-era past.
descriptions.29936379-8628-4125-8f2b-25d841e8eb5e: Occupied since 2500 BC, this coastal village sat at the edge of the Wantsum Channel that once separated the Isle of Thanet from the mainland.
descriptions.2f86a187-f279-46e6-81b5-0ad66b46caea: Southwest of the village, just beyond the motorway, lies the Aubreys — a prehistoric hillfort. To the north, a complex of Roman temples completes a layered landscape of occupation.
descriptions.d48e920c-f57c-4f20-8bdf-df646d31029b: At 105 m tall and 220 m wide, the Red Pyramid at Dahshur is the third-largest pyramid ever built — after Khufu and Khafre at Giza. Its red limestone casing gives it a distinctive rusty hue.
descriptions.2207dced-e1db-4547-bac5-2d90984550a3: A Roman garrison at the Danube's northernmost point, founded in the 1st century AD. Its medieval old town preserves the most intact medieval centre in the region.
descriptions.ed334343-bff8-4397-b8b6-889903614fd4: Dated 3300–1900 BC, this Pre-Harappan site 22 km north of Dera Ismail Khan enclosed a planned urban area within a wall — one of the earliest gridded cities found in South Asia.
descriptions.4626dd74-00a2-4796-91b6-cc737f96d08a: Over 3,000 dolmens spread along 2 km of cliff edge in the northeast — the largest prehistoric necropolis of its type in North Africa.
descriptions.317436c1-4827-4db2-acf6-1238452a5e86: 1st-century AD Roman city on the Via Militaris between Naissus and Serdica. Its bishop Nicetas (c.335–414), patron saint of Romania, is credited by many scholars as author of the Te Deum.
descriptions.1374c196-3e09-44d3-b2a8-ac326f6bd14c: A Bronze Age stone circle near Corfe Castle, hidden in dense woodland. Ten surviving gritstone boulders form an arc suggesting an original oval of ~26 m — Dorset's second-largest stone circle.
descriptions.49695e70-c15a-482d-ad6c-7bdf7467b8f8: A Phoenician temple layered over itself — the L-shaped base from 2600 BC sits beneath an Obelisk temple from 1600 BC, built on the same footprint.
descriptions.a56bd06f-2305-409d-99e5-47e4f7e29ae4: The Chachapoya built cliff-face tombs resembling miniature houses at 2,800 m altitude. Funerary buildings cling to the limestone rock like birdhouses.
descriptions.3df5f75c-51c1-45a7-bf4c-fdb80f9f585d: A coastal city in Attica overlooking the Euboean Strait, Rhamnous held antiquity's most revered sanctuary of Nemesis. Two temples stood there — the larger Doric temple built around 436 BC.
descriptions.d0901b94-6ede-4c1a-9498-7e8bf16a2bb3: Planned in 408 BC by uniting three older settlements, Rhodes hosted the Colossus — a 33-metre bronze statue — and later a Hospitaller citadel whose medieval town survives largely intact today.
descriptions.1a3bf98d-c88e-485c-8c4c-96c124f89e7b: A compact Roman city in Lycia with a uniquely dense layout — buildings packed into difficult terrain without leaving empty space between streets.
descriptions.3cb81240-5b1e-4505-a73a-4c0d02fd439c: An early monastic site with low stone walls and a cross-slab standing stone. Artefacts found here date the community to the early Christian era.
descriptions.84b456ff-0b44-4d75-92a4-5cbe22026b95: A 40 km wide geological dome in the Sahara exposing concentric rings of rock. It is visible from orbit and was once proposed as Plato's Atlantis.
descriptions.2d35e0fe-b551-47db-b86d-30b2c3aad3aa: A massive Saxon Shore fort founded after the conquest of 43 AD, with substantial walls still standing. Rutupiae was the main Roman gateway into the province and the origin of the name Britannia.
descriptions.cc89fe8f-328b-470e-adcd-0d1244f28acf: Bronze Age barrows from around 800 BC survive within this royal deer park. Ancient burial mounds now share the landscape with free-roaming deer.
descriptions.920b1e8b-7b15-48bf-8352-e48ea2cdc264: Standing 1.1 km north of Wolfershausen, this menhir is the largest megalith in Schwalm-Eder-Kreis district. Erected around 3000 BC, it rises from the corner of a small woodland.
descriptions.bc55dd6f-a972-4caa-af6a-e4e96f65d0f5: A 25-metre-wide round barrow on eastern Bodmin Moor, opened in 1837 to reveal a stone cist and a corrugated gold cup — held at Buckingham Palace for centuries before entering the Royal Collection.
descriptions.fea39465-ffe1-4c93-a5af-2f6490484307: A megalithic site from around 3000 BC, part of a cluster that includes stone alignments and a dolmen within 300 m. Corsica's ancient ritual landscape.
descriptions.08122cd2-522f-4ebc-b363-aabc7bd60de3: A funerary complex near Sandwich, Kent, dated to c. 2300 BC — identified only after the 2001 discovery of the Ringlemere gold cup. The cup now resides in a London museum.
descriptions.7793574e-f857-4526-bfc4-d9a64281f303: A stone row stretching across Ringmoor Down, paired with a cairn circle. Dartmoor holds the densest concentration of stone rows in the world.
descriptions.4656cc72-cea3-407e-a61c-314450ff6c62: A double-banked Iron Age fort covering 3.4 hectares, dating to around 50 BC. Its multivallate design suggests a community expecting serious threats.
descriptions.ab336181-36c6-4505-b52b-181bed507d50: The original Greek acropolis of Dicearkia, later the Roman port city of Puteoli, built in the 6th century BC. It sits on an active volcanic field.
descriptions.f6916087-0021-44fe-af7e-5111e67f660a: Set 17 m above the Kubršnica river at the edge of Aranđelovac, this Paleolithic cave confirmed human occupation south of the Sava–Danube line. Its finds span tens of thousands of years.
descriptions.1327e266-b4d2-484a-a6c8-f165ec0e0716: A 2800 BC site on Bornholm island with both a Neolithic sun temple and Iron Age earthworks. Two civilizations millennia apart chose the same spot.
descriptions.5137c62f-7a51-4144-9ee1-9bd565b10bc8: A settlement occupied 750–1500 AD near a major tectonic boundary. The Talamancan people built communities on geologically volatile land.
descriptions.3f004b9f-812c-4bd8-b7d8-554f7e9ce926: A group of nine Bronze Age barrows on the Blackdown Hills, named after the legendary outlaw Robin Hood. The bowl barrows date from 3300–1200 BC.
descriptions.91d662b0-f64e-4b15-81c6-bb5a05a1796e: An Iron Age enclosure on a steep hillside above the East Lyn River at 320 m elevation. Its promontory position gave natural defence on three sides.
descriptions.ee091b60-f72c-4e85-be61-baa970aa0630: A Bronze Age coastal settlement with some of the best-preserved monumental architecture of the 2nd millennium BC anywhere in the Mediterranean.
descriptions.e17ba5d6-296f-4441-85cb-8bff98ef2f7e: Neanderthals sheltered at "Bull's Rock" in the Catalan Pyrenees around 50,000 years ago. Since 1988, researchers here have used a unique digital system to document the fossil sequence.
descriptions.86b67ab6-879c-4b80-a6ab-7bae209b8dc4: A rock shelter in El Cogul, Catalonia, bearing Levantine rock art and schematic art from two distinct prehistoric traditions. Latin inscriptions confirm its use as a sanctuary into historical times.
descriptions.1d65f378-c797-47d7-827c-252df5243d13: A town built around a sulphurous volcanic spring called the Mefite, sacred since the 7th century BC. Ancient peoples thought it was a gate to the underworld.
descriptions.cc3e0e34-8532-41dd-9988-6c20e37be8e6: A 1st-century BC pre-Roman temple carved into a natural schist spur, dedicated to the Lusitanian god Endovellicus. Steps are cut directly into bedrock.
descriptions.940444fb-1897-4c1f-bdc2-30e967df95c8: A large upright granite stone sometimes called a menhir, though it may be naturally positioned. Its name translates to "Lovers' Rock."
descriptions.bf00a8de-4b2d-4cbd-9078-0923ed709dc0: Over 700 sites of Paleolithic to Neolithic rock art spanning 14,000 years across the Mediterranean coast. UNESCO-protected since 1998.
descriptions.23ddb957-c31f-4ec9-9fcc-e02bc5316c5c: A Roman courtyard villa from the 1st century AD with well-preserved mosaic floors. It grew from a simple farmhouse into a sprawling estate.
descriptions.280e2bbb-e4cf-4705-88a7-3ebcdd441d0b: Over 6,000 rock carvings spanning 4200–500 BC in the Arctic, the largest concentration in northern Europe. They depict boats, animals, and ceremonies.
descriptions.baa9dcab-849f-46ae-b6eb-eabaa8ed2eaa: Rock carvings at Drotten, Fåberg, dated to the 6th millennium BC — the oldest known petroglyphs from a hunting culture in Scandinavia.
descriptions.6290bb50-27f9-412e-86d8-0c9faf98dfc1: Stone carvings of moose and other animals covering about 20 sq m. The largest figure spans 90 cm, etched by Stone Age hunters millennia ago.
descriptions.a776d595-3309-45c7-9c7f-014181af2a84: Rock carvings spanning 4600–2600 BC — the first hunting-culture petroglyphs ever found in Scandinavia. They redefined what we knew about Arctic art.
descriptions.d928b37a-38d1-4c34-8e89-49703f92f313: Around 300 petroglyph and painting sites from the Stone Age and Bronze Age across a single region. The Stone Age images favour naturalism over abstraction.
descriptions.6de2b431-29c0-41e2-822e-91d99f46f7cb: Bronze Age petroglyphs from 1500–500 BC in Uppland province, part of a complex with multiple rock art panels. They were carved during the Nordic Bronze Age.
descriptions.2b43af76-29cd-4b3f-a784-e9a673e54c04: Roughly 1,500 rock inscriptions spanning from the 3rd century BC to the 16th century AD, carved into coastal cliffs on the Ionian Sea.
descriptions.58ad6c3e-49ea-4a21-ab5b-2735d30298d1: Covering 0.84 hectares in Somerset's Selwood parish, this univallate hillfort retains a bank up to 1.6 m high with a 1.8 m ditch below it. It sits close to the later Hales Castle.
descriptions.0db059e7-fd17-408c-9953-db7391aabf75: A small oval Iron Age enclosure on open moorland. Single-rampart forts like this typically sheltered a handful of farming families.
descriptions.f30145f9-4f34-4a4f-9553-5d42001da5a5: Three Neolithic and Bronze Age megalithic monuments built from local oolitic limestone, spanning 4000–2000 BC. Legend says a king and his army were turned to stone.
descriptions.2acd40c5-e1dd-4ea1-9378-8c4e28acd415: Remains of a Roman amphitheatre rebuilt by Julius Caesar with a capacity of 30,000. Its podium was built in opus quadratum — precisely cut stone blocks.
descriptions.9aedc6a3-1681-4ee3-8d6c-4386de4bba1d: A 2nd-century AD amphitheatre half-carved into rock, half-built in limestone, seating over 10,000. It is the largest Roman monument on the island.
descriptions.d37895cc-6801-418e-a4b2-29b7001566ef: Built under Hadrian (117–138 AD) near his birthplace of Italica, this amphitheatre seated roughly 25,000 spectators — a footprint rivalled by few in the empire — 300 m from the city's north gate.
descriptions.fedd9198-56b3-4810-bcba-33f382a6240c: A 2nd-century AD aqueduct delivering water over 26 km using only gravity. It was the engineering lifeline of Roman Paris, then called Lutetia.
descriptions.91ad730f-4a6d-48c3-aa2d-e79d940878ca: A Roman underground aqueduct from the 2nd century AD, classified as a historic monument since 1840. It has survived almost 2,000 years underground.
descriptions.d849ed4e-d1bc-47f3-9721-247006e54a3c: A 1st-century AD triumphal arch at Medinaceli in opus quadratum, built at nearly 1,200 m elevation. Its three barrel vaults are rare — only a handful of triple-arched Roman arches survive anywhere.
descriptions.0b681115-78b6-409f-b780-4330392e5b40: Roman baths built around 60–70 AD over natural hot springs sacred to the goddess Sulis. The water still flows at 46°C after nearly 2,000 years.
descriptions.d7cecc1a-ed47-4dd6-a335-69e1233d47aa: 1st–2nd c. AD public baths buried beneath the old city. Hypocaust heating, three bathing halls, and a Greek marble statue of a dancing satyr found during 1986 excavations.
descriptions.70037a24-6487-4834-9b50-5242289009fe: A 1st-century military bathhouse 15 feet underground, complete with tepidarium, caldarium, and frigidarium. Tiles stamped with legion identities suggest the Ninth Legion built it.
descriptions.15cf53da-ecf4-4681-a2a7-63984886562f: A 1st-century AD Roman bridge on the road from Lisbon to Mérida. It wasn't identified as Roman until the 1980s despite being there for 2,000 years.
descriptions.ac24586e-d09c-422c-be37-d3a3fb34891b: A bridge originally crossing the Guadalquivir in the early 1st century BC, rebuilt many times since. For two thousand years, until a modern bridge opened, it was the city's only river crossing.
descriptions.19bf50b2-2ed2-4f63-a9b5-c5932439c190: A 1st-century AD Roman bridge on Via XIX, linking Lucus Augusti to Bracara Augusta. Eight stone arches span 104 m over the Minho — carried traffic for nearly 2,000 years, pedestrian-only since 2012.
descriptions.0a36e25e-4aaa-431f-bcde-843fc01353a1: A Roman bridge whose image appears on the city's coat of arms. It crossed the Tormes starting from the 1st century BC and is still standing.
descriptions.6d615647-22ef-4614-abca-fad00fc83994: A 148-metre, five-arch limestone bridge remodelled in medieval times. The Jarama River has since migrated entirely, leaving all five arches spanning dry ground.
descriptions.754f8aff-b1ac-4650-a0db-89bf64dbbba5: A 1st–2nd c. AD bridge on the Lisbon–Mérida road: six arches, each 8.95 m wide with 33 voussoirs, spanning 116.5 metres. Flood-relief eyeholes were built between the piers to survive flash floods.
descriptions.5cc613ff-ad80-4906-9103-6d1035eaea3e: A Roman bridge still in use today, part of an ancient road from Faro to Beja. Nearly 2,000 years of continuous traffic across the same stone arches.
descriptions.0a3362a9-23ba-41f8-83d6-88e727059f95: A Roman bridge on the Via Domitia with nine arches spanning 10–12 m each, built during Augustus's reign. Only parts survive today.
descriptions.6c7352e9-2e99-4dd7-b2c8-93a883b69d4f: The oldest standing bridge north of the Alps, with pillars from the 2nd century AD. It replaced two older wooden bridges on the same spot.
descriptions.c3fda873-10be-4040-878f-350d6da7d70d: A 1st-century AD single-arch bridge spanning 17 m, still in daily use. It survived a 1992 flood that killed 37 people in the town around it.
descriptions.a9acce8d-1324-434d-913d-519e7c4eb619: Over 400 m long and 30 m wide, Mérida's circus held 30,000 spectators for chariot racing from c. 20 BC. Its starting gates and central spine are the most legible of any surviving Roman circus.
descriptions.d4fbbaf4-742a-448f-a424-6f3ddf573c31: Built in the 1st century AD, roughly 423 metres long with room for 15,000 spectators. One of Hispania's largest Roman circuses; chariot races thundered here until Christianity shuttered the games.
descriptions.43cc8f86-b6cc-4064-b3fa-e333077b938e: An ancient city founded in the 7th century BC that rose to Roman colony status. Originally a port, it passed from Phoenician to Carthaginian to Roman hands.
descriptions.63d4e2b3-4dad-438d-be14-34bd79cf9842: Capital of Roman Dalmatia, Salona held an amphitheatre and basilicas before Avars and Slavs destroyed it in 614 AD. Refugees fled to Diocletian's palace at Split, which still stands today.
descriptions.4561c396-b590-47a8-b6da-c177870361bb: A 1st-century AD Roman column that originally supported a great hall. It was built by Legion IX and reused by Legion VI three centuries later.
descriptions.591cee00-2570-4cf4-94d8-a141cf6e9854: A 3rd-century dam across the Carenque River near Sintra, built to supply Olisipo (Lisbon) with water. Its mortar-bonded masonry survives partially buried beneath a modern road.
descriptions.190fdea4-2036-47fa-a6ca-81b3b0ab2e93: A Roman dam about 70 m long and up to 8 m tall, built during the Romanization period. It supplied water to the surrounding agricultural estate.
descriptions.384133aa-dc2d-4f86-9f20-e53c98e5c5be: A small buttress dam in Grândola, built in two phases during Roman occupation. Its rectilinear wall stretched 40 m, supported by six downstream buttresses spaced 2.5 m apart.
descriptions.fee2da6d-ac67-4e7c-92b9-fbb82ae6bf8a: A 600 km tourism route linking the birthplaces and estates of 18 Roman emperors. More Roman emperors came from this region than any other outside Italy.
descriptions.e578e7e9-a9ec-48d0-9f9f-64f3f1b64a5e: 1st–4th century AD. Vats cut into the floor produced garum — fermented fish gut sauce — from local mackerel and tuna. The southern tip of Hispania was one of Rome's biggest garum hubs.
descriptions.5a68414e-22b9-4e2e-a9b7-d2a46b25be9b: The political heart of ancient Rome, a forum surrounded by temples, basilicas, and government buildings. Decisions made here shaped the Western world.
descriptions.15ecd8c5-1887-4162-8b42-d2315b15f65a: A cylindrical Roman funerary monument near Córdoba built in Republican-era style. Tombs like this lined the roads leading out of Roman cities during the early centuries AD.
descriptions.e07a4878-eb3c-4174-8762-61a94eaf8629: A 2nd-century AD mausoleum near Fabara built in opus quadratum for Lucius Aemilius Lupus. Its cella and portico survive in better condition than almost any comparable tomb on the peninsula.
descriptions.8e50020c-5483-4331-a8e2-e46feaa60098: A Roman salt-production town called Salinae, founded in the 1st century AD. Romans prized salt so highly that soldiers were partly paid in it.
descriptions.725d79b1-6918-484c-97eb-ff6ae947f840: Roman milestones from the 1st century AD marking the ancient road to Guimarães. They measured distances in Roman miles — each about 1.48 km.
descriptions.67afbdc6-2f22-4678-88aa-df76baf9f7ea: A partially preserved 2nd-century AD Roman public fountain. Nymphaea were elaborate water displays that showcased Roman hydraulic engineering.
descriptions.88e024ff-c9a8-4ab6-9158-23033f5356fc: A 2nd-century AD Roman odeon that once seated 1,200 guests. Odeons were roofed theatres for musical performances, smaller and more intimate than open-air venues.
descriptions.9192a16a-acc4-4aea-9d6e-19e74b9d8a38: Gallo-Roman baths from the 2nd century AD, partially built into a church with the hypocaust heating system preserved beneath the nave.
descriptions.2cc719f3-4797-4137-a5b2-7b41d15b8d3a: Roman industrial ovens from the 1st–2nd century AD, used for mass-producing large ceramic materials. Ancient factory-scale manufacturing.
descriptions.b4990b79-a0d1-45e7-9d03-635362c0b2cf: A 1st-century AD forum in the capital of Roman Lusitania, founded in 25 BC. It served as the civic heart of the province's most powerful city.
descriptions.8c66d030-330a-4f76-9e07-8e1ed0b0f706: A series of earthworks forming a dyke once running from Sheffield to Mexborough. Its purpose and date of construction remain genuinely unknown.
descriptions.b048a095-8e3e-41af-a715-e785e3a1a51d: 1st–5th century AD. Linked Calleva Atrebatum (Silchester) to Aquae Sulis (Bath) — a military highway later used by medieval drovers. Its earthwork ghost survives as part of the Wansdyke.
descriptions.c3c4e677-a96a-41bc-aea7-7a6882e8dd1a: Roman ruins including baths, cemeteries, and wall remains, dated to the 2nd century AD. The villa was occupied for at least three centuries.
descriptions.91f09c72-5e12-49da-bce4-9f139d7e8e2a: A Roman villa near modern Vilamoura, occupied from the 1st century AD. Its ruins sit incongruously next to a contemporary luxury resort.
descriptions.d9d26446-9348-4f16-b5e4-c4c11e8ccffb: Ruins of a Roman fish-salting factory and baths from the 1st century AD. Garum production was big business — the Roman appetite for fish sauce was enormous.
descriptions.9bf829da-096e-41c6-b175-f3436c1ce18c: A Roman town adapted to mountain terrain, with forum, temples, and triumphal arches. Its grid plan bent around the topography rather than fighting it.
descriptions.cc413994-12b4-4d0c-b143-739d21992542: 1st century AD, occupied until the 10th century. The thermal baths feature mosaic floors with fish designs. A temple to an aquatic deity stood here before being converted to a Christian church.
descriptions.addfeb62-4424-4c58-8a2a-0c5e26a98df9: A Roman villa dating from the 1st century AD with an olive-oil production facility. Rome's insatiable demand for oil drove estates across the empire.
descriptions.3cd39d3e-def2-4565-b4c8-9673cbdb5443: A Roman villa active 1st–5th centuries AD in the colony of Ipses, Lusitania — where Pompeia Exoce buried her grandson, recorded in a funerary inscription. The nearby port Portus Magnus was a key hub.
descriptions.9c776b7e-cc75-46e4-a169-2aa16b47ae86: A Roman agricultural estate occupied from the 1st to 4th century AD. A monastery was later built directly on the villa's foundations.
descriptions.8c84668c-5362-4b99-84a1-470534b0f02a: An ancient city called Theveste in Roman times, with 3rd-century AD ruins. Its strategic position made it a key garrison on the empire's African frontier.
descriptions.1b824103-b553-450d-9901-ba645d7d7a09: Roman ruins from the 1st–6th century AD, including fish-processing facilities and thermal baths. The site industrialised fish sauce production at massive scale.
descriptions.bab3e7ad-3795-42e6-8a05-b65606e7d708: Active 1st–4th centuries AD near Torres Novas, this villa takes its name from a mosaic pavement whose inscription remains untranslated. Excavation in 1962 recovered hundreds of coins and bronzes.
descriptions.17ddf3b5-0e0f-4f9b-9f65-88ba2fde7f90: Roman ruins featuring a perfect grid plan with a 12 m triumphal arch. One of the best-surviving examples of Roman urban planning anywhere.
descriptions.b54580b3-4201-4cc6-9588-785d365974d6: A 1st-century AD Roman temple beside the Alcántara Bridge. The bridge, arch, and temple were all designed by the same Roman architect.
descriptions.5bfa1075-d0f7-4b73-82e9-90091e4b9ca9: Hexastyle, Corinthian, and 32 m long, this temple in Córdoba lay hidden beneath City Hall until the 1950s. Its columns and podium have since been re-erected in the city centre.
descriptions.9152beea-f7ab-40ef-a692-ef63ac8e9ca6: A Roman temple wrongly named after Diana for centuries — its dedication remains unknown. Fourteen Corinthian columns still stand from the 1st century AD.
descriptions.4e0540cd-333a-4808-8c4e-fa136957c934: Built 162–166 AD but never finished — the marble was stripped for a Byzantine church. A colossal 13-metre Hercules once stood here; only three fingers and an elbow remain.
descriptions.e056946d-fd09-43f2-8d45-648121ace99d: An early 2nd-century AD Corinthian temple in Vic — unknown until 1882, having been concealed inside a medieval tower. Fully restored after that tower's demolition, it stands in the town centre.
descriptions.0f654bf4-86b7-4602-8bee-c8da00f3edee: A Roman temple built on a high platform with a wide staircase, its collapsed façade now reconstructed. It once faced the rising sun.
descriptions.e45af002-3182-479c-984e-0692325c40c7: A 2nd-century AD theatre built by Emperor Hadrian, surrounded by the medieval quarter that grew around its ruins. It is still used for performances.
descriptions.2d76f228-e78d-4e1a-934e-cf8eef944e37: A 1st-century AD Roman theatre seating 2,000 — far exceeding Brigantium's population. Stone base, timber superstructure, semicircular cavea; rediscovered by targeted excavations in 2013 and 2019.
descriptions.0bd5fa99-83d0-4443-86f4-20510d2a4ab1: With a cavea exceeding 120 m in diameter, the 1st-century BC theatre at Cádiz ranks among the Roman world's largest. Abandoned by the 4th century, a fortress was built over it by Alfonso X.
descriptions.51e00207-24c0-4f44-b581-4d8584df5296: Built 5–1 BC and buried under a medieval cathedral by the 13th century. Rediscovered in 1988 during construction work; excavations revealed Carrara marble columns carved in Rome.
descriptions.1bda8d7d-01e8-4063-b1c1-c2f46c6b9a64: Once the largest Roman theatre north of the Alps, with a 116 m diameter and room for 10,000. It now sits beside a modern train station.
descriptions.7630e743-d719-486b-9be7-aa06d9bcab71: Built 16–15 BC by consul Agrippa in the capital of Lusitania. Its 86-metre cavea seated 6,000 and is still used for live theatre — named one of Spain's 12 national treasures.
descriptions.2c4d2e4b-57b5-4788-8ba6-22955dac6448: Built under Augustus, the theatre at Arles held 8,000 spectators across 33 tiers. Pillaged for stone in the medieval period, two columns of its scaenae frons still stand.
descriptions.8de309a1-1291-4878-8f63-694b2276b934: Built for the colony of Arausio, founded 40 BC, this theatre at Orange preserves its 103-metre stage wall nearly intact — the best-surviving scaenae frons in the Roman world.
descriptions.44428a81-cfc8-4e6b-9671-f40a385b2c4f: A superbly preserved 1st-century AD Roman theatre seating 7,000, built into the hillside of ancient Philippopolis. It still hosts live events.
descriptions.1dd3a790-bf81-49e2-b516-dcc04a14328f: Built 140 AD in Verulamium — the only theatre-with-a-stage in Roman Britain, not an amphitheatre. The stage was added in 160 AD. By 300 AD it seated 2,000. A secret shrine was found just beside it.
descriptions.a71bf02d-0df6-4b15-8436-be73a43950f4: A theatre built in Augustus's time using the natural hillside for seating. Much was destroyed, but the ingenious slope-built design is still visible.
descriptions.6d2b0b49-565b-41ed-8763-aa0f35d7c627: A 1st-century AD theatre seating 6,000, modelled on the Theatre of Marcellus in Rome. It was active until the 3rd century, then repurposed.
descriptions.cab346d8-176c-429d-830c-2f1ac68e2eb9: A monumental Roman public bathhouse from the 1st century BC, part of the provincial capital's urban renewal. The complex was enormous for its era.
