descriptions.f859776a-9e93-4c62-9585-1f4aed2cbaa0: The largest Roman baths in the Balkans, covering 7,000 sq m. They are the fourth-largest surviving Roman thermae in all of Europe.
descriptions.cf46928b-ed62-4b81-acbd-8822349ca58a: Built around 300 AD and found in 1895 with two sarcophagi — a family tomb. Legend insists Christian martyrs Hermylus and Stratonicus, drowned in 314 AD, floated here in a coffin.
descriptions.61c3203a-1363-412c-8977-a32cbb67b3cc: A 4th-century AD tomb famous for exceptional wall paintings — among the finest examples of late antique art anywhere in the Balkans.
descriptions.df304236-53ea-44a0-8c2c-ef6a4b459728: A 4th-century AD Roman town house with well-preserved mosaic floors found during construction work for a county government building.
descriptions.27df72a6-018c-4870-ba5b-c719dca6c570: A reconstructed Roman villa with buildings spread over a full estate. It shows how a working Roman farm operated, from kitchens to bathhouses.
descriptions.9431fc19-12a8-4ec7-ac30-183d2d110cf3: A Roman villa known since the 1890s but neglected by archaeologists. Decades of neglect destroyed artefacts including Roman-era mosaics.
descriptions.0fb3b6cd-57cc-4ed6-b4a3-97a580cadfcc: A Roman town founded in the 1st century AD within a mountain nature park. The town of Ammaia was large enough to have its own forum and baths.
descriptions.a36951c3-c172-4782-8fa0-a0cfd2e7650c: A 1st-century AD Roman villa with an exceptional mosaic floor — the primary surviving treasure from one of the province's most significant estates.
descriptions.1994047b-25e3-4702-9449-4bf7324f2827: A 1st-century BC Roman villa with rich marble and mosaic decor, remodelled in the 3rd century. Traces of painted stucco still survive on the walls.
descriptions.581afa31-d38d-43a5-8cfc-50cb95a96aa8: 4th-century AD dome holds the oldest surviving Christian mosaic in the Roman world. Three tiers show a hunt, biblical scenes, and the four seasons — possibly the tomb of Constans, son of Constantine.
descriptions.b04ee52d-6549-4877-8131-2475c9989299: Spanning 16 hectares on the Garonne near Toulouse, this 1st–4th century estate's walls yielded 70 imperial portrait busts — the largest such collection found outside Rome.
descriptions.2882893b-da7b-4afa-bd4a-e8d4ffb76dcd: Near Cascais, this villa shows gradual Romanisation — imported Iron Age goods giving way to local production, then full Roman villa construction from the 1st century AD onward.
descriptions.fabd8d1b-1a9c-4266-8ff6-d764c6229943: A 3rd–4th century villa in the Loures municipality within Roman Olisipo's territory. Excavations since 1997 have traced its reuse into the medieval Islamic period; classified heritage since 2012.
descriptions.a0c839b2-5efa-409c-852a-dcaf88507e64: A Roman villa near the road from Lisbon to Braga, occupied 1st–5th century AD. Its octagonal peristyle design is architecturally unique in the region.
descriptions.32008339-d027-4578-b76a-915e5464f6c0: Roman ruins from the 3rd–5th century AD with structural elements deemed worthy of preservation. The villa was part of a larger agricultural estate.
descriptions.9ec68853-e08d-4b35-af4a-177e756eed3e: A 4th-century AD Roman villa near the Vizela River basin. It was built on a platform with views over the valley — Romans always chose the best views.
descriptions.d0f09ee9-6684-44d7-92cb-56c85ea6cb35: Active 1st–4th centuries AD near Évora in Lusitania, this villa sat at the junction of two Roman roads — to Salacia and Pax Julia. Excavations have uncovered mosaics, coins, and architecture.
descriptions.473987c8-f684-4c4a-8c23-633821731f1e: Built in 206 BC after Rome seized the city, the walls ran 2,650 metres with a rubble-filled gap between inner and outer faces. Semicircular towers punctuated the circuit.
descriptions.b98dd630-7010-4134-869f-e546b258f646: 3rd-century AD Roman walls that still encircle the entire old town — the best-preserved complete Roman wall circuit in the world. UNESCO-listed.
descriptions.55ac13ab-3693-4e65-af02-a6b424d0e345: A 2nd-century AD theatre built from black basalt. Its dark stone gives it a dramatically different look from any other Roman theatre.
descriptions.06f6cb37-39f4-4785-b6ec-7ec6272ac7d4: A late Iron Age and Romano-period farmstead on Cranborne Chase, covering about 2 hectares. Augustus Pitt Rivers excavated it in the 1880s — an early landmark of stratigraphic excavation.
descriptions.424a8ef0-74a3-48ab-bdaf-8df3d957e36c: A cave with over 250 Paleolithic engravings and paintings from around 11,000 BC, including remarkable depictions of mammoths and bison.
descriptions.5d3ec998-b314-4e52-bf91-3f2a90f8afaf: A tor with a Neolithic enclosure, Bronze Age hut circles, and a summit Logan Stone. Four millennia of human activity stacked on one hilltop.
descriptions.4505d766-7814-4693-9ca3-04d707883088: Built around 400 BC, this massive hillfort on Roulston Scar south of Sutton Bank is the largest prehistoric monument in the North York Moors, with sweeping views over two adjacent vales.
descriptions.2fe636b2-9d02-434e-8c26-889601e30190: A Late Neolithic or Bronze Age bowl barrow on Anglezarke Moor, measuring 73 m by 66 m and up to 5.5 m high. Unexcavated and scheduled, it aligns between Great Hill and the Pikestones long cairn.
descriptions.003428cd-6046-41c9-a687-a8a2b392e19d: A steep 370 m volcanic hill with an Iron Age fort from around 800 BC. Its fortifications exploited the natural defences of the volcanic terrain.
descriptions.b864c402-1d93-4376-b37c-f5b89874afec: A Minoan city near Palekastro, Crete, occupied from Early Minoan IIA to Late Minoan IIIB. In myth it was the birthplace of Diktaian Zeus and where the Argonauts confronted Talos the bronze giant.
descriptions.c3bf5c7e-26d4-4441-95ea-990a5c82c4ae: A tourist route linking megalithic sites from 4000–3000 BC between Osnabrück and Oldenburg. The region has one of the densest concentrations of megaliths in Europe.
descriptions.4acf93dc-6942-41bf-90f2-107407872c9a: A circular stone mausoleum built around 3 BC for the kings of Mauretania. Its round form with a pyramid top blends Berber and Hellenistic styles.
descriptions.60f955a7-4e61-4feb-9203-318af677053a: Nine royal shaft-and-chamber tombs cut beneath the city, holding sarcophagi from the 19th century BC. Heavy Egyptian influence on the funerary goods reflects Byblos's role as Egypt's timber supplier.
descriptions.63ae296b-eca5-4df7-b7f3-64d6cd4d6eef: Royal tombs from the 4th–3rd century BC of the ancient Illyrian city of Pelion. Traces of human activity here go back to the Bronze Age.
descriptions.332d3d4c-4dfd-4a7a-8f79-0db277b1f4c6: A hilltop castle inhabited since the 9th century BC, with ruins of a 13th-century Venetian church inside. It now forms an archaeological park.
descriptions.29446177-8f7d-4e23-9a9c-6c9ba2959472: A 3rd-millennium BC passage grave on a headland below the Cuillin hills. Designated a nationally important historic monument in 2017.
descriptions.9b682dd4-674c-4713-9cdc-55723a5f25bf: Triangular in plan on a Quantock Hills spur, this univallate fort encloses 1.8 hectares. A linear outwork 120 m beyond the rampart and ditch adds a second defensive line to the north.
descriptions.3fe3b8d1-a2a0-4d11-8bed-68f33110fb57: Founded by Messapians in the 8th c. BC, Rudiae covered 100 hectares — twice the size of nearby Lecce. A 2011 dig uncovered an amphitheatre seating 8,000. Birthplace of the poet Ennius.
descriptions.1065be39-af74-4a22-8f95-ffc846068367: At over 7.6 m, this is the tallest standing stone in the UK. It now stands in a churchyard — Christians built around it rather than topple it.
descriptions.8080e03e-2603-4665-915e-db88291d434c: 3rd–4th century AD courtyard villa famous for its Venus mosaic — a naively charming British-made image of the goddess surrounded by lion, stag, leopard, and bull.
descriptions.a4a3242d-7110-406e-ba77-af035c6cf560: Founded by Phoenicians around the 12th century BC, later a Berber capital and then a Roman city. It passed through more civilizations than most cities on Earth.
descriptions.6a48cd85-a104-4e10-a3d8-e804922d1552: A 2nd-century AD Roman theatre unique in the region — built on flat ground and raised with vaults instead of being carved into a hillside.
descriptions.22362770-e393-48d3-812d-34c7e772cf4c: Roman-era ruins declared a protected monument in 1931. Positioned on a road node by the Jarama river, the site sat within the epigraphic orbit of Complutum, one of Hispania's key Roman cities.
descriptions.d747c493-89ff-4471-ac39-17dbd5a5614c: Phoenician port known to Rome as Cartenna, trading since the 8th century BC. The Roman cisterns built here are still in use today, 2,000 years after they were cut from stone.
descriptions.ad1ee295-b7b8-47bf-a8d6-8a14ce362d32: Concentric stone circles spanning 150 m with a tumulus at centre, built 3000–2700 BC. Seen from above, the rings look strikingly like a target.
descriptions.36408f22-774c-4626-a92f-e0c231f69206: A monumental gateway from the Wari era, built between the 5th and 10th century AD. Local folklore says the Wari people walked through it into legend.
descriptions.b3d487a0-2f8b-4eb0-b6b8-7560377ebe9f: An Inca-period settlement from around 1400 AD near central San Sebastián. It sits within what is now an urban neighbourhood in Cusco.
descriptions.2e4b8483-8599-458c-abcc-29e4e92e2ee3: Over 2,500 runestones survive across the country, most from the late Viking Age. Each was a public monument — carved to be read by passersby.
descriptions.5200dee4-0688-4447-b671-1b6fbf39fa7f: Built 1438–1530 AD. Perched at 3,750 metres on the Inca Trail, its semicircular rooms served as a royal rest stop and surveillance post. In Quechua its name means 'basket-shaped.'
descriptions.10fc71fe-5305-497e-8642-4219e822223a: A 13th-century sandstone cross shaft marking the 1-mile point on the medieval Guisborough-to-Kildale packhorse route, still standing at the crossroads of Ruthergate and Hutton Lane.
descriptions.82a98ba6-5bd5-4a0c-8170-5ac93df1a89b: An ancient road mentioned in early charters, now disused. It may have originated as a Roman route — the name might derive from a Roman personal name.
descriptions.48767303-6f43-4ddb-88e5-fb43ea3dfd89: A Roman villa with the first mosaic in Britain depicting scenes from Homer's Iliad. A 2021 geophysical survey revealed a larger complex than expected.
descriptions.99b1e4ac-3157-4120-b015-8f72d9c9fe35: A Dilmun-era temple from 2050–1800 BC designed to mark the summer solstice. The Dilmun civilization was the "garden of the gods" in Sumerian myth.
descriptions.e5079e17-27bc-4c6a-897d-68134cf661c7: A sacred pit with a 7 m corridor carved into the ground in the 11th century BC. Water from surrounding springs may have held ritual significance.
descriptions.61e8d3cd-1e93-4c78-a558-f2955a9fe221: A 15th-century Inca citadel built with dry-stone walls of boulders so massive — up to 200 tonnes — and fitted so precisely that no mortar was needed.
descriptions.5d316e03-60c3-47c0-ae67-3f432cdc9050: A Talaiotic culture site from the 2nd–1st millennium BC. These Bronze Age island people built massive stone towers called talaiots found nowhere else.
descriptions.abe8f81a-dcdb-42b8-9f99-a763c858fd7f: A cairn at Ljungarums parish near Jönköping, dated c. 1700–500 BC — originally encircled by up to 100 sandstone slabs. Four smaller graves were added at its foot some 1,500 years later.
descriptions.fa2075b9-ae78-4ce0-b00f-673d0139f0ff: Home to petroglyphs left by the Hohokam people (200–1450 AD) alongside the iconic saguaro cacti. The carvings survive in one of America's hottest deserts.
descriptions.f5131959-47d4-4052-a049-a92f51837614: In 219 BC, Carthage's siege of Saguntum — 30 km north of Valencia — triggered the Second Punic War. The hilltop still holds ruins of the ancient settlement alongside a later medieval castle.
descriptions.13ad29f2-194e-4391-a038-c4bb8c7419ec: A 1st-century AD Roman theatre at the foot of a castle-topped mountain, with the civic forum on the platform above. A vertical slice of Roman city planning.
descriptions.075337ec-9108-431f-ae90-d5d0e795f23a: Around a thousand lingas carved into rocks in and along a river, dating from 1678–1718 AD. The carvings turn the riverbed itself into a sacred space.
descriptions.29e8f8a9-119e-4cb7-8c24-c1ebd943cfe3: The largest grave mound in continental Europe, 125 m long and 50 m wide, dating to the 5th millennium BC. It took a massive communal effort to build.
descriptions.17c20887-877e-4427-8728-4c856cc8c0c3: A prehistoric gold mine active from the 4th–3rd millennium BC — among the oldest known gold mines in the world. The tunnels still survive.
descriptions.c7a242e3-1638-4260-82da-ec130f9cc023: Remains of a fort built around 300 BC, attributed to Chandragupta Maurya. The Mauryan Empire was the first to unite most of the Indian subcontinent.
descriptions.f064d736-e58e-4505-b634-b5f18052e293: Occupied since the 11th century BC on the island's east coast, Salamis hosted a Late Bronze Age harbour. Its gymnasium, theatre, and royal tombs span a thousand years of urban occupation.
descriptions.64fe03e2-33c3-4836-b012-b3e50917fcf6: One of the first farming settlements in the Cyclades, dating to 5000–4500 BC. It is the oldest known permanent habitation in this island chain.
descriptions.f10115c4-5ca9-4d69-990c-8054f9962ea3: A cluster of small catacombs from 500–1000 AD. Though modest compared to larger sites, they reveal a substantial early Christian community.
descriptions.e6f2a294-6c1d-4607-8f2c-ee6ee8614518: A circular stone tower at the south-eastern end of Loch Shin near Lairg, Sutherland — built between 800 BC and the 1st century AD. A characteristic defended farmstead of the Atlantic Iron Age.
descriptions.bf0d9250-fe2f-4f04-9dc7-28bcbfd6da20: Capital of Roman Dalmatia and last residence of the final Western Roman Emperor, Julius Nepos. For four years, it was the de facto capital of the Western Empire.
descriptions.8fc0c418-49b4-459a-abc9-9c54c09ef5ba: Greeks who named it Salauris founded this coastal port around 600 BC. A commercial hub through medieval times, the harbour — 10 km from Tarragona — now underpins a major tourist resort.
descriptions.6d530908-adfd-44bf-b0dc-d4a02d2cdefb: Flourishing 5500–3900 BC on the east bank of the Tigris, Samarra is the type site for a pottery culture that spread across the ancient Near East. UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 2007.
descriptions.16d9eae9-81b1-436e-bd93-e6aea4b4c818: A 4th-century BC fortified town on a spur above the coast, built where the mountains nearly touch the sea. It guarded a crucial coastal pass.
descriptions.e4f6fa32-6aff-4539-b40b-ab73f9e94cec: Thirty-three granite burial cairns near Rauma, dated 1500–500 BC — the most complete Bronze Age burial landscape in Fennoscandia. UNESCO listed the site in 1999.
descriptions.b1b150e6-ebca-4c21-ad56-ddccd8c9afcc: Pre-dating colonist arrival in the 7th century BC, Samothrace's sanctuary centred on the Great Mother — a chthonic deity. Its Kabeiric mysteries drew initiates from across the ancient world.
descriptions.43d64ea4-8c7e-4bca-bcfe-04b4e6e6b437: A fortified city spanning the 3rd century BC to the 18th century AD, with mostly medieval ruins stretching 2.5 km. Twenty centuries of continuous habitation.
descriptions.49835383-20b8-44e0-9bf1-9e06cf2ecbb1: An island inhabited since 7000 BC, used as a Viking-era meeting place due to its central location. Its name's etymology is completely unknown.
descriptions.da9cf7e0-8fd0-41be-9af7-8c6e8bfb9213: A Classic-period Maya city with an acropolis and two ballcourts. Ballgames in Maya culture could end with the ritual sacrifice of players.
descriptions.31490608-0d55-49b1-843b-b983ed37ae64: A Bronze Age hilltop site with stone cists and burial mounds dating from 3300–500 BC. The beacon summit was a ritual focus for millennia.
descriptions.b9a13520-b2dc-4bb8-80d7-10626ad9ef7a: Northwest of the Athenian Agora, a marble altar to Aphrodite Urania was laid around 500 BC and buried as ground levels rose. A colonnaded hall was added by the early imperial era.
descriptions.610ecf75-d2ea-4377-a26a-1f6b521bfcbc: A sanctuary of Artemis Orthia, where Spartan boys endured ritual flogging to prove endurance. The Romans later built seating to watch.
descriptions.ce101d86-8313-4fe1-bb90-9c74fba2a76e: The most important healing sanctuary in the ancient world, dedicated to Asclepius. Patients slept in sacred halls hoping for a cure in their dreams.
descriptions.9e4cc13d-57c5-484f-9a55-8770ac95019a: A 40 x 17 m open-air sanctuary from the 5th century BC on the Acropolis. Its exact purpose is debated — it may have hosted sacred animal sacrifices.
descriptions.9785a238-2527-4fdc-891a-93ebfcdfd9ce: An open-air sanctuary to Zeus the City Protector, built around 500 BC on the Acropolis. No foundations survive — its plan was worked out from cuttings in bedrock.
descriptions.0b15deb1-cfb6-4f85-ab6c-ef09ceef175f: Known as Sorviodunum in Roman times and settled before 250 BC, Sandy in Bedfordshire sat at the junction of the Ivel River and a Roman road. Extensive Iron Age and Roman remains underlie the town.
descriptions.7149fb1e-d88f-459a-88e1-c5547c8b1138: A Maya sacred site occupied from 250 AD to the Spanish conquest. It was the main pilgrimage centre on the island, dedicated to the goddess Ixchel.
descriptions.e3cf8ea1-6146-400c-a642-6f855dd88031: A Paleolithic cave with evidence of human activity spanning 48,000–10,000 BC. Stone tools found here track the evolution of toolmaking techniques.
descriptions.1196cd92-ce30-4a47-97f4-51f7a3694ebc: A Roman town mentioned by Pliny the Elder in the 1st century BC. It sits in a natural port that has sheltered ships for over two millennia.
descriptions.32124d0d-d0af-4613-a3f1-b1e5f1a14f0c: Declared a national monument in 1912, this 1st-century BC aqueduct in Mérida channelled water to Emerita Augusta. Its arches follow the valley terrain north of the city centre.
descriptions.5af64ae1-13fb-4693-a070-fa3628f8f78e: Home to a collection of Olmec colossal heads — massive basalt portraits weighing up to 50 tonnes, carved without metal tools around 1200 BC.
descriptions.c9066b1a-0da8-436f-ad87-cdec31e99366: A Roman-period agricultural villa from 300 BC with a pagan temple — the most extensive ever found on the island. A Christian church was built on top.
descriptions.658c8147-803d-4fa5-a335-bd1fe3573a28: Beneath this Naples church, excavations from 1979 revealed a 4th-century BC double curtain wall. The building was bombed in 1943 and left as a ruin until recent restoration reopened it.
descriptions.b5269a8f-b1fd-448a-a0ef-72142e188006: A Maya site near Corozal identified with ancient Chetumal, occupied 2000 BC–6th century AD. Its sole standing structure holds a ceremonial chamber connected by passages to two burial rooms.
descriptions.bf6ada10-e9c6-49f0-b911-52e277f4368b: A major Maya Chenes-region town that peaked in the Late Classic era. Its largest structure, "Hill Stars," has at least ten interconnected buildings.
descriptions.f8ccb519-328b-4b91-8c67-3416ee2aa788: A Neolithic temple site in Xaghra, Gozo, occupied from around 5000 BC. Though heavily damaged, it was among the archipelago's major megalithic temples — named for a later chapel to Saint Venera.
descriptions.f1dc14c0-5f0b-4bf1-a7ee-cecfb00514a5: A cave spanning the Middle Paleolithic to the Iron Age, best known for Magdalenian bison paintings. It holds one of the longest habitation sequences in the region.
descriptions.25432451-b8e5-4f62-956e-bcc3859d54d5: A 6th-century BC Greek settlement that served as the county seat for centuries. It was eventually abandoned for a location less exposed to pirate attacks.
descriptions.788f9236-c12f-4f94-9dc6-4f3a3d682626: A 2nd-century AD Roman sanctuary with cavities of various sizes carved into three large cliffs. Steps cut into the rock lead to ritual platforms.
descriptions.68859b06-2135-4711-a160-da003d18ccca: Two Beinan culture standing stones, 5.75 m and 3.99 m tall, raised 2,000-3,000 years ago within an oval site 600 m long. Their purpose remains unknown.
descriptions.4770146e-aaa9-49ca-a35e-76ec91b5ea94: The necropolis for ancient Memphis, with burials spanning 3150 BC to the 15th century AD. It contains the Step Pyramid and dozens of other monuments.
descriptions.4d0928dd-8050-4e45-a9d2-f9a8331fa425: Rock paintings from 4400 BC on a cliff rising from a lake. The site sits on an important water route and was painted by Stone Age hunter-gatherers.
descriptions.16bdc3b7-0e3b-4c6f-9313-6988d76fa673: A 5,505 m volcano formed during four stages of Pleistocene volcanic activity. Ancient peoples lived in the shadow of a mountain that could erupt again.
descriptions.ff3dcd2e-6e3b-405b-a532-09b7cf71dff0: Eight Chachapoya mummy bundles in human-shaped clay sarcophagi, 2 m tall, perched on a cliff ledge. No one knows how they got them up there.
descriptions.a0736505-9ca5-4361-bc0a-f0a47b6fed7e: A Roman fish farm from 146 BC with a connecting aqueduct carved into coastal rock. Romans engineered saltwater ponds to breed fish on an industrial scale.
descriptions.9e37c354-9a78-4372-90cf-6fae13200286: A 5th-century BC Cappadocian city with a theatre, Roman doorway, and milestones still in their original roadside positions. Traces of a Severan road survive.
descriptions.3b61e6c5-a06b-4239-bbd9-23edc83e2497: A Scordisci tribal settlement from the late La Tène period, 1st century BC. The Scordisci were Celtic warriors who fought Rome for decades.
descriptions.b0b461de-f74e-47b9-8b91-32c35b7c89c6: Cave dwellings inhabited since 7000 BC — among the oldest continuously lived-in settlements on Earth. People lived in these caves until the 1950s.
descriptions.c8b957fb-37fa-46eb-84fd-39e572072d05: A satellite pyramid beside the Bent Pyramid, originally 26 m tall. It may have housed the pharaoh's ka — his spiritual life force.
descriptions.31860bc4-476a-49bc-9f97-e25220063d19: A Paleolithic cave first occupied around 23,500 BC. In the Middle Ages it was reused — ancient humans and medieval people sheltered in the same cavern.
descriptions.efa38e30-8e64-431b-8f87-2b55d8d05968: An Inca waystation between Runkuraqay pass and Phuyupatamarka on the trail to Machu Picchu. Its name means "inaccessible town" in Quechua.
descriptions.6228ca17-0d5a-4142-85df-4474a8eb6943: An Inca religious centre focused on water worship. Its carved "Sayhuite Stone" is a boulder mapped with over 200 figures of animals and waterways.
descriptions.257ce429-7d0c-4444-8ed5-57d129c25d50: A circular rampart fortification from 1200–450 BC on a wooded hilltop at the Hesse-Bavaria border. Such ring forts controlled strategic forest passes.
descriptions.b8117d4b-647c-4efd-815f-e0a427adf357: A wooded hilltop in the Spessart forest with ancient earthworks. Its peak at 343 m was a natural vantage point over the surrounding forest.
descriptions.3db38675-ded2-42a9-968f-b22744e5faff: Within Scholes Wood near Kimberworth, South Yorkshire, a hillfort known as Caesar's Camp preserves an outer rampart and inner enclosure. Partial excavation in the 1990s confirmed its Iron Age date.
descriptions.111a0de2-2005-43a9-947f-c5d1bddda27d: Wooden hunting spears from 300,000 BC — the oldest hunting weapons ever found. They prove early humans were skilled predators, not just scavengers.
descriptions.4fbef8ee-1d95-429f-ae1d-bf525dab7ab1: A Roman open-air museum on a 1st-century BC settlement destroyed in the 3rd century AD. Excavations revealed streets, houses, and taverns.
descriptions.c5f8bd3a-c334-453c-b99b-9509aac6ea90: A cave with over 13,000 Mousterian stone tools and a fossilised Neanderthal child's jaw from 127,000 BC. One of the richest Neanderthal sites in Europe.
descriptions.768114a3-1ebc-476b-8dcb-5883278071bf: One of Dartmoor's biggest and most intact stone circles, dating from 3300–500 BC. Its remote moorland setting has protected it from disturbance.
descriptions.57196b23-2217-4d5e-ae1b-9b2080956e5b: Covering 15 hectares on Scratchbury Hill, Wiltshire, this univallate hillfort dates to around 100 BC. It encloses an earlier Bronze Age enclosure whose earthworks remain visible within the perimeter.
descriptions.333b1b12-dfb2-4ee3-a3c0-4af360dd498f: A Roman military camp from the 2nd century BC that grew into a major city. It lies beneath modern Skopje — the capital sits on Roman foundations.
descriptions.79484b17-4db6-454c-aacb-a3cb5eafaec9: Known as Cwichelm's Barrow, this Iron Age round barrow on the Oxfordshire Ridgeway marks where King Edwin killed Cwichelm of Wessex in 636 AD. It later served as the shire moot meeting point.
descriptions.806f831d-3aa7-40be-a792-8e9ad6287b20: Greek-founded city, Roman colony from 124 BC. Its park contains a theatre and the only Roman amphitheatre in Calabria. Tradition held it was built by followers of Odysseus after the Trojan War.
descriptions.2607b059-3e7c-4eb3-97b2-737e1517c526: Capital of the late Scythians from the 3rd century BC, an Iranic people who controlled Crimea. Their culture blended steppe nomadism with Greek urban life.
descriptions.951c140b-1698-4495-9c6b-c78254c2b4cd: A timber circle from 2049 BC with an upturned oak tree root at its centre. The upside-down tree may symbolise a world turned on its head — death itself.
descriptions.1e46077d-d963-46f5-aa22-dbff17bb7b9b: A Roman-period village on the River Derwent, occupied in the 1st–2nd century AD. It sat near the route that would later become a major medieval road.
descriptions.ad11d27d-d6ad-4384-bf32-ef4e74e0fee2: Dated to 3500 BC — roughly contemporary with the earliest Mesopotamian cities — Sechin Bajo in the Sechin River valley is among the oldest civilisation centres in the Western Hemisphere.
descriptions.cf6f7651-a72a-40c5-b423-459a2225f3d1: In 2009, construction beneath Zürich's main square uncovered 2nd-millennium BC pile dwellings. The square — site of the annual Sechseläuten festival — overlies this prehistoric lake-edge settlement.
descriptions.a55ddaef-8835-4749-ab18-978c295cf1b5: Built in the late 1st century BC on Pefkakia hill in Larissa, this theatre replaced the city's original venue — converted to a gladiatorial arena after Rome's conquest of the region.
descriptions.594fb89c-b8fc-4990-9818-35a82c9ffbfa: Built around 460–450 BC in the Doric order at Paestum, this temple has six columns on its short sides and fourteen on its long sides. Its interior colonnade survives intact on both levels.
descriptions.e50caf34-c829-4f2c-b87c-3311958ef369: A Celtiberian town whose expansion in 153 BC triggered the Roman Senate to move the consular year from March to January — changing the calendar forever.
descriptions.efa6ff4f-1d6a-4121-b1c0-f3d21a6c4ce6: Built 122 AD at the eastern terminus of Hadrian's Wall. Garrisoned for 300 years by a mixed unit of 480 infantry and 120 cavalry. Its lost bathhouse was rediscovered in 2014, buried 3 m beneath.
descriptions.d83c15cf-679a-4e80-b138-344df541e860: A 6th-century BC city of the Elymians, one of three indigenous peoples of Sicily. Its unfinished Doric temple stands roofless but otherwise remarkably intact.
descriptions.51ec5b10-cd97-4fc2-a827-fc265910d873: A Celtic and Roman city on a hilltop, active from the 2nd century BC. It sat atop massive lapis specularis mines — "window glass" for the Roman world.
descriptions.c40df04b-563c-45b1-80db-82e646445531: Crowning the Berkshire Downs above Wantage with four gateways, this hillfort was occupied 6th–2nd century BC. A 1871 excavation on the south side found a cist grave floored with stone slabs.
descriptions.28b1639a-d35e-4fef-bfac-78dbb00a1d69: A Roman bridge connecting two modern countries, built over the Erges river in the 1st century AD. Only two of its five arches are original Roman stonework.
descriptions.1d78a562-f1e1-4115-8172-9ef13c7dfe1b: Dated to 800 BC near Asmara, Sembel is the earliest known archaeological site in East Africa. Excavations in the Maekel Region have yielded remains spanning its long pre-urban occupation.
descriptions.1eb455d8-2117-4094-8c4d-76707b3a4890: Over 1,000 megalithic stone circles across 30,000 sq km, built from the 3rd century BC to the 16th century AD. The largest concentration of stone circles on Earth.
descriptions.03d28afb-c252-423e-9b4f-2815cfaed6c5: A Ptolemaic temple to Serapis from the 3rd century BC. Pompey's Pillar nearby is the tallest ancient monolith outside of obelisks.
descriptions.50d4292b-caee-4819-8aaa-64b94187fce8: The burial place of at least 60 sacred Apis bulls over 1,400 years. Each bull was mummified and placed in a massive stone sarcophagus weighing up to 70 tonnes.
descriptions.1e7ec452-34c4-4630-ac4e-e53d0dcbd184: A Kushan-period town paired with Takht-i-Bahi monastery 5 km away — together a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980. Its stone fortified wall crowns a mound rising 9 m above the plain.
descriptions.7ee8535b-b034-498c-9311-466662e75e58: Ancient earthworks stretching across hundreds of kilometres through the Dnieper region. They parallel the Danube's Trajan's Wall in both mystery and scale.
descriptions.a694497b-30ab-4283-be76-d1570d7c90ad: The type site for the Sesklo culture — Neolithic mainland Europe's earliest, c. 7000 BC — this settlement near Volos predates the Bronze Age by millennia. Its name defines a ceramic tradition.
descriptions.a7ea17b2-3760-4724-9672-38bc0687da0c: A Talayotic settlement at Artà, Majorca, centred on a talaiot built c. 900–800 BC. Largely overgrown with holm oak, its triclinium hall used for communal gatherings survives largely intact.
descriptions.20a18387-7871-456c-967a-c94abd69e3e0: An ancient Thracian capital founded 325–315 BC, now entirely submerged beneath a reservoir. It can only be studied when water levels drop.
descriptions.22f53fa2-6170-4d7b-ac52-5904861bb47c: Over 40 barrows clustered at Upper Lambourn, Berkshire, the earliest dating to c. 2200 BC. The 4-hectare site is also a biological SSSI — its chalk grassland supports more than 100 herb species.
descriptions.db35f2ee-809e-45ab-997b-50a3b0135c44: Founded as the Roman city of Hispalis. Under Islamic rule as Isbiliya, it became a capital of Al-Andalus and one of Europe's greatest medieval cities.
descriptions.73cd4580-09d7-4bd4-9ec1-58c1fd18ef67: A Phoenician colony near modern Almuñécar, active from at least the 3rd century BC. Its mint issued coins depicting Melqart — evidence of sustained Punic cultural identity even under Roman rule.
descriptions.94fc8fb4-4792-418c-bee0-65c3ec4b8a71: A stone-and-earth rampart 7 m wide curves southeast from Salters Nick at Shaftoe Crags, enclosing an irregular area supplemented by natural crags. The site spans Iron Age and Romano-period use.
descriptions.ef73ab96-3f35-4e88-8586-2740f5cdae65: A village with rock inscriptions of Ashoka's edicts from the 3rd century BC — rare surviving examples of written text, and the northwesternmost edicts recorded in the subcontinent.
descriptions.b24418d7-adfc-4d2a-89a3-f57ef83bd2c1: Founded 631 BC, Cyrene (modern Shahhat) held a Temple of Zeus larger than the Parthenon, plus temples to Apollo, a Greek agora, and baths. It anchored the Pentapolis for over a millennium.
descriptions.2ed572b3-bf48-4f8d-a638-387b6484c962: About 6 km from Peshawar, the Kanishka stupa was raised in the 2nd century AD and yielded the Kanishka casket — a reliquary inscribed with the emperor's name, now in Peshawar Museum.
descriptions.9f823459-f4ce-43cc-a433-b1cdaf9f89ad: Built c.1729–1737 AD at 1,133 m elevation by a prince of the Al-Baqum tribe. Guarded the northwestern tribal border of Turubah valley in the Makkah Region, now a dramatic ruin on a rocky slope.
descriptions.9190f012-5a73-4f94-9f39-9c870a7bdf4c: A 3.2 km megalithic avenue of stones linking stone circles and burial mounds, built 3000–2000 BC. One of only three such complexes in the region.
descriptions.b9f26550-7988-4a34-a3ff-7ef9cb69c838: A Mughal-era fort from 1607 AD. The Tuzk-e-Jahangiri records that Emperor Jahangir ordered its construction during a hunting trip.
descriptions.565483ad-e6c8-4053-9d06-dfd254daa246: A Jeulmun pottery-period shell midden on Yeong-do Island in Busan — among the oldest such deposits in the region. Three excavations from 1969 recovered mollusc shells, fish bones, and pottery.
descriptions.ef1ee8c0-f6bd-4886-bd66-8a6106ac5ca4: An Early Bronze Age settlement occupied from 3000 to 2200 BC. It belonged to the Kura-Araxes culture, which spread from the Caucasus to the Levant.
descriptions.945eea72-1e1d-4156-bd45-d68c250b959b: A Buddhist stupa from the 3rd–4th century AD with 13 narrative panels depicting the life of Buddha. The village name derives from "Shiva."
descriptions.c5d612d7-5604-4de3-b797-7cbcbdafdde7: Opened in 1998 in Bali District, New Taipei, this museum conserves finds from the adjacent 3rd-century AD iron-smelting site. Its "Bridge of Time" walkway spans the original excavation trench.
descriptions.126756cf-1651-49dd-8075-11e19248b37f: Early Saka kurgans from the 8th–6th century BC in a river basin. Carbon-14 dating pushed the timeline of Saka culture earlier than expected.
descriptions.1eaf26d7-d381-4796-ad1c-605833ec077a: A Late Bronze Age platform settlement from 2500–800 BC, found during lake clearance work in 1995. It had been hiding underwater for 3,000 years.
descriptions.b306aff1-60d0-4d34-85e3-fe206911dc65: An Iron Age defended settlement — a rare monument type found only in the uplands. Such sites sheltered small communities in troubled times.
descriptions.38e9688f-57a8-4e96-b465-d685bccdfb3f: A Byzantine farming colony in the middle of the desert, also a pilgrimage way station. The colonists somehow grew crops where nothing should grow.
descriptions.84e3e5e3-f92c-4222-b6ca-0123c0945812: Perched at 472 m on Shoulsbarrow Common near Challacombe, Devon, this unusually rectangular hillfort has multiple ditches and ramparts. Its hill spur shape suggests dual defensive and signalling use.
descriptions.1032047c-3a0c-413b-bd70-23b81f64487e: Dartmoor megaliths including stone rows, a fourfold stone circle, and standing stones from 3300–500 BC. Four concentric circles in one site is exceptionally rare.
descriptions.18ab996a-0aea-4f62-bd8d-3461adda0c88: A Neolithic cairn from the 4th–3rd millennium BC atop a prominent tor on Bodmin Moor. The rocky outcrop served as a landmark visible for miles.
descriptions.f9534330-fcf4-4a34-a8ca-6b63fce8362b: An Italic sanctuary of Hercules Curinus from 89 BC. The epithet "Curinus" was a local Italic name that connected Hercules to an older, indigenous god.
descriptions.76220eb6-d405-4d79-a0a7-d36c4809094f: An Early Neolithic long barrow from the 4th millennium BC, built of earth. Unchambered barrows like this held the dead but had no accessible burial room.
descriptions.d88cdea2-b3af-4627-884a-b15d9a9a74f1: A 2nd-century AD fort built according to Punjabi folklore by Raja Sálbán. It was later rebuilt by multiple conquerors across a thousand years.
descriptions.10f42fef-61bd-46a1-b2e7-f35e0c84f9b4: Replacing a tholos and a monopteros at Delphi's sanctuary of Apollo, this treasury was built by Sicyon after Cleisthenes won the First Sacred War in the early 6th century BC.
descriptions.598a622b-0034-4e9b-92ed-9f82a44bc5c7: At roughly 185 m above sea level near Sidbury, Devon, this hillfort overlooks both the town and the River Sid. Its substantial earthworks enclosed a hilltop settlement during the Iron Age.
descriptions.e95ae624-060a-40ef-a821-0983a25b68bb: Sub-triangular and 6.9 hectares in area, this bivallate hillfort on the eastern edge of Salisbury Plain was raised over a Neolithic settlement. Double ditches reinforce natural defensive slopes.
descriptions.a4ac2a6f-0159-447e-a6d2-7300fbc986ef: A limestone cave housing Neanderthal fossils from around 47,000 BC. The remains of over a dozen individuals include evidence of cannibalism.
descriptions.415f4848-7b6c-4da9-9713-684fcb67c6a7: A group of five dolmens from 3500–2800 BC on the Lüneburg Heath, built by the Funnelbeaker culture. They are among northern Europe's oldest stone tombs.
descriptions.dbbef6f8-f2bb-4ea3-9691-90c09205f678: Paleolithic rock carvings from around 18,000 BC, part of the UNESCO-listed Côa Valley art network. The images include horses, aurochs, and ibex.
descriptions.051aa298-6b64-49ef-af78-efb53fa1d3a1: Capital of the Masaesyli under King Syphax (c. 215 BC). A Numidian royal mausoleum still rises above the Tafna valley. Later became a Roman border port between two Mauretanian provinces.
descriptions.1ec1e384-fe4a-4cf5-bffd-f342e5daa228: A 200 m rock column with 1,200 steps to the summit and 22 surrounding caves. The fortress dates to the 5th century AD reign of King Kasyapa.
descriptions.ebadc068-2bac-468f-9b3c-df5c12bf446f: An area rich in archaeology from the Early Bronze Age through the Iron Age, overlooking Cadbury Castle. Multiple eras of activity layer the landscape.
descriptions.33ac2b60-4a42-4331-9c91-93388429ada0: A 3rd–4th century AD Kushan Buddhist stupa with 13 narrative panels of Buddha's life. Modern restoration arranged the panels in their original sequence.
descriptions.21d63980-32dc-43cc-baa1-06c9e2f15335: Europe's tallest prehistoric man-made mound at 39 m, built around 2400 BC from chalk. It took 18 million man-hours to construct and no one knows why.
descriptions.8126681d-e2a2-49f2-ab9a-4695c751ce23: A pre-Inca cemetery with above-ground chullpa towers that housed entire families. Grave robbers dynamited many, but the remaining towers still stand.
descriptions.5f3e3b85-6a44-4dfa-a2e3-998d779037b8: Ruins spanning Hellenistic through Seljuk eras, including a stadium, amphitheatre, and temple. Multiple civilizations built on the same hilltop.
descriptions.d0b8b206-14b2-4b9d-856a-ee978836c7a8: A 4th-century AD Roman gate into what was Diocletian's Palace, now the old town of Split. You can still walk through this 1,700-year-old entrance.
descriptions.801f9478-d27d-4c58-919b-2e14a07ca1a4: A cave inhabited for tens of thousands of years by Neanderthals and later humans. It contains over a dozen Neanderthal fossils and Paleolithic rock art.
descriptions.fbe0c4cf-1863-4930-9bca-1557de689b67: A cave in a limestone massif with a 372 m route and an entrance at 885 m elevation. It preserves evidence of prehistoric use deep within.
descriptions.fdafef27-24a2-4939-b2b0-7f3852676e82: A 3rd-century BC Celtic city that later became Roman Singidunum — the foundation beneath modern Belgrade. The Scordisci tribe named it.
descriptions.9624278c-1080-4a2a-ae2e-11829bda299a: Erected on the Sacred Way at Delphi in the early 6th century BC to display Siphnos's silver wealth, this treasury bore a continuous Ionic frieze — a landmark of archaic sculptural decoration.
descriptions.7cfc73a7-180b-4378-a14a-785e9cab28a4: An ancient port town from the 3rd century BC abandoned after earthquakes in the 13th century. Legend says it was founded by the Greek hero Diomedes.
descriptions.7ee6d3f9-e9cc-43d1-8747-17d15e31ba16: An ancient city built on the Hippodamian grid plan around 180 BC by a Greco-Bactrian king. Greek urban planning transplanted to the edge of South Asia.
descriptions.f0e4bbe8-a16f-46af-a1fe-0ba46a127c89: A massive settlement mound measuring 400 x 300 m and 30 m high, occupied from the 5th millennium BC. It spans over 5,000 years of continuous habitation.
descriptions.cc38f616-81ad-4cfc-9732-c57b0302cb20: Named a tetrarchic capital in 293 AD alongside Trier and Nicomedia. Beneath modern Sremska Mitrovica lie a 450 m hippodrome, imperial palace, mint, and baths — 17 emperors ruled from here.
descriptions.cac857fa-bbb6-4364-a0f3-64bb9b9a7e4b: The last of Taxila's great ancient cities, founded around 80 AD during the Kushan era. Each successive ruler abandoned the old city and built a new one.
descriptions.4f739f05-0a2b-4e7a-93e8-36ad775f4b20: An ancient well named after the Canaanite commander Sisera from the Book of Judges. It sits near the 2,000-year-old castle of Zaabal.
descriptions.3666230f-bc1f-4871-887f-db49556f9e3f: A cave associated with Sita from the Ramayana, dating to around 250 AD. It is a living pilgrimage site where mythology and archaeology overlap.
descriptions.37321e41-a629-4d79-820d-3104c7713860: Augustus settled military veterans at Tubusuctu — modern El Kseur — after 30 BC, founding a colony in Mauretania Caesariensis known for olive oil. Well-preserved Roman bath ruins remain on the site.
descriptions.a7e88abd-9d65-4a68-bec6-d9d527f3c172: An ancient city spanning the 4th to 14th century AD, bridging Dvaravati and Khmer cultural periods. It shows how Southeast Asian civilizations overlapped.
descriptions.becd7970-8a7a-4a21-9832-889d66c4e5fc: The ceremonial heart of the Chavín culture (1500–300 BC), built as a truncated pyramid with a maze of interior stone passages and hidden galleries.
descriptions.fd7f614f-4547-4b2d-9534-a0b7f61d20eb: Capital of the Kaqchikel Maya from 1470 to 1524, with pyramid-temples and palace complexes. It was abandoned after the Spanish arrived.
descriptions.87033d8b-bb1e-48c4-a743-7dde02b2db33: A Maya site in northern Petén active c. 900 BC–1200 AD, La Blanca features a large acropolis in the Mopan River valley. Its Middle Preclassic core predates most regional ceremonial centres.
descriptions.79287e36-88cb-434f-8fa3-a259f235a089: Occupied 1000 BC–250 AD by Proto-Lencan ancestors, Yarumela holds more than 60 structures in the Comayagua Valley. Only 9 are surface-visible; the rest await excavation beneath the overburden.
descriptions.658a18d9-ae09-4a8b-b16e-abeb92fa91bc: A Coclé chiefdom necropolis used 450–900 AD. Burial 11 alone held 23 individuals and over 7,500 grave goods — gold plaques, emerald pendants, and 228 dogs buried across the site.
descriptions.cca3b72c-8ad4-481b-838f-64bc69cf11a0: The largest surviving group of Roman barrows in Britain, from the 1st–2nd century AD. Six burial mounds line the old Great North Road.
descriptions.2cbc1c11-5750-4b96-973b-7f1f8c847003: A Neolithic stone village from around 3100 BC with ten houses featuring built-in stone furniture — beds, shelves, and dressers still in place.
descriptions.8f32afcc-457a-4143-8862-ebc774736fb3: Mid-3rd-millennium BC Cycladic settlement on Ios, excavated 1984–1997. Stone buildings survive in exceptional condition, revealing dense multi-room architecture rare for the Aegean Bronze Age.
descriptions.cb1b00bc-0495-43d9-8a69-c54aa3fb93b4: Rydno on the Kamienna River is the world's largest concentration of late Paleolithic campsites — hundreds of sites where reindeer hunters mined hematite for red ochre ritual dye from 13,000 BC.
descriptions.701203f2-92b6-4631-ab3e-aab9a5a796be: A 15th-century BC Bronze Age burial mound near the Kongeå River. It is part of a chain of 26 mounds along the river — a landscape of the dead.
descriptions.45b4e76d-0430-4abe-acfd-af61e2938421: A Late Minoan settlement from the 2nd millennium BC. The villa-style buildings suggest a prosperous community connected to Minoan palace culture.
descriptions.d570a6d4-f4a9-4a82-856f-e66c4b55d056: The only aqueduct in the entire country, one of the three largest and best-preserved in the wider region. Its exact construction date remains debated.
descriptions.2e648c8e-56af-4349-8064-6372c29b3d25: Megalithic temples from 3600 BC with torba cement floors and libation holes. These are among the oldest freestanding stone structures on Earth—older than the pyramids.
descriptions.22221e3a-aa5d-4dc4-83e8-fc1b12f67b1e: A cave 160 m deep and 36 m wide used as a Minoan cult site from the 4th millennium BC. Figurines found inside suggest rituals spanning over 3,000 years.
descriptions.d3887b75-e839-48a9-ac9c-d24684bd0d91: A Kashubian settlement with roots in the 5th century BC. An Iron Age cemetery here confirms continuous habitation through to the medieval period.
descriptions.dee36d33-1911-4cc8-9aa7-c7ad207298d1: Perched at 65 m on a promontory east of a hilltop, this Iron Age fort used the sheer terrain as its primary defence above Slapton Ley.
descriptions.cc7e7e8a-ad91-4001-9849-bfcd41168369: A defended Iron Age settlement first built between the 7th and 5th centuries BC. Enclosures like these housed several round timber buildings inside.
descriptions.2d12562b-e482-4a6b-8329-5d7a22667a86: Concave grooves in a Scanian sandstone outcrop, traditionally read as axe-sharpening marks. Modern surveys show the motion was rotary or pendulum-based, not linear.
descriptions.5a5beef1-9bd1-472e-b77d-eefe6092cb06: Roughly rectangular hillfort near Brecon, measuring 187 by 242 m with a single encircling rampart. Hedges and trees now obscure its form almost entirely.
descriptions.e55a8540-286d-4182-8370-3ffc69280f6d: A temple to the sun-disc Aten built in 1346 BC at Akhenaten's new capital. It was dismantled so thoroughly that only tomb paintings record how it looked.
descriptions.841f862f-a312-4794-a490-aefbeadd2994: A Bronze Age hilltop fort with multiple concentric ramparts enclosing 2.4 hectares. Flint finds show people lived here as far back as the Mesolithic.
descriptions.f9ccac76-d1c7-46c4-9c70-4748ce838527: A Roman-era agora from the 4th century BC. Agoras were the hearts of ancient cities—marketplace, courthouse, and public square in one.
descriptions.32f8606a-075b-4e6c-afae-427a49ef9df4: A 4th-millennium BC chambered tomb built from local sarsen megaliths. It was dismantled when found in 1822 and the human remains inside were scattered.
descriptions.b777562e-098d-4091-988f-79fe2b58db6c: A Neolithic stone circle from around 4300 BC, hidden under dense heather for decades. A robber trench of unknown date cuts through its center.
descriptions.b427d092-8349-4f90-b2e9-6fb6036fb3e2: Known as Serdica in antiquity, this city sits on hot springs that have drawn settlers for 7,000 years. Neolithic dwellings from the 6th millennium BC survive here.
descriptions.34898f1b-9aa7-42e2-8847-4f78639c6e67: A 4.5-hectare mound 13 m high near Nal, occupied 3800–2300 BC. Its layered Togau, Kili Ghul Mohammad, and Kechi Beg pottery connects pre-Indus traditions to the Amri-Nal culture.
descriptions.81a32f2d-5102-47f9-adf3-4f5f8fb54561: Harappan outpost on the Makran coast, occupied 2600–1900 BC, about 24 km north of Pasni. Its coastal position aligns with evidence for Bronze Age overseas maritime commerce.
descriptions.f69cf72f-d7b2-48d8-996d-82e19c289eee: A Greek city whose entire urban plan was reportedly designed by Solon during a ten-year journey. It thrived from the 3rd century BC to the 4th century AD.
descriptions.235d48e6-9c13-4de6-a0d1-96bde161338d: Built on ancient Salona, capital of Roman Dalmatia and birthplace of Emperor Diocletian. When Avars destroyed it, refugees moved into his nearby palace.
descriptions.e8bb0905-e8ca-441d-a35b-041af4645ffb: Bronze Age cairns and around 400 runestones scattered across this parish. The runestones are among the densest concentrations in all of Scandinavia.
descriptions.4541e162-c69b-49d8-a4db-04e66089e8fd: A fortified town from 4700–4200 BC whose walls protected a salt production facility. Salt was so valuable in antiquity it was worth fortifying a city for.
descriptions.76924f6f-c141-4d1b-8b29-80ca09fa2c9d: A 19 m tall Scythian burial mound from the 4th century BC. The intact side tomb held a royal burial with gold weapons and a gold comb depicting a battle.
descriptions.69e786d2-00e3-4872-af8f-031fa6201248: Flat-topped hill rising 191 m above the Avon, defended 300–100 BC and showing evidence of burning from a violent attack. It is among the proposed locations of the Battle of Badon.
descriptions.861136bb-c3b6-4cf6-8e0c-ff756d744c12: Octagonal-chambered Neolithic tomb on Møn, dated to 3400 BC. Its capstone boulder holds over 180 bowl-shaped carvings added roughly 1,000 years later during the Bronze Age.
descriptions.b66e9572-4469-4d1a-b13f-b927af5d79db: Buried by Vesuvius in 472 AD—not the famous 79 AD blast. This later eruption preserved a different era of Roman life under a shallower layer of ash.
descriptions.c18ed010-6938-4961-83ff-0e9e6ec640c7: A 13th-century ceremonial site built by the Chanka people. Some call Chanka culture a step backward from the Wari, but others argue they had massive populations.
descriptions.c57686bf-acf3-42c3-afce-fb93f65b1547: Near a 2nd-millennium BC park with Talaiotic watchtowers—stone towers unique to the Balearic Islands and found nowhere else on Earth.
descriptions.885f5a1c-3453-4017-98a5-7e0d2b0151e7: Founded 147 AD by Antoninus Pius — an inscription confirms it. The fort's walls rose 11 metres; watchtowers reached 16. A 500 sq m luxury mansio beside the Via Traiana served passing travellers.
descriptions.9b42d08a-5048-42bb-8527-8e26a4f6bbe2: Late La Tène Scordisci site beside the Danube, southeast of Vukovar, with a settlement and necropolis. Rescue excavations in the 1970s–80s traced the tribe's deep reach into eastern Slavonia.
descriptions.5e384859-dede-47ed-8d4e-0509d425234e: Augustan-era Ionic octostyle temple in the Agora's southeast corner, assembled from architectural fragments stripped from the Temple of Athena at Sounion in Attica.
descriptions.9bec7da2-8ff6-46be-a2cf-34d689358bf2: A two-aisled stoa from 425 BC with 15 rooms, each with an off-center door and a couch. It may have housed officials who dined at public expense.
descriptions.b0f8cf11-8472-422b-9e00-cf45b1d80683: A circular Iron Age fort covering 2.8 hectares, linked to the Catuvellauni and Trinovantes tribes. Its rampart and steep bank survive today.
descriptions.ae79d7fc-8820-4ca0-baf1-b162e08ecc86: Doric tetrastyle temple in the Agora's southwest, built under Augustus from spoliated Hellenistic blocks and material from a 5th-century BC stoa at Thorikos.
descriptions.27190db9-7e95-4f0e-a757-a897fcf7c390: Settled in the Bronze Age and formalised as the colony Apollonia in the 7th century BC, this Black Sea port had an ancient harbour whose ruins and amphorae lie visible on the seabed.
descriptions.3dde8dfa-0538-4c2e-9236-1dcb5e24693a: Built in phases from the 2nd to 5th century AD. A fresco portrait of a woman — possibly the mistress of the house — survives. One reconstructed wing still stands at Butser Ancient Farm.
descriptions.0b2d26e4-2441-4333-900d-fc4119c03166: A Late Bronze Age necropolis on Mount Olympus with tombs from the 14th to 12th century BC. Burial offerings in Mycenaean style were found far from Mycenae.
descriptions.5bdfb4fe-496d-4c3a-9032-d5677201fca8: Ruined quoit in West Penwith, dated variously to the Late or Post-Neolithic and as far back as 5000 BC. Two uprights and a displaced capstone survive on a moor near Zennor.
descriptions.a25c9c7d-58f2-402a-a484-ac9ec953979f: A Buddhist stupa in the Khyber Pass with a dome on a three-tiered stone base. Large sections have fallen away, exposing the raw construction underneath.
descriptions.b01e5465-5f19-408e-8a56-4d04f6575537: Three granite uprights carry a 4.5 by 3.1 m capstone on Shilstone Farm near Drewsteignton. The structure collapsed in 1862 and was rebuilt the same year.
descriptions.67bb2bbe-a409-498b-acae-b1fa0e389cf4: A Roman courtyard villa with a mosaic still viewable under a corrugated roof. Finds include Samian Ware pottery and hundreds of Roman coins.
descriptions.e3e42f8a-9a6e-438b-bd2f-69b883334600: A Paleolithic cave ranked among the most significant in Europe. Two Neanderthal skeletons—Spy I and Spy II—found here were among the first ever identified.
descriptions.d7a107f8-b228-48a7-97c5-081dc67c0469: Begun around 300 BC and abandoned unfinished by 275 BC, this large peristyle served briefly as Athens' law courts before being demolished for material reused in South Stoa II.
descriptions.0e7825f5-26f0-483e-8cd0-687a9228a894: Buried under up to 5 m of tephra in the 79 AD eruption of Vesuvius, Stabiae held luxury resort villas 4.5 km southwest of Pompeii. Excavation of the villa frescoes continues today.
descriptions.b33b1575-195d-4c86-b927-cd5804b41528: The oldest and largest of Pompeii's five public baths, built in 125 BC. A sundial with an Oscan inscription names the magistrate who ordered its construction.
descriptions.1bc57ad9-041a-42de-b0a1-c361a7beb531: Athletes competed in foot races just metres from the Temple of Zeus. A rectangular starting block—the ancient equivalent of a starting line—was found on site.
descriptions.403e3c53-6a70-49cc-81b8-2014542e53d3: The Olympic stadium: a 212 m clay track where the fastest person in the ancient world was crowned. It held 45,000 spectators—and had no seats.
descriptions.8b1bec65-9c91-4ba1-a8c9-ccde8579e04c: The best-preserved ancient stadium in the Hellenic world, built in the 4th century BC at Delphi's highest point. Stone seating for 6,500 was added later by the Romans.
descriptions.8747ac16-0730-4bdc-8afa-49c3d8d6819b: Remains of a probable Iron Age broch from around 800 BC. Brochs are hollow-walled stone towers—engineering feats built without mortar.
descriptions.9957740f-918a-4c11-b3f4-abc1bfc988dd: A long Bronze Age stone row near a stone circle on Stall Moor. Stone rows can stretch for kilometres, yet their purpose remains unknown.
descriptions.861015a5-d704-4231-a835-069e4ee5b4a4: A Roman military road built around 80 AD linking forts across the north. It predated Hadrian's Wall by 40 years and formed the empire's original frontier.
descriptions.4d70c735-5eb1-4907-a2a3-9c25871a951b: A 91 km road linking Londinium to Chichester, in use by 70 AD. Construction may date to within the first decade of the Roman occupation, as early as 43–53 AD.
descriptions.cbea941d-7c4d-44b4-9b0a-ea20827e7cbb: A 63 km Roman road from Braughing to Colchester. Roman roads formed a network so well-built that many still define modern road routes today.
descriptions.0a5920b9-0a15-48f6-bd19-cc8bdd75f26c: 47 upright stones, 30 recumbent, and 4 outliers in an oval 43 by 40 m on Bodmin Moor. Cornish circles use local granite and typically count far more stones than inland examples.
descriptions.0dd83b62-fce8-4143-9d25-ed7de89933d8: Hillfort from 1200 BC on an isolated Oolitic Limestone outcrop near Marksbury. Iron sickle blades and the tip of a prehistoric ard found here now reside in the collection of a national museum.
descriptions.0c259791-b095-4347-8e59-2172d8791617: The Great Circle here is 113 m across—the second largest stone circle in Britain after Avebury. Geophysics revealed a massive timber building beneath it.
descriptions.d34a4c75-f3e7-42e8-accb-1e2329dc27fa: Over 9 km of ditches and ramparts enclosing 300 hectares, built in the early Roman era. Venutius or Cartimandua — or both before their split after 51 AD — held this North Yorkshire stronghold.
descriptions.805a50cd-f05e-4f4d-b7af-395948a00fff: 2nd century AD. Uxelodunum was the largest fort on Hadrian's Wall, garrisoning the Ala Petriana — 1,000 elite cavalry. Its prefect held the highest military rank on the entire frontier.
descriptions.60722e7e-587a-46fb-b09c-e6e82f1b74f7: A Neolithic building on Shetland so unusually large it was likely communal or belonged to someone important. Only the massive walled enclosure survives.
descriptions.1a3c1c74-6536-4d2f-bd49-259c36e10357: A settlement with ceramic, tool, and weapon remains from the 5th to 1st millennium BC. Even in the Iron Age, this place was thriving.
descriptions.ac5e0ce6-db45-4199-a285-83941a839851: A sacred hill home to a stone circle, Bronze Age cairns, and a solitary menhir called the Cow Stone. Multiple monuments share this one stretch of common.
descriptions.a979b657-533e-4561-aa38-8b889f449c59: Traces of civilization here reach the 7th millennium BC. Neolithic dwellings from the 6th millennium BC are among the best preserved in all of Europe.
descriptions.af010237-a119-4b7b-8a37-802f22d82708: A Mesolithic site from 9300–8480 BC, as important to its era as Stonehenge is to the Neolithic. Twenty-one red deer skull headdresses were found here.
descriptions.f95bef03-ef56-40c2-9ee8-bb27572c9277: The Neolithic Starcevo culture—one of Europe's first farming societies—was named after this site. Settlers here were among the earliest to cultivate crops.
descriptions.f666ad09-20d2-4078-ba70-77d96662acbd: Late La Tène Scordisci site in Slavonia, with a settlement and necropolis. Rescue excavations from the 1970s–80s exposed the tribe's westernmost reach into Srijem.
descriptions.3f348969-d6bd-4b9b-a657-a5aa7a8e5e7f: A Celtic settlement from the 3rd century BC where the Tisa meets the Danube. Romans conquered it and renamed it Acumincum, a strategic frontier fortress.
descriptions.72980dbd-dee9-446e-b694-a16515924c10: Four stones set at the corners of a rectangle straddling Stonehenge's sarsen circle. Two stood on mounds that resemble barrows but never held burials.
descriptions.c34bf073-ed1e-4626-8cc8-8cbd724d9b93: The largest and heaviest prehistoric standing stone in Cornwall, weighing 16.5 tonnes. Made of Devonian shale with striking feldspar veining.
descriptions.e432d0fb-25a7-4c3d-808a-faf304c1ca8e: Chalk hilltop above Winchester topped by a hillfort, then scarred by Black Death plague pits on its south slope, then marked by a mizmaze cut into the turf in the Early Modern period.
descriptions.894e8180-b166-4986-b273-ea719c7c3a34: A church stands on this hilltop where an Iron Age fort once dominated the Cornish clay country. Discovery of china clay nearby caused the village's population to explode.
descriptions.e2f2dee4-9e70-41b8-a7f5-be7aa07ea807: Funerary stele of 510 BC carved from Pentelic marble at 2.02 m tall, showing a warrior in full armour. Traces of polychrome paint survive—confirming ancient sculpture was vividly coloured.
descriptions.394676cb-8534-4424-b387-800c59f5993b: 6th-century BC Archaic stele from Corfu marking the grave of a warrior killed near the river Arachthos. Its epitaph enumerates his bravery in one of antiquity's earliest surviving verse inscriptions.
descriptions.f2b64b04-bcd7-4333-ac21-2641a667bef2: An Iron Age grave field with 45 burials, a stone ship, and menhirs arranged by height—tallest to shortest. The gradient is deliberate.
descriptions.2c621de8-bfe8-4f0f-96a9-01b3761ea97a: A Neolithic passage grave where hundreds of amber beads, flint tools, and a decorated bone tube were found. It dates to roughly 4500 BC.
descriptions.0bee1a58-01b6-4d51-8caa-782b194828fb: Iron Age burials from the 1st–3rd century AD with Roman ceramics—rare this far north. Trade between Rome and Scandinavia reached further than most assume.
descriptions.cd10aef4-26b6-477b-bc12-de3786c10594: A 15-hectare Cucuteni-Trypillian settlement from 5000–4300 BC. These proto-cities are among the earliest urban experiments in human history.
descriptions.f78f8d70-ca5f-4831-9475-e4369414c5b1: At least 260 earthwork figures up to 400 m across, visible from space. Some date to 8000 BC, predating most known monumental construction.
descriptions.678f0897-ca66-404c-a678-7255000117ac: A Minoan settlement and cemetery active from 3100–1100 BC. A potter's kiln and a tholos tomb were found, showing both craft and ritual in one place.
descriptions.412fddc2-44a1-4fb6-b272-4d38cc7cd56c: A 4th-century AD baptistery—the cathedral it served no longer exists. Its Late Roman and Early Byzantine architecture survives in this frontier city.
descriptions.44cf60cc-9ced-49af-acc5-9922cc3d6f38: Excavations in 2003 beneath a school's sports fields at Bradford on Avon revealed Roman-era floor mosaics and a stone structure identified as an early Christian baptistery.
descriptions.94a3c919-e3f9-4d26-9e15-46ed22ac2f93: A 4 x 3 metre mudstone capstone rests on three uprights, its rear stone pierced by a port-hole. Built 1,500 years before Stonehenge, it once formed the east end of a 27-metre long barrow.
descriptions.904babe6-e678-4a59-be5f-89228d5cbb59: Doric stoa from around 500 BC, seat of the Archon Basileus and repository of Athenian law. Incoming magistrates swore their oaths on a sacred stone kept within its walls.
descriptions.d09330b1-d704-4e42-8ad1-39d6a1178704: A 150 BC stoa built by King Attalos II of Pergamon. Fully reconstructed in the 1950s, it now houses the Museum of the Ancient Agora.
descriptions.75374382-c6a7-4fb5-b9fb-cb1cd29fd7f2: A gallery donated by King Eumenes II around 160 BC as shelter for theatre spectators. It connected the Theatre of Dionysus to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus.
descriptions.cb2858ad-2ca7-4d48-9d71-0e3ced3a2d31: A 5th-century BC portico at Delphi built by Athens after the Persian Wars. Its back wall is formed by the famous polygonal masonry of the temple platform.
descriptions.748bda90-84cd-452b-8cff-25d9185bab43: A stoa to Zeus Eleutherios built around 425 BC—a rare cult center rather than a marketplace. It was founded to celebrate freedom after the Persian War.
descriptions.bfa06d13-88b7-4e88-913b-1f06f7c5305b: Doric stoa erected around 460 BC on the Agora's north side, its name lives on in Stoicism—Zeno taught there. Its walls displayed trophy armour and the famous paintings of the Battle of Marathon.
descriptions.94e18246-8ec7-4da8-9bad-ea33e78d2dcb: A Roman crossroads city where the Crna meets the Vardar. Stobi was capital of Macedonia Salutaris and a strategic center for trade and military campaigns.
descriptions.bcf9d5f0-42b5-4065-b897-c458eb5ee4bd: Bronze Age and Hallstatt period burial cairns in a valley shaped by melting glaciers. The landscape itself is a relic of deep geological time.
descriptions.ce9c68cf-97b7-4ef2-8301-0a3907d2608d: Two Iron Age hillforts sharing one hill, barely 1 km apart. Paired hillforts are rare and may indicate rival communities or complementary functions.
descriptions.aa60e5f1-a3f5-4f27-b152-44ad38e72f54: Two superimposed sites on a hill 159 m above Exeter: a hillfort at 145 m placed for simultaneous sight-lines to neighbouring forts, and a later Roman signal station at the summit.
descriptions.40d5953a-8816-462d-8ea6-4e9bc78a6af5: A 7.5-acre Iron Age promontory fort of the Dobunni, occupied from the 3rd century BC for 400 years. Its innermost rampart stands over 30 feet high, backed by a sheer gorge drop.
descriptions.c28a832f-4e26-482b-9cb1-93f5d4dce5f1: The lowest hillfort in Britain at just 2 m above sea level. Around 500 BC this gravel bank was an island fortress amid flooded marshland.
descriptions.21b2278e-c3f2-4723-ae40-fa8a6161e3fb: Sarsen stones weighing 25 tonnes capped with lintels, enclosing bluestones hauled 240 km. Built 3000–2000 BC; why they built it is still debated.
descriptions.4b29999c-68c7-4726-9c5a-47ea177779f4: A 3 km avenue linking Stonehenge to the River Avon, aligned with the summer solstice sunrise. A vanished stone circle once stood at the river end.
descriptions.3d1c5bc3-f16b-4459-afd5-0d4034875aa2: A 3 km Neolithic earthwork from 3630–3375 BC—centuries before Stonehenge itself. It was the first monument built in this vast ritual landscape.
descriptions.f3ab5721-49ad-4aa7-b2f2-1ac7604d8ae2: An engraved volcanic stele elevated on three rocks like a table. It is linked to Guanche mummification practices—the indigenous people of the Canary Islands.
descriptions.fc215bfb-e68e-4aa0-844a-c15d8047f62f: Neolithic henge on Orkney dated to the 4th millennium BC, among the oldest such sites in the archipelago. Its standing stones form part of the Heart of Neolithic Orkney World Heritage Site.
descriptions.6d84eb20-870b-43b1-ba78-25e3a0e4954f: Over 300 stone spheres up to 2 m in diameter, nearly perfect in roundness. Nobody knows how the Diquis people achieved such precision around 600–1000 AD.
descriptions.3f06d44f-7bcc-4a9e-882f-c19f436b0612: Built around 3500 BC. A 30-metre mound hides a 12.8-metre gallery with seven chambers holding bones of multiple generations. Centuries later, Romans left pottery offerings inside.
descriptions.e5e6bcbc-23d3-482f-9126-becfcc26ab80: A Roman road station that grew into a 31,000 sq m fortress after Gothic raids began in 238 AD. Its walls stood 2.2 m thick with semicircular towers.
descriptions.17a5dcfe-4f54-467a-9399-ce1a6c72f267: An underground catacomb complex from the 3rd–8th centuries AD with over 30 hypogea. Some feature agape tables where mourners shared ritual meals with the dead.
descriptions.8426a941-5472-44b1-b7aa-0872fa5ae26d: Granite circle 44.3 m across on Bodmin Moor, dated 4300–3300 BC, enclosed within a 53 m ditch-and-bank platform. A fallen menhir 3.7 m long lies at its centre.
descriptions.3195c970-3603-4a2c-9810-7031b5120420: The only archaeological reserve in the country, home to hunebedden—megalithic tombs built from glacial boulders. Over 50 survive in this province alone.
descriptions.ac2ef60c-347b-491c-a31b-39204e932a94: A Roman fort built around 50 AD and replaced within 30 years by a new one across the river. The military kept upgrading positions during the conquest.
descriptions.7583e021-25bc-41d7-8e48-d00d6f38a495: Pompeii's newest public baths, built outside the walls near the Porta Marina. Erotic frescoes in the changing room may have served as locker number labels.
descriptions.5b4e478e-a052-46d9-b892-c3894bd8c3ae: A strategic Roman city fought over during the Samnite and Punic wars. Oscan tombstones at the site confirm pre-Roman Italic inhabitants.
descriptions.58c0a320-200d-42ce-9477-2148736e6a65: Ruins of a Roman aqueduct in ancient Phaselis. Aqueducts like this carried water across kilometres using only gravity and precise engineering.
descriptions.f26676eb-8ab7-4032-86de-b28e992373f8: Archaeological finds from the Stone Age through Roman times prove millennia of continuous habitation. Layers of settlement are stacked deep beneath the surface.
descriptions.480e074e-f607-44d7-8bad-753453941c0c: Kushan fire temple founded under Kanishka, atop 200+ stone steps and four terraces. A Bactrian inscription in Greek script names the architect — a Greek named Palamedes.
descriptions.30cff220-3dbe-433c-8f8c-81e9bd4699af: A Roman east-west road linking north-south routes across a free-draining greensand ridge. It was a planned military route, not a paved-over Iron Age track.
descriptions.37d8c068-dfb3-4fc5-a99e-a09c4aad18d3: An archaeological site at over 3,800 m in the Andes. Living this high forced adaptation to extreme cold, thin air, and limited growing seasons.
descriptions.76d37f57-f64c-4579-8e60-1f47f781940c: Elongated ovoid hillfort 6.4 km north of Hereford, with V-shaped ditches and timber-revetted banks begun by 100 BC. Skeletal remains found here suggest the settlement met a violent end.
descriptions.2c170344-d5e4-46ad-9239-68959f5436f5: A Roman-era site where 21,000 coins were found in a single excavation. That volume of coinage suggests a treasury or major commercial hub.
descriptions.322cd09d-45f7-4cea-aaac-d1d973910935: A sandstone runestone from 1–250 AD—the oldest datable runestone known. Its Elder Futhark inscriptions push the origins of runic writing back centuries.
descriptions.519f6ff4-934d-46c5-8d84-b73ca0e4d594: A Bronze Age mound that served as the meeting place of Swanborough Hundred (183 hides). In 871 AD, King Aethelred and his brother Alfred the Great convened here before fighting the Danes.
descriptions.6e49927e-99cd-480d-8474-4da41b51ae46: A carved swastika-like design from around 3300 BC—millennia before the symbol gained modern associations. It closely matches a motif found in Scandinavia.
descriptions.a627df4e-f241-478e-b8ab-273e67f52441: Timber causeway built in 3807 BC across the Somerset Levels—dendrochronology dated it to the exact year. The second-oldest timber trackway of its type found in the islands.
descriptions.07ae3cb5-efbc-4d97-b3bf-f6d1aeca168c: Two Iron Age enclosures plus a deserted medieval settlement, all layered on one hillside. Each era built on the bones of the last.
descriptions.c097eec0-60d9-4c1c-84f7-16e869dd5ccd: A circle of 55 close-set slate stones, 26.8 m across, with a southeast entrance gap. The Lake District saw more stone circles built than almost anywhere.
descriptions.991bd627-65d9-40d3-a97d-dfa879756da0: Founded 720 BC, Sybaris grew so wealthy that "sybarite" still means lover of luxury. Jealous neighbors destroyed the city completely in 510 BC.
descriptions.70762563-db82-43f3-ad30-bce5fde9c9bd: A hill with Neolithic and Bronze Age remains where Charlemagne captured a Saxon fortress during the Saxon Wars. Roman coins were also found at the summit.
descriptions.a90a07b9-221b-4078-8cb6-931df31296ac: Thousands of rock engravings carved into sandstone by Aboriginal artists. Many locations remain secret to prevent damage—these sites are still sacred today.
descriptions.57ded976-9874-4832-8716-2b54c1fee102: A 4000 BC dolmen whose capstone bears a carved axe and a plough pulled by oxen. The capstone was part of a broken menhir—the carving matches across the break.
descriptions.a2df5acf-6b70-48e1-a8e6-869e1d0dffbc: Punic-Roman tower in San Gwann with origins that may reach into prehistory. The site later served as a Muslim cemetery, then a church—three faiths layered onto a single structure.
descriptions.5e13b5f1-b63f-49fa-96e9-7adad6c1d136: The best-preserved of six Punic-Roman towers, standing seven courses high with 3 m thick walls at the base. It served from the Punic Wars into Roman times.
descriptions.7d8df981-b89f-4d88-809d-205d2d11c160: A cave inhabited from 62,000 to 22,000 BC with over 7,000 stone tools found inside. Mousterian culture artifacts link it to Neanderthal occupation.
descriptions.fcc4232a-0c79-42c7-ae83-cb6bd8fa98bd: UNESCO-listed temples from 3600–3000 BC, among the oldest religious structures on Earth. The facade closely resembles the nearby Ggantija temples.
descriptions.d972a5b7-866c-48d6-af54-d9ac91f00b0b: Three moai platforms, one topped by a statue with restored white coral eyes. It shows how moai originally looked—wide-eyed and watching.
descriptions.e6b90e74-f7c5-40fa-846f-6ffab5ac8beb: A Punic-era rustic villa that confirms a thriving olive oil industry in ancient times. Rooms surround a courtyard with fluted pillars hewn from local stone.
descriptions.c71054c1-6e0b-4e14-a8c8-83ffc79db502: An archaeological site at nearly 4,000 m in the Andes. At this altitude, ancient inhabitants endured extreme cold, thin air, and limited growing seasons.
descriptions.592c7bd0-4cff-4910-a55e-b50ea0e59897: A Buddhist monastery carved entirely from bedrock, with a lotus-decorated dome. An adjacent carved hill holds a stupa surmounted by a harmika.
descriptions.49037cfb-5c88-4863-aa23-c317502fc6d8: A UNESCO-listed Buddhist monastery used for 600 years from its founding in the early centuries AD. It is the most representative example of Gandharan monastic architecture.
descriptions.e9d94ed6-b8f1-489a-baa3-0934e14fff08: Saka burial mounds from around 500 BC, including the tomb of a "Golden Lady" with Achaemenid-style ornaments. These nomads traded directly with Persia.
descriptions.3d12019c-b7fc-4966-8f9e-c6eab13b6f18: A Talaiotic village with a taula sanctuary—T-shaped stone monuments found only on Menorca. The village once spanned 5 hectares behind Cyclopean walls.
descriptions.d321b4b1-0103-4190-ace4-125339800e75: Thirty rock-cut caves with 15 water tanks used by Jain and Buddhist monks. The unique Ebhal Mandapa style marks where both religions first entered the region.
descriptions.9703779d-9bc9-4e82-8daf-053842127c98: A Talaiotic settlement with a taula—a T-shaped stone pillar unique to Menorca. Centuries of farming damaged the site, but the taula enclosure survives.
descriptions.ad16f637-fa0c-4920-bfae-7a53dee2593a: A Roman-era agricultural zone with tomb clusters, field systems, and Byzantine catacombs. A Christian catacomb and four rock-cut tombs were found in 1915.
descriptions.d4151e8f-d299-434d-9f75-1287f1a99677: Cave burial site dated 1000–900 BC in the Olancho Valley. Calcite coating ancient skeletal remains causes them to glow when lit—the origin of the name 'Cave of the Glowing Skulls.'
descriptions.a692e959-c6b4-45b5-96f6-65b82c883a35: A Roman Danubian fort (134 x 126 m) in the Moesian Limes frontier system. Its walls were upgraded from wood to stone before Domitian's Dacian War in 87 AD.
descriptions.ad191503-1e6b-405c-bd52-fca93895617e: Three aligned hypogea dug side by side, originally separate but later joined by passages. Each has a unique plan, but all share interconnecting galleries.
descriptions.78aacfb6-8feb-4240-998e-d1a1feeae92a: Megalithic temple at Salina dated 3300–3000 BC, now reduced to its ground outline. A stone slab found at the site bears star-like carvings, read by some researchers as a night sky or calendar.
descriptions.cd88cf76-8b62-4b6a-ab57-fbbdbdcb445f: A Maya city that was capital of the Petexbatun region before Dos Pilas conquered it. In the 8th century it turned on its overlord and helped destroy it.
descriptions.c947e9b6-41c7-4c94-81c3-d79fc9e601b2: A rare Inca adobe complex still showing original red, yellow, and white paint. Most Inca sites are bare stone—this one reveals how vibrant they once looked.
descriptions.91889130-bd24-42d1-a128-89527ebf79f2: Inca aqueducts, canals, and waterfalls running through terraced rock. Whether it was a ritual bath, water temple, or engineering showcase remains uncertain.
descriptions.0aa03558-b60a-46d3-8a77-7dcce6f7e015: An Inca-era settlement with layers from early Nasca pottery through to Spanish colonial ruins. Each culture left its mark stacked in sequence.
descriptions.681b6f74-7b5c-4c1a-99b4-0f58822e5e39: A Huastec city with over 70 structures, including a 21 m pyramid. Active from 600–1100 AD, it was a major center in an often-overlooked region.
descriptions.a3047874-7d9a-429c-ba0a-b2448e6e88e6: A hill with a vanished white horse figure called the Tan Hill Donkey for its oversized head. It measured 23 m from nose to tail before vanishing under growth.
descriptions.6fb66867-1ba1-405d-b451-14767885ab53: An ancient city with Greek roots predating the first Greek colony on the island in 734 BC. Its ancient theater, still in use, overlooks the sea.
descriptions.e911a780-13d9-401b-ae9d-4d1f5d4cc22b: Pre-monastic phase dates to Azes II (35–12 BC). Clay sculptures here are the 'missing link' between Hellenistic Bactrian art and later stucco Buddhist work — looted and burned by the Taliban in 1992.
descriptions.5b66df99-d730-4aaa-aef0-2d6bf3c53d17: A temple in ancient Phaselis whose ruins include baths, an amphitheatre, and a gate built for Emperor Hadrian's visit. Even emperors played tourist.
descriptions.270a7cb6-a601-4414-9f4a-6105c74ba674: Named from Anglo-Saxon for "Taeppa's barrow"—a 7th-century burial mound survives here. The village name itself is a 1,300-year-old grave marker.
descriptions.61f1e287-c3bc-40ad-b3fe-af956af4cb1b: Woodland broch near Falkirk, first studied in 1864 by Colonel Dundas and later laser-scanned after conservation work cleared the scrub. The circular chamber measured about 9 m across.
descriptions.f81ac74d-ecfc-4970-9b11-8a4202305724: The central temple of Eastern Polynesia, on the island once called Havai'i. Marae complexes were political and spiritual power centers.
descriptions.88feb4fd-5d22-4766-8637-fd910c3bc8f3: Rock reliefs from the Sassanid Empire that have survived 1,700 years of wind and rain. They depict royal investiture ceremonies in extraordinary detail.
descriptions.aa0e933b-2f4d-4ce0-aac5-84666d1f80c3: A Sasanian arch with the second-largest unreinforced brick vault in the world. It was the facade of Ctesiphon's main palace, capital of the Persian Empire.
descriptions.ce4fd9fc-65cc-45b8-935a-a24099d3dba4: An archaeological site at 3,800 m in the Andes. High-altitude sites like this required extraordinary adaptation to thin air and freezing temperatures.
descriptions.3223ecb5-4712-44c1-b02b-f9fabe186d09: A 15th-century Inca rest stop for travelers and royal messengers called chasquis. Its walls are octagonally carved stone blocks fitted without mortar.
descriptions.6b808340-302a-4866-9c2d-46391aff4ce3: Known as Roman Turiaso, this city passed through Visigothic, Muslim, and Christian rule. A textbook example of layered history in a single place.
descriptions.33e2399e-fd68-4aab-bf79-c5695a6c0bf0: Inca tambo in the Junín highlands, part of the road-station network that linked the Inca empire's thousands of kilometres of road. Such way stations supplied travellers, armies, and state runners.
descriptions.dbb1be2f-16a7-4447-aa92-e83b7eb8c280: Settlements here date back 20,000 years, with Bronze Age tools found along the river Stola. Silver and lead mining later made this one of the richest towns.
descriptions.865dcc6d-fa4c-429b-8c16-908cb96dcec2: Roman Tarraco was capital of Hispania Tarraconensis, the largest province in the west. Cyclopean wall bases near the old prison predate the Romans, belonging to an earlier 5th-century BC settlement.
descriptions.b68b5ee3-74cb-41bf-8033-8678da454cf9: A 2nd-century AD Roman amphitheatre that held 15,000 spectators. It was built close to the forum of this major provincial capital.
descriptions.4a5a324f-832f-4dca-b688-d4a006d297c7: Three connected temples from 3150 BC, among the last in the Megalithic temple tradition. Decorated slabs with spirals and animal reliefs were found throughout.
descriptions.767b931c-d5d6-4da3-80fd-bdd8b72f8663: Romans quarried white limestone here from around 69 AD to build the walls of Singidunum. The Turkish name means "stone mine." An underground cave complex from the workings survives today.
descriptions.ddeef34a-1bf9-4066-9871-d894d7f7bf1f: A sanctuary spanning 4,000 years—Megalithic temple, Phoenician shrine, Roman pilgrimage site. The goddess worshipped here changed names but never left.
descriptions.7caf1620-133b-4038-bc01-0ba854a84505: A Thracian sanctuary dating to 4000 BC with a rock-hewn surface tomb. It was an exclusive religious center for the surrounding region.
descriptions.2c1d6960-56c3-425c-8bf5-199f40562a50: T-shaped stone monuments up to 5 m tall, found only on Menorca. Built 500–300 BC, their exact purpose—religious, astronomical, or both—remains unknown.
descriptions.641eee4d-d29c-42a6-9bf0-c8ac34e8cbc4: Birthplace of Byzantine Emperor Justinian I around 482 AD. From this small settlement came the ruler who reconquered half the fallen Roman Empire.
descriptions.cc5d8fbd-741d-4da3-9ac4-c7bd797d4fd8: An ancient Bruttian city on the border between Reggio and Locri. Its Tyrrhenian coast position made it a flashpoint between rival Greek colonies.
descriptions.bf53f267-7a43-4af9-a8d3-1e270d40b85e: A Neolithic burial cairn with a rare double-tiered chamber—upper and lower, originally separate. Why they stacked the chambers remains unknown.
descriptions.6af23268-e00e-481b-ac50-8fc3901be8be: Hexastyle peripteral temple from the 6th century BC on a sandbank near the Bradano river, dedicated to Hera and Apollo. Remains of the temenos wall and an ancient altar survive at Metapontum.
descriptions.7d39dd8c-cca7-4b3a-a412-6bbe5afa9307: A vast site active from 1000 BC to the 7th century AD with Neolithic remains dating to 3360 BC. It passed through Persian, Greek, Mauryan, and Kushan hands.
descriptions.5ef32845-6e06-422d-bb99-e1e7c898749a: Babylonian king Nabonidus abandoned his capital and lived at this oasis for ten years. Its city wall ran 11 km—enclosing an area among the largest of any walled site in the ancient Near East.
descriptions.ce733a7d-a3e2-463d-b09e-2bdac5ea6dcb: Aramaic inscriptions from the 5th–6th centuries BC carved in limestone. They record life at a desert oasis along ancient trade routes.
descriptions.c15b3210-d987-4ced-9d94-1f3af0d41905: A Roman legionary camp founded 123–129 AD that became a major military base. The Third Legion anchored Roman power across North Africa from here.
descriptions.c86669d0-04df-4bfb-9453-40f7d927f8f9: A village with a medieval castle and a Roman road from different eras. The road linked the fort at Low Borrowbridge to routes heading south.
descriptions.5fe6dbf7-9f00-49aa-b9ed-7aa643ac1305: Multivallate promontory fort near Great Elm covering 24 hectares, its inner bank reaching 4.6 m high in places. A hoard of Roman coins dated 337–366 AD was recovered from within the fort.
descriptions.9d65d8dd-ef7f-4479-ad2b-1fde36484e23: One of ancient Arcadia's most powerful cities, home to the Temple of Athena Alea. Votive bronzes found here date to the 8th century BC.
