descriptions.e6b17dcc-68fc-40ff-b2ab-b541655e14e2: Capital of Urartu's Transcaucasian provinces in the 7th century BC. Its ground floor was entirely filled with storage rooms for grain and oil reserves.
descriptions.27defc87-bd64-47ea-ae01-9d5bc0129f87: Largest archaeological site in Israel at 200 acres. A cuneiform tablet with Hammurabi-style laws, a six-chamber Solomonic gate, and a 19-metre bedrock water shaft have all been unearthed here.
descriptions.0608f0dc-4dd4-420e-ad27-ea59fe561212: A fortified settlement dating to 7000 BC—one of the earliest walled sites known. It preserves the development of pre-Hassuna culture in Mesopotamia.
descriptions.18f488c0-fce6-4ea4-b732-d23fe5759cd1: A 12 m high tell with 5,000 years of stacked layers—Medieval, Roman, Iron Age, Bronze Age, and Copper Age. Each era is literally built on top of the last.
descriptions.a1999e42-e24d-4e35-b44f-8164349735b6: A 450 BC Doric temple with fire damage from 406 BC still visible in the stone. Romans restored it with marble tiles, replacing the original clay roof.
descriptions.7759e372-b62e-424a-a726-d078a5a49e54: Once the largest temple in Greece, dedicated to Olympian Zeus. Hadrian finally completed it and placed a gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus inside.
descriptions.c4bb47e2-6e2e-49e6-a17b-e9c2ad9c9129: A small Neolithic stone circle also known as The Druid's Temple. An Early Christian site lies nearby, layering pagan and Christian sacred space.
descriptions.27309875-001f-4c13-a005-17cde60e415c: Doric temple on Selinus's acropolis built shortly after the mid-6th century BC, dedicated to Apollo as confirmed by inscription. Hundreds of clay seals recovered suggest it doubled as an archive.
descriptions.ad2eb54f-98a3-4299-8cd5-56e3ddc0b48f: Mid-6th-century BC Doric temple on Selinus's east hill, raised on the foundations of an earlier structure. Debate over its dedication—Hera or Aphrodite—remains unresolved.
descriptions.b13caf27-5754-44a2-b13d-ec8824ac95f4: Mid-6th-century BC Doric temple at Selinus with six front columns and fourteen on the flanks, dedicated to Dionysus or Athena. Its cella was screened by a row of small internal columns.
descriptions.e507b1a6-966b-4dec-88fc-e167e3915821: Built around 1450 BC by Thutmose III and extended by Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV, this is the oldest pharaonic temple surviving in Nubia. Its interior reliefs are finely cut and retain vivid pigment.
descriptions.9abf8d9a-b474-44cf-b9da-1761e7a6d1ad: The central temple of the vast Karnak complex, built during the New Kingdom. It was the house of Amun—the sun god and king of all deities.
descriptions.d3272ca0-0c72-4c97-a745-762e9ed77416: A Carthaginian temple rededicated to Sardus Pater Babai, chief god of the Nuragic civilization. Roman layers sit on Punic foundations like a cultural sandwich.
descriptions.4bf50d9c-aa7f-4283-83d6-5519e1793a03: A 500 BC Doric temple on Aegina dedicated to the goddess Aphaia. Its sculptural pediments depicted the Trojan War in vivid detail.
descriptions.12851166-9039-4782-b5e3-98bce8e3ccc7: Ancient Kassope, built on a Hippodamian grid—one of the best surviving examples in the Hellenic world. A temple to Aphrodite stood among its Cyclopean walls.
descriptions.56836aa2-1680-43fb-aeef-1edcc33e2c91: Home to the Oracle of Delphi, where the Pythia's prophecies shaped wars and empires. The visible ruins date to the 4th century BC.
descriptions.7bffddb6-2fc1-49cf-987a-d7e78bdc98c5: Doric temple at 1,131 m in Arcadia, built 450–400 BC and attributed to Iktinos—Parthenon's architect. Its interior holds the earliest surviving Corinthian capital in world architecture.
descriptions.0b2dbda6-0bd0-4e07-89e8-bbe4792cdfcf: A temple to Apollo "of the fathers" rebuilt around 306 BC with an unusual L-shaped plan. Its colossal cult statue by Euphranor survives headless.
descriptions.b07d443c-8ef1-460a-900d-dc4113ce03e3: Pompeii's most important religious building, dedicated to Apollo since 120 BC. Bronze statues of Apollo and Diana flanked the main altar.
descriptions.3fbcee0b-5778-4897-ba4a-9b792fd5305d: A 6th-century BC temple to Apollo Zoster with a unique floor of large rectangular slabs. A later wall separated the inner sanctuary from the main chamber.
descriptions.15511706-1e3e-4b7f-974d-7464988b0462: Doric hexastyle temple to Ares, physically dismantled and rebuilt stone by stone in the Agora during the Augustan period. It had a large altar to the east and was surrounded by statues.
descriptions.caf19500-efd7-4258-b429-2b41bec64d3e: Temple to Atargatis in Dura-Europos, raised under Parthian rule in the 1st century AD. This multicultural frontier garrison city sheltered a half-dozen temples of competing traditions side by side.
descriptions.e9a3f325-9632-4f10-a0a4-b04048f0b117: Sanctuary at Tegea active from the 10th century BC, dedicated to Athena under a fusion with the local deity Alea. Its status as asylum was so absolute that no one could be seized within its walls.
descriptions.83013ef0-17e6-4d64-84bc-464e1855c86f: 4th-century BC temple to Athena on the Lindos acropolis in Rhodes, built above a natural cliff cave. The site overlaid the cult of an older local goddess worshipped before the sanctuary's foundation.
descriptions.8d8753ae-9935-4ffb-b578-de5907999f68: The smallest Acropolis temple, built 426–421 BC for Athena Nike. Mycenaean ritual fragments in its basement are a thousand years older than the temple itself.
descriptions.0e12027e-9a65-470f-aca7-2cb1eb408120: A 500 BC Greek temple long misidentified as dedicated to Ceres. Terracotta figurines of Athena finally corrected the attribution centuries later.
descriptions.83822807-fe8c-4ca5-946e-17c5e7c5cf25: Three successive temples at Delphi from the 7th to 4th centuries BC, each replacing its predecessor. The famous Tholos stands in the same sanctuary.
descriptions.24009e21-6345-4cee-81d6-4b6c8ae39fc4: A Roman temple from 20–25 AD. Carved into its walls is the Res Gestae—Augustus' political testament listing his achievements for all to read.
descriptions.2fecf287-b758-45e4-bc5c-81c6d1196f2f: A Roman temple on the highest point of ancient Barcino. Four Corinthian columns still stand in a medieval courtyard, hidden in the Gothic Quarter.
descriptions.85652e72-e8d5-4c37-8c60-f5d9fd0b1edd: A Roman temple built over a Greek or Samnite capitolium, later converted into a cathedral. Layers of pagan and Christian worship stack on top of each other.
descriptions.4a07cc38-1b55-4254-b0ad-fe875310caf7: A Roman temple to Augustus built 27 BC–14 AD with a richly decorated frieze. It survived by being repurposed as a church, then a granary, then a museum.
descriptions.8ee9e59b-a2fd-4a46-b3a6-a9ae4efc0500: Commissioned around 150 AD, its 66 m x 35 m footprint surpasses the Parthenon. Nineteen of its 42 Corinthian columns still stand 19 m tall, and its entrance doorway soars 11 m high.
descriptions.6e807534-9daa-4656-9cbd-a4c8dd0d65dc: The largest temple in Roman Britain, built 49–60 AD. Boudica's army burned it during the revolt of 60 AD; a Norman castle now sits on its foundation.
descriptions.03b9c5be-ec62-4fe7-8231-c098a4d2b921: The largest and best-preserved Doric temple in Sicily, built around 440 BC. It survived because it was converted into a Christian church in the 6th century.
descriptions.903285ef-5216-4d41-88ee-8d386d6865f3: A temple to Thoth begun jointly by a Meroitic king and a Ptolemaic pharaoh in the 3rd century BC. Nubian and Ptolemaic power cooperated to build it.
descriptions.da62b3af-331d-461c-a715-d64e35870466: A temple to the Nubian god Dedun from 2040–1780 BC. Dedun was a god of wealth and incense—the luxuries that flowed from Nubia into the north.
descriptions.c7ce50b5-7f16-41a7-844b-d0d7b419d549: Augustan building near Nimes's sacred spring, long misnamed 'Temple of Diana.' Its basilica-like floor plan and absence of any cult evidence point instead to a library.
descriptions.139ade22-bf52-47ca-8f98-632fa877adc3: A sanctuary to Eshmun, the Phoenician healing god, expanded from the 7th century BC to the 8th century AD. Each era—Phoenician, Persian, Hellenistic—added a new layer.
descriptions.79bdd238-3531-426f-a51b-fd304d21581e: A fortified caravan city between Rome and Parthia that thrived in the 2nd century AD. Its concentric walls and temples withstood Roman sieges before falling.
descriptions.9d1f90a0-7c45-4903-a83c-7503daf3db1b: Doric peripteral temple to Hephaestus, standing largely intact since 415 BC on the Agoraios Kolonos. It survived by serving as the Orthodox church of Saint George Akamates for over 1,200 years.
descriptions.4c7f6521-241f-48c0-93da-f8d7893f5446: The oldest temple at Olympia, built around 590 BC, originally shared by Hera and Zeus. The Olympic flame is still lit at its altar today.
descriptions.6493afc6-9665-440c-90ea-1e7d9fc28e6b: Founded as early as the 8th century BC at Gadir for Phoenician Melqart, later rededicated under Rome. Hannibal, Scipio Africanus, and Caesar each visited before launching their greatest campaigns.
descriptions.cb3119c9-4740-4255-a825-21816d822ff1: The largest temple in Kharga Oasis, and the only surviving Saite-Persian period structure. Its sanctuary depicts hundreds of deities.
descriptions.383214cc-1b63-4ea9-b5aa-3bf851e0826f: Rebuilt after the 62 AD earthquake by a freedman who registered it in his infant son's name — a legal trick to buy the boy social status. Murals and cult statues are now in Naples.
descriptions.31189b26-92cd-4486-a696-35cc37daf70b: A Romano-Celtic temple at the center of a vast sanctuary. Its site has Neolithic roots but was monumentally rebuilt under Roman rule.
descriptions.5adaee62-3e90-4550-930c-6cd9039c223d: The main temple of the Pompeii forum, where Roman Jupiter superseded Greek Apollo. This temple proclaimed Rome's supremacy over the old Greek gods.
descriptions.ff55d038-92b0-4fad-9973-96cab63ec8db: Built inside Diocletian's Palace between 295 and 305 AD, later converted into a baptistery. An Egyptian sphinx 3,500 years older than the temple flanks its door.
descriptions.08f27e9a-8ad4-49b2-8676-a9c7a43cde8b: A temple to Khnum begun in the Ptolemaic era but mostly built by Rome. Its columns are carved with astronomical calendars and ritual texts.
descriptions.1c3a15dd-4add-4c8b-84ef-3e638ce46b1b: A New Kingdom temple to Khonsu at Karnak, built by Ramesses III. Ptolemy III later added a grand gateway—all that survives of his contribution.
descriptions.669d6f3d-fb65-47ce-907a-3b6c847666d4: A unique "double temple" with mirrored courts for two gods: crocodile-headed Sobek and falcon-headed Horus. Mummified sacred crocodiles were found on site.
descriptions.e255c084-20ff-49d1-a93e-883578b94758: A Roman-built temple that was never completed or inscribed. It was dismantled and relocated in the 1960s to save it from the rising Aswan Dam waters.
descriptions.a8238496-728d-4971-9f4d-3ed5ce0f9ff8: A Romano-Celtic temple whose ruins sit beside a 16th-century farm built directly on the sanctuary's foundations. Old stones are reused forever.
descriptions.04b79866-b13b-4b76-ae03-6392651eecab: A 2nd-century AD temple built atop a volcanic summit to replace a smaller version that couldn't handle the pilgrim crowds. Its facade faced east toward sunrise.
descriptions.9031494a-4710-430f-975c-18c9a5990592: Colossi over 10 m high flank the entrance, with the queen's statues as tall as the king's—unprecedented in ancient art. Dedicated to Hathor and Nefertari.
descriptions.cf772251-cfa0-47e5-ad66-fa56770aaa41: An island temple complex moved piece by piece to save it from the Aswan Dam. The oldest temple here, dedicated to Isis, was begun around 380 BC.
descriptions.100ab5ea-fdf9-4d78-9f65-961ee8190b7b: A 5th-century BC marble temple built on the ruins of one the Persians destroyed in 490 BC. Fifteen of its original columns still stand.
descriptions.e7bb01c3-14d8-4dd1-9e63-5d804927a032: A Roman temple to Proserpina, goddess of the underworld. Its marble was later stripped and reused across Valletta—only one piece survives in place.
descriptions.860263d7-1a2f-43d7-b739-fc7145caacf9: A temple built by Ramesses II in Nubia, partly rock-cut and partly freestanding. It was dedicated to Ptah, Hathor, and the pharaoh's own divine image.
descriptions.39e49c72-4037-487c-8402-409d00f7026e: Four 20 m colossi of Ramesses II guard a temple carved into the cliff. Twice a year, sunlight penetrates 60 m deep to illuminate the inner sanctuary.
descriptions.0ea92399-96d7-4b98-839f-5ac77983e576: A circular Ionic temple built on the Acropolis around 19 BC, aligned with the Parthenon's entrance. It was Roman propaganda in Athens' most sacred space.
descriptions.07318b0f-10b0-4637-95e1-d170923d33ca: Marble temple on Naxos built around 530 BC, among the earliest Ionic examples on the islands. Its unusual plan—resembling a telesterion—suggests use as an initiation hall for mystery rites.
descriptions.248951cd-2522-4a50-8cb4-aeeef742576e: Founded around 3200 BC to track the Nile floods, rebuilt by dynasty after dynasty for 3,000 years. A living record of architectural evolution across the ancient world.
descriptions.60d35c77-9be8-4d45-a774-37c6d2f99426: Known as the Temple of the Oracle after Alexander the Great's visit. Its reputation drew visitors from across the ancient Mediterranean world.
descriptions.5573e1bf-b642-4860-a51b-86e1455a6d46: Once connected by a causeway to the Temple of the Oracle, forming an integrated ritual complex. Together they served the Amun cult in the Siwa Oasis.
descriptions.7abb834a-305d-43b5-b0fe-283261d83cf0: A temple built around 480 BC to celebrate victory over a Carthaginian invasion. The battle was fought the same year as Thermopylae and Salamis.
descriptions.349e080c-0b4f-4708-8744-d1b1c6a0b83e: Built mid-5th century BC; its cult statue by Phidias (c.435 BC) stood 12.4 m tall in gold and ivory. Strabo wrote that if Zeus stood up, he would lift the roof off. Lost before 600 AD.
descriptions.a62177c7-346f-4323-a896-087f608ea5be: A 2nd-century AD temple to Zeus Theos in Dura-Europos. The city blended Greek, Parthian, and Roman religion in one multicultural frontier post.
descriptions.8ed8a300-acf7-4287-8b86-6a6185e3a8a2: Use began before 3000 BC and continued for 2,000 years. One stone bears a spiral motif mirroring Irish passage-grave art — evidence of prehistoric sea contact with Ireland.
descriptions.76c51ba8-fb3f-4a54-9cc2-8f6feafa9594: A temple to the Semitic god Bel, built in 32 AD on a stratified hill. It was converted to a mosque in 1132, which preserved it for centuries.
descriptions.e06caf0a-2a7c-44d5-8cdb-5473d995f896: An Inca temple with a throne carved into the rock of a shallow cave. The caves are thought to have housed mummies of important ancestors.
descriptions.07fb4e2f-26e5-4720-a949-9c28d4712e11: A 1st-century AD Roman temple in Evora's city centre, its 14 surviving Corinthian columns standing to full height. Construction was linked to the imperial cult and dedicated to Augustus.
descriptions.318414bc-098b-4459-95c0-41e1ec49c8a8: Megalithic temples from 2800 BC, first built with rubble, later upgraded to decorated limestone. Most slabs are carved with foliar motifs.
descriptions.d9543648-1f50-4614-b33e-398edff7d7d6: A 21-hectare Lenca fortress from 250–950 AD on a difficult mountaintop. Mounds up to 15 m high and interior fortifications made it a natural stronghold.
descriptions.50873aa8-b4da-4b2c-99a9-b9e7859bf44b: A Maya city on massive platforms, thriving in the early Postclassic as Classic sites fell. While other cities collapsed, this one rose to fill the void.
descriptions.852f3856-ecaa-4bab-82c8-a0ab2d11f94f: A double pyramid with twin shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli. It was rebuilt six times, each layer encasing the last like a nesting doll.
descriptions.6a28da7c-1e74-4f45-b49c-03c2af224c86: The Aztec capital's main temple, rebuilt seven times with twin shrines to the war god and rain god. Each expansion required mass sacrifice to consecrate it.
descriptions.6e8ac9be-7600-4248-921b-0477ca4a70dc: A settlement from 8000–5000 BC with circular stone houses and flat roofs. Its inhabitants were among the earliest in the Mediterranean.
descriptions.1e2fb44b-2c93-4ad8-827c-e9f1b61136ff: A fortified city founded as Teotihuacan declined. The Matlatzincas later conquered and expanded it, adding plazas and pyramid complexes.
descriptions.de42523e-9322-4dba-9448-016174872c48: At its peak a city of 100,000 with an Avenue of the Dead flanked by pyramids, Teotihuacan dominated Mesoamerica from 600 BC to 750 AD. The Pyramid of the Sun stands 65 m tall and covers 4.5 hectares.
descriptions.5d975f0c-bbe4-4bd4-9436-5bf4f2bd59b6: Built in 7 phases from 100 to 450 AD. Its largest burial chamber held 12 human sacrifices and over 100 animals. At 148 ft tall, it mirrors the mountain Cerro Gordo visible behind it.
descriptions.a0f66e3c-744c-493c-8584-ad80194ee21d: The largest building in Teotihuacan, with a base nearly as large as the Great Pyramid of Giza. It was raised in two major phases around 200 AD.
descriptions.ad5aeac3-c555-41d9-b0c6-3665aaefa949: The Feathered Serpent temple, built 150–200 AD with Quetzalcoatl carvings on every face. Over 100 sacrificial victims were buried beneath its foundations.
descriptions.a53220ca-2676-4d39-971d-6dd256ada114: A residential compound at Teotihuacan housing 20–100 people from 350–550 AD. Two independent room groups gradually merged into one sprawling complex.
descriptions.559dfb7c-6754-408f-923b-035500a31213: Buddhist monastery near Ghazni displaying two successive artistic phases: Hellenistic sculpture from the 3rd–6th century AD, then Sinicized-Indian styles from the 7th–9th century.
descriptions.24de1fb5-935c-4fc0-89d0-00539a0ce610: Paro stood 10 m tall and weighed over 80 tonnes — the largest moai ever raised. It fell around 1840, cracking in two. Its 10-tonne pukao headdress still lies at its head.
descriptions.62131a06-8c8c-4c55-bf8a-c19abbca2048: A town at the foot of a mountain temple dedicated to Quetzalcoatl. Nearby Amatlan is the mythical birthplace of the feathered serpent god's human form.
descriptions.93391ee6-8e80-42db-922c-11f64ea57db9: A Celtiberian hill fort allied with Numantia against Rome. Buildings were carved directly into the red sandstone, giving the hill a sculpted appearance.
descriptions.341dc7e6-fb0d-4f41-a0dd-35897aca134a: Ruins of the Pisidian city of Termessos. Alexander the Great besieged it but gave up—the mountain terrain made it nearly impregnable.
descriptions.c250e4dc-81e8-4b7b-8da5-3947e346e2ef: A Celtic stronghold from the 5th century BC. Local legend says the devil was tricked into sliding down the stony slope on his bare bottom and never returned.
descriptions.6a111273-edf6-44f2-b282-a7ac9477aa98: A hilltop monolith with traces of ancient cult activity. Local legend says the devil tried to hurl it at an abbey being built on the opposite hill.
descriptions.f46af5ba-a3d9-4d5f-9d73-0f610b666060: Roman Teurnia was capital of the province Noricum Mediterraneum in late antiquity. It also served as a bishop's see—where the empire ended, the church began.
descriptions.972a2d53-376a-4f73-98bb-7a408040de58: A 15th-century botanical garden by the ruler Nezahualcoyotl—one of the first in the Americas. It collected plant and animal specimens for encyclopedic study.
descriptions.a29d5e41-b7ef-4f9d-baf2-33c562ba9273: A 735 BC Urartian fortress, the best preserved in the Sevan basin. Foundations of city walls, gates, and grain storage rooms survive among the ruins.
descriptions.3a8d94d2-e851-4e74-9ef2-9df7da8172de: A Phoenician city from the 8th century BC, occupied continuously through the Islamic era. Ruins from six civilizations overlap at this single site.
descriptions.337fa8ef-09c7-4419-ab8c-af277ee10cee: Ruins of a city first settled by Greek immigrants from Cyme. Continuous occupation from the 7th century BC to the 10th century AD left deep layers.
descriptions.a965d140-d212-45f5-a269-1945fc8432b3: A Nabataean caravan station from the 2nd century BC on the Incense Road. Excavations uncovered 195 papyri — the Nessana documents — recording life here from 505 to 689 AD in Greek and Arabic.
descriptions.7a21a398-cac6-4446-a619-fa0cd8f5203f: Neolithic remains from 7500 BC through Roman golden age to the 749 AD earthquake. Its colonnaded streets and oval plaza rival Pompeii in preservation.
descriptions.3c412ef3-5dd8-4079-b1b9-d38b7f711edd: A triumphal arch commissioned by Septimius Severus, born in nearby Leptis Magna. Found in ruins, it was pieced back together by archaeologists.
descriptions.e1e4e79c-a9c4-4169-8fde-371c0df79061: Pompeii had permanent stone theatres decades before Rome built its first. The Large Theatre seated 5,000 and was carved into a natural hillside.
descriptions.90f8d91e-5465-41c2-a297-8f33269c241e: A Roman theatre at 1,000 m elevation built for the region's most important city. Its stage wall is carved directly into the hilltop rock.
descriptions.cb039044-f134-4131-9d34-148eaf14840e: Drama's birthplace: the first orchestra terrace was laid out on the Acropolis slope in the late 6th century BC. By the 4th century BC it seated 25,000—Sophocles and Euripides premiereed here.
descriptions.d60110a3-f57d-4fd1-afaf-05740fdef6a6: A Roman theatre from the 2nd or 3rd century AD in ancient Thubursicum. The city was founded by Trajan around 100 AD on an older Berber settlement.
descriptions.c7a71867-0a74-4bf4-a77a-a0d53acbf2bb: A treasury at Delphi built after Thebes' shock victory at Leuctra in 371 BC. It marked the brief moment when Thebes was the most powerful city in the Hellenic world.
descriptions.76cd8b60-c373-4f26-85ac-2827b0797b15: Known to the ancients as Waset, this was the pharaonic capital for much of its greatest era. The temples of Karnak and Luxor are among the largest ever built.
descriptions.ce14b760-db1b-4b4d-93eb-8654952d9450: Continuously settled since the 4th millennium BC, Thebes in Boeotia left clay tablets in Linear B script confirming Mycenaean importance. Myth placed Cadmus, Oedipus, Dionysus, and Heracles here.
descriptions.aea029cf-6583-48a3-9c2e-67376db31da8: A Neolithic cairn once 110 m long, now reduced to one surviving compartment. Built between 3500 and 2400 BC from massive stone slabs.
descriptions.31efd673-3b29-4dbc-acb2-2d9179d7a972: A 90-metre-diameter Neolithic henge built around 3500 BC, once enclosing a stone circle whose massive stones were hauled away in the 19th century to build a local road. Two barrows stand 20 m away.
descriptions.4e7d2543-42a8-476a-846b-f587950c12df: Promontory fort above the Bristol Channel near Rhoose, with well-preserved ramparts and ditches on the west side. Occupation continued into the Roman period, controlling coastal movement.
descriptions.a705abb0-2fda-42d2-9eaa-dee12b190ce4: A Neolithic dolmen with a 15.4-tonne capstone bearing cup markings, last remnant of a 70-metre-long burial mound. The fallen stones were reassembled in 1921 to produce what you see today.
descriptions.1516a14a-9185-4adb-a7f9-c3b5cb14fa13: Univallate hillfort just north of Roman Calleva Atrebatum (Silchester), with a single bank up to 1.5 m high. Its proximity to the Roman town suggests it was integrated rather than abandoned.
descriptions.a07daa54-5e5d-48c7-a95f-097ce085c9fb: A tumulus from 600–500 BC so large it gave the town its name—which literally means "large steep hill." It was built by the Kalenderberg culture.
descriptions.db61f285-8d98-417e-9f7e-52b6745a2eb6: Four stones in a 4 m square, the tallest just 0.8 m. The flattest stone bears 13 cup-mark carvings. Beneath the circle lies an older Bronze Age burial cairn it was built over.
descriptions.6313cd62-456d-4a85-8782-57613c7fc0e1: Built over 27 years in the 26th century BC, it was the tallest structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years. An estimated 2.3 million stone blocks were used.
descriptions.b5958bf8-444c-4966-8d9b-2a6ad8197350: Chambered long barrow 24 m long and 13 m wide at the east end, built 3400–2400 BC near Abbotsbury. Early 19th-century excavations recovered human bones and pottery fragments.
descriptions.c2984c15-07c8-4109-ad99-0ecc2e2e2d82: Three stone circles set in a precise line on Bodmin Moor. The alignment is so deliberate it implies astronomical or ritual purpose, but which remains debated.
descriptions.2b0f2420-5602-471f-b4be-eb03e7d33151: Ruins of Hwangnyongsa Temple, once the largest in the Silla Kingdom. An 80 m nine-story wooden pagoda once stood here, built to project power over rivals.
descriptions.d7c688fd-ca27-4a8b-91fd-affbcc948eee: A 75 m wide Bronze Age double burial—uniquely grand for the Nordic world. Its cist stones bear petroglyphs of processions and ships.
descriptions.a2d92ad7-ebd8-4445-9f48-a1458fd302fe: Unfinished step pyramid at Zawyet El Aryan dated to around 2630 BC, 3rd Dynasty. Its owner is unconfirmed—attribution to pharaoh Khaba rests on a nearby stone vessel bearing his name.
descriptions.fe268a4c-2d51-42f9-a00e-addd8fe217da: The only megalithic monument on the Isle of Wight—two greensand stones, the taller standing 3.9 m. The village name Mottistone means "assembly stone."
descriptions.a06ad29e-06f0-450b-bf8e-cd3b7231f096: Two standing stones, remnants of a prehistoric cove near Beckhampton. "Adam" is a surviving piece of the avenue that once connected to Avebury.
descriptions.58286d95-1d76-4513-b5ca-dc386c3033a8: An ancient port city now lying 7 km offshore under 5.8 m of water. It sank gradually, taking temples and shipwrecks to the sea floor.
descriptions.b6af84c5-21f1-4c8a-94d1-2d925bd04725: Late Neolithic, 24 metres across. Nineteen granite megaliths graded in height, tallest to the southwest. The two Pipers stones nearby reach 4.6 metres — the tallest standing stones in Cornwall.
descriptions.192467da-7219-4481-9b2d-34fc4cd5c6fd: Athens' emergency wall, built in 479 BC from rubble of temples the Persians had just destroyed. Speed mattered—they used whatever was at hand.
descriptions.452d8602-3ae3-4386-bfed-e1b3776dd298: Two standing stones near the Hurlers stone circles, each about 2 m high. Legend says they were men turned to stone for playing music on the Sabbath.
descriptions.6b6a62fc-a743-47a2-9caf-9d41ee6a36e7: Two standing stones 90 m apart, aligned to point at the Merry Maidens stone circle. The taller reaches 4.7 m—one of the tallest in Cornwall.
descriptions.dc277dc8-5631-484f-b07a-d1462403dd92: A Neolithic burial cairn 14 m across with a 2 m standing stone beside it. This paired monument type recurs across prehistoric northern regions.
descriptions.e6de5091-b046-45e8-bb6a-a81c99b2fbe2: 13th century BC. Ramesses II's mortuary temple measured 210 by 178 metres. Its shattered 1,000-tonne colossus — once 17 metres tall — inspired Shelley's poem 'Ozymandias' in 1818.
descriptions.5bb2f3b5-7bc6-4cf8-a3b4-cbb4b6e35595: Often called Britain's oldest road, used since 3000 BC. It follows a chalk ridge from Wiltshire to the Thames, connecting Stonehenge to East Anglia.
descriptions.f8571940-a590-4f5f-a2bc-c57efd1853b7: 3rd-century AD baths in central Paris, their frigidarium still standing with intact Gallo-Roman vaults. The ruins form roughly a third of the original bath complex, now folded into a medieval museum.
descriptions.be8b2fd9-d7fb-4f8e-905a-9d237f21b59b: Aetolian sanctuary at Thermos with a Doric temple of Apollo dated to about 630 BC. Its painted terracotta metopes rank among the earliest surviving examples of narrative architectural decoration.
descriptions.6a43a3e7-66c7-4133-a91c-58a52cc5e0dc: A Roman bridge spanning a gorge the legion called "Hercules' Kick." The gorge is only 40 m wide but its walls rise 120 m—a gateway to the desert.
descriptions.11b0139d-eb15-4ea7-9bf2-699a39d2c731: A twin-headland Iron Age fort of basaltic rock projecting into the Atlantic. Mediterranean pottery finds show trade links reaching far beyond Britain.
descriptions.18253743-256d-497f-be7b-6a7400d33593: Holds over 100,000 objects including the Amesbury Archer and the Wardour Hoard of 100+ Bronze Age weapons. The Grade I listed King's House inspired Thomas Hardy's Jude the Obscure.
descriptions.fe7c453a-cabe-4fb2-9009-2ed71a7632fd: A timber and stone ritual site connected to Avebury via the West Kennet Avenue. Originally 58 stone sockets and 62 post-holes formed concentric circles here.
descriptions.49af6562-eae0-42b1-8a52-6d808ae415ea: A sanctuary to Hylates, a local god later merged with Apollo. The cult predates Greek influence—the god changed, but the sacred ground didn't.
descriptions.5d7bd109-0da2-4c89-b92e-aba77991d673: Roman wooden ships recovered near the Rhine frontier from 1997 to 2008. They patrolled the limes—where the Roman Empire ended and the "barbarian" world began.
descriptions.03be9fbc-965c-4c56-8d33-11b954d78353: A Roman road crossing the limestone plateau from Buxton to Derby. Its medieval name "The Street" preserves the memory of a road built 2,000 years ago.
descriptions.a939e800-06e4-4719-a000-165e7f5efe92: 7th–5th-century BC temple or sanctuary ruins on Thasos in the North Aegean. Artemis held cult sites across the entire Aegean archipelago, reflecting her role as protector of coasts and borderlands.
descriptions.e60fc487-9fb9-4e37-b590-4a035e591c7e: One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, now reduced to a single reconstructed column. Three versions of this temple were built over a thousand years.
descriptions.0312b756-2f79-4b8e-bcef-d00885080bca: Built 237–57 BC during the Ptolemaic period, this temple at Edfu stands in near-complete condition. Its inscribed walls are a primary source for Hellenistic-era myth, religious language, and ritual.
descriptions.05ee235c-2ded-4af5-9e94-980c7750bc52: Iron Age fort on St Roche's Hill raised over a causewayed enclosure built before 3500 BC. Two cultures 3,000 years apart chose the same hilltop—each for strikingly similar defensive reasons.
descriptions.44d6f27b-3a9f-49d3-99fa-b1a65380776a: Three groups of Silla-era royal tombs, most shaped like domed mounds. Some contain gold crowns rivaling anything found in European royal burials.
descriptions.f4955fe7-d4e9-4de7-9812-0fc7e94c0620: The largest known ancient obelisk, abandoned after cracks appeared during carving. Had it been finished, it would have stood 42 m tall and weighed 1,200 tonnes.
descriptions.f244de05-4191-4cac-a25d-ea7fc38a6961: Ancient defensive ditches crossed by a Roman road, spanning 3300 to 600 BC. Dense vegetation now conceals what was once a formidable barrier system.
descriptions.1b51e95a-6d3b-4cd1-b3ed-da5f4ab8a501: An 800 BC Iron Age hillfort atop a 407 m landmark. The Cornovii tribe here gave their name to the county—a linguistic survival of 2,800 years.
descriptions.b9024baf-e614-498c-aa14-5c14d2c525b4: A Numidian city that became a Roman municipality. Excavations uncovered a forum, temple, and baths from what was a bustling North African town.
descriptions.c4ee2569-7555-47a2-8d4c-71fcae8468fb: Two Neolithic long barrows near the Dorset Cursus. The unexcavated one, 44 by 18 m, still holds its secrets—its contents remain unknown.
descriptions.f0ca6709-214b-4f96-9ddc-069990a45034: Dolmens modified into corbelled stone structures using a technique common among the Berbers. The monuments line both sides of a valley.
descriptions.f23a31c3-6833-4df6-8583-3b3930b5a74f: A building with a 2nd-century Roman hypocaust and a medieval undercroft side by side in its cellar. Two thousand years of heating systems, one basement.
descriptions.e11457a6-9938-45af-9b8e-00cdbc929123: Roman-era settlement in Rutland with a large temple precinct. Ironstone quarried north of the village supplied building material for churches and structures across the region for centuries.
descriptions.a0d8cc79-b3fd-448f-b983-8155c26de853: Corbelled tholos tomb at Antequera dated to 1800 BC, with a 43 m entrance passage ending in a domed chamber. Two flanking tombs—Dolmen de Menga and Dolmen de Viera—lie to the southwest.
descriptions.20cb6548-7b52-4764-b473-8d2422bf018d: A Copper Age domed tomb from 2500–2200 BC built of block masonry. Flint tools, bone implements, and limestone objects were found inside.
descriptions.e34f699d-7025-4f41-ab0c-fdb54d6a672c: A circular tholos at the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia. Its three restored columns are among the most photographed images from all of the ancient world.
descriptions.15e0fbf2-7d64-46c8-a5ed-8b8830b17b9c: Three aligned henges forming a ritual landscape comparable to Salisbury Plain. The complex dates from 3500–2500 BC and includes a cursus and burial sites.
descriptions.a29a678a-721c-48ae-9d1d-02fdda6c4aa5: A village near two hillforts—one with a 12.5 m high bank. Multiple fortified sites this close together suggest a fiercely contested Iron Age landscape.
descriptions.519a09b3-c3dc-4760-a0b6-30cb2267cd4e: A peat bog where the Angles deposited votive offerings for 400 years. Finds include a Roman helmet, runic inscriptions, and socks attached to trousers.
descriptions.c9ab63ba-44f8-4e52-aec1-2e305191abf6: A cave with a dramatic 10 m entrance, occupied since 9650 BC. Bone tools and Roman coins span the entire human timeline in one location.
descriptions.fd5d7c13-ee71-4b5c-a386-404f446b315f: A 5th-century BC Thracian tomb with a domed chamber sealed by double stone doors. A granite block in the floor hides a cavity—a possible ritual deposit.
descriptions.a6f8838d-ff92-4aef-9723-5ce4b3605fae: A 5th-century BC Thracian tomb whose pediment ends resemble griffin heads. Decorative plastic columns on the facade are a uniquely Thracian feature.
descriptions.75839a02-22e1-4aa0-8954-be8d0922cff9: A 4th-century BC Thracian tomb with a ceiling that shifts from double-pitched to semi-cylindrical. A key moment in the evolution of Thracian architecture.
descriptions.d1f638bc-edc3-4669-b390-20b2df56348b: A 4th-century BC Thracian tomb with vivid frescoes, uncovered by a bulldozer in 2000. Looters damaged some paintings before archaeologists arrived.
descriptions.7ff27a12-f5eb-46e4-b875-310c171a926a: A "beehive" tholos tomb in the Valley of the Thracian Rulers, where over a thousand royal tombs cluster. Its frescoes are UNESCO-protected.
descriptions.8fd7cbfa-01d7-429a-8f97-0592f44ac152: A 300 BC Thracian royal tomb, likely belonging to King Dromichaetes of the Getae. He famously captured Lysimachus, a general of Alexander the Great.
descriptions.37e3f5fe-576c-4b49-a987-9f8c4aa3be3d: A 4th-century BC Thracian temple-turned-tomb with sacrificed horses and dogs inside. The column's knucklebone capital may symbolize fate or games.
descriptions.084a4187-0251-4788-b714-212f796c2642: Three boulders on a hilltop above Morecambe Bay. Whether they are natural erratics or deliberately placed standing stone altars remains debated.
descriptions.171c0658-fbad-43fd-9764-fa7b37c5ba28: Neolithic dolmen near St Keverne dated to 3300 BC, its two orthostats supporting a capstone with possible cup-mark depressions. The enclosed chamber measures roughly 4 by 2 m.
descriptions.257fe33f-735b-46d0-9cb6-83ca0e03937f: A late Neolithic stone circle with 32 stones and cup-and-ring carvings. These are among the northernmost examples of such rock art found in Britain.
descriptions.cab41f26-0bf2-4078-a0c9-6e173fcdc837: A 10th-century BC Sabaean temple dedicated to the moon god Al-Maqah. Six columns and a sacred well survive from this ancient Arabian kingdom.
descriptions.ae2d2c32-689c-443f-ba05-e70023619136: The oldest throne room in Europe, from the 15th century BC at the palace of Knossos. Griffin frescoes flank the gypsum throne, which still sits in place.
descriptions.3fccdb58-627d-4e17-b711-15921d2b681d: Ruins of a large Roman city with a forum, amphitheatre, temples, baths, and houses. None are fully restored, but the scale reveals a prosperous settlement.
descriptions.16419886-7d47-4007-86ae-2fef6dd1fa38: 5th–7th century AD stupa of mud and baked brick in the Kachho plains of Sindh, standing 15.2 m high. Buddhism coexisted with Hinduism in this region until the 13th century Soomra dynasty.
descriptions.e66552b1-7b57-4b1a-a3dd-dded213cfc82: Chalk ridge site on the South Downs with three overlapping phases: a Bronze Age bowl barrow, a 1.33-hectare univallate fort, and a Roman-era farming village traced above it.
descriptions.e69a6a9f-9adf-4927-833d-5d5d0d0d7112: Founded 443 BC as a Panhellenic colony by Athens and Sybaris exiles. Herodotus settled here; Hippodamus laid out its grid streets; Protagoras wrote its constitution.
descriptions.b2a97f1e-1f85-4f7f-97d0-38da53be836a: A Bronze Age cairn near a summit with a stone cist holding cremated remains and pottery. The original cairn survives as a ring of stones around a mound.
descriptions.1e5f61dd-b362-4985-b235-dadeea0eca0f: Agropastoral settlement at Dhar Tichitt occupied from 2000 BC, with dwellings placed on Saharan cliff edges. Among the earliest farming communities identified in West Africa.
descriptions.99b054a0-54c7-44e5-b5e7-28cb8ca28d56: Univallate Iron Age fort in Hampshire dated from 800 BC, later reused in the Roman period. Two structures found inside—consistent with a courtyard villa complex—overlie the earlier earthworks.
descriptions.b30f9252-e3c4-4d53-a13e-7a10b1c6a501: A Roman city with both a Mithras sanctuary and a Christian chapel on the same hilltop—two rival religions, one plateau. A Temple of Saturn crowns the crag.
descriptions.84ef64f3-394a-4b35-ba4a-7e81b3b6a317: A Celtiberian hillfort that allied with Numantia against Rome. Buildings carved directly into the red sandstone give the hill itself a sculpted look.
descriptions.fd94d469-92a0-4796-a7a8-64f925f01773: A Neolithic axe quarry producing porcellanite tools traded across the British Isles. Axes from this mountain have surfaced from the Outer Hebrides to the south coast.
descriptions.4b6407b2-f099-4fd2-a837-0b7a9b263b51: Ruined Hellenistic city in the Aghdam District, named for the Armenian king Tigranes the Great (r. 95–55 BC). Several cities across the Armenian plateau shared the same royal name.
descriptions.30d3fb78-6b80-42f9-87f8-7616e63bec4f: An ancient Maya complex with pyramids in an E-Group alignment that tracked the sun at solstices and equinoxes. Astronomy and architecture merged as one.
descriptions.f7a58094-985b-4f4c-ad0e-c7d8b4c5c2f4: Circular dwellings alongside rectangular chullpa burial towers at high altitude. Chullpas housed the dead above ground, as if they never truly left.
descriptions.74a81d2a-f0a4-482b-ae66-15b51bbdb7ee: Six burial mounds from the 1st century BC yielded 20,600 gold, silver, and ivory artifacts. Five tombs held women; only one held a man.
descriptions.070dcea0-d528-4f58-bd97-7b3ad5a5d73e: An Illyrian fortified settlement of the Delmatae. Under Rome, stone workshops here crafted tombstones for soldiers of the 7th Legion.
descriptions.d5a5f6ff-a9cd-424e-9af9-572b0844f980: Middle Bronze Age hill near Francavilla Marittima where Oenotrians built the first known temples on the peninsula — predating any colonial foundation by generations.
descriptions.05f23376-78dc-4cb6-941d-faaea3abe6aa: Founded in 396 BC, ancient Tyndaris sits on a dramatic hilltop. Its theatre, basilica, and floor mosaics are still being excavated today.
descriptions.3fc93551-df6e-4279-8879-ac5c5e84f330: Two construction phases: Teotihuacan-style taluds from 450–600 AD, then expanded platforms with a ball court. Two empires left their stamp on one site.
descriptions.446c8f5c-fbaa-4344-ae81-4b59d21f5c1a: Severn-Cotswold burial chamber near Cardiff, built about 6,000 years ago. Its capstone weighs an estimated 40 tonnes—the heaviest in the region—requiring hundreds of people to place.
descriptions.e6bfc8ce-6dd4-43b8-9e58-3a56b6ee7163: A Gallic sanctuary where seven carnyces (war trumpets) and ornamented helmets were found buried. These are among the rarest surviving Celtic instruments.
descriptions.d2b71745-bf32-4027-8920-18fcd5600c8d: An Inca park with monumental terraces irrigated by canals fed by a natural spring. The hydraulic precision here rivals modern irrigation systems.
descriptions.e2fab8b2-fe0a-4691-9556-3fc8d71ed312: Lismore broch set on a rocky eastern height, 4 km north of Achnacroish. Clear-day views reach Ben Nevis to the north, Ben Cruachan to the east, and the Paps of Jura to the south.
descriptions.e180ea7b-079b-44f8-88db-128ddc3ee492: A Mycenaean fortress from 1400–1200 BC with walls so massive the Greeks thought Cyclopes built them. Legend says Heracles performed his Labours from here.
descriptions.e355bfda-5a11-4b50-813f-8212abdd0009: A 40 m cave once shared by cave bears and Paleolithic humans. Bone tools made from bear skulls, dated to 27,000 years ago, were found inside.
descriptions.2bf713bc-9782-4f70-9a9f-4b93fd1d5b15: A Paleolithic cave sealed by a collapsed entrance before 10,000 BC. The collapse preserved wall paintings, tools, and objects perfectly.
descriptions.00cb2c16-2b30-42ce-aeb0-b258761ea754: Bronze Age flint tools give way to Cranmore Castle hillfort on Exeter Hill, with a Roman marching camp later sited on the hillside below Knightshayes Court.
descriptions.b1e7b190-e66c-49da-8df8-2b1345fa68fd: A pre-Columbian site at 3,800 m with megalithic blocks and decorated ceramics. It was capital of an empire that controlled much of the Andes for 700 years.
descriptions.52827c54-91cb-4902-99fb-7b0860a71e36: "Over the earth" in Nahuatl—a crossroads linking the Aztec capital to points south. The name refers to the ancient roads that converged here.
descriptions.1212f6ee-6fdc-4b75-8277-5efe8f60086c: An Aztec site centered on Three Cultures Square. Pre-Hispanic temples, a colonial church, and modern buildings share one plaza in three eras.
descriptions.ed7bb62e-95da-4f8a-9c42-869be8bfe912: An ancient Lycian city dating to the 2nd millennium BC with an acropolis, stadium, and a Roman amphitheatre for 20,000. The rock-cut tombs are carved into cliffs.
descriptions.b3d37445-fbc6-479b-8f04-d4cbf95f2292: The "City of Three Cultures" for its layered Christian, Muslim, and Jewish heritage. It was the Visigothic capital from 542 to 725 AD.
descriptions.6d5f0432-6f3d-44af-9119-e8d744b890f0: A rocky hill at a strategic crossroads between the central plateau and the Mediterranean coast. Every passing empire—Roman, Medieval, Islamic—left its mark.
descriptions.9a4ccc75-d0d1-4bf8-8068-ef4cf3221aaf: A Neolithic holed stone 2.3 m tall with a 43 cm hole near its base — the largest of its type in Cornwall. It was moved to its present spot in 1847.
descriptions.79a1bd1f-b28c-49ff-a80d-b882196b3d92: A Bronze Age "Giants' Grave" with a stele and gallery grave. Giants' Graves are long communal tombs unique to Sardinia's Nuragic culture.
descriptions.041499b8-dddc-4b67-9185-dafff2dadf35: A Nuragic funerary chamber 7.1 m long, built from squared trachytic stones. Giants' Graves like this held collective burials for entire communities.
descriptions.1bb82113-962e-4782-9e83-9e3f19470949: One of Sardinia's most important sepulchral monuments. Giants' Graves held dozens of burials—tombs not for individuals but for whole lineages.
descriptions.b27222dd-e77f-419d-9f1b-55bafcf61cc0: A Neolithic dolmen in the legendary Forest of Broceliande, called Merlin's tomb since the 12th century. Grave robbers destroyed much of it, but visitors still come.
descriptions.e256cfc9-63fe-4f27-b7e9-6778a8317eb7: A Mycenaean tholos tomb from 1510–1450 BC, the third largest at Mycenae. Its architecture bridges the oldest and newest tomb styles at the site.
descriptions.58d46ab0-7fc9-4dfa-bf40-a5042d4a91be: Built 1656–57 for the Kurdish engineer who channelled Ravi River water over 100 miles to feed Lahore's Shalamar Gardens. An octagonal brick tomb with a soaring dome, now stripped of all ornament.
descriptions.8a30c67b-4f3e-4e14-b249-bf7de6d7ff31: Built around 1250 BC, this Mycenaean tholos tomb pioneered the semi-column facade that later Hellenistic and Roman builders would copy across the Mediterranean.
descriptions.695ddb9f-70cb-4e8a-9020-4bebf0b06227: The tomb of Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid Empire. Its base-isolated design is the oldest known earthquake-resistant structure in the world.
descriptions.edfe7ad8-3180-442e-890f-e68f0981394e: A rock-cut tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, likely belonging to Darius II. Four Achaemenid kings are buried in the same cliff—a royal gallery carved in stone.
descriptions.1a2c2dc7-7003-4025-a8ce-f3401a10134f: A site some consider the burial place of Eve, with an estimated tomb length of 130 m. It was sealed with concrete in 1975 to discourage pilgrimage.
descriptions.50e5e380-1f89-4fa3-88de-e6ad35241316: A 1637 Mughal mausoleum for Emperor Jahangir, lavished with frescoes, marble, and pietra dura. It sits along the Ravi River in a grand funerary ensemble.
descriptions.e4c7f9de-4dbb-47bc-9586-216f486ac86a: A 3rd-century BC Macedonian tomb with a monumental painted facade depicting scenes of judgment in the afterlife. Two vaulted chambers survive under the tumulus.
descriptions.f906b412-ef19-4865-91ed-26582ed6a332: A mausoleum complex of 63 tombs honoring Jumong, the legendary founder of the Goguryeo Kingdom in 37 BC. He unified rival tribes by age 19.
descriptions.36b645fb-d402-4609-a842-623f8dc0f0e3: Built for two brothers around 250 BC, this Macedonian tomb held a century of family burials. Its painted walls preserve Hellenistic art in vivid color.
descriptions.2590803d-1be8-4d57-abc5-2b10da46806d: Built around 600 BC in ancient Korkyra, this cenotaph honors a warrior lost at sea — its circular stone tomb and guardian lion sculpture among the oldest funerary monuments on the island.
descriptions.c889f267-d523-4253-8bc4-ec3eec0244c2: Called the "fourth pyramid of Giza," this two-stepped Fourth Dynasty tomb was built for Queen Khentkawes I — whose royal title "King of Upper and Lower Kemet" still divides scholars.
descriptions.b70e1353-dfa2-456c-925c-2256195a22c6: A 1st-century AD Roman tomb carved into the bedrock of the Carmona necropolis. Elite Roman burials here mixed cremation urns with elaborate painted chambers.
descriptions.120f7321-78f7-4786-a3a3-13d6b3c9d0f6: Originally a 5th-century BC temple, this mound was repurposed around 300 BC to entomb Seuthes III, a Thracian king. His lifelike bronze portrait head survived intact.
descriptions.a80f19c6-ffde-4350-b122-095a4ef5c97a: The oldest elaborately painted tomb in the Monterozzi necropolis, dating to ~530 BC. Its frescoes blend Etruscan and Ionian Greek styles in vivid mythological scenes.
descriptions.4bb445e0-c605-4f40-ae13-4532fbdb8867: A 470 BC slab tomb whose frescoes show a man diving into water -- the only known Greek painting of its kind. What the dive symbolizes remains an open question.
descriptions.5aaf8925-6b79-4b61-9933-be252c6f2ff6: A Neolithic cairn holding 16,000 bones from at least 324 people, mixed with eagle talons and skulls. Whether the eagles were totems or scavengers is still debated.
descriptions.f4864569-5406-4e10-ac59-0385cc1ad6a4: Built in the 3rd century BC at Mieza, this Macedonian tomb features painted palmette decorations of exceptional quality — the finest surviving Hellenistic funerary painting in the region.
descriptions.f927f3d3-7149-4786-94ac-412652b5123f: An Achaemenid-era tomb standing 15 meters high with two rooms and three burial chambers. Two attendants were entombed alongside the governor they served.
descriptions.ea25fd7b-6bae-4a45-8a75-60ef783a9230: A network of prehistoric tombs spanning multiple islands, dating to around 4000 BC. The archipelago's temple builders left burial traditions found nowhere else in Europe.
descriptions.1b3a3297-9a51-4abf-8528-f194ef9161a0: A rock-cut funerary complex from ~50 AD so grand it was mistaken for royal tombs. It actually belonged to Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism.
descriptions.15e95e05-6fb3-4779-bbcd-375cd2f031e0: Carved from solid rock starting in the 4th century BC, these underground tombs housed aristocrats, not kings. The name stuck because of their sheer opulence.
descriptions.3845e670-6a97-47b6-b6c4-2387e7465523: Over 415 decorated tombs of courtiers and officials from the New Kingdom era. Clay funerary cones stamped with the dead's titles were placed above each entrance.
descriptions.51db73ea-a48b-40dc-9d9e-f0f9b3a27cf6: The oldest town in its country, founded as Atuatuca Tungrorum -- a Roman administrative capital for the Tungri tribe. It has been continuously inhabited for over 2,000 years.
descriptions.4f94a1d6-ed13-4311-adfd-c7b0f2ba3756: The ruins of a Galician-Roman city sprawling across 15 hectares. Its baths, forum, and houses map the daily life of a provincial Roman town in the 2nd century AD.
descriptions.7c6a563b-df2f-4c13-b743-76efc1a67382: A Maya city whose temple-pyramids rise 71 meters above the plaza, with over 100 carved monuments. It waged war against Palenque and captured one of its kings.
descriptions.9b3a978b-e3d2-4257-845e-a435d92bd535: Settled since 4000 BC, this island site holds traces of the Funnelbeaker culture, Bronze Age activity, Iron Age life, and Viking occupation all layered together.
descriptions.07a246e5-5ca7-454b-b10e-a7a8f320384c: Perched on a narrow Hampshire spur, this univallate fort channels all attackers through a single entrance, with a counterscarp bank reinforcing the main rampart and ditch.
descriptions.2b7bb7a9-4759-41bf-a703-8f4da42a1b5c: Cave paintings from 8000 BC depicting communal hunts with dozens of human figures driving animals. Among the oldest evidence of organized hunting in the Americas.
descriptions.b2a6a85b-d671-41a5-b939-f22ddf32ee59: A hillfort occupied in two phases: an early Iron Age ring fort from ~800 BC and a later promontory fort from ~300 BC. Folklore calls the hill a giant's grave.
descriptions.dff560c6-2128-4e34-b738-e7248403a237: Some 3,000 volcanic boulders covered in petroglyphs from the Wari culture, dating to 500-1000 AD. One of the densest concentrations of rock art in the Americas.
descriptions.2121c097-4bc4-4763-9534-ba57efa1437d: A 350,000-year-old site with Acheulean stone tools found alongside elephant and other megafauna remains. Whether early humans hunted or scavenged here is still debated.
descriptions.aad935a4-efbd-4133-94ac-ce7d12789e9c: A Roman suburb of Herculaneum buried alongside it by Vesuvius in 79 AD. The area's ancient coral reefs fueled a jewelry trade that continued for centuries.
descriptions.3d576cfb-2228-45a3-a05e-8433b80d88bc: A 1st-century AD Roman funerary tower standing along the Via Augusta. Its carved relief figures were long mistaken for the Scipio brothers, giving it its name.
descriptions.4b5e5d49-dc89-4a64-9c7d-d2dc63aa7127: The largest Talayotic settlement on Menorca, occupied from 1400 BC through Roman and Muslim eras. Its horseshoe-shaped taula enclosures are unique to the island.
descriptions.fe5d4d6d-a5f0-41eb-ad92-cb3d1b8215b2: A hillfort on Gotland with walls nearly 2 km long, raised in the early centuries AD and reinforced until 1100 AD. Its name means "Thor's fortress" and it features in the medieval Gutasaga.
descriptions.a86f1885-cf64-4dfc-bbec-b388a3ae2ebf: A Roman courtyard villa of 14 rooms with mosaics, underfloor heating, and painted walls. Pottery dates it mainly to the late 4th century AD.
descriptions.e40b24fc-ef7b-4ca8-a0a8-10c2f313f2fb: A 6-meter-high cylindrical Roman tower from the city's original rampart. It gets its name from nuns at a nearby 6th-century monastery.
descriptions.3009852f-6e47-44b6-882b-91471dadf4c5: A Neolithic menhir known as "La Pierre au Bordeu," standing since around 3300 BC. Menhirs like this may have marked territory, tracked seasons, or honored the dead.
descriptions.65936955-be6f-43cc-a306-fc879106f442: Built atop an earlier structure when the city was Caesarodunum, this 1st-century AD arena once seated 34,000 spectators before its ruins were folded into the medieval city walls.
descriptions.fc8f7864-e56c-4e21-a4c1-57c18e31d358: A two-story Roman villa rustica from the 1st century AD whose tower-like stone skeleton still stands — its purpose debated for centuries, theories ranging from villa to watchtower.
descriptions.d9ad0ebd-039e-4cc6-990a-41f690e94795: A citadel rebuilt by every empire that held the city -- Hasmonean, Herodian, Byzantine, Crusader, Mamluk, and Ottoman. Its quarry dates to the First Temple period.
descriptions.8797faec-8590-4716-9763-310be93ef6ea: A four-story sandstone tower tomb built in 103 AD outside Palmyra's city walls. Tower tombs like this could hold hundreds of burials in stacked compartments.
descriptions.d36d9012-fba6-40fc-9f0d-ff865ef0f2a4: A Roman lighthouse from the 1st century AD that still functions as a navigational beacon. At 55 meters tall, it is the oldest working lighthouse in the world.
descriptions.8dedf95c-00b3-490e-94fa-3d558e4bc6be: The remains of a Gallo-Roman temple to Vesunna, a local tutelary goddess. Legend says a saint cracked the tower by driving out demons -- the real cause was stone robbing.
descriptions.e569fdb5-f2fd-4054-8aec-74d21e99a70f: A Neolithic passage grave near the Boyne Valley megaliths. Unlike its famous neighbors, this tomb started as a settlement that was converted into a burial site.
descriptions.4b635088-8799-4dc1-99de-b2b224a71d28: Roman defensive walls built around Durnovaria starting about 130 AD. The earthen bank and stone walls were recut in the medieval period and became public walks.
descriptions.e0bdbec4-268a-4b70-bb73-3e0a74351b9d: A Roman frontier fort on the Rhine, fortified in 47 AD under Emperor Claudius. The modern city that grew on its ruins still carries a version of its Latin name.
descriptions.e9f5f160-fb1f-4497-b89c-e3e3d4f1e8e7: Late 2nd to early 3rd century AD. This 12-metre sandstone arch guarded Timgad's western gate — centuries of wagon wheels carved deep ruts into the stone beneath the central arch.
descriptions.1d6c490a-ef60-42ae-85d8-4ba27c1b8d3e: Completed in 105 AD, this bridge over the Danube was likely the longest arch bridge in the world for over 1,000 years. It was deliberately destroyed to stop barbarian crossings.
descriptions.fea0865c-9b28-4d88-9f66-36e61ed0f0e2: A Roman bridge built under Trajan around 100 AD, paid for by local citizens. A commemorative column from 104 AD still records their contribution.
descriptions.787c014a-347b-4426-ab01-fd3eefe61aa8: The last and largest of Rome's Imperial Fora, built 105-113 AD. Workers excavated over 300,000 cubic meters of rock to eliminate an entire ridge between two hills.
descriptions.716136a2-65cf-4741-8874-9d09b17b8b91: An unfinished open-air temple on Philae island, attributed to Emperor Trajan. It was dismantled and relocated in the 1960s to save it from rising Nile waters.
descriptions.d213752b-d8df-4d17-bd75-63538e87b8ab: A Minoan peak sanctuary on Crete whose clay figurines include a female figure with a swollen leg — a healing votive — alongside ceramic boats and stone objects unique to this site.
descriptions.5007aaf4-5baa-4f8a-b0ed-95e6352d511b: A sacred cave used from the Neolithic through the Bronze Age, called "the table of Minos." Its pottery matches finds from Knossos and Vasiliki.
descriptions.99a98235-4cba-484b-b179-c3e34ed89908: A 3rd-century AD burial of a Vandalic king containing Germanic and Roman objects. The treasure reveals the deep trade networks between barbarian rulers and Rome.
descriptions.67661f87-a03e-4e21-b8d1-c62fbf91361d: A 1250 BC beehive tomb with the largest corbelled dome in the world until the Roman Pantheon. Its 120-tonne lintel stone is the heaviest in Mycenaean architecture.
descriptions.ee80f50f-49c5-49c1-b3a6-76cce8d757a3: Built of Parian marble with rare Aeolian capitals, this Delphi treasury was dedicated by the colony of Massalia — modern Marseille — and stood within the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaea.
descriptions.64a2c786-64cc-43e4-945f-52bc889ac3b1: A 7th-century BC Iron Age necropolis whose gold death masks are among the most striking finds in the Balkans. The culture that made them is still debated.
descriptions.046ccbd9-e5a6-4050-9dfb-83c578344fc1: An ancient Campanian city whose citizens were specifically identified to distinguish them from two other towns with the same name. Roman bureaucracy at its finest.
descriptions.ef0072cc-9021-4f21-8e22-4163967650d6: A restored stone circle of 19 granite blocks, the sole survivor of three circles once aligned east-west. Its Cornish name means "Stones of the Dance."
descriptions.0a82ea91-7f4e-4f1c-89c8-2e1115c1176c: A rare entrance grave from ~4000 BC with a stone-lined passage leading to a central chamber. This tomb type is found almost exclusively in far western Cornwall and the Scilly Isles.
descriptions.8d46f810-cc6f-41c8-b840-8d16efc5deab: A Neolithic hilltop enclosure reused as an Iron Age fort. Hut circles and cairns survive within its stone banks, and a holy well sits just below the ramparts.
descriptions.c57ba273-883f-47c3-a464-12bc976f1821: A circular earthwork whose name literally means "circle ring" -- a tautological name suggesting its shape was always its defining feature. It covers less than one hectare.
descriptions.b249f6b3-60af-4879-be7c-c3924e866d76: "Town of the giants" in the local tongue, this hilltop fort holds over 150 stone roundhouses occupied from 200 BC through the Roman period — the most intact Iron Age settlement on the Llŷn Peninsula.
descriptions.0020c4e1-21fd-4174-94ae-912703cb7ec6: The Logan Rock — an 80-tonne granite boulder once balanced to rock at a touch — crowns this Penwith headland fort, defended on the landward side by widely spaced earthworks.
descriptions.d1bbea1c-28b0-4441-a944-be72f9a40da1: Occupied from before 1000 BC to 900 AD, Tres Zapotes bridged the Olmec and epi-Olmec eras. Stela C found here bears a Long Count date of 31 BC — among the first confirmed uses of that system.
descriptions.cb9eb967-f8ee-4c08-98f5-c2a0a181bc81: A 2.7-meter-tall megalithic tomb known locally as "The Giant's House," originally covered by an earthen mound. Its portal-stone design is typical of Cornwall's Neolithic builders.
descriptions.489ca9da-126d-463b-b792-a1b39a555e3e: A 1st-century AD Roman marching camp at the site of modern Hamburg, built where ships from Flevum could dock. Rome abandoned it when the frontier pulled back to the Rhine.
descriptions.dae23b93-8b4c-4e7c-961b-ca9bd54c4871: A headland near Newquay whose cliffs defend three sides naturally, with ramparts crossing the landward approach. Two Bronze Age round barrows predate the Iron Age fortifications here.
descriptions.0259ff6b-ef34-4a7e-93ef-78e2729e45a6: Rock art spanning the Mesolithic to the Middle Bronze Age, including geometric, animal, and human images. Part of the Council of Europe's Prehistoric Rock Art Trails.
descriptions.6b2cc1ad-eb68-4f1d-9181-42cc5f84cda0: Uncovered during railway construction near modern Thessaloniki, this 4th-century BC farmhouse yielded olive remains that gave researchers a detailed picture of ancient oil production.
descriptions.728762be-061a-4f8a-b03f-980153495b02: A 2nd-century AD Roman arena built into a hillside at Augusta Treverorum — now Trier — part of a World Heritage Site recognizing the city's status as a major Roman center north of the Alps.
descriptions.265f7928-8587-4158-b02f-6e5b779ae7ab: A 4th-century AD imperial bathhouse with pools heated to 40 degrees Celsius. An underground network of service passageways beneath the complex is still visible today.
descriptions.d013bd60-0008-4319-85ff-1523f13edf5b: A hilltop with a Bronze Age barrow, a menhir, and a logan stone that supposedly could only be rocked at midnight. The menhir stands on the western slope near an old mine.
descriptions.53837f96-d32c-4abb-b461-bcf45d914e0f: A stone circle of 12 surviving stones on Bodmin Moor, originally built with up to 20. The circle spans 32 meters, with stones spaced evenly about 4 meters apart.
descriptions.6d2ffc46-f990-4ec7-9d69-94029e8e98ed: A triumphal arch from the reign of Augustus, built to honor veterans of the Gallic Wars. Later rebuilt by Tiberius to celebrate Germanicus's victories over Germanic tribes.
descriptions.71765908-34a8-4811-8e82-2e238a2bddfe: Settled in the 3rd century BC as Tragurion, this small-island town preserves 2,300 years of continuous urban fabric. Its ancient name derives from the Doric word for "goat."
descriptions.e1581c93-ce65-45e9-8d83-3392e9fc8a31: A 3rd-century AD Roman fortress on Mt. Cer at 607 m, on a ridge road linking Balkan strongholds. Slavic folklore attributed it to a mythical Emperor Trajan; only one wall fragment survives.
descriptions.2141f6e0-ab5c-4108-9f2e-8110f1585f43: A 2nd-century AD Iron Age fortification encircling 1,700 square meters on a hilltop. One side drops 70 meters into a ravine called the Devil's Valley.
descriptions.944099e9-5dfb-435f-a1a2-0c87eb4660be: A 5,000-year-old Neolithic long barrow marked by 47 megaliths, stretching 50 meters. Its polygonal dolmen capstone still sits on top. The name means "Church of the Troll."
descriptions.996b223e-5644-4305-9ca6-bd42ca657856: A Roman trophy from 6 BC celebrating Augustus's conquest of all 45 Alpine tribes. The inscribed names of every defeated people were carved into its base.
descriptions.b27d56e3-58e8-4ee7-b32f-2f7d58d737ed: A karst cave with Mousterian tools and a Neanderthal molar, dating occupation back 50,000 years. The cave has two levels with a large terrace at the entrance.
descriptions.a0aec173-1e85-4832-8be6-99ebcdfeb247: A burial mound nearly 20 meters high with a corbelled dome chamber reaching 8.8 meters inside. The dromos entrance passage is 20 meters long.
descriptions.8df1e714-b5bb-4d4b-846b-71cdf7cb3d21: A 1st-century BC fortified acropolis of ancient Iberia, overlooking a pagan temple on Mount Zedazeni. A Christian monastery was later built directly over the sacred site.
descriptions.aba339e0-48a6-44d3-ad40-247c76200b1b: The first pre-Columbian port discovered on the Gulf Coast, with a 15-meter plastered retaining wall of beach rock. It likely served maritime trade routes around 900-1200 AD.
descriptions.e48a661d-c148-4a0f-abff-f862d61524b7: A complex of 26 pyramids and mounds that served as a capital for three successive cultures: Lambayeque, Chimu, and Inca. Local shamans still invoke its spiritual power.
descriptions.9a57f2b6-71ce-449d-8c83-d1e6c8f36f3a: Capital of the Toltec Empire, famous for its 4.6-meter-tall warrior statues atop a pyramid. It rose to power between the fall of Teotihuacan and the rise of the Aztecs.
descriptions.8dace4e6-f6f7-4901-8132-897017b01700: A 2,500-year-old city with four distinct archaeological layers from Hindu, Buddhist, Muslim, and Sikh civilizations stacked on top of each other.
descriptions.0185cd5a-0d05-4720-bc1c-6ea0e809f3a6: Around 200 rock-cut Buddhist caves from the Hinayana phase, carved into the hills near Junnar. They date from the 3rd century BC to the 3rd century AD.
descriptions.b7deb2fd-c322-4c36-a4b5-7b6551ade780: A walled Maya port city built atop 12-meter cliffs on the Caribbean coast. One of the last Maya cities inhabited -- occupied for 70 years after the Spanish arrived.
descriptions.56f3ec0c-0610-4701-8a4e-727b7d3a2512: Home to the earliest known Trincheras village, with 160 stone structure foundations from the ancient Hohokam people. The site dates back to at least 2100 BC.
descriptions.ab28cd35-6f8c-4789-80df-a123993db0b0: Dating 4200–2500 BC, this pictograph on Hisingen island is the southernmost rock painting in the country — and among the rarest, with fewer than a handful known from the western provinces.
descriptions.7797f819-742d-44a1-9df8-f412d513e54a: A Late Preceramic site near Caraz at 2,285 meters on the Cordillera Blanca's western flank, predating pottery in the region. Structures on the Llullán river bank date to around 2000 BC.
descriptions.de449341-fecc-48c2-ab1d-0087ce60e174: A group of five Neolithic barrows with structures dating to 4800 BC. The 1,000-year evolution of burial architecture here spans round mounds, long mounds, and stone chambers.
descriptions.622658a7-db08-4b38-8c80-023702db4a8f: A pre-Inca archaeological site at high elevation in the Andes. Sites like this dotted the highlands as fortified hilltop settlements before Inca expansion absorbed them.
descriptions.bfe38998-f394-4d5e-9a90-1fe222f8f106: A Proto-Norse runestone from 200-450 AD, inscribed in Elder Futhark runes. It may be the oldest written record of burial rites and inheritance in its region.
descriptions.0f113d77-f9a6-4f54-858e-89a99bba03b4: A 6 km tunnel built by 30,000 workers to partially drain a lake, completed by 52 AD. Emperor Claudius's drainage project ranks among the grandest engineering feats of antiquity.
descriptions.ff687661-ccd0-484c-9fe7-c966649818c0: A Gallo-Roman settlement at the foot of Lake Zurich and precursor of modern Zurich. It sat on the border between two Roman provinces and served as a tax-collection point.
descriptions.94bed1bf-8ce1-44b3-a5a3-91860cf1b558: A Bavarian municipality with Neolithic settlement evidence and Bronze Age tumuli nearby. Its name — "Turkfield" in the local language — has no historical connection to the Turks.
descriptions.e3ac6021-f7ef-464d-a6d0-e0df9e91f553: Home to the 14th-century Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi — a Timurid masterpiece and World Heritage Site — this Syr Darya city has been occupied since at least the 4th century AD.
descriptions.2cea8e97-21f2-4d79-95f3-c00ef69985eb: A decorated granite stone from ~100 BC covered in swirling La Tene-style Celtic patterns. The top half is carved; the bottom half was left rough, meant to be buried in the earth.
descriptions.7c562ff4-eefb-4a42-b58a-a013cf1cb970: Small watchtowers spaced every 495 meters along Hadrian's Wall, two between each milecastle. Some still stand several courses high after nearly 2,000 years.
descriptions.4e399e7e-d5e9-49f8-a1de-6e404a740a55: In the 5th century BC this Tartessian building was ritually burned and deliberately buried. Excavators found horse skulls arranged in the rubble — a mass sacrifice with no parallel on the peninsula.
descriptions.2655cac3-4a76-4ea5-bc1e-9922ce8c08c7: A single diorite block with 12 precisely fitted angles, set into an Inca palace wall without mortar. It demonstrates the extreme precision of Inca stonework.
descriptions.55f1b595-fef2-4d16-9dfc-fb5e22634b07: A stone circle of 12 remaining millstone grit blocks, originally 16-20 stones, spanning 15 meters in diameter. All stones had toppled by the mid-20th century before restoration.
descriptions.585ae9f5-c9ef-4446-84e9-a2c5825f5eda: A two-chambered Goguryeo tomb (37 BC-668 AD) with plaster walls once decorated with chariots, musicians, and horsemen. Nearly all the paintings have now vanished.
descriptions.f5df832e-ab5e-4e9c-b6c9-037441011945: Roman double-arched gates from the 2nd century AD that served as the entrance to an ancient theatre. A portcullis slot above the arches shows they doubled as defense.
descriptions.9ba07ea3-0efb-41eb-a65d-e7c5d4c2fe2d: Locals call the summit mound "the Pimple" or "the Nipple." The hillfort defenses date from 800 BC through the Roman period, with earthworks still visible around the distinctive knoll.
descriptions.bf24be84-f6ea-4f68-9b22-2274d0a4c6e5: A Minoan town and peak sanctuary in use from the Early Bronze Age. Excavations uncovered a pithos with Linear A script, stone horns, and clay figurines.
descriptions.e77b1f25-4675-472d-b63d-ff76fae4c08d: A collapsed Neolithic dolmen with a 3.6 by 2.6 meter capstone resting on two support stones. A missing stone, removed before 1873, likely caused the collapse.
descriptions.41eb7a6d-7eb0-4842-b25a-52cca7b3355e: A ruined Neolithic dolmen set on a natural rock outcrop, once covered by a mound or cairn. The cracked capstone measures 4 by 1.8 meters and is 1.2 meters thick.
descriptions.f1a5b6af-b0d7-4784-9edc-8fe83f78730b: A necropolis along a Roman avenue lined with hundreds of stone and marble sarcophagi. A triumphal arch, aqueduct, and hippodrome mark the ancient city entrance.
descriptions.8e1838d6-ec4c-4813-b331-7c745f8aa67e: Capital of the Purepecha Empire, which held off Aztec attacks until the Spanish arrived. Its five yacata pyramids line up along a platform overlooking Lake Patzcuaro.
descriptions.067d1bca-c9e0-45dd-afa8-4a4d474efbd0: A historic Punjab city that may trace its founding to 325 BC as Alexander the Great's Alexandria on the Indus. It later sheltered scholars fleeing Mongol destruction of Central Asian cities.
descriptions.14e9a488-b7a0-4205-aed8-a02d5ded87b5: A high-altitude archaeological site in the Andes. Sites like this served as waypoints along the vast Inca road network connecting the empire's far-flung provinces.
descriptions.bdbe5ee5-28a4-4f75-9777-e9d733738451: From the 8th century BC, this Oxfordshire hillfort has two earth banks, a ditch, and an original western entrance. A second eastern entrance was deliberately blocked a few centuries later.
descriptions.81724be4-6588-41b1-8efc-364637456cdf: A 110-meter-long horse figure from ~1000 BC, carved by filling trenches with crushed white chalk. It must be re-scoured every few decades or the grass reclaims it.
descriptions.4a1c0e1a-7ef6-4e1f-bbdb-6334304bcf52: Settled from 6000 BC, this fortified city produced the world's earliest known alphabet around 1300 BC. Its 90-room royal palace and twin temples crowned a 20-meter mound.
descriptions.eaac27c7-d027-442a-ae0d-49d9e27dfb69: A sacred island in Lake Inari, revered by the Inari Sami as a powerful sieidi — used as a sacrificial site perhaps as recently as the early 19th century. Both Sami and Finnic names invoke sky deities.
descriptions.e1548be0-b310-4afd-82dc-bce186b01410: A Roman temple in Gloucestershire built over an earlier prehistoric shrine. Lead curse tablets recovered here spell out exactly what ordinary worshippers asked their gods to avenge.
descriptions.63d56bb0-10de-42e3-ab43-c76ffca8c323: A 13-hectare Iron Age hillfort occupied from 300 BC to 100 AD, with evidence of extensive settlement. It stands 230 meters above sea level with sweeping valley views.
descriptions.0cd2e708-f7f6-412d-91ba-6d00420b5056: A Neolithic gallery grave known locally as "Hetty Pegler's Tump," built before 3000 BC. Its 37-meter mound hides a central passage with five stone chambers.
descriptions.a6d23a55-e3d1-4846-a7c9-ca5856a9e0cf: A town founded around 1800 BC that became a major regional center during the Ptolemaic period. Greek and Roman buildings filled this once-wealthy settlement.
descriptions.c68b5a7f-8fb5-426e-b73e-7743264afc87: A village with substantial Byzantine and early Islamic ruins visible above ground, alongside an older Roman settlement. Its black basalt buildings earned it the nickname "Black Gem."
descriptions.fa58a468-7383-43cd-ae53-202b74c07f14: Known in antiquity as Gadara, one of the Decapolis cities. The ruins preserve a Roman theater, colonnaded streets, and a view across three countries.
descriptions.5be3cff9-8b07-4cfc-b667-933e2d0ae302: A four-story rock-cut temple carved from solid sandstone, with a massive reclining Vishnu sculpted from a single granite block on the second floor.
descriptions.1e50d2b6-86e7-4b5b-b19d-1682d3304539: A museum built atop a Roman domus that was later converted into a private Mithraeum -- a secret temple for the cult of Mithras, a mystery religion popular with Roman soldiers.
descriptions.63348c8b-a2f1-4d03-8752-cbc9343e51ab: Built around 3400 BC on Mainland Orkney, this chambered cairn is an atypical hybrid of the two main regional tomb types. The pottery style called "Unstan ware" takes its name from finds here.
descriptions.a0c043a9-fc02-49d8-93e8-39100e5ed8c7: Rock-hewn into the Mtkvari River's left bank, this ancient town spans Early Iron Age through Late Medieval structures — blending Anatolian and Iranian rock-cut architectural styles in a single site.
descriptions.4fa134fd-f016-4acf-a2a1-e9e2d2ed3321: Occupied 1st century BC through the Viking Age, this Scanian village sat on a major ancient road. Excavations since 1996 have revealed ritual gold deposits and weapon caches from a major cult center.
descriptions.6b9aa503-6d6a-44b1-a9d0-c165294808df: An Iron Age temple rebuilt six times on the same floor plan over seven centuries. Its elevated central section was supported by four pillars, suggesting a ritual focal point.
descriptions.1b25156f-6212-4c62-a58e-9c6b846fa8f1: Over 300 Bronze Age and medieval sites across 15.5 square kilometers of Dartmoor moorland make the Upper Plym Valley among the most archaeologically dense landscapes on the moor.
descriptions.3dbbef3c-4605-4a1f-b04f-cadd63462673: Founded around 3800 BC, this Sumerian city reached its height under the Third Dynasty of Ur. Its Royal Tombs held gold, lapis lazuli, and mass ritual burials of royal attendants.
descriptions.31fabe04-8275-48fc-bdbc-85073302026a: A Bronze Age five-stone circle with boulder burials, set between two lakes on the Beara Peninsula. The axial stone aligns with the portal stones in a pattern unique to this region.
descriptions.aeee41a7-f003-4d34-ba18-6f9b96563c4d: The second most important city in ancient Iberia after the capital Mtskheta. Archaeological layers go back to the 3rd millennium BC, with early wattle-and-daub buildings.
descriptions.f2da07c6-4f70-4620-989c-f9f3c5ec07e6: A hilltop site with 6 to 8 meter stone structures surrounded by a 10-meter wall. Petroglyphs of spirals and human faces cover some of the walls.
descriptions.d0b9e72f-73a8-4671-a01f-5cafa6e53bf8: Multiple cities stacked atop each other mark this Sumerian site. Proto-cuneiform clay tablets found here — dating to approximately 3300 BC — represent the birth of writing.
descriptions.679bb2a2-0107-4af9-a3d8-9d78539dea20: An Iron Age fortress whose walls have almost entirely collapsed. Large stone piles mark where fortifications and interior structures once stood.
descriptions.f9daddce-2c64-460a-97f8-73046547e10e: An Inca administrative center in the town of Vilcashuaman. A Spanish chronicler described it as "principal and very important," with beautiful buildings and a wealthy temple.
descriptions.7b2aa41c-d24b-4c4c-8ee1-cc0bc461d18c: An amphitheatre half-carved into a hillside, seating 16,000. Underground vaulted galleries and symmetrical chambers lie beneath the arena floor.
descriptions.99115b5a-460c-41e5-98f0-be47a7235402: A cave carved to resemble a human womb, used as a Thracian fertility shrine from around 480 BC. The interior narrows into a symbolic birth canal.
descriptions.608d793c-bd69-41e7-9330-17f35558f8d4: A Celtiberian and Roman city that fought in the Celtiberian Wars, was conquered by Rome in 99 BC, then supported a rebel general before being destroyed by Pompey in 72 BC.
descriptions.b577f36e-74a7-4433-a24f-de51defcfca5: The earliest known Maya polity in the southern lowlands, with 13 identified stelae. Settlement may have originated from Peten peoples during the Early Classic period.
descriptions.3651b680-869e-4ee1-835a-1c0c2305eb5b: The last Gallic stronghold to resist Rome, brutally punished after the final revolt. Caesar reportedly had the hands of all defenders cut off as a warning.
descriptions.ec987c81-f12a-429d-b312-7bd15d98412c: A major Maya city in the Puuc style, with the Pyramid of the Magician rising in an unusual elliptical shape. The Governor's Palace contains 20,000 individually carved stone elements.
descriptions.ab76ee0e-ba9c-4cfc-b68d-c3b47c35497c: A Classic-period Maya city whose water reservoirs had bottoms sealed with clay -- a rare waterproofing technique that allowed it to survive dry seasons.
descriptions.ca826aa3-d4f8-4ca3-ba60-5fc434bcaf96: A pre-Inca archaeological site on the bank of the Qullqa River. Highland sites like this typically served as agricultural or ceremonial centers before Inca consolidation.
descriptions.a81c53d3-e5ad-4aba-a7d1-ee84dc383e03: A Neolithic site where objects may date to 125,000 years ago, which would make them the only known Neanderthal artifacts in the region. The claim remains controversial.
descriptions.1e492f5e-7913-49a5-8d9c-3f9ee581361a: Perched at 185 meters on Woodbury Common, this Devon fort commands views of the Exe Estuary from a ridgeline 12.9 km southeast of Exeter. Earthwork defenses remain visible across the summit.
descriptions.4b4a9785-3993-4bc1-91f2-6df76949b100: A city on the Oude Rijn where a Roman fort once guarded a strategic junction of the Rhine delta. A well-preserved Roman ship was found in the city center in 2003.
descriptions.0f43e795-0348-4bfd-bfea-386ab6e59b68: A mountain cave where objects found in 1996 may date to 125,000 years ago. If authentic, they would be the only Neanderthal artifacts known this far north.
descriptions.7cf17ac2-f8e5-43a4-a31d-3c89370c7cea: Enclosing about 5 hectares on a chalk outcrop near Bere Regis, this hillfort hosted an annual medieval fair until the mid-20th century — over a thousand years of continuous public use.
descriptions.f0b4765f-f0ab-46bf-bfb0-900cd3914323: Covering 11 hectares near Great Witley, dating from around 1200 BC. Its single rampart extends roughly 600 meters east to west, with inturned entrance ramparts forming a defensive corridor.
descriptions.f8beb699-0b16-4b18-b322-bdf7ca612ac9: A Roman villa whose Orpheus mosaic is the second largest in Europe, dating to ~325 AD. The mosaic is now buried under a churchyard, only uncovered for rare public viewings.
descriptions.e7ad39e0-062c-4fe6-a534-3126b72c9e9c: A late Iron Age farmstead on Cranborne Chase, occupied through the 4th century AD. Below ground, storage pits and a small enclosure were the only traces before systematic excavation began.
descriptions.c452fb9a-2718-4a74-81aa-1a5d9b0ba566: A Neolithic timber circle within the Stonehenge World Heritage Site, built with concentric rings of wooden posts. The postholes reveal it was contemporary with Stonehenge itself.
descriptions.310cc15d-fd30-4fe7-b7a6-3f138f44a1e9: Perched on the Mid Cheshire Ridge above Frodsham, this fort's stone-revetted rampart once stood 4 meters high. Slingstones from 1950s excavations confirm ranged weapons were kept here.
descriptions.fd7b2e9e-b11e-4d94-83b4-c94b03f323d1: Covering 8 hectares on Stockbridge Down, this univallate fort has a single bank rising 2.7 meters. Ploughing erased the eastern defenses, leaving the western rampart sharply defined.
descriptions.fff0e7ae-45b8-49c3-8ce4-8bf72cf03d04: Sitting at just 67 meters on Bloxworth Heath, this Late Bronze Age to Early Iron Age fort is unusual for lowland heath — despite its modest elevation it dominates the flat surrounding landscape.
descriptions.c930964b-b6de-4f06-a421-af0c183431fc: Set at 200 meters above the Teign Valley, just 3 km from both Prestonbury Castle and Cranbrook Castle — a density pointing to fierce territorial competition in the Devon Iron Age.
descriptions.337b115e-72c8-4919-b008-b82b86303247: Dating 3400–2400 BC on Cranborne Chase, this Neolithic long mound stands 1.6 km east of Sixpenny Handley. Its presence drew Bronze Age communities to build further round barrows nearby.
descriptions.271aef65-62aa-4e64-9107-140f96633ea3: Nearly 100 bedrock-cut pits at this Somerset hillfort held human bones, coins, and animal remains — evidence of a violent end, perhaps a massacre, around the time of the Roman conquest.
descriptions.74e4bdc2-675e-42b9-b390-898eabed0224: Rising 109 meters above North Somerset, its western end juts as a peninsula into the Bristol Channel. The western cliffs made ramparts unnecessary on that side — only the eastern approach is defended.
descriptions.15d92d09-d2ec-415d-87ea-88535744e27f: A menhir from the 3rd century BC standing at a crossroads. Its earlier name, "Malstein," and its association with Wotan hint at pre-Christian ritual use.
descriptions.d138312f-d127-427e-beac-f0210cf41ba8: A small round earthwork that looks defensive but was actually an Iron Age farmstead. Dense woodland now obscures its modest banks and ditches.
descriptions.417def78-8c53-40cd-96bc-9e56578e9aac: A village whose name means "a nook of land frequented by buzzards." Earthwork remains of an oval Iron Age settlement with bank and ditch defenses survive nearby.
descriptions.dae9bc10-f90d-45d4-9ab6-1408912b461e: An inscribed stone from ~75-460 AD bearing Primitive Irish text in a partly-Latinized form. It bridges the gap between Roman Britain and early Celtic literacy.
