descriptions.cf8b5d56-cbc8-4550-bd77-4dc259020bad: Around 50 meters across in an irregular egg shape, this ~9,000-year-old basalt stone arrangement aligns with equinox and solstice sunset positions — a stone calendar built into the landscape.
descriptions.f75a7bb2-603b-4d3a-858f-88847af51793: From 1200 BC, this 2.93-hectare fort near Hagley has two ramparts and a sacred spring called St. Anthony's Well. Local tradition holds it as the Dobunni tribe's last stand against Rome.
descriptions.f064bba9-1ebd-46b7-a9e4-28e45972e44f: A village with two Iron Age archaeological sites: a cemetery and a settlement. Human habitation here stretches back to the 5th century BC.
descriptions.0490ef6d-5381-449d-aa8c-385ab7dbd8e7: A Neolithic funerary complex in caves surrounded by a walled enclosure, dating to 4100-2400 BC. The caves collapsed before 2000 BC and were never used for burial again.
descriptions.e64b6d10-04bb-4f31-a5e4-a9d132d42b92: A coastal Maya settlement and commercial port, serving as an embarkation point to the sacred shrines on Cozumel island. Its Post-Classic structures use the East Coast style.
descriptions.36bcd304-458f-4727-95f1-716b73d87676: A Maya port city active from 250-600 AD, linking into a vast trade network across the peninsula. Its earliest structures feature Peten-style architecture from the Early Classic.
descriptions.cad0ee78-1954-4ca9-b8e4-dde794c99117: A Maya port city occupied from 200 to 1500 AD. Most of its visible buildings date to the period from 1200 to 1550 AD and include a small temple and residential compounds.
descriptions.9b543ec0-a5ab-49bd-abb3-183570b39989: A Maya coastal city active from the 1st century through the Post-Classic period. It served as both a commercial hub and a port on the Caribbean trade routes.
descriptions.b6ba249d-9287-4be7-b332-59b9cabe509e: A megalithic complex relocated in 2002 to save it from flooding by a hydroelectric dam. The original cromlech dates to the 5th or 4th millennium BC.
descriptions.e284429d-db64-478d-becd-20faf2a1b847: An 18th-century mosque with lead-covered cupolas, built by a pasha who wanted to give his hometown the feel of a capital. It has nothing to do with ancient archaeology.
descriptions.1bdbaf2e-333f-4fcc-b48b-0b0ef244b7e7: A site occupied for over 3,000 years by three cultures, with contact reaching Teotihuacan and the Olmec. A carved stele and ballcourt rings were found before formal excavation began.
descriptions.d9d21ff1-e341-42ac-8283-9d570097a9c6: A Maya site built in the Puuc style, active from 600-900 AD. Its architecture links it to the broader Classic-period civilization of the northwestern Yucatan.
descriptions.8466f428-5e7d-4d8b-bf67-68cc758c6f01: A small Puuc-style Maya site with three palace groups in a valley of the Puuc Hills. Its carved facade masks are characteristic of the ornate Late Classic tradition.
descriptions.3cfc623b-724a-4b48-9c86-2889278efe57: Built 5th–8th centuries AD on a ridge from the Maya Mountains, Xnaheb's architectural similarities to nearby Nim Li Punit suggest a deliberate founding as a satellite or offshoot center.
descriptions.16bc7c0d-247d-4de5-960c-d870236b7bb1: A Maya city whose Temple of the Feathered Serpent blends Teotihuacan and Maya artistic styles. An underground observatory tracked the sun's zenith passage twice yearly.
descriptions.dc2dad07-a240-4111-9a03-4093ef65301a: Active 800 BC–950 AD on a volcanic dome in Tlaxcala, this ceremonial center has Middle Preclassic pyramids. Over 200 female figurines recovered here point to a fertility or goddess-focused cult.
descriptions.27c3bfef-7374-4231-9c14-3c1c09ee6ec2: A Maya site in the Rio Bec style with a famous triple-towered structure. The towers are purely decorative -- their steep stairs lead nowhere and were never meant to be climbed.
descriptions.a72bf9fc-f2ef-4f84-b322-f9707dac50f5: A ruined megalithic temple with a typical two-apse plan and paved court. Coastal erosion was believed to have destroyed it, but 2015 investigations found the remains intact.
descriptions.03d63367-fb7a-4014-b1db-a704e99a10f3: A Maya ceremonial center with over 500 structures, 40 stelae, and 9 temple pyramids. It was the third-largest city in its region during the Early Classic period.
descriptions.a2ddd76f-1c37-4ac9-971b-d9682384141d: A Late Classic Maya centre (7th–10th c. AD). El Castillo rises 40 m and carries a stucco frieze depicting the Sun god, Moon, and Venus — one side preserved behind a fiberglass replica made in 1996.
descriptions.f9f8e1fa-4460-419a-97cf-1e0e2fb6a565: An ancient city that controlled strategic passages near Lake Xynias. During the Second Macedonian War, its location made it a key point of contention.
descriptions.b6ecca26-a3f9-437e-bda5-aa52368598d7: A Zapotec city-state occupied from 500 BC to 1521 AD. Most visible remains date from its final phase as a Postclassic capital, built around and into a hill.
descriptions.a82ec27f-4d6b-4218-924a-f8d01f6ce6ca: A group of pre-Incan towns in the Andes. The first settlers likely arrived around 2000 BC, based on evidence from other archaeological sites in the area.
descriptions.6ecce501-caff-4b88-bc2a-9e6d91656bbc: Near Nanjing, this ancient quarry preserves a gigantic unfinished stele from the Yongle Emperor's reign — a partially cut block estimated at over 16,000 tonnes, abandoned in the early 15th century.
descriptions.9e17ecc2-7c59-4f03-bea4-8d32de261d3e: An early farming settlement from 6000 BC with layers from the Hassuna, Halaf, and Ubaid cultures. Three of Mesopotamia's earliest civilizations are stacked in one tell.
descriptions.f7145c9f-7760-447f-989c-0f6868405cbb: A multivallate hillfort near Steeple Langford, Wiltshire, occupied from around 300 BC. A 1991 survey found 130 internal structures alongside Iron Age and Roman coins, pottery, and human burials.
descriptions.6f759cf6-fe55-4567-b1d1-26b536e8352e: A Maya city whose carved stone lintels are among the finest surviving examples of Classic Maya art. The hieroglyphic texts record detailed dynastic histories.
descriptions.4b0f332b-9289-4a80-9843-3df96b119343: A Maya city with over 500 structures, 9 temple pyramids, and 2 ballcourts. A network of causeways connected its distinct urban districts.
descriptions.fce870cc-5856-4801-80e9-2b7a9ef96b1c: A Maya site with continuous occupation from the Middle Formative through the Post-Classic. The city-state of Coba conquered it in the Late Classic and built a 100 km causeway to it.
descriptions.13b836d4-2d0d-4295-90e4-57fa86d9e359: The largest known Recuay settlement, perched above 4,000 meters in the Andes. Its stone constructions mark the most important evidence of this pre-Inca culture.
descriptions.85a6ae2e-6f62-44f2-9dfd-fd81b229d56d: A Hittite open-air rock sanctuary with two chambers covered in carved reliefs of gods. Over 60 deities from the Hittite pantheon march in procession across the walls.
descriptions.ff824fd2-59cd-49dc-ad4f-21c437f20189: A twin-peaked Iron Age hillfort enclosing 4.9 hectares, the tribal center of the Votadini. Its stone wall encircles the summit at 353 meters above sea level.
descriptions.2d61ebea-06e2-4163-b610-a1a5187ed6d6: Prehistoric stone rows on tidal mudflats, now buried under silt and debris since the 1990s. At least 18 sandstone pieces once formed two parallel alignments.
descriptions.79ad41ce-15fc-471a-8a95-b79a859cf139: A Bronze Age concentric stone circle of four rings nested inside one another. The largest spans 20 meters, the smallest just 6. A vanished burial cairn once stood at the center.
descriptions.b3ebd837-d8b7-4e16-8fd9-c4018ed3f9e0: A circular Kushan-era fortress of 20 hectares with walls and multiple gates. Its round plan -- unusual for the region -- may reflect Hellenistic design traditions.
descriptions.d6d44645-a99b-4826-85b3-eb0123faadd2: An Ottoman fortress built in 1699, covering 25,000 square meters. Its powder-magazines, arsenal, bathhouse, and mosque served a garrison guarding the strait.
descriptions.8f0bd6a2-46b6-46cb-afbb-efd18b2471d8: A 4th–6th-century basilica near ancient Ani, built on a plateau above the Akhurian River. Its plan ranks it among the oldest surviving examples of early church architecture in the Caucasus.
descriptions.ba74c51b-0b28-4e93-aadb-7da862f574da: A tiny island that once held a late Hellenistic sanctuary to Apollo. Ancient writers called it "Holy Island" -- a name preserved in its modern form, Yeronisos.
descriptions.454b824c-cc1a-4846-97d8-7c036712895b: A hillfort so large it is considered one of the biggest Iron Age enclosures in its region. Its stone-walled defenses stretch along the summit at 350 meters elevation.
descriptions.6e01b8ff-f4c3-4eaf-88d5-418482b1c90d: Roman-founded walls that form the most complete medieval circuit of any city in its country. They stretch over 3 km and have been maintained since the fortress was built in 71 AD.
descriptions.be2bb871-ba24-49cf-9172-d20d673a2c3d: Populated since the Late Stone Age, Zadar has accumulated Roman, Byzantine, and Venetian layers across 3,000-plus years of unbroken habitation — the Adriatic coast's longest urban record.
descriptions.fc337c87-1194-4407-b440-2b91f93dbdc7: A cave where a Neanderthal jawbone dated to 28,000 BC was found alongside Mousterian tools. At the time, it was the youngest-known Neanderthal specimen ever identified.
descriptions.f0ac24b0-babb-4e1d-9d56-423ad12d6206: A Minoan palace rebuilt around 1600 BC after an earlier version, destroyed along with other Minoan centers around 1450 BC. Its harbor made it a key hub for eastern trade.
descriptions.7d24037c-4afc-49e7-a13e-713769bf8208: Built atop a leveled natural hill 1 km long in the Petén, this 600–800 AD Maya center pairs a royal palace and temple-pyramids with an unusually high density of royal stelae for its size.
descriptions.ebf816e0-2353-4ed3-81bd-685d6480973f: A Roman villa with original tiling and colored stucco, active from the Bronze Age through Late Antiquity. Punic and Roman tombs surround the complex.
descriptions.f947a367-a17a-4cb3-9d43-93965c88d3bf: The Totonac capital of Totonacapan, occupied from around 1000 AD. Hernán Cortés arrived here in 1519 — the first major city the Spanish encountered — a meeting that shaped the entire conquest.
descriptions.775adc1b-7af2-4452-824b-5cc575b2ec8c: An ancient settlement absorbed into the modern capital in 1934. Its strategic position on the Danube made it a contested border town for centuries.
descriptions.18462ce6-cfb7-43ba-83cd-d44c26395227: A ruined megalithic burial chamber dating to 2500-1500 BC, with a 12.5-tonne roof that collapsed sometime between 1770 and 1865. Bodies were cremated and replaced over time.
descriptions.1fe816f4-f921-45ff-97b7-0ca7d1d0d009: The remains of an Eastern Roman castle from the 4th century AD. Both above-ground fortifications and underground chambers survive at the site.
descriptions.c928294a-3522-4b13-b6ab-1721bebbeb2a: A tell with layers spanning the Bronze Age through the La Tene period. A famous treasure found here reflects the site's role as a trading hub for over 3,000 years.
descriptions.319a1c6f-465d-47bb-b498-2e760d62cd8f: A town whose origins trace to the Byzantine settlement "Ad Herculum" from the 4th century. The fortress ruins sit atop a nearby mountain.
descriptions.3a229dc1-93fd-4ff5-93a9-6c3c61cc9e22: A Minoan building from 1800-1600 BC on the path from Knossos to the great cave sanctuary of Mount Ida. Signs of permanent settlement include a large two-story structure.
descriptions.02436343-8cca-4d64-9927-3b2aa6fd8240: A Maya city that flourished from the 3rd to 9th century, with hieroglyphic inscriptions spanning 591 to 897 AD. Post-Classic occupation continued until the 13th century.
descriptions.f2de39f0-bf5a-4da0-8be0-d06bb65f1af2: Home to the largest pyramid by volume in the world, dwarfing even Egypt's Great Pyramid. The massive structure accumulated over centuries of successive cultures building on top of each other.
descriptions.885ee465-142a-4368-a08c-66295e94cfab: An Aztec ceremonial site now surrounded by the modern city of Cuernavaca. Its dual-staircase pyramid follows the classic Aztec double-temple design.
descriptions.ed186ea9-9ed1-415d-828b-97d9f21401d2: A regional center from 700-500 BC that controlled trade routes to the Soconusco region. It rose during the Middle Formative period when Olmec influence was waning.
descriptions.2d765805-aec0-4616-b547-4ec57a70fbd6: A village with two Iron Age settlements and a cemetery. Human habitation stretches back to the Bronze Age, with finds from the 12th century BC.
descriptions.129465fa-008c-481b-9491-b3cb80ee6294: A late 4th-millennium BC gallery grave near Fritzlar in Hesse. Its stone slabs bear carved symbols including cattle-drawn carts — rare early depictions of wheeled vehicles from Central Europe.
descriptions.54bbb6a0-65d3-42c2-a995-0469957a1313: A prehistoric hilltop settlement occupied in the Early Bronze Age, Late Bronze Age, and La Tene period. Its defensive position 410 meters up controlled a Carpathian pass.
descriptions.0c00d8bd-d6b3-4237-b4c9-9a86748ee5ab: An ancient Greek amphitheatre initially built in the 2nd century BC. It was expanded under Trajan, then modified for gladiatorial games, and finally converted into a Christian basilica.
descriptions.cfc78356-fc53-48b9-b1d5-6bb1c7f86426: The ancient city where the sanctuary of Zeus Sotiros once stood. Remains of the theatre, agora, and bouleuterium mark it as a major center of Arcadian civic life.
descriptions.e9731acc-69e0-4c54-80ed-73dc1c0751c5: A ridge of seven Doric temples from the 5th century BC, among the finest Greek temples outside of Greece itself. The "valley" name is misleading -- they sit on high ground.
descriptions.6e6a831d-bdce-400c-86af-9238e6af3e89: A valley with an estimated 1,500 burial mounds spanning two millennia of Thracian civilization. Each new dig reveals painted tombs, gold treasure, or bronze armor.
descriptions.ea209a12-df80-46f7-9985-4ccd0ae5fc99: Four layers of uninterrupted occupation from the 8th to 1st century BC mark this as a city of ancient Colchis. Sophisticated local goldwork rivals imported Greek pottery.
descriptions.e8ecb6c3-4f2c-4505-9b66-ac3743b02e54: The best-studied site in ancient Colchis, inscribed as a national cultural monument. Excavations revealed temples, fortifications, and gold jewelry of exceptional craftsmanship.
descriptions.5075fcfd-fd0b-4b63-ae8d-7d43e1964554: A Mycenaean tholos tomb from ~1500 BC famous for two gold cups depicting bull-catching scenes. The cups rank among the finest examples of Aegean metalwork ever found.
descriptions.0ee44ac1-3636-4c0f-ad66-05370f8b0c55: An ancient town whose monumental stoa and acropolis date to Early Antiquity. Archaeological excavations continue to reveal its layout at this strategic valley position.
descriptions.e6a32ed2-57ae-48ba-ad7c-bbeeba5f31f1: A small cave shrine dedicated to Apollo, Pan, and the Nymphs, occupied from the 6th to 2nd century BC. One devotee carved elaborate reliefs directly into the cave walls.
descriptions.e5558c53-90b5-42ca-aa79-ba2d05d56eac: Home to the oldest processed gold in the world, belonging to the Varna culture from ~4600 BC. The city itself was founded as a Greek colony called Odessos around 575 BC.
descriptions.fe6a7e02-39e4-46bf-abb9-b1862974f252: A burial site with the oldest gold treasure in the world, dating to 4600-4200 BC. Over 3,000 gold objects were found in 294 graves -- unprecedented for the era.
descriptions.5e32bbc3-17d5-415c-9c66-db088b25685e: A Minoan settlement on a small hill, active from the Early Bronze Age. Its distinctive pottery style -- dark-on-light with mottled surfaces -- is named after this site.
descriptions.46f747db-300f-49fb-bf4a-d2857eee3dee: A Minoan estate containing some of the oldest wine presses in the world, dating to ~1600 BC. The complex included a manor house, courtyards, and workshops.
descriptions.a6d5b07a-c9ea-4e5a-a82d-4416a045f1bc: This Scanian grave field holds 183 menhirs, 15 stone ships — the largest 25 meters long and 8 meters wide — and 2 circles, dating 400–900 AD. Few sites in Scandinavia match this monument density.
descriptions.aaeb620b-8363-45e2-b9f5-4dc46320aff5: The largest petroglyph site in the Verde Valley, with 1,032 carvings across 13 panels. Created by the Southern Sinagua between 1150 and 1400 AD.
descriptions.8c44a3a9-c945-44e8-8dc2-1baab82890ea: A Greek colony from 538 BC that became home to the Eleatic school of philosophy. Parmenides and Zeno -- who changed Western thought forever -- taught here.
descriptions.46be23ba-b785-4a9f-bcd7-c98b01ff445f: A settlement added to the list of sites of exceptional importance. Sparse details survive, but its protected status confirms archaeological significance.
descriptions.2ad2ae09-19fb-4994-8f1d-33d84694c5fb: A Neolithic settlement from the 5th millennium BC where pottery and stone tools were found. The earliest layers of habitation in this region date to this period.
descriptions.ad75ba60-6517-4a16-a529-7c2ba101c40f: A pre-Columbian site with gold offerings and evidence of human sacrifice in its burials. Radiocarbon dates place the main occupation between 200 and 900 AD.
descriptions.ae70d78a-1aa9-43b6-b311-369e1c314343: Established around 70 AD over an abandoned Iron Age enclosure called Oram's Arbour, this Belgae civitas capital later became Winchester. Dere Street connected it northward through the province.
descriptions.d8f8e827-efeb-4169-b55e-e6ee4718d3d6: The capital town of the Iceni -- the tribe whose queen Boudica led a famous revolt against Rome in 61 AD. The town itself was built after the rebellion was crushed.
descriptions.c1e90f5b-8650-46f1-ad58-b61c2e8e069b: Funerary niches carved into volcanic rock covering 1,700 square meters. These "little windows" held the dead of the Chavin and Moche cultures from 1000 BC to 700 AD.
descriptions.d025918d-e26d-4ba9-a4e5-ab60509b55e0: A 4,500-year-old temple with what may be the oldest mural in the Americas, radiocarbon dated to 2000 BC. Four successive cultures occupied the site over 2,700 years.
descriptions.2bf8b01e-8bc2-4f0e-a66e-130b085e83ae: The first capital of ancient Macedon, where Philip II was assassinated and Alexander the Great was proclaimed king in 336 BC. The royal tombs survived unlooted.
descriptions.9553ca4b-63bb-4aa9-bf83-7d3befaf023a: A major center of the Catuvellauni tribe from about 20 BC. King Tasciovanus minted coins here that circulated across southeastern Britain.
descriptions.7c901711-227a-416e-b281-588e67eb1cc6: Guarding a key Roman road in Cumbria from the 1st to 5th century AD, this fort at Brough was later used as the foundation for an 11th-century Norman castle, its Roman walls still visible.
descriptions.56686df2-f3f4-468a-83b8-6a3ae164b9f6: A Gallo-Roman settlement covering 25 hectares with ramparts, baths, and a temple. A stone wall with gates enclosed the original Gallic oppidum.
descriptions.7bd8951e-8693-423f-ae6f-f56713813262: The third-largest Roman city in Britain, with a population over 15,000 at its peak. Settlement continued until the 7th or 8th century -- unusually late for a Roman town.
descriptions.dce4d9db-1bf4-4430-b5e6-2e13e63e4813: A 4.35-meter sandstone monolith at Bois-lès-Pargny, dating to around 3500 BC. A twin menhir was demolished for building material in the 19th century; legend links both stones to the giant Gargantua.
descriptions.ae3b5deb-3b9c-42ec-8610-445c99f5b1a8: Less than 3 km from Stonehenge, built beside the ceremonial Stonehenge Avenue, this ~800 BC hillfort has the River Avon as its southern boundary — a naturally defensible position on three sides.
descriptions.0f20e3ec-b709-4cb9-8859-8125c5576fbf: The grand circular vestibule of Diocletian's Palace, once topped with a dome 17 meters high. It served as the emperor's private receiving hall for select audiences.
descriptions.77809c8e-181c-4e4e-b879-dfb7fb63c220: A Gallo-Roman wall 1,150 meters long with 39 semicircular watchtowers and two monumental gates. It was built under Diocletian to defend what was then an imperial capital.
descriptions.6e87a51f-2dbb-4c7c-8d00-388dbf2b41a2: A Roman military road running from Colchester to Chester, connecting two major garrison towns. The Latin name means "The Chester Road."
descriptions.feccbb16-9c3a-4d0e-9aac-ca8cf3d370d8: A 1,120 km Roman road from the Adriatic to Constantinople, about 6 meters wide, paved with polygonal stone slabs. It connected Rome's western and eastern provinces.
descriptions.0c491ed6-51ca-4189-8db1-6b481f0862e3: The eastern section of a 1,120 km Roman road connecting the Adriatic to Constantinople. Key towns along this stretch served as major military and trade waypoints.
descriptions.eff9d2c5-6e15-4aed-ae90-a81c4efe9f13: A Roman road running from Belgrade to Constantinople, linking the Danube frontier to the imperial capital. It connected major cities including Nis, Sofia, and Plovdiv.
descriptions.4efaf96b-44db-4931-a070-33ad9fcc7232: A Gallo-Roman country town founded in the 1st century AD at a crossroads. Excavations since 2001 have uncovered its streets, buildings, and development over several centuries.
descriptions.f3df5faa-2f56-492b-b526-a229f971d12a: An Inca administrative center with a large plaza where sacrificial ceremonies were performed. A Sun Temple and Moon Temple flanked the central square.
descriptions.c2d8b523-cc72-4987-bc2c-99fd5e5af3c2: A sumptuous 1st-century AD Roman palace villa with elaborate mosaics and frescoes. It is classified as a monument of national importance.
descriptions.8438e161-08c5-48a3-88dd-923b99b9bdd6: Roman villas buried and preserved by Vesuvius in 79 AD. One villa, the Villa Regina, is the only one still visible -- the others were reburied after excavation.
descriptions.102d6fc1-6d23-418c-85a5-27039abee01d: A rock settlement in the Canalotto valley showing Byzantine then Arab occupation. Rooms dug from rock include churches, colombariums, and millstones.
descriptions.fc5e2174-402b-4fcf-9826-77bf9be90957: Emperor Tiberius ruled the Roman Empire from this clifftop palace on Capri from 27 AD until his death in 37 AD. It was the largest of his twelve villas on the island.
descriptions.5f0df994-58d2-4bd5-91be-252d6ae06f76: A Roman villa near Pompeii with storage rooms where 20 bodies were found huddled together during the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD.
descriptions.43fc125a-8617-45d6-a2ad-24f4a1a7f9b8: A 2nd-century AD villa of Herodes Atticus, the wealthiest man in the Roman Empire. He spent his fortune on public buildings across the ancient world.
descriptions.e2a04b44-a3e7-47fc-a217-0689fab93524: A Roman villa with piers stretching into the sea, fish ponds, moray eel farms, and a rich library. Consul Lucullus was famous for his legendary feasts.
descriptions.0b9d33a6-c4b2-4b7a-8209-63feefd129f1: A suburban Roman villa buried by Vesuvius in 79 AD, famous for frescoes showing what appears to be a mystery cult initiation. The exact ritual depicted is still debated.
descriptions.ba877057-f093-46ef-80b9-762e1859b320: A Roman villa in Herculaneum with the only intact library from antiquity -- 1,785 carbonized papyrus scrolls. Scientists are using AI to read them without unrolling.
descriptions.4190c8a6-db2f-442b-8125-f2df42cf51a0: The residence of a Roman governor, named for its mosaic of Theseus fighting the Minotaur. The villa was occupied from the 2nd to the 7th century AD.
descriptions.8d5b27e6-c0ab-4c08-8742-7bb0c59bcfa5: A Roman villa near Monforte in Lusitania, occupied from the 1st to 5th century AD. Its extensive floor mosaics and courtyard shrine make it among the largest villa complexes on the peninsula.
descriptions.ee159937-ce30-40a0-b657-48e29c4df37b: A luxurious Roman seaside villa buried by Vesuvius in 79 AD, attributed to Emperor Nero. An inscription mentions Nero's second wife, Poppaea Sabina.
descriptions.b51b2f98-a99a-4742-ac2a-28df400dae47: A Roman villa in Cuenca province whose floor mosaics — the Noheda mosaics — rank among the largest figurative panels surviving from the Roman world, with scenes spanning mythology and spectacle.
descriptions.2990f219-d421-4474-b478-6b9b0f81990b: A coastal Roman villa whose kitchen mosaic depicts fish and marine scenes -- reflecting the villa's role in fish salting, a major industry of the Roman coast.
descriptions.ab524e5e-2c34-4564-ab3a-f7ab487116f4: A 1st-century AD Roman villa on the Amalfi Coast, where aristocrats built seaside residences. Its remains sit at the point where the Regina Minor river meets the sea.
descriptions.4897c012-56c6-470b-85fa-a89d7e23a6c6: A Roman military capital with an estimated 40,000 inhabitants at its peak. Only 3-4% has been explored -- the vast majority lies untouched underground.
descriptions.fe0f04f9-f65a-4798-93d9-f037383cdb44: A tell almost entirely made of human settlement debris, occupied from ~5700 BC through the Middle Ages. It is the type site of the Vinca culture, one of Europe's earliest civilizations.
descriptions.ef396d45-3f62-4b03-a15b-ae3666c2af7f: A cave where Neanderthals lived about 40,000 years ago -- roughly 8,000 years before modern humans reached the area. DNA extracted here helped sequence the Neanderthal genome.
descriptions.c7459d30-d8e5-46af-ad54-46fcf6b1384a: The fourth fort on Hadrian's Wall, measuring 157 by 117 meters. It is bisected by a modern road that follows the ancient wall's route.
descriptions.e2bb7b81-bdd5-4713-893f-3c2c516a3d7a: A Roman military camp on the Danube that became the foundation of modern Vienna. Emperor Marcus Aurelius reportedly died here in 180 AD.
descriptions.115be95f-85b1-472e-86b4-e68c8f55bdd5: A Roman fort predating Hadrian's Wall, famous for the Vindolanda tablets -- thin wooden letters that are among the oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain.
descriptions.cbfd3d2a-70f5-41f4-a3db-298b56040fea: An auxiliary fort on Dere Street in Lower Britain, positioned between Corbridge and Bywell to control a key supply corridor. Its ruins — Ebchester Roman Fort — sit in County Durham north of Consett.
descriptions.19ecf84c-4c48-46ec-9685-c87ddfdf65ef: A Roman legionary camp that became the predecessor of modern Windisch. Excavations found Bronze Age graves beneath the Roman layers, showing 3,000 years of habitation.
descriptions.f978251d-d093-415a-8be0-c0e0de5d9d8e: A Roman fort and settlement at Bishop Auckland whose military bathhouse preserves a near-complete hypocaust heating system — the most intact example of its type from Roman Britain.
descriptions.e8f52f85-51d3-426c-8c5b-117fb9dfd6c3: A restored Maeshowe-type Neolithic tomb on Eday island, built on the highest point with sweeping views. It dates to the early 3rd millennium BC.
descriptions.28579aa8-dab5-444d-9ee0-61c95cd1c073: A Wari administrative center at over 3,000 meters elevation. The Wari built standardized planned cities across their empire, connected by road networks.
descriptions.e2032339-c139-444d-9347-5d30ecd0b048: The surviving arch of a Roman theatre entrance, popularly called the "Ruined Gate." During the Roman period, it led to the Asklepion healing sanctuary.
descriptions.c8d355dd-e6f9-44bd-b73b-a23f9e550590: Said to be the tomb of Virgil, Rome's greatest poet, at the entrance to a Roman tunnel. The site became a medieval pilgrimage destination surrounded by legends of magic.
descriptions.b40d492a-193f-422b-bd42-559624dd2079: A hill and ancient monument area with cremation cemeteries and cup-marked stones from the Bronze Age. The 1.5 km nature trail passes through this layered cultural landscape.
descriptions.a5d15136-a50e-4c19-8d9e-02efa520ec8f: The 4th-largest Roman settlement in Britain, with over 15,000 inhabitants. It survived as a functioning city until the 7th or 8th century, long after Rome fell.
descriptions.75644a1d-350a-4750-a17f-bdae9a0e139f: A Roman fort controlling a Pennine pass between Stainmore and the Aire gap. Its hilltop position provided unobstructed views across the entire valley.
descriptions.297e5e17-96b1-4df9-88ac-638b1231a654: A Roman city in the province of Noricum, where temples to Jupiter Dolichenus and Mithras served the garrison. Its name survives as a Catholic titular see.
descriptions.0689fd2e-b56c-4c35-adb5-e4ef34083174: A ceremonial center and noble residence of the Neo-Inca State on a ridge above two rivers. Spanish forces overran this last stronghold in 1572, ending four decades of Inca armed resistance.
descriptions.856fe292-38b8-433d-8cde-052863c98659: A Roman vicus from the 1st century BC whose remains lie beneath Oberwinterthur in Zürich canton. Excavations around the medieval St. Arbogast church have uncovered commercial and religious buildings.
descriptions.6a7ed782-d72d-4eeb-8df6-634a27140019: A Celtic burial mound from ~500 BC containing the "Lady of Vix" and her treasures, including the largest known bronze krater from the ancient world -- 1.63 meters tall.
descriptions.1803acf9-1c91-4958-aa2c-3a6a83ff8e77: A village with Neolithic Vinca culture circles 300 meters in diameter, visible only from the air. Bronze Age steppe nomad graves were also found here.
descriptions.c2739b78-39a2-4641-9f68-0ea17d8f1603: A large ancient city whose identity remains unknown -- no ancient source can be securely matched to it. Its size suggests it was a major regional capital.
descriptions.45ed713b-bab5-429b-aa62-2f26a08e2a69: An ancient capital inhabited from the 12th century BC through the Early Middle Ages. Its 121-hectare urban area and harbor made it a major Cycladic center.
descriptions.77e3f3a1-163d-4925-88c5-86456fc81dd7: Home to roughly 3,000 people on the right Danube bank in the 3rd millennium BC, this site lent its name to the entire Vučedol culture — a label now applied to sites across a wide swath of Europe.
descriptions.8f918a04-656c-42c4-a6f1-460a066cfd7d: Above the Mells Stream in Somerset, this promontory fort guarded the Mendip Hills mining district. Newbury Camp 1.6 km north and Tedbury Camp across the river extended the lookout network.
descriptions.6148883a-659c-40c4-bcf4-ef086f860f40: Positioned on a narrow ridge at 210 meters near Beaminster, with steep natural slopes for defense. The Wessex Ridgeway passes just north of the summit, placing it on a major ancient route.
descriptions.eab8cd53-0fe7-4b42-a9cc-8b9ec68ae133: A sinuous stone monument up to 6,000 years old, stretching across moorland for potentially 40 km. The visible section on Wheeldale Moor runs just over 1.6 km.
descriptions.3efdc2f9-61ef-40b9-8d93-0f61668d8418: Perched above Clevedon with steep natural slopes to south and north and two ramparts closing the eastern approach, this univallate fort guards a river valley entrance in North Somerset.
descriptions.b7e6747e-9081-404a-b294-f53ea0b8e3f3: A Maya site dated to the Classic period, considered the most important archaeological complex in its area. Three separate levels of construction span a ridge.
descriptions.9b4bc2f9-521a-467f-a1a6-ebd4563221e9: At 297 metres, this is the highest natural point in the South East. A hillfort crowns the summit, its banks and ditch cut into the chalk downs above the village of Combe.
descriptions.bf372514-0d2b-4f83-b16a-7e4a2c9c97d7: Defensive walls maintained since Roman times through Visigoth, Islamic, and Castilian periods. Parts survived intact until 1868 when revolution prompted their partial demolition.
descriptions.5c40d704-05a0-4951-a5cf-20066d444d81: A common with two saucer-shaped Bronze Age round barrows, now both a Scheduled Monument and an SSSI. The barrows are the low, dish-like type used for cremation burials.
descriptions.6cf9cf72-ba27-4843-bbd4-e9acfabec124: At 4,089 meters near Cusco, Wanakawri was the most sacred wak'a in the Inca religious system — central to founding myths and visited in major state rituals from 1438 until the Spanish conquest.
descriptions.3bb2d9e1-7e77-4582-8b28-92ab27133a9a: First built around 400 BC with a chalk rampart and ditch, Wandlebury Ring is the largest of three hillforts in the Gog Magog Hills. At 74 meters it is the highest point of this Cambridge-area ridge.
descriptions.b319970d-efcd-4f5c-9d9b-55535771676b: The same Iron Age hillfort as Wandlebury Ring, first constructed around 400 BC. A later rebuild added a flat-bottomed ditch and new rampart, showing two phases of defense.
descriptions.67b3a2f7-5f1b-46cc-893a-6cc48b2908c4: Wapley Hill's ramparts stand 5.6 meters high, enclosing 6 hectares. Its 90-meter entrance passage — longer than most in the region — forced all visitors through a controlled single-file corridor.
descriptions.b8244ad8-45ad-411c-a3f3-053aa0a3d4aa: A small Inca site in Acomayo Province near the Apurímac River. Its position within the Inca network of Cusco Region marks it as a waypoint, though sparse remains leave its precise function unclear.
descriptions.dc7253ce-0ab9-43eb-a8ca-a254f77e2d96: An Inca complex built under Pachakutiq, with buildings named Inkawasi ("Inca house"), Warmiwasi ("Woman house"), and Phaqcha -- an altar for water ceremonies.
descriptions.b2a9c061-0761-4f66-9406-130bf68f6770: An oval Cornwall hillfort covering 7.5 hectares at 246 meters, with two concentric ramparts rising up to 4.5 meters. Clear days offer views as far as Lundy Island and Dartmoor.
descriptions.582777a5-6a82-4883-8092-ef8c9b4dc78d: A perfectly circular Iron Age fort with a 212-meter diameter, dating to around 300 BC. A later river channel was cut straight through the middle, splitting it in two.
descriptions.d6c6520a-dc96-4a47-bb30-3c742c4509dc: An archaeological site whose name is all that survives. Highland Andean sites like this typically served as regional administrative or ceremonial centers.
descriptions.fdeca69b-4a68-455c-a865-044b37ccfd21: A site with finds stretching back over 10,000 years, including Paleolithic through Iron Age layers. Its elevated position dominated the bay and served as a natural lookout.
descriptions.6dfdc2fb-802e-4193-b9c9-15684d50bea8: An archaeological site in the high Andes. Pre-Inca highland settlements like this typically sat on defensible ridges above river valleys.
descriptions.1145b2f6-41b7-470f-ac32-cbea87e0a646: A village where a Bronze Age log boat and bronze sword were found in a nearby riverbed -- evidence of a once-busy waterway connecting inland communities.
descriptions.6b730ea0-cd85-423c-a537-4b1097b86031: A mountaintop site at 3,889 meters between two rivers. Andean sites at this altitude often served as pilgrimage or astronomical observation points.
descriptions.41552c37-9349-4c1d-a6e6-a7493f8b16bf: A road used since the Bronze Age, paved by the Romans as one of Britain's main arteries. It linked Dover to London and onward to Wroxeter, spanning the island.
descriptions.ab699722-9c7e-464a-b507-74a21078411c: A Roman town beside the modern A2 in Kent, hidden for nearly 2,000 years. A 2019 dig across 7.2 hectares exposed iron furnaces, pottery kilns, a 7-meter-wide Roman road, and a temple.
descriptions.cc5fb86d-5a12-4ff9-85dc-5c02534e9d7a: A 64 km earthwork running parallel to the famous Offa's Dyke, sometimes within yards of it. Its purpose and the relationship between the two dykes remains a puzzle.
descriptions.1fff5c49-9169-490f-947e-bd5cc8cca4c6: A possible Neolithic henge from 3000 BC, enclosing 7 hectares with a chalk bank and ditch. The River Lea has its source within the surrounding marshland.
descriptions.bf395f91-b77b-460f-802b-20cf52a73bfb: A postulated Neolithic stone circle in the Preseli Mountains, estimated at 110 meters diameter — third largest in Britain. Several of its stones are thought to have been transported to Stonehenge.
descriptions.c4ec69f3-aed5-4c87-8a94-808639ab5544: A chambered long barrow from ~3600 BC, named after a mythical blacksmith god. Legend says if you leave a horse and a coin overnight, the horse will be shod by morning.
descriptions.12e0a51b-54c4-4d30-abcb-7ef995ccd49f: At 3,600 meters on Mount Tawqaray, about 5 km southeast of Cusco, Wayna Tawqaray commands the Watanay River valley. Its position above key routes marks it as a high-altitude Inca landscape node.
descriptions.264ac74e-f5bc-4b73-b28a-c2db99132c50: A market town where a large Iron Age ditch was found in 2008, confirming a long-suspected hilltop enclosure. Anglo-Saxon battles were fought here centuries later.
descriptions.7ef9ec08-db40-406b-b2bd-330e6f3b28ad: A moor with 26 panels of cup-and-ring mark petroglyphs carved into sandstone, dated between 3800 and 1500 BC. These abstract symbols appear across Britain but their meaning is unknown.
descriptions.54782fbd-0ba3-4673-941a-3f5cf1fc8290: A site with Roman and Saxon pottery and an Anglo-Saxon cemetery. The hillside earthworks were noted as early as 1832 as possible ancient defenses.
descriptions.57acda9c-ea62-47b0-be94-a5ac7be9ac3a: From 1600 BC near Mitcheldean in Gloucestershire, this hillfort is traditionally linked to the Dobunni tribe's last guerrilla stand against Rome. St. Anthony's Well survives on the slopes below.
descriptions.7c097275-ba5b-44f8-852b-77f450b7b813: An Iron Age trade route crossing the Cotswolds, linking the Thames to the Severn. The Romans later upgraded it to connect their major roads Akeman Street and the Fosse Way.
descriptions.ae4088f2-d0f0-472e-a783-459f246811c6: 3rd-century AD Roman baths sealed beneath a motorway north of Welwyn Garden City. When the A1(M) was built, engineers constructed a steel vault around the ruins, preserving a near-complete hypocaust.
descriptions.72599653-52d6-4d02-8c11-a7654f010780: A town at the foot of the Chilterns, inhabited since the Iron Age. Its strategic position at the intersection of two ancient routes ensured continuous settlement.
descriptions.50abd026-06c4-4790-a102-26da88b3eae4: A megalithic site stretching over 8 km near the village of Weris, unique in its country. Two well-preserved dolmens and numerous menhirs date to around 3000 BC.
descriptions.8bb46f97-8983-4cba-9519-4d4d9ab7e480: A village near concentrations of stone circles and burials from the Wielbark Culture, a Germanic Iron Age people. The stone circles are rare for this part of northern Europe.
descriptions.ba452543-f3d8-436b-bef5-4329382d234e: A retaining wall from 19 BC that is all that remains of the Temple Mount's western side. It has been a site of Jewish prayer for centuries, earning it the name "Wailing Wall."
descriptions.adbd9b2f-be83-4b3a-a368-2fa7c9928874: City walls stretching 4 km, built around 390 AD and incorporating earlier Hellenistic foundations. The seaward walls were demolished in the 19th century by Ottoman urban planners.
descriptions.92cad00e-4027-4e01-bb7d-2da01760d197: A 3700 BC chambered long barrow and one of the longest Neolithic burial mounds in Britain at 100 meters. It held the remains of at least 46 individuals over 1,000 years.
descriptions.81be53ae-7297-4cf9-8f9f-96f6ac1ebfe8: A collapsed Neolithic dolmen with one standing stone 1.6 meters high and a fallen capstone. Much of the structure was destroyed after its 18th-century excavation.
descriptions.e7e82839-72a2-466c-93ee-7292571e8506: A Wiltshire woodland identified in 2020 as the likely source of most Stonehenge sarsen stones. Geochemical analysis of a core sample drilled from one stone clinched it.
descriptions.0ccb45b7-c632-4f9f-b3d2-698d397ac9b3: Occupied since the 5th century BC, West Wycombe Hill's summit holds a hillfort, an 18th-century mausoleum, and a golden ball — three eras of use stacked on one chalk ridge in Buckinghamshire.
descriptions.b1410fda-e006-411f-a8ce-64513976d158: A Bronze Age henge on Eyam Moor in the Peak District with 10 upright orthostats. Its earthen bank exceeds 30 metres in diameter — the largest stone circle of its type in the county.
descriptions.f3fa78cb-e363-43e8-971e-954d4e9f9b27: A hamlet that is the site of an Iron Age hillfort. Small hillforts like this dotted the landscape as defended farmsteads or local gathering points.
descriptions.ab2ae6ec-ad7c-469b-a03d-b925beaaa21a: A working farm where an Iron Age roundhouse site from ~600 BC was found beneath the modern fields. Two ancient cruck barns in the farmyard are Grade II listed.
descriptions.b774f9cc-ea01-4658-b12c-c66add4453d1: At 77.5 meters long on Salisbury Plain near Tilshead, this Neolithic long barrow dates to 4000–3500 BC. Never fully excavated, it sits within the broader Stonehenge ritual landscape.
descriptions.bfa3495a-39f7-4ba8-a110-eff95d15f05c: Dating 3700–3500 BC on Whitehawk Hill, this causewayed enclosure has ditches broken by deliberate gaps. Such earthworks served as meeting places or ritual arenas — the gaps remain unexplained.
descriptions.f524b8bf-c69d-4dd3-8fb6-549de566d297: A Neolithic sarsen on Blue Bell Hill in Kent, likely the capstone of a chambered long barrow. Its lower companion was destroyed before 1834; this stone then inherited the name and its folklore.
descriptions.c54a5e46-c856-46be-b638-62d6fda1c8e5: A chalk hill carving of unknown age and origin, mentioned as an antiquity in 1742. Whether it dates to the medieval or prehistoric period remains an open question.
descriptions.c87764f1-460f-46b0-8fc3-ddd115a6c9f3: One of only two intact Assyrian obelisks ever found, dating to about 1000 BC. Its carved reliefs depict military campaigns and tribute from conquered peoples.
descriptions.21ba0be2-3da7-40f7-8f99-aece38b3ea17: A hilltop with 12 Bronze Age burial mounds dating from 1800 BC and a large Iron Age hillfort. The chalk landscape preserves rare flora alongside the ancient earthworks.
descriptions.290410a4-c7ed-4fe7-842d-bfe7ab97e899: A desert park with seven Hohokam villages occupied between 500 and 1100 AD. Over 100 petroglyphs are scattered across the mountain's boulder-strewn trails.
descriptions.7ab48a71-0bbd-49a3-b562-563dc5e26bf6: Built early in the 2nd century AD and partly rebuilt around 200 AD, this Cumbria fort has a diamond shape unique along Hadrian's Wall — adapted to hilltop terrain while guarding nearby lead mining.
descriptions.34b70381-5c31-45d0-8a80-62fd28229ba4: Pear-shaped and covering 6.5 hectares on a chalk outcrop near Whitsbury, Hampshire. Two large ramparts with outer ditches and a counterscarp bank protect the northern half of this univallate fort.
descriptions.1328e959-ddab-4dd5-bc24-071540a6ce0d: A Romano-Celtic temple discovered from cropmarks in 1959. Its rectangular plan with an inner cella follows the standard design of temples across Roman Britain.
descriptions.9a219745-8e06-4d8a-8396-c5d5656990a5: A Neolithic cairn on Orkney similar in design to the famous Maeshowe tomb, dating to around 2000 BC. It sits on a steep west-facing hill overlooking the bays.
descriptions.6287ace1-7bcd-4b92-91c9-5cc2be238981: A village with an Iron Age cemetery dating to around 500 BC. Sites like this in the Pomeranian region preserve traces of the Wielbark and Oksywie cultures.
descriptions.19e57e66-7781-42ef-88d6-cb2d5327b8f2: Funnelbeaker culture burial mounds up to 150 meters long, dating to around 4000 BC. Nicknamed "Kuyavian Pyramids," they form a rare megalithic long-barrow cluster preserved in the adjacent forest.
descriptions.a7abbf5d-8bea-4e7f-9df8-bb82169889ab: A Wari culture complex at 3,400 meters near Huaraz, dating to around 1100 AD. Its multi-story stone structures preserve the highland architecture of this pre-Inca civilization in the Ancash region.
descriptions.a2151986-ba6c-4676-ae54-220d2d21e0e0: Three interlinked caves at 1,477 meters with traces of Paleolithic Neanderthal habitation. A full bear skeleton was found in one of the caves.
descriptions.7e5a3822-699c-4603-be7a-ea8ba8278e15: In 1908 a ~30,000-year-old limestone figurine was found in the Wachau valley. The Venus of Willendorf became the defining artifact of Upper Paleolithic portable art — the most studied of its type.
descriptions.7667ebc2-c948-414d-badd-31dbe04b60c4: A circular earthwork 27.47 meters across and 2.74 meters high near Babcary, Somerset. Whether it was a Bronze Age bowl barrow (2600–700 BC) or a medieval motte has never been conclusively settled.
descriptions.7b4c1efe-0e33-453c-bf29-2bece9b96248: An Inca settlement at 2,650 meters on the trail to Machu Picchu, with upper and lower house complexes connected by stairs and fountains. Agricultural terraces cling to the steep hillside.
descriptions.7c3cb1c4-0431-4ebb-96e0-a3238de40ca0: An oval Iron Age hillfort covering 1 hectare on a sandstone hill above the River Don. A rubble-core rampart and ditch surround the entire fort.
descriptions.6c4d8b74-697a-46f7-a000-bf92b702f87a: A headland fort on the Hartland Peninsula, now reduced by coastal erosion. Only the southern ramparts remain at ~100 meters above sea level — the seaward defenses long since collapsed into the sea.
descriptions.cd7f64d3-c693-4955-88e3-638fbea42afd: An Iron Age "spur" fort between a steep river valley and sea cliffs. Its enormous earthworks defend the eastern approach at a lower elevation than the 261-meter summit.
descriptions.fa2bcb15-3d7f-4c62-8215-514ae296e375: The largest known causewayed enclosure in Britain, built around 3700 BC near Avebury. Three concentric segmented ditches surrounded the hilltop as part of the Avebury ritual landscape.
descriptions.7f9f3957-7fc4-4775-8c45-93c279feb753: A Neolithic stone tomb near Rodmarton, covered by a cairn mound. Trees have grown over the site, but the stone chamber structure remains beneath.
descriptions.b2e10c58-6558-4472-93c5-c167a7d17ee7: Winsford Hill holds the Wambarrows Bronze Age burial mounds and the Caratacus Stone — a standing stone bearing a 5th-century inscription linked to a legendary king who resisted Rome.
descriptions.ebd73df9-93c3-4466-8d55-2b7fbceb5df2: A 2nd-century AD villa in North Lincolnshire whose 4th-century mosaics are among the most complete from Roman Britain north of the Humber. The 1958–1967 dig produced a benchmark site report.
descriptions.c5c5f2da-a5ea-41c6-807d-4c8ad7af03ba: A decorated Iron Age bronze shield from ~400 BC, found in a river alongside a sword fragment lodged in a human skull. The shield's La Tene metalwork is exquisite.
descriptions.90cfd278-3aac-40b9-9d3c-d50a40bd3051: A stone circle on Exmoor moorland, part of a Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age tradition. The purpose of these rings is unknown, though ritual gathering is widely suspected.
descriptions.89dd0394-47e5-479e-a2a7-6e78b3d7a267: Castle Hill rises 110 meters above the Thames Valley, its summit enclosed by an Iron Age fort with ditches carved into chalk bedrock. A second wooded hill, Round Hill, reaches 120 meters nearby.
descriptions.bf35f488-6864-4eaf-853b-3c654085af85: Danesborough Camp, a 500 BC hillfort, represents the earliest known occupation on this Buckinghamshire–Bedfordshire ridge. Earthwork defenses are still traceable across the wooded hill above the town.
descriptions.92d7c758-2244-465f-ac17-a6f8ca51a3cf: A 7.5-meter-high tumulus in the Wolds that yielded no burial despite multiple excavations. Medieval folklore connected it to fairies and hidden treasure.
descriptions.5614b867-438c-4c38-9a43-e2d04abe6dc0: The second-largest collection of open-air Bronze Age petroglyphs in Europe, with carvings dating from 3300 to 1200 BC. Over 40,000 engravings cover the mountain boulders.
descriptions.610fdab9-c6f1-4076-b0ad-e36f4e5035f8: A Roman city founded on conquered Celtiberian land between 93 and 82 BC. Its spectacular ruins include a nymphaeum and forum terraces cut into the hillside.
descriptions.86a32957-57c8-424d-bc27-78c2d3ebaedc: Founded as the Roman colony Valentía Edetanorum in 138 BC, this city has passed through Roman, Visigoth, Byzantine, Moorish, and Aragonese rule — six civilizations across roughly 2,200 years.
descriptions.9adf8063-9af0-4610-b021-0e9f0cef4c02: A megalithic stone circle from the 5th millennium BC in the Alentejo region. It sits in one of the densest concentrations of megalithic monuments in Western Europe.
descriptions.d70dd131-fac7-4c7e-b367-95c2ac945339: Known in antiquity as Ta-Set-Neferu — "the place of beauty" — this necropolis across five valleys holds 110 royal tombs. Nefertari's tomb contains wall paintings of extraordinary preservation.
descriptions.ed78d548-5409-4909-abc0-793390dfed1c: For 500 years, pharaohs were buried in rock-cut tombs hidden in this desert valley. Over 60 tombs have been found -- and more may still lie undiscovered.
descriptions.f5c6a56e-79b4-4f06-a064-d0e33524a118: A town where 2,000 years of Roman, medieval, and modern history sit side by side. Its Roman ruins include a colonnaded street, houses with mosaics, and a theater.
descriptions.f7dc20d6-aa71-46fa-8e27-19779a1187fb: Cliff dwellings built by the Mogollon culture in natural caves of Huapoca Canyon, the southernmost site linked to Mogollon influence. The best-known cave holds 40 rooms.
descriptions.0fd636ac-1a80-4a77-b9d0-a065ae811656: Natural hill near Visoko claimed since 2005 to be a pyramid built 12,000 BC. Geologists confirm a natural flatiron; the site now draws a New Age pilgrimage despite unanimous scientific refutation.
descriptions.3c466fde-b751-4065-8de2-bd5c9280afe5: Largest of the Visoko hills, claimed to exceed the Great Pyramid of Khufu. Geologists confirm a natural flatiron; the European Association of Archaeologists called the pyramid claim a 'cruel hoax.'
descriptions.9446bdcb-861c-4073-91dd-35248a1363d5: Petroglyph site carved into an elevated boulder above Lonya Grande valley. Name means 'opossum' in Quechua. Rock art here depicts social hierarchies, distinguishing it from most regional petroglyph.
descriptions.0943934a-6b61-416c-a382-8493a2d9db7f: Castle ruins perched on a high rock cliff. Two lion reliefs face each other in high relief over the arched entrance; a cross carved in a circle flanks the door. Period and builder remain unidentified.
descriptions.be5e8af5-aaee-4119-9572-a66ee691f455: Occupied from ~48,000 BC. Three ground bone beads found here — dating to 19,000 BP — are among the oldest evidence of symbolic behaviour in Australia. Over 100 distinct sediment layers record it all.
descriptions.7ca988d4-73af-4ed2-b4ab-d93d080aa486: Founded 1964 near the ruins of Ephesus. Houses 60,000 artefacts including a 2.9 m marble Artemis covered in bulls, griffins, and rows of mysterious orbs
descriptions.7155aa5a-4eff-4b1d-a105-b15d17b786c6: Hyena den 121,000 years old — bones of elephants, rhinos, hippos and cave lions found here in 1821. The northernmost hippo remains ever found. Buckland's analysis earned the Copley Medal in 1822.
descriptions.2133d54c-f352-4325-ae0c-dd532f9a65d3: Established 1974 across 370 km² of Western Ghats forest. Harbours tigers, leopards, gaur and dholes alongside an ancient hilltop temple bearing a 40-foot iron pillar of pre-modern metallurgical.
descriptions.3bcf804a-ff18-4066-89bd-cfaa8a3b5a46: Founded 1870 in Palazzo Antignano, Capua. Houses 160+ tuff statues of matres matutae — mother goddesses with infants — from the Fondo Patturelli sanctuary, plus the region's second-largest lapidarium.
descriptions.470169f0-deb7-4c7c-b912-90a98acede1d: Built inside a Great Tumulus, this underground museum holds four royal Macedonian tombs including Philip II's — unopened since 336 BC.
descriptions.0abf05cb-0fda-4567-9d9d-0829911a8c66: Sealed for millennia, stumbled upon in 1963 by two students. Inside: 47,000 stalactites, Neanderthal flint tools dating to 60,000 years ago, and bones of mammoth, woolly rhino, and cave hyena.
descriptions.eb80c959-82f5-4288-9a3d-02c2695e583a: Mountain homeland of the Shor people, famed for iron-smelting and shamanism. Over 60 named caves cut the terrain; the Moonlight cave alone stretches 200 metres and is encrusted with stalactites.
descriptions.b89bd9e5-053b-4d85-a2a9-1f79a6c3b452: Three rounded Carboniferous sandstone boulders in the Irthing Gorge SSSI. Pre-1870 photos show a single much larger stone — dramatically reshaped in the 1870s.
descriptions.045f1593-1dac-4504-9c53-ee8644a3134c: Shiny black boulders over ten tonnes each line the Arguenon riverbank. A metallic stone that rings like a bell when struck — no volcanic geology nearby explains their presence or how they arrived.
descriptions.79898fb7-ea09-4366-93ee-d87e379e1aca: Excavated from 1987 to 1999 — diggers opened a 50 m tunnel but found no temple. The Finnish Heritage Agency calls it a natural formation.
descriptions.01296632-a2a1-4610-a4a9-d0c3be77b788: Discovered in 1986, 25 m below sea level. Flat terraces, right angles, and sharp-cut channels span 150 m — still fiercely contested: natural geology or submerged ruins?
descriptions.6d3bc9c6-2672-49a9-9934-9f56e37c8fde: Built 3700–3600 BC, this Neolithic earthwork features ditches cut by deliberate gaps called causeways. Was it a settlement, gathering place, or ritual ground? Archaeologists still disagree.
descriptions.cafcb3e7-fc61-4867-98ba-0a5f3cf68d6e: Mid-3rd millennium BC Sumerian city-state buried under low mounds. Culturally tied to Kish, Mari, and Ebla — a minor outpost in the web of the ancient world’s greatest urban centres.
descriptions.89f1d2b7-2579-4c33-82b3-8b58d7857c53: Founded as Colonia Julia Gemella Accitana by Julius Caesar or Augustus, settled by legions III and VI. Coins bearing Tiberius, Caligula, and Germanicus were minted here in the 1st century AD.
descriptions.34182e34-cef8-4fe8-bcd0-bb1640be1cec: 214 BC — Quintus Fabius Maximus recovered this small Apulian town from the Carthaginians during the Second Punic War. The exact location of Accua has never been found.
descriptions.7d24f980-7f63-4e6a-8bb1-1f83d16435f2: 8th millennium BC Early Neolithic mound in Thessaly, excavated by Marija Gimbutas. Practically untouched, it is packed wall-to-wall with Neolithic debris and hundreds of earthen mounds.
descriptions.ca60cec6-9909-4285-bc0f-0fe3f063546d: 4th-century BC settlement on the Via Egnatia, linking the Adriatic to Byzantium. Its pass harbour sat on the Macedon–Thrace border, 13–15 km east of modern Kavala.
descriptions.03c54b35-5554-497f-b91e-a2a77f3325e1: Around 1830 BC, massive Cyclopean walls enclosed a trapezoid acropolis at Alatri. The outer circuit is nearly intact — block upon block, fitted to extraordinary heights, still standing today.
descriptions.2c9bdc10-4f98-4737-bab7-fc73822d584a: 5th-century BC acropolis with the Temple of Athena Polias, the Temple of Apollo, a stadium, an odeon, and a gymnasium — a complete civic centre on the heights of ancient Rhodes.
descriptions.61092d36-78c1-4aa9-b830-7bcef7673225: 2nd-century BC Pisidian city with a theatre, necropolis, Imperial residences, and tomb monuments. Its temples are among the finest examples of Pisidian sacred architecture in the region.
descriptions.fe4edbed-be84-4b80-b5de-62ab3e4c88ef: Prehistoric archaeological site in the southern Corsican commune of Sartène — a locality known for its concentration of ancient monuments set among the island's interior hills.
descriptions.c0e10d6e-fb0e-4e9c-a910-631da9e578ea: 3rd-century BC sanctuary of Aphrodite at Aphrodisias, with temples, a theatre, an agora, and two baths. Nearby marble quarries made it one of antiquity’s great sculptural centres.
descriptions.a9c5d1bf-b6d0-4486-a507-8dddfdc57a02: Iron Age necropolis where the dead were buried inside massive ceramic jars. Discovered when a tractor accidentally split one of the burial urns open during agricultural work.
descriptions.40229d13-d7b7-4b8f-acb3-7ae19fb085ba: Mycenaean palace stumbled upon when a Linear B clay tablet slid out of a hillside in 2008. Excavations since have uncovered archives reshaping what we know about Bronze Age Laconia.
descriptions.f984f67d-95a3-4a2d-9e69-977cfb7a2e4f: Built 114–115 AD in limestone, one of the Levant’s best-preserved Roman temples. The pediment and west wall survive intact, carved with busts of Selene and Helios watching over the fields.
descriptions.1ce06cbc-5f4e-4114-82f8-3bae6bc40a16: 3rd–4th century AD Roman villa found only in 2013 when a bypass survey was run. No prior evidence hinted at its existence — the county archaeologist called it a shock and a surprise.
descriptions.a9f3224a-798f-43ab-b3ea-41be12a41074: Pitted Ware culture settlement on Gotland, active 3100–2700 BC. Around 2900 BC, the sea rose and flooded part of the site — Mesolithic and Bronze Age layers survive beneath the ground.
descriptions.e1a5a808-87ce-461a-8b3f-dba7d50656c9: 4th-century AD tomb carved into a freestanding 4.5 × 4.5 m rock cube with a surrounding passage. The upper elements are gone; the chamber itself survives exactly as quarried.
descriptions.2a262303-2cf1-4f9a-97d7-e8a7fc194530: Theatre of Alabanda, active from the 5th century BC through the 6th century AD — over a thousand years of continuous performance. Only ruins remain of a stage that outlasted empires.
descriptions.0386a5a3-8842-4da8-ba7c-13e5fbcb46a0: 1st-century AD Roman frontier line stretching 135 km across the Swabian Jura, anchored at Rottweil in the southwest and Heidenheim in the northeast. It marked the outer edge of Rome.
descriptions.b0d0089a-a59e-435f-bef3-468d610507ca: 1st-century AD Roman town whose Latin name is entirely unknown — no ancient text ever mentions it. Yet it commanded a road crossroads 3 km south of modern Bicester in Oxfordshire.
descriptions.1d25e910-a12c-41a1-a7c9-caf4aa769fde: 2nd-century BC residential complex near Jubail with water facilities, reception rooms, and storage. Occupied continuously from ~200 BC into the 3rd century AD in a strategically key locale.
descriptions.2910c599-c631-4c92-a342-75be81adb95a: 3rd-century AD northern gate of Roman London, built into the great London Wall. Aldersgate’s Ward still splits today into ‘Within’ and ‘Without’ — inside or outside the ancient wall.
descriptions.95af4ca2-80d9-4b18-81d9-05c8477213cb: 1st-century AD triclinium at Hegra, carved into a hillside to shelter feasts from the desert wind. Niches once held Nabataean deity figures; one of the few non-funerary structures at this site.
descriptions.54afc94b-b7e1-469c-9e54-9d838d101acf: 1st-century AD Nabataean tomb at Hegra, cut into a single massive boulder. It was never finished — the carved facade stops halfway up, frozen mid-chisel for two thousand years.
descriptions.7191058f-3722-49ac-abcf-2d25e68f580c: 3rd millennium BC Dilmun burial field, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 2019. Spanning the Dilmun era through the Tylos period (300 BC), it holds millennia of funerary tradition.
descriptions.1cc5420b-1545-470c-bff0-dacfea7ec800: Late 6th-century BC Greek rock tomb cut into a cliff above Wadi Taybsillu, visible for miles. Built for a high-ranking individual whose identity has been completely lost to history.
descriptions.0f015b68-0253-4c1f-a1a5-0c8401a51c2b: 3300–900 BC stone settings on Exmoor moorland — upright stones in patterns whose purpose is unknown. Barrows and cairns layer 2,400 years of prehistoric use across this open hilltop.
descriptions.ad70541b-145f-449c-b91d-28f1e281fff1: 3rd-century BC Meroitic temple city with a Lion Temple and two enormous water reservoirs. Elephant sculptures and pilgrims' marks cover the walls, but no formal decorated inscriptions have been found.
descriptions.4e2aaa20-44e6-4023-b127-a91b4ca8fe08: 1st millennium BC Messenian town near temples of Bacchus and Minerva. Only a single ancient passage confirms its existence; its ruins have never been securely identified on the ground.
descriptions.af8e0293-7e40-45db-986b-b2382e5bc272: 1st-century AD Nabataean tomb at al-Hijr — one of the very first carved there. Its clean facade set the template for the elaborate rock-cut tombs that would follow across this necropolis.
descriptions.04fe73f5-72d9-4990-88f9-507c7e75719f: 4th-century BC marble altar of Zeus, 9 m deep and 5.5 m wide — one of the first objects unearthed in the 1931 Agora excavations. Augustan-era mason marks were later carved directly into its stone.
descriptions.fa59ed73-d877-48a6-89e2-1fb458c9a512: 1st-century AD site carved with hands, horses, camels, and snakes. Alongside the rock art are remnants of a mosque and early Islamic Kufic inscriptions — two thousand years of devotion.
descriptions.0e3698c6-006c-4161-a8c3-8dfac5bdf2cc: Built 1700–1550 BC for an obscure 13th Dynasty pharaoh of the turbulent Second Intermediate Period. Every stone of its upper structure was stripped by robbers; only the substructure survives.
descriptions.8802e0ba-d052-43d1-91b1-b23feff05f6d: 2nd-century AD Roman theatre at Kasserine with its seating hewn from rock. Only a fragment of the stage remains — and the small dressing room actors used before taking the stage.
descriptions.26c567ca-9af0-486b-9599-dcb0b7792628: 5th-century BC Athenian sanctuary of Castor and Pollux. In 415 and 411 BC, citizens mustered here before military campaigns — making it as much a war ground as a sacred precinct.
descriptions.bff9c3d8-4897-417b-9ef1-0bd7aae62826: Founded 19 BC, Anavarza had a 1,500-metre city wall with 20 bastions and a triple-arched triumphal arch. A colonnaded street, stadium, theatre, and aqueducts made it one of Cilicia’s grandest cities.
descriptions.40e48fb3-769d-47c5-ac69-995bcd9e86b8: Founded 1894 BC, Babylon rose to dominate Mesopotamia under the Old Babylonian Empire and again as the Neo-Babylonian Empire in the 7th–6th century BC — one of the ancient world's defining capitals.
descriptions.0f5bb5fa-e4a9-4e6e-ae02-48929ed84921: Occupied since 8800 BC, Byblos is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth. Over millennia it passed through Egyptian, Phoenician, Assyrian, Persian, Roman, and Ottoman hands.
descriptions.e8879fb9-adb0-48f3-8672-51923c57047d: 3rd-century BC Greek city with a stadium, a theatre, an Ionic temple, aqueducts, and rock tombs cut into the hillsides — a provincial Hellenistic city that still tells its story in stone.
descriptions.7af83a27-7b99-4486-a607-85020bc7819e: Ancient city on a 200-metre mesa ringed by sheer cliffs, divided into upper and lower city by the terrain. Hellenistic, Roman, and Byzantine layers span over a thousand years of occupation.
descriptions.ccf40c39-5f83-4bc4-bf28-23d0a7e4fa59: 500 BC — irregular polygonal wall blocks at ancient Eleon have stood for 2,500 years. Excavations revealed Late Bronze Age, Archaic-Classical, and Ottoman layers stacked on one acropolis.
descriptions.e2aa3754-8d32-4455-bf6d-9077f18d50d2: From the 3rd millennium to the 1st century BC, Lilaia controlled the Cephissus headwaters. Its walls, gates, and a temple at the sacred springs are still visible east of the modern village.
descriptions.9001cee0-cda8-4309-917f-c0bece02e5e6: 4th-century AD Roman amphitheatre in Alexandria — remarkably intimate for an imperial venue. It seated just 700 spectators, carved into the city's dense urban fabric at the heart of the ancient port.
descriptions.2e53c7cf-072e-465a-a53a-ba2128f50c08: 650 BC — Sparta led the unified resistance against Persia. The so-called Tomb of Leonidas, a quadrangular structure, survives near a theatre whose retaining walls still stand above ground.
descriptions.5dd5ecd6-2cd4-4e37-ae35-51da8f716d07: 776–724 BC — athletes competed in the stadion metres from the Temple of Zeus. The Nemean Games drew competitors from across the ancient world to this sacred ground beside the temple.
descriptions.f284934a-a5b3-4c85-ba90-953aa9e72bc5: 300 BC theatre of one of the most important cities of ancient Aetolia, set on the hills of Adirion on the eastern side of the ancient city, looking out across the plain below.
descriptions.aa75397c-7bdf-4b31-bbfc-1aa544fe91b5: Built 356 BC by Philip II, the theatre of Philippi braces against the city’s eastern wall and the acropolis slope. Excavations exposed Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, and Paleochristian layers.
descriptions.d5fc9a81-4a7a-427d-8f28-244eff8582ac: 5th-century BC theatre at Thassos, carved into a natural hollow in the acropolis hill. Its oldest phase dates to the very start of the Hellenistic period — an early theatrical tradition on the island.
descriptions.a4990269-42fc-45f8-9849-905dbf3f68fb: 1st-century BC Goguryeo military fortress with three separate forts — inner, outer, and new — built in different eras as the kingdom’s northern frontier after its capital moved to Pyongyang.
descriptions.6763f7a6-45af-4b74-8ef6-2cbda7cdd0e8: High-altitude site at 3,900 m in the Andes. Its remote mountain position hints at a settlement built to control surrounding valleys — full details await future excavation.
descriptions.6e1bc7d5-624c-41c8-b69b-e64917ae5164: 2nd-century AD Roman dam built across a narrow ravine — a feat of hydraulic engineering in an arid landscape where water control was the difference between survival and collapse.
descriptions.02c083c6-8552-4edb-8b3d-26d649280de5: Built 521–515 BC as the winter palace of Darius I on the ruins of an Elamite city. Alexander burned it in 330 BC. A handful of pillars and partial walls survive of one of antiquity’s grandest courts.
descriptions.01cdc8e2-56b7-4c9d-b6d0-68c290a65e55: Prehistoric archaeological site near Sartène in Corsica — a commune noted for its exceptional concentration of ancient monuments across the southern part of the island.
descriptions.996e0b32-f8ca-4d04-8900-ed937b729269: Karstic sea cliff housing one of Europe’s most significant Palaeolithic cave sites. Accessible only by boat today — during the ice ages, the sea level stood more than 100 metres lower.
descriptions.820bbc57-f448-4e1a-8912-d097977fd739: 4th to 2nd millennium BC Minoan mansion at 450 m above the Libyan Sea, yielding Linear A inscriptions — rare traces of an undeciphered Bronze Age script at a clifftop ceremonial building.
descriptions.bdc9be4b-30c5-4cd0-b72f-d07782a4aa46: 1st-century BC sanctuary of Apollo Smintheus, destroyer of mice and bringer of plague. Mouse figurines line the entrance stairs. The complex included baths, water tanks, and a sacred road.
descriptions.bb392843-3d7e-40c0-9cda-0e93ddc47a60: 5th-century BC temple left unfinished, permanently facing Delos, birthplace of Apollo. The foundation and massive doorway survive. Later converted to a church — the same portal that once framed a god.
descriptions.0d9bd81d-d41c-4381-8e2e-7626928fedc1: 3600–2700 BC mega-settlement of the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture, covering 90–120 hectares. One of the largest among 2,440 known settlements of this proto-urban culture spread across eastern Europe.
descriptions.3f170e16-175a-4e4c-9717-1f0e32d05e8e: 2nd-century AD Temple of Apollo set inside the Apollonia Archaeological Park — a sanctuary to the god of light and prophecy, its columns and foundations preserved in the open-air museum.
descriptions.cb659fbe-0f1c-43dc-9c40-4517c0974a79: Founded around 20 AD near a Roman legionary camp, Aquae Helveticae was built around mineral hot springs at 47°C. The baths drew soldiers and civilians to healing waters at a Limmat river bend.
descriptions.a85d081b-f87c-49fe-937e-3a13ce212d48: 3rd–4th century AD Roman water structure in Constantine built directly above a Numidian necropolis — Roman hydraulics sitting atop an older North African burial ground.
descriptions.af25c5ad-8050-456e-94bd-c8f6e5fa1715: Prehistoric rock shelter at Bonifacio, on Corsica’s southern tip, overlooking the strait to Sardinia — one of the island’s most evocative prehistoric sites at the edge of the sea.
descriptions.42e81a5c-fcc3-40ab-a5eb-c9a9c55e53ad: Late 1st-century BC Roman sanctuary dedicated to Rome and the Emperor in the Ubii capital. Conquered Germans were required to make offerings here to demonstrate loyalty — devotion as politics.
descriptions.3722c54c-716e-4a23-9877-d23c3ff1358b: 4th-century BC gate of ancient Messene, built from massive limestone blocks fitted without mortar. One of the best-preserved city gates of the ancient world — still standing and still imposing.
descriptions.c44ec5d4-313d-4a18-8b2b-45b0f2c4a0e1: 4th millennium BC necropolis of ten domus de Janas tombs carved from volcanic tuff near Alghero. Above the burial chambers rises a nuraghe tower — the dead watched over by a Bronze Age sentinel.
descriptions.56c0445a-ac05-4950-a847-b6b267d19402: Occupied from 3000 BC through Roman times, when Visigoths destroyed it in 395 AD. Mycenaean tombs, a 2nd-century Roman bath, an odeon, and a sanctuary of Aphrodite layer six thousand years here.
descriptions.ef4a8fe6-c961-4521-9242-9d3ac1168846: 1st-century BC to 4th-century AD Roman city at Makthar — one of the region's most extensive sites. Much remains unexcavated; a monumental gate, amphitheatre, forum, and triumphal arches still stand.
descriptions.b991992b-4895-4e18-b3eb-4fa954a1007e: 8th-century BC Dorian city — the smallest and most agricultural of Rhodes’ three great cities. Beneath the classical ruins lies a Mycenaean cemetery, proof of Achaean settlement centuries earlier.
descriptions.a945d5ef-bbbf-42bd-be5b-27c25eda9df1: Spanning 20–30 hectares, this site was inhabited from the Copper Age through the Roman era — one of the longest-occupied settlements in the Almería region, first found in 1859.
descriptions.4df06c48-82c5-46d6-b82f-6b5023b1220e: 1600–1100 BC — Mycenae dominated the eastern Mediterranean. The Lion Gate, Cyclopean walls, grave circles, and the Treasury of Atreus make this the richest Late Bronze Age palace site on record.
descriptions.0d7c325a-5370-4a95-b048-8e599f69892c: Inhabited since 4000 BC, Olympia became a sanctuary of Zeus in the 10th century BC. From 776 BC, athletes competed here every four years on the very ground where the temples still stand.
descriptions.34fd3d60-f6b8-4ea4-8d6d-36ec82d70a5f: 12th-century BC Mycenaean city built around the cult of the Great Goddess of fertility, worshipped here since the Neolithic. The goddess who became Aphrodite drew pilgrims for centuries.
descriptions.c31699a9-a0e0-46d3-ba59-15f508f4014d: 600–475 BC royal city with a temple of Aphrodite, two majestic royal tombs, copper-processing workshops, and six oversized limestone statues. Bronze Age copper from here fed the ancient Mediterranean.
descriptions.a2df90a7-df37-483b-b899-f0623f2e61b1: 3rd-century BC Greek temple of Dionysus, rebuilt in Ionic order in the 2nd century AD. Excavations revealed the earlier Hellenistic temple still buried directly beneath the Roman one.
descriptions.2d4eb24d-1348-4458-aa4a-68a9a50cd804: 1250 BC tholos tomb on Panagitsa Hill at Mycenae. The lintel above its doorway weighs 120 tonnes — the heaviest lintel in the ancient world. How they moved it remains an open question.
descriptions.c5d05e95-f6a3-454f-85ba-6ebb4736b7bb: 27 BC triumphal arch flanked by fluted Corinthian columns. Four carved shields display Jupiter, Apollo, Neptune, and Roma — one of Rome’s oldest surviving arches, still standing after two millennia.
descriptions.13c3f25f-3887-49c1-9492-cf7e512e5782: Founded 303 BC as a Roman Latin colony, Alba Fucens’ polygonal walls enclosed a grid of public buildings. A temple of Apollo on the hill of San Pietro was later swallowed by a Roman amphitheatre.
descriptions.2d0c0ca8-b7cf-41a8-b938-1e58ee9fdc63: 10th to 5th millennium BC Neolithic settlement mound in Thessaly. Excavators controversially claimed to have found an aceramic Neolithic layer — pottery-free farming — that others have disputed.
descriptions.1fd1292d-5dbf-4bbf-a501-6a0e094da785: Homer named it Argissa in the Iliad — the 7th-century BC town of Argura on the Peneus near Larissa. Ancient scholars debated whether it was simply a neighbourhood of the larger city.
descriptions.b1eabcf0-cc21-4053-92a1-285b30da510b: Standing stone in the Gorbea Natural Park, dragged from the mountain’s southern slopes and erected in the Albian Age. The park’s most visited attraction, rediscovered in the 20th century.
descriptions.3c601353-b55a-4dc8-80c1-9b8c5ca24d31: 4th to 2nd millennium BC settlement at 700–850 m on the Taygetus range, where Mycenaean chamber tombs were cut into the hillside at the Arkina site. Altitude made it a natural Bronze Age stronghold.
descriptions.a4856c44-4e78-4a45-b618-d558b763942d: Mid-Classic Maya site, 2–3 km from Dos Pilas. Its architecture closely mirrors nearby Tamarindito but diverges sharply from Dos Pilas — two adjacent sites with entirely distinct royal identities.
descriptions.ec87f52c-4fd5-4be1-9754-494de52afb91: 4th millennium BC Sardinian park with the Necropolis of Li Muri and two Giants’ Graves — Li Lolghi and Coddu Vecchiu. Nuragic monumental culture distilled into one concentrated landscape.
descriptions.e5948e02-efb2-4c4e-b3e6-8295aa3cdcac: Phrygian rock tomb reused in the Roman period, known locally as the Tomb of Solon. Carved into a natural rock mass in the Anatolian plateau, it reflects the classic Phrygian rock monument form.
descriptions.2a486734-8365-4c1e-93b2-f1c2f092789e: Occupied from the 6th millennium BC, Arslantepe peaked in the Late Chalcolithic. Its palace complex is one of the earliest known — contemporary with the earliest urbanism in southern Mesopotamia.
descriptions.9740df69-d050-4a92-9e96-6e797ff98266: Roman aqueduct carrying water 19 km to Aspendos. Its most remarkable feature: the final 2 km used pressurised inverted siphon pipes to push water uphill — a feat rarely attempted in the ancient world.
descriptions.6a8bc59c-77c3-4359-8f65-19f67ee0ac04: 1st-century BC Roman port town on northern Crete, the harbour for inland Axus. Excavations confirmed the site; it appears in the ancient Stadiasmus Maris Magni as a named coastal waypoint.
descriptions.5f10ac9c-682b-41cf-9eeb-7c2825b0ea4d: Karstic hills with fossil deposits and stone tools of Western Europe’s earliest known hominins. Ongoing excavations have repeatedly reshaped understanding of when humans first spread across Europe.
descriptions.d83ce2b4-77cf-4b1f-b993-28cfb17d313a: 2nd millennium BC Late Bronze Age capital of the Amorite kingdom of Alalakh — buried beneath a tell on the Orontes plain, its layered remains have yielded cuneiform tablets and palatial architecture.
descriptions.2c05946f-80d4-4caf-8294-f1e2948d69b9: 3rd-century BC Oscan city 20 km north of Naples, crossed by the Via Atellana. Atella gave its name to the Fabula Atellana — an early form of Roman comic theatre that shaped Latin comedy.
descriptions.e1976732-579b-4f25-be81-626008526093: 530 BC Doric temple of Athena with an unusual Ionic frieze below the roofline — a blending of orders found in few surviving temples. Several columns still stand on their two-step podium.
descriptions.2dd6aaa9-95bb-4c96-a3e2-ae7864fb8748: High-altitude site at 3,700 m on the mountain of Jircan in the Andes. Its remote elevation and proximity to Urpish village suggest a ceremonial or defensive outpost above the valley floor.
descriptions.2c1c70ac-91df-4577-ac77-3bedd6c521ee: Late pre-Columbian site in the Yarowilca highlands, declared part of the National Cultural Heritage in 2006. The region's Inca-era settlements are only beginning to receive systematic study.
descriptions.53b027b5-8d22-4339-a218-41dcb158a4e6: Stone chullpa tombs at 3,932 m in the Huamalíes highlands, above the village of Carhuapata. Chullpa towers housed the mummified dead — ancestors kept visible among the living on the Andean altiplano.
descriptions.a2772b36-6951-45a7-ab30-42e1d959e88a: Site at 4,000 m on the Andean border of two districts in the Apurimác Region. Its elevated position on a named mountain suggests a place chosen for visibility or ritual significance.
descriptions.454ecea0-4c69-48a1-8fb3-5e96b53f683c: Pre-Columbian site in the Huánuco highlands, in the Ambo Province region where multiple Andean cultures left traces before Inca consolidation. Its full extent remains under active investigation.
descriptions.a7dcc8b1-678d-458b-a0a7-31fca6f4c866: Iron Age to early modern necropolis at Axura, with burials spanning the 1st through 18th centuries AD. Part of the cemetery was destroyed when the Axurachay river eroded its bank.
descriptions.8a68279e-6456-48ab-9543-7c33376fac42: Rock paintings in white showing abstract and geometric figures above the Salqa river near Oroscocha. A companion site, Llamachayuq Qaqa, lies to the west of Ayamachay in the same Andean valley.
descriptions.134e6d5f-86de-4c3a-afc6-2959a360db15: Site declared National Cultural Heritage in 2003. Its Quechua name — aya (corpse) and muqu (hill) — hints at funerary use in an Andean landscape where the living and dead shared the high ground.
descriptions.4132d835-b56c-4117-93b9-26296695832e: 645–643 BC Urartian fortress of Rusa son of Argishti, guarded by two concentric andesite walls. Inside: a temple, a pier hall, and interlocking storage warehouses with cubed chambers.
descriptions.05c89db6-7e37-495d-9859-544bc6cb60e0: Rock art at 3,100 m on the slope of Kapillayuq mountain in the Urubamba valley. A companion site, T’uqu T’uquyuq, lies 800 m away — two galleries of Andean imagery sharing the same ridgeline.
descriptions.cae9d762-cdd4-4833-adc3-c426b7a79948: 1st–8th century AD Nabataean port at Leuke Kome on the Red Sea. Strabo named it a key waypoint on the Arabia–Egypt trade route; an 8–9 day caravan journey linked Aqaba to Petra through this coast.
descriptions.3ff78ce4-ac80-4902-9bb9-20eab8a16a4a: Cave structures with a rock-cut burial field, suggesting use as both shelter and sacred ground. The visible grave monuments served a community’s dead across multiple generations.
descriptions.03f33939-7a7b-49f1-8ed1-99fb54897ae6: 330 BC — Alexander the Great commissioned a Greek temple at Babylon, inserting a Hellenistic structure into the heart of one of the ancient world’s greatest Mesopotamian capitals.
descriptions.14eceb81-5819-4fb7-ac10-dfdb26ce63d1: Iron Age hillfort discovered in 1933 with a ditch-and-bank on two of three sides. In 1956, quarrying at Coles Quarry nearly obliterated it — the site survived, but barely, on the quarry’s edge.
descriptions.2f44fbd5-7420-4904-8ef9-3bb2c7a15064: Around 3000 BC, hundreds of mysterious stone megaliths were erected in the Lore Lindu highlands. Purpose and builders remain unknown. First recorded by Western observers in 1908 — still no answers.
descriptions.5d252b0e-96d1-4857-9883-72f508cabcd9: 4th millennium BC long barrow in Surrey, built in the Early Neolithic. A communal tomb raised before the age of individual monuments — part of a burial tradition widespread across Neolithic Europe.
descriptions.b11a5e2b-e4ac-4480-8575-98282c2de8de: 3rd-century AD Gandharan Buddhist stupa in Swabi, claimed to be the largest in the region. Over 400 artifacts recovered so far; excavations of the Gandhara Kingdom’s remains continue.
descriptions.8c4d854b-55f3-4004-bc87-cffe5a431a2e: 2200–1750 BC Dilmun burial mounds at Janabiyah — hundreds of them. Inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage in 2019 and regarded as one of the most important heritage sites in the entire region.
descriptions.9ac59d75-ae27-4515-8430-32ba6a23669e: Phrygian rock monument with a gable roof and a deep niche symbolising a doorway. Known locally as the ‘Tip Fountain’, a well descends from its roof — sacred and practical fused in one carved mass.
descriptions.94090aa6-490e-4b0b-8253-404391232b24: Active 1000 BC–900 AD, this Maya river valley site ran lithic workshops and possibly cash-cropped cacao — a long, continuous occupation from Preclassic through to the Postclassic.
descriptions.c54b1f6c-0870-401c-8857-5b4aac198056: 2nd–3rd century AD Roman temple on a massive limestone podium, its interior stripped bare. No inscription survived to name the deity worshipped here — the god remains unknown.
descriptions.90bf9ebf-4050-433f-aaef-3b31dd3053d6: Built 200–400 AD on the Pacific coastal plain, Balberta is the only known Early Classic Maya site there with exposed architecture not buried by later construction.
descriptions.12aadb2a-b677-4750-91e3-bea81d76351b: Late Bronze Age hill fort, originally triangular and commanding river views. Most of it was destroyed by a modern bypass — only the southwest corner survives, reaching 1 metre high.
descriptions.50f3f5c5-fcc1-443e-b516-9aaf6ca13d0c: Neolithic court cairn set on a rock outcrop, 4th–1st millennium BC. Its chamber yielded human bones, flint tools, and distinctive pottery now known as Ballyalton bowls.
descriptions.f0bcab22-b5ea-43e1-ace1-c9adc5d6e0db: 1st century BC. The Ax Gate -- surviving arch of an entrance to the ancient city of Mylasa. A single arch standing where a city once thrived.
